papers.title: Data augmentation using generative networks to identify dementia
papers.abstract: Data limitation is one of the most common issues in training machine learning classifiers for medical applications. Due to ethical concerns and data privacy, the number of people that can be recruited to such experiments is generally smaller than the number of participants contributing to non-healthcare datasets. Recent research showed that generative models can be used as an effective approach for data augmentation, which can ultimately help to train more robust classifiers sparse data domains. A number of studies proved that this data augmentation technique works for image and audio data sets. In this paper, we investigate the application of a similar approach to different types of speech and audio-based features extracted from interactions recorded with our automatic dementia detection system. Using two generative models we show how the generated synthesized samples can improve the performance of a DNN based classifier. The variational autoencoder increased the F-score of a four-way classifier distinguishing the typical patient groups seen in memory clinics from 58% to around 74%, a 16% improvement
papers.summary: Medical classifiers are often trained on very small datasets because recruiting patients is constrained by ethics and privacy. Two generative models are used to synthesize additional speech- and audio-based feature samples drawn from interactions recorded by an automatic dementia detection system, and the synthetic samples are added to the training data of a deep neural network classifier. With variational autoencoder augmentation, the F-score of a four-way classifier separating the typical patient groups seen in memory clinics rose **from 58% to around 74%**.

papers.title: Differential Diagnosis of Frontotemporal Dementia and Alzheimer's Disease using Generative Adversarial Network
papers.abstract: Frontotemporal dementia and Alzheimer's disease are two common forms of dementia and are easily misdiagnosed as each other due to their similar pattern of clinical symptoms. Differentiating between the two dementia types is crucial for determining disease-specific intervention and treatment. Recent development of Deep-learning-based approaches in the field of medical image computing are delivering some of the best performance for many binary classification tasks, although its application in differential diagnosis, such as neuroimage-based differentiation for multiple types of dementia, has not been explored. In this study, a novel framework was proposed by using the Generative Adversarial Network technique to distinguish FTD, AD and normal control subjects, using volumetric features extracted at coarse-to-fine structural scales from Magnetic Resonance Imaging scans. Experiments of 10-folds cross-validation on 1,954 images achieved high accuracy. With the proposed framework, we have demonstrated that the combination of multi-scale structural features and synthetic data augmentation based on generative adversarial network can improve the performance of challenging tasks such as differentiating Dementia sub-types.
papers.summary: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) show similar clinical symptoms and are easily misdiagnosed as one another, yet deep learning has mostly been applied to binary rather than differential diagnosis. The proposed framework uses a generative adversarial network to separate FTD, AD and normal control subjects from volumetric features extracted at coarse-to-fine structural scales of magnetic resonance imaging scans. In 10-fold cross-validation on 1,954 images, the authors report high accuracy and conclude that **combining multi-scale structural features with GAN-based synthetic data augmentation improves differentiation of dementia sub-types**.

papers.title: Causal Time Series Modeling of Supraglacial Lake Evolution in Greenland under Distribution Shift
papers.abstract: Causal modeling offers a principled foundation for uncovering stable, invariant relationships in time-series data, thereby improving robustness and generalization under distribution shifts. Yet its potential is underutilized in spatiotemporal Earth observation, where models often depend on purely correlational features that fail to transfer across heterogeneous domains. We propose RIC-TSC, a regionally-informed causal time-series classification framework that embeds lag-aware causal discovery directly into sequence modeling, enabling both predictive accuracy and scientific interpretability. Using multi-modal satellite and reanalysis data-including Sentinel-1 microwave backscatter, Sentinel-2 and Landsat-8 optical reflectance, and CARRA meteorological variables-we leverage Joint PCMCI+ (J-PCMCI+) to identify region-specific and invariant predictors of supraglacial lake evolution in Greenland. Causal graphs are estimated globally and per basin, with validated predictors and their time lags supplied to lightweight classifiers. On a balanced benchmark of 1000 manually labeled lakes from two contrasting melt seasons (2018-2019), causal models achieve up to 12.59% higher accuracy than correlation-based baselines under out-of-distribution evaluation. These results show that causal discovery is not only a means of feature selection but also a pathway to generalizable and mechanistically grounded models of dynamic Earth surface processes.
papers.summary: Earth-observation models often rely on correlational features that fail to transfer across regions and seasons. `RIC-TSC` is a regionally informed causal time-series classification framework that uses `J-PCMCI+` causal discovery on `Sentinel-1`, `Sentinel-2`, `Landsat-8` and `CARRA` meteorological data to find region-specific and invariant predictors of supraglacial lake evolution in Greenland, then feeds the validated predictors and their time lags to lightweight classifiers. On a balanced benchmark of 1000 manually labeled lakes from the 2018 and 2019 melt seasons, the causal models reach **up to 12.59% higher accuracy** than correlation-based baselines under out-of-distribution evaluation.

papers.title: Textual Response-Aware Guidance for Zero-Shot Adversarial Robustness of Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong zero-shot generalization but remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Existing adversarial fine-tuning methods often use pre-trained model guidance to preserve image--text alignment while improving robustness. Our analysis of visual representation drift reveals complementary limitations of two representative forms of guidance. Matching visual features constrains all directions equally, providing broad coverage without semantic emphasis. Matching prediction distributions prioritizes semantically relevant directions, but remains limited by the candidate texts and prediction probabilities. These limitations can hinder preservation of pre-trained image--text relationships and degrade zero-shot performance. We therefore propose Textual Response-Aware Guidance (TRAG), which constrains visual representation drift using the pre-trained text encoder's responses to local variations in input embeddings. TRAG constructs anchor-level constraints from the response directions and magnitudes around semantic anchors, then aggregates them using pre-trained image--anchor relevance, yielding an image-adaptive constraint. Extensive experiments across architectures and tasks demonstrate state-of-the-art clean and robust performance. Further analysis shows that TRAG helps preserve pre-trained image--text relationships.
papers.summary: Adversarial fine-tuning of vision-language models (VLMs) typically uses the pre-trained model as guidance, either by matching visual features, which constrains all directions equally, or by matching prediction distributions, which is limited by the candidate texts. Textual Response-Aware Guidance (`TRAG`) instead constrains visual representation drift using how the pre-trained text encoder responds to local variations around semantic anchors, aggregating these anchor-level constraints by image-anchor relevance into an image-adaptive constraint. Experiments across architectures and tasks are reported to give **state-of-the-art clean and robust zero-shot performance**, with further analysis indicating better preservation of pre-trained image-text relationships.

papers.title: Alchemically Transferable Parameters for Variational Quantum Eigensolvers
papers.abstract: Machine-learned circuit parameters could remove one of the main bottlenecks of variational quantum eigensolvers: the classical optimization loop, with its typical barren plateaus, local minima, and costly energy and gradient evaluations, is replaced by a direct prediction. Prior work showed that machine-learning models paired with a structured circuit design can transfer across system size and structure within hydrogenic systems. The next step: Extending them to organic molecules would seem to require re-training on use-case-specific training sets. In this work, we show that this is not necessary by establishing an alchemical approach. A geometric projection places surrogate hydrogen atoms along the bond directions of the target molecule and so maps its local bonding environment onto small hydrogenic fragments. Existing hydrogenic solvers can then be reused as they are. The only new quantity is a single projection radius per bond type, which is fitted once on a small reference molecule and reused unchanged thereafter. We demonstrate the approach on the separable-pair circuit designs that have been used in prior work and extend the approach to multi-circuit approaches that span effective bases for quantum subspaces.
papers.summary: Variational quantum eigensolvers are slowed by a classical optimization loop prone to barren plateaus and local minima, and machine-learned circuit parameters that replace it have so far transferred only within hydrogenic systems. An alchemical geometric projection places surrogate hydrogen atoms along the bond directions of an organic molecule, mapping its local bonding environment onto small hydrogenic fragments so that existing hydrogenic solvers can be reused without retraining. **The only new quantity is a single projection radius per bond type, fitted once on a small reference molecule**, and the approach is demonstrated on separable-pair circuit designs and extended to multi-circuit approaches spanning quantum subspaces.

papers.title: D-TINs for Track-Sampled Ice Sheet Surface Reconstruction from Satellite Altimetry Data
papers.abstract: Satellite altimetry samples ice sheets densely along tracks but sparsely across tracks, with frequent gaps in spatial coverage. We study the impact of this irregular support on surface reconstruction and introduce a new method, D-TIN, that applies Delaunay triangulation and barycentric interpolation directly to observed locations. A spatial holdout removes contiguous track intervals and nearby same-pass observations. We compare D-TIN with two common workflows, kriging and tile-based polynomial interpolation, to evaluate its accuracy and computational efficiency. Across seven ICESat-1 campaigns, D-TIN reduces RMSE by 12.1 m to 23.6 m relative to independent 5 km tile and polynomial based reconstruction. Its aggregate accuracy is close to the ordinary kriging workflow using a 1 km grid on the commonly used GStatSim platform while its median runtime is 252 times lower. A fixed-weight multiscale extension of D-TIN, called MS-D-TIN, gives the lowest aggregate RMSE, 67.5 m, while retaining the low computational cost of the D-TIN family.
papers.summary: Satellite altimetry samples ice sheets densely along tracks but sparsely across them, which complicates surface reconstruction. `D-TIN` applies Delaunay triangulation and barycentric interpolation directly at the observed locations and is evaluated with a spatial holdout that removes contiguous track intervals, against kriging and tile-based polynomial interpolation. Across seven `ICESat-1` campaigns it reduces RMSE by 12.1 m to 23.6 m relative to 5 km tile polynomial reconstruction and comes close to ordinary kriging on `GStatSim` with a **median runtime 252 times lower**, while the multiscale extension `MS-D-TIN` gives the lowest aggregate RMSE of 67.5 m.

papers.title: AFNO: Universal Certifiably-Arbitrage-Free Operator Learning Framework for European Call-Price Surfaces
papers.abstract:
Neural operators (NOs) have been introduced as deep learning-powered solutions to the computational bottleneck of solving families of problems. Once trained, an NO can rapidly output approximate solutions, avoiding the need to rerun classical solvers. However, standard NO architectures cannot guarantee static no-arbitrage when predicting European call-price surfaces from market or model features and, as we verify experimentally, can yield negative PnL in downstream trading tasks.
  We introduce a certifiably arbitrage-free (AF) and universal encoder-decoder NO framework, continuously mapping inputs from a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) $\mathcal{H}$ over any fixed subset of $[0,\infty)^2$ to a convex combination of arbitrage-free European call-price surfaces by continuously solving an approximate nearest-neighbour problem. We show that a nearest arbitrage-free correction of an unconstrained predicted surface need not exist, implying that no-arbitrage cannot, in general, be restored through post-processing. Further, we show that standard NOs, such as the FNO and certain encoder-decoder NOs, admit parameter configurations whose outputs violate static no-arbitrage. Thus, out-of-the-box NOs generally cannot be certifiably restricted to arbitrage-free configurations, but may only be guided towards them through PINN-type regularization during training.
papers.summary: Neural operators (NOs) can quickly predict European call-price surfaces from market or model features, but standard architectures cannot guarantee static no-arbitrage and are shown experimentally to yield negative profit and loss in downstream trading. `AFNO` is a universal encoder-decoder NO framework that maps inputs from a reproducing kernel Hilbert space to a convex combination of arbitrage-free call-price surfaces by continuously solving an approximate nearest-neighbour problem. The authors prove that **a nearest arbitrage-free correction of an unconstrained predicted surface need not exist, so no-arbitrage cannot in general be restored by post-processing**, and that the `FNO` and certain encoder-decoder NOs admit parameter configurations that violate it.

papers.title: From Relevant Posts to Attributable Spans: Explicit Symptom Evidence for Depression Questionnaire Inference
papers.abstract: Longitudinal social-media histories offer an opportunity to assess depression, potentially supporting the inference of standardized depression questionnaire responses. However, this task requires evidence that is semantically relevant to a symptom and attributable to the user, while being sufficiently specific to support an individual questionnaire item. Existing approaches rely on semantic similarity to retrieve posts, which can introduce misleading or non-attributable evidence, particularly in multi-symptom posts and discussions of others' experiences. We propose SREE (Symptom Retrieval and Evidence-Grounded InfErence), an evidence-grounded pipeline that extracts first-person and symptom-specific text spans, selects a representative subset using a Facility Location-inspired objective, and performs Evidence-Gated Inference over the selected evidence. We evaluate evidence retrieval on BDI-Sen and evidence-conditioned questionnaire inference on eRisk 2019-2021. Compared with state-of-the-art retrieval approaches, SREE achieves relative improvements of 70% in post-level precision and 59% in F1, while retaining at least 30% fewer posts. On multi-symptom sentences, it also outperforms dense retrieval in precision and F1 even with twice the retrieval budget. Across all three eRisk collections, SREE achieves the highest exact item-level agreement while remaining competitive on ordinal and aggregate metrics. These results highlight the importance of localizing attributable evidence and controlling its composition before inferring depression questionnaire responses.
papers.summary: Inferring depression questionnaire responses from social-media histories requires evidence that is symptom-specific and attributable to the user, whereas similarity-based post retrieval pulls in multi-symptom posts and discussions of other people's experiences. `SREE` (Symptom Retrieval and Evidence-Grounded Inference) extracts first-person, symptom-specific text spans, selects a representative subset with a facility-location-inspired objective, and performs evidence-gated inference over it. On `BDI-Sen` it achieves relative improvements of **70% in post-level precision** and 59% in F1 over state-of-the-art retrieval while retaining at least 30% fewer posts, and on `eRisk` 2019-2021 it reaches the highest exact item-level agreement.

papers.title: Rethinking in Spikes: Mitigating Hallucinations in MDLMs with Step-Aware Decoding
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in multimodal diffusion language models (MDLMs) have exhibited strong global modeling capabilities through iterative refinement. We observe that mask uncertainty follows an overall downward trend during iterative denoising, while a few denoising steps exhibit localized entropy spikes closely associated with hallucinations. We argue that anomalous steps can be identified by measuring the entropy deviation of each denoising step from its neighboring temporal window. We hypothesize that discrete token commitment discards the distributional information at masked positions, limiting the continued interaction between candidate semantics and the context during entropy spikes. With this goal, we present StepRefine, a plug-and-play decoding strategy that leverages semantic context to achieve reliable denoising. The core of our method lies in a step-aware switch between discrete denoising and latent refinement. The model employs probability-weighted embeddings at entropy spike steps to preserve diverse reasoning hypotheses and performs multiple rounds of continuous refinement. Meanwhile, a refinement controller monitors distributional stability to reduce unnecessary loops and switch the model back to standard discrete denoising. Through extensive experiments, StepRefine demonstrates significant hallucination mitigation across different MDLMs on multimodal benchmarks.
papers.summary: In multimodal diffusion language models (MDLMs), mask uncertainty generally falls during iterative denoising, but **a few steps show localized entropy spikes that are closely associated with hallucinations**. `StepRefine` is a plug-and-play decoding strategy that detects such steps by comparing each step's entropy to its neighboring temporal window, then switches from discrete token commitment to several rounds of continuous latent refinement using probability-weighted embeddings. A refinement controller monitors distributional stability and returns the model to standard discrete denoising, and experiments report reduced hallucination across different MDLMs on multimodal benchmarks.

papers.title: TimeOmni-o1: Bidirectionally Coupling Time Series Foundation Models and LLMs for Multimodal Reasoning and Forecasting
papers.abstract: Time series from real-world systems are often accompanied by text, such as a report on an event that affects them. Two common tasks on these series are understanding, e.g., answering questions about a series, and forecasting its future values. Both tasks require reasoning over the series and the text together. Moreover, understanding outputs text while forecasting outputs a time series, so serving both requires a model that reads and generates both modalities. Large language models (LLMs) read time series as digit tokens and handle long series poorly. Time series foundation models (TSFMs) forecast well from large-scale pretraining but typically neither read nor generate text. Time series language models add a time series modality to the LLM but forecast on the LLM side, leaving the TSFM's pretrained forecasting ability unused. We present TimeOmni-o1, which couples a pretrained TSFM and an LLM bidirectionally. In one direction, the TSFM encodes the series in compressed form for the LLM, which reasons over it together with the text. In the other, the LLM's reasoning is fed back into the TSFM, which produces the forecast conditioned on it. One model architecture thus reads and generates both series and text, reasons in text, and draws on the TSFM's pretrained forecasting ability. To train it, we build MMTR, a multimodal time series reasoning dataset with annotated reasoning traces, covering both tasks across 12 domains with 500k+ samples. On MMTR, TimeOmni-o1 outperforms existing models on both understanding and forecasting across most domains, as well as the LLM and the TSFM inside it when used individually. The gains carry over to three open benchmarks, where it outperforms the dedicated time series models.
papers.summary: Understanding and forecasting time series that come with related text require reasoning over both modalities, but large language models (LLMs) handle long numeric series poorly and time series foundation models (TSFMs) neither read nor generate text. `TimeOmni-o1` couples the two bidirectionally: the TSFM encodes the series in compressed form for the LLM to reason over alongside the text, and the LLM's reasoning is fed back into the TSFM to condition the forecast. Trained on `MMTR`, a new reasoning-annotated dataset with 500k+ samples across 12 domains, it **outperforms existing models and its own LLM and TSFM components used individually** on both tasks across most domains, with gains carrying over to three open benchmarks.

papers.title: SELD: Detecting Silent Evidence Loss in Context Compression beyond the Answer
papers.abstract: Context compression is now routine for language models with long inputs, but a compressed context is useful only if it keeps the evidence for the answer. Existing checks compare the reader model's answer or its most likely words, and thus miss a frequent failure, silent evidence loss: key evidence is removed while the answer stays the same, leaving the answer unsupported and risky for other models that reuse the context. To address this challenge, we propose SELD (Silent Evidence Loss Detector), which needs no training and no labels. Its principle is that when evidence is lost, a reader model's preferences among the answers it leaves unsaid shift even if its answer does not, so comparing these preferences before and after compression reveals losses that answer checks cannot see. We also build SEL-Pairs, a benchmark of length-matched evidence and control deletions from three question-answering datasets. Quantitative and qualitative experiments with five reader models on it show that SELD consistently outperforms strong and recent baselines across compressors, compression rates and models, identifying the evidence-removing edit in 83% of matched pairs with unchanged answers, against 70% for the strongest baseline. These results show that evidence loss in compressed contexts can be detected even when the answer is unchanged.
papers.summary: Context compression for long language-model inputs can remove key evidence while leaving the answer unchanged, a failure the authors call silent evidence loss that answer-based checks cannot see. `SELD` (Silent Evidence Loss Detector) needs no training or labels and compares a reader model's preferences among the answers it did not give before and after compression, since these shift when evidence is lost. On `SEL-Pairs`, a new benchmark of length-matched evidence and control deletions built from three question-answering datasets, it identifies the evidence-removing edit in **83% of matched pairs with unchanged answers, against 70% for the strongest baseline**, across five reader models.

papers.title: Actionable Feedback: Improving Model Capabilities from User Edit Data on Clinical Documentation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being deployed in clinical documentation workflows, where clinicians review and edit their outputs before use. In principle, these clinician edits represent a scalable source of supervision for model training. In practice, not all edits represent actionable feedback: for instance, on data drawn from real-world deployment of an AI clinical documentation product, our review suggests that over 45% of edited outputs contain user-added information that is not directly supported by the inputs to the model. Naively fine-tuning on such edits risks teaching the model to hallucinate. In this paper, we develop a method to address this challenge. Given that real clinician edits on deployed documentation tools are not publicly available, we first develop a taxonomy of clinician-editing behaviors, informed by data from a deployed AI clinical documentation product. Then, we develop a method for generating semi-synthetic clinician-edit data, informed by our taxonomy, on a discharge-summary generation task based on MIMIC-III, a public dataset. Finally, we introduce simple filtering methods for identifying actionable edits, with accuracy evaluated by expert review. We show empirically, on our semi-synthetic dataset, that naive fine-tuning on raw edited output increases ungrounded content, while our approach of progressively filtering toward grounded edits enables improvement on clinician-alignment metrics while retaining faithfulness to the input context.
papers.summary: Clinician edits to large language model (LLM) outputs look like a scalable training signal, but a review of data from a deployed clinical documentation product suggests that **over 45% of edited outputs contain user-added information not supported by the model's inputs**. The authors build a taxonomy of clinician editing behaviors, use it to generate semi-synthetic edit data for discharge-summary generation on `MIMIC-III`, and introduce simple filters for identifying actionable edits, validated by expert review. Naive fine-tuning on raw edits increases ungrounded content, whereas progressively filtering toward grounded edits improves clinician-alignment metrics while retaining faithfulness to the input.

papers.title: Brasilidade: Measuring Brazilian Identity for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: This work presents a new benchmark that aims to address the limitations of current methods for evaluating LLMs in Brazilian Portuguese. We introduced Brasilidade, an assessment methodology comprised of standardized tasks distributed across four different domains, and we are making available the tasks from its first domain, which address nuances of the language, grammar, and variations of Brazilian Portuguese. The results show that model size, by itself, does not determine performance; several medium-sized models outperformed larger models in the protocols evaluated. Specific models for Portuguese, in general, did not perform above average, despite their targeted training. Different task levels revealed significant nuances: while some tasks proved easy for most models, others posed extreme challenges, and some yielded mixed results, with wide variations in performance. This clearly illustrates the need for benchmarks that address the limitations of the models in Brazilian Portuguese, allowing future training cycles to seek to overcome them. Project repository https://github.com/soberania-oficial/brasilidade
papers.summary: `Brasilidade` is a benchmark methodology for evaluating large language models in Brazilian Portuguese, organized as standardized tasks across four domains, with the first domain, covering language nuances, grammar and regional variation, now released. Results show that **model size alone does not determine performance**, with several medium-sized models outperforming larger ones. Models trained specifically for Portuguese generally did not score above average, and task difficulty ranged from easy for most models to extremely challenging.

papers.title: Generative Learning on Manifolds for Probabilistic Seismic Performance Assessment and Structural Identifiability
papers.abstract: Seismic performance assessment relies on computationally expensive nonlinear simulations, limiting uncertainty quantification and inference of structural properties from observed responses. We develop a manifold-based generative framework that learns the joint distribution of uncertain structural parameters and seismic-response trajectories from limited high-fidelity simulations. Combining Diffusion Maps, score-based Diffusion Modeling, and Geometric Harmonics, the framework enables both forward probabilistic prediction and inverse inference. Applied to a nine-story steel moment-resisting frame, the results reveal which structural properties are identifiable from seismic performance and how uncertainty in these properties influences response. In particular, the learned representation captures post-capping degradation characteristics more effectively than individual strength parameters. Inverse inference identifies distinct structural configurations that produce similar seismic performance, with representative solutions independently validated using nonlinear simulations. These findings demonstrate how generative learning can support uncertainty-aware seismic assessment while revealing structural non-identifiability and alternative mechanisms underlying observed performance
papers.summary: Seismic performance assessment depends on expensive nonlinear simulations, which limits uncertainty quantification and the inference of structural properties from observed responses. A manifold-based generative framework combining Diffusion Maps, score-based diffusion modeling and Geometric Harmonics learns the joint distribution of uncertain structural parameters and seismic-response trajectories from limited high-fidelity simulations, supporting both forward prediction and inverse inference. Applied to a nine-story steel moment-resisting frame, the learned representation captures post-capping degradation characteristics better than individual strength parameters, and **inverse inference finds distinct structural configurations that produce similar seismic performance**, validated with nonlinear simulations.

papers.title: M\"obius Interaction Filtering: Order-Selective Spectral Regularization for Multimodal Humor Detection
papers.abstract: Multimodal humor detection requires interpreting language, vocal delivery, and visual behavior jointly. Expressive fusion must also regulate how interactions of different orders enter the final judgment. We propose M\"obius Interaction Filtering (MoIF), which learns a modality-subset prediction function and imposes order-selective spectral regularization through its aggregation structure. Private temporal encoders and balanced reciprocal interaction construct supervised unimodal, bimodal, and trimodal predictors. Their uniform aggregate is exactly a M\"obius-domain filter with a geometrically decreasing interaction-order response. This formulation retains higher-order representations while regulating their contribution to prediction. Controlled UR-FUNNY perturbations reveal a pronounced decline in label-aligned signal-to-noise ratio across interaction orders. The induced filter improves the final ratio by 1.62-2.79 times relative to the co-trained trimodal predictor while preserving its own clean class-aligned signal under perturbation. Five-seed experiments achieve 70.6% accuracy and weighted F1 on UR-FUNNY, exceeding thirteen reproduced methods on these detection metrics. CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI evaluations establish applicability to sentiment prediction, and cross-seed analyses show more stable estimates on all three datasets. MoIF connects the organization of multimodal interactions to their statistical reliability through an executable spectral constraint. Code is available at https://github.com/D-ST-Sword/MoIF.
papers.summary: Multimodal humor detection must fuse language, vocal delivery and visual behavior while controlling how much unimodal, bimodal and trimodal interactions each contribute. Möbius Interaction Filtering (`MoIF`) trains supervised predictors for every modality subset and aggregates them uniformly, which is shown to act exactly as a Möbius-domain filter whose response decreases geometrically with interaction order. Under controlled perturbations the filter improves the label-aligned signal-to-noise ratio by 1.62-2.79 times over the co-trained trimodal predictor, and five-seed experiments reach **70.6% accuracy and weighted F1 on `UR-FUNNY`**, exceeding thirteen reproduced methods, with further evaluations on `CMU-MOSI` and `CMU-MOSEI`.

papers.title: IntentTwin: Deconfounding Candidate Support and the Oracle-to-Deployment Gap in Offline Web Behavior Prediction
papers.abstract: Offline web-behavior benchmarks frequently insert the demonstrated action into a finite candidate set and then measure reranking. We show that this protocol can create a candidate-support confound: when the target is outside training support while all distractors are sampled from that support, support membership identifies the gold action without modeling behavior. We formalize this effect with support-identifiability rate (SIR), construct support-balanced candidate sets, and evaluate a target-free dual-path proposer that combines support retrieval with open-vocabulary DOM/LM proposals. On filtered OPeRA (4,282/469/992 train/dev/test steps), the original protocol has SIR 1.0000 on target-OOV rows and a support-only rule reaches 1.0000 OOV Exact@1. Support balancing reduces SIR to 0.0000; the strongest conditional reranker obtains 0.7214 overall Exact@1, 0.7988 on IV rows, and 0.5668 on OOV rows. The target-free dual-path system reaches Proposal Recall@16 0.6915 and end-to-end Exact@1 0.5212, compared with oracle conditional Exact@1 0.7450. On Mind2Web, the same audit yields SIR 0.2380 and an oracle-to-proposal gap of 0.2125. A 200-row semantic audit labels 0.7150 of exact-key OOV targets as semantically novel, 0.2450 as locator/string variation, and 0.0400 as ambiguous (Cohen's $\kappa=0.8173$). These measurements show why support composition must be controlled alongside candidate accuracy when offline results are used to reason about deployment.
papers.summary: Offline web-behavior benchmarks often insert the demonstrated action into a candidate set and measure reranking, which creates a confound when the target lies outside training support while all distractors are sampled from it. The authors formalize this with a support-identifiability rate (SIR), build support-balanced candidate sets, and evaluate a target-free dual-path proposer combining support retrieval with open-vocabulary DOM and language-model proposals. On filtered `OPeRA`, **a support-only rule reaches perfect Exact@1 on out-of-vocabulary targets under the original protocol** without modeling behavior; after balancing, the strongest reranker scores 0.7214 Exact@1 and the end-to-end target-free system 0.5212, and the same audit on `Mind2Web` gives an SIR of 0.2380.

papers.title: Using LLM Agents to Evaluate Prosocial Interventions on Social Media Platforms
papers.abstract: Social media platforms are a primary source of information for many users. Although research explores various interventions to promote prosocial content or demote harmful content on platforms, there are few systematic methods for evaluating competing intervention designs before conducting costly human-subject experiments. We develop a simulation-based evaluation pipeline built on the OASIS framework. We generate 13,835 LLM-based agents, each with a unique profile. Over 20 time steps, we expose them to real-world Twitter/X posts and let them comment, like, repost, or follow. We use those agents to systematically evaluate three interventions that increase exposure to verified news: adding content, upranking content, and celebrity source cues. All interventions significantly increase news engagement, with upranking news to prominent feed positions producing the largest effects. These effects hold across agents' gender, age, and education levels. We validate our injection treatment results against a comparable human-subject study and find strong directional alignment and similar dose-normalized efficiency. Our results suggest that LLM-based agent simulations can support early-stage evaluation of platform interventions before human-subject deployment, and upranking may be more effective than news volume or source.
papers.summary: Few systematic methods exist for comparing social media intervention designs before running costly human-subject experiments. A simulation pipeline built on the `OASIS` framework generates **13,835 LLM-based agents** with unique profiles, exposes them to real Twitter/X posts over 20 time steps, and tests three interventions that increase exposure to verified news: adding content, upranking content, and celebrity source cues. All three significantly increase news engagement, with upranking to prominent feed positions producing the largest effects, and the content-injection results show strong directional alignment with a comparable human-subject study.

papers.title: An ensemble of graph generative models for assisted history matching of the Brugge field case
papers.abstract: Assisted history matching remains non-unique because many geological realisations can reproduce equivalent production responses with substantial differences between individual well matches. This ambiguity increases when a field comprises several depositional settings and modelling strategies. The paper applied a graph autoencoder approach to history matching of a benchmark Brugge field that comprises different depositional zones. Each stratigraphic zone is modelled with its dedicated generative model that comprises a joint latent space for optimisation history matching loops. Graph-based generators operate directly on the active cells of the corner-point grid, so its irregular geometry is handled without conversion to a regular lattice. The optimisation search in the 160-dimensional joint latent space is done with the Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy. The multi-component objective function includes static well data mismatch, dynamic production mismatch, and a geological realism penalty based on the Decoder induced latent metric. Latent space diagnostics with topological data analysis are applied prior to history matching to test whether one generator is sufficient or whether a multiple generator formulation is required. The results show that the zone-based formulation gives coherent latent spaces, preserves the main porosity and permeability relations that vary from one zone to another, and supports history matching while keeping the solutions within the learned geological manifold. The matched models reproduce field oil and water production within the prior uncertainty range and provide a comparable well-level match to previously published Brugge studies based on Ensemble Kalman Filter, Particle Swarm Optimisation with principal component analysis of parameterisation, and Multiple Kernel Learning with Particle Swarm Optimisation.
papers.summary: Assisted history matching of oil reservoirs is non-unique, and the ambiguity grows when a field spans several depositional settings. For the benchmark Brugge field, each stratigraphic zone gets a dedicated graph autoencoder generator operating directly on the active cells of the corner-point grid, and the resulting 160-dimensional joint latent space is searched with the Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy using an objective that combines well-data mismatch, production mismatch and a geological realism penalty. The matched models **reproduce field oil and water production within the prior uncertainty range**, with well-level matches comparable to previously published Ensemble Kalman Filter and Particle Swarm Optimisation studies.

papers.title: Token Importance-Aware Semantic Communication Enabled Robust Video Transmission
papers.abstract: Video applications are increasingly prevalent, yet their high data volume and temporal dependency make robust wireless transmission challenging under limited communication resources. To address this issue, we propose a token importance-aware semantic communication (Ti-SemCom) framework for bandwidth-efficient video transmission. Specifically, object and motion information is jointly extracted to identify communication-relevant regions, which are hierarchically associated with semantic tokens according to their importance. The transmitted tokens are then dynamically selected based on both token importance and the available bandwidth, prioritizing more informative video content under resource constraints. At the receiver, untransmitted regions reuse recently reconstructed references to further reduce redundant transmission. Experiments on the CAVIAR dataset show that Ti-SemCom can achieve an 88.3\% reduction in communication cost while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality.
papers.summary: Video is hard to transmit robustly over wireless links because of its data volume and temporal dependency. The token importance-aware semantic communication framework `Ti-SemCom` jointly extracts object and motion information to identify communication-relevant regions, ranks the associated semantic tokens by importance, and selects which tokens to send according to importance and available bandwidth, while the receiver fills untransmitted regions from recently reconstructed references. On the `CAVIAR` dataset it achieves an **88.3% reduction in communication cost** while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality.

papers.title: Topology-Aware Reinforcement Learning for CAD Decomposition toward All-Hexahedral Meshing
papers.abstract: Automatic hexahedral meshing for complex CAD models has long been regarded as the "holy grail" of mesh generation. The fundamental challenge arises from feature misalignment, where orthogonal or interacting features coexist, making direct hexahedral meshing infeasible and requiring decomposition into simpler, meshable blocks. While existing decomposition methods, including frame-field pipelines and learning-based techniques, have reduced manual intervention, they can remain sensitive to geometric and topological complexity and may fail to produce valid decompositions for challenging feature configurations. Specifically, their action spaces are typically restricted to surface-based splitting, which often yields invalid or unmeshable decompositions. To address these limitations, we propose DecompRL, a deep reinforcement learning framework for CAD decomposition toward hexahedral meshing. We design a set of topology-aware internal-splitting actions that leverage both global topological structure and local geometric property to effectively separate misaligned features. Furthermore, we introduce geometric rewards together with meshability feedback to guide the learning process toward valid decompositions and high-quality meshes. Extensive experiments on ABC, Fusion360, NIST, and DeepCAD show that DecompRL achieves the highest success rate among the evaluated learning-based methods on three of the four benchmarks, while maintaining competitive mesh quality. The measured LMFF-to-DecompRL runtime ratio reaches up to two orders of magnitude; this compares the full LMFF procedure with DecompRL decomposition alone, excluding subsequent mesh generation. The largest SR improvement is observed on Fusion360, where DecompRL reaches a success rate of 59.6%.
papers.summary: All-hexahedral meshing of complex CAD models requires first decomposing them into simpler meshable blocks, and existing learning-based methods restrict themselves to surface-based splits that often yield invalid decompositions. `DecompRL` is a deep reinforcement learning framework with topology-aware internal-splitting actions and rewards that combine geometric terms with meshability feedback. Across `ABC`, `Fusion360`, `NIST` and `DeepCAD`, it achieves **the highest success rate among the evaluated learning-based methods on three of the four benchmarks**, reaching 59.6% on `Fusion360`, and its decomposition step runs up to two orders of magnitude faster than the full `LMFF` procedure.

papers.title: Auditable Human-Agent Teams for Autonomous X-ray Experimentation
papers.abstract: Closed-loop autonomous experimentation can accelerate scientific discovery, but implementation effort limits accessibility. Agentic systems may lower this barrier, although sustained operation on physical instruments remains largely unexplored. Here, using coding-agent infrastructure grounded in validated scientific methods, we demonstrate autonomous synchrotron X-ray experiments on nanoparticle superlattices under evolving, human-defined objectives. Complete human-agent and agent-agent transcripts enable an audit that reconstructs decision provenance and characterizes the division of cognitive labor. Across three experiments, 61-67% of messages involved interpretation or judgment, while the share of methodological and scientific contributions increased from 46% in the setup-focused first experiment to 56-61% in later experiments. Provenance showed that 59-68% of error corrections involved multiple participants and that about half of all decisions incorporated the input of another participant. These results may guide design principles for multi-agent scientific systems and inform future agent harnesses, model training, and accessible autonomous experimentation.
papers.summary: Closed-loop autonomous experiments on physical instruments are costly to set up, and sustained agent operation on real hardware is largely untested. Using coding-agent infrastructure grounded in validated scientific methods, the authors ran autonomous synchrotron X-ray experiments on nanoparticle superlattices under changing human-set objectives, then audited the complete human-agent and agent-agent transcripts to reconstruct who decided what. Across three experiments, 61-67% of messages involved interpretation or judgment, and **59-68% of error corrections involved multiple participants**, with about half of all decisions incorporating another participant's input.

papers.title: EarthRecord: From Pixels to Land Change with Multimodal Agents over Four Decades of Satellite Imagery
papers.abstract: While multimodal agents now carry out complex data analysis with tools, their ability to turn decades of satellite imagery into reliable land-change analysis, crucial for Earth observation science, remains unmeasured. Existing benchmarks fall short: they pose questions on curated images or give agents preprocessed inputs, leaving out the raw multi-sensor archives where such analysis begins. We introduce EarthRecord, a benchmark built on the raw record of 56 sites: four decades of Landsat, MODIS, VIIRS, and Sentinel-2 data, with cloud masking and cross-sensor harmonization left to the agent. It poses 238 land-change questions across ten analysis tasks, scored against withheld references from global products, agreement among methods, and visual interpretation. Two controls test what answers rest on: the closed book removes the record, and instrument pairs alter one satellite's data while nothing changes on the ground. Evaluations of twelve multimodal agents reveal that leading agents complete most analyses end to end but falter when an answer requires mapping from imagery. Further analysis shows that the record moves answers from prior knowledge to the pixels but not yet to the real change on the ground: when one satellite's data are altered, half of the right answers follow the alteration. EarthRecord thus provides a principled platform for measuring and advancing agents from pixels to land change.
papers.summary: `EarthRecord` is a benchmark that tests whether multimodal agents can turn raw multi-sensor satellite archives into land-change analysis, leaving cloud masking and cross-sensor harmonization to the agent. It covers 56 sites with four decades of `Landsat`, `MODIS`, `VIIRS`, and `Sentinel-2` data and poses 238 questions across ten tasks, with two controls: removing the record entirely, and altering one satellite's data while nothing changes on the ground. Among twelve agents evaluated, leading ones complete most analyses end to end but struggle when an answer requires mapping from imagery, and **when one satellite's data are altered, half of the right answers follow the alteration** rather than the real ground change.
papers.highlight_summary:
`EarthRecord` benchmarks whether multimodal agents can turn four decades of raw, multi-sensor satellite archives into reliable land-change analysis, instead of answering questions on curated or preprocessed imagery. Its two controls test whether a right answer rests on regional priors, on unverified pixels, or on change that actually happened on the ground.

- The benchmark gives agents the unscaled `Landsat`, `MODIS`, `VIIRS` and `Sentinel-2` record for 56 sites (1984–2026) in an offline CPU-only sandbox, leaves cloud masking and cross-sensor harmonization to them, and scores 238 questions across ten tasks by `pass^3` (right in all three passes).
- Of twelve agents, the top four (`Opus 5.5`, `GPT-6 Sol`, `GPT-6.1 Sol`, `Sonnet 5.5`) reach **81.0–85.4%** on the 226 computable and recognition questions with overlapping confidence intervals, while `GPT-6 Luna` and `Qwen 3.7 Flash` fall below the **23.9%** majority-class baseline.
- Mapping from imagery is the main bottleneck: the six leading models score **92.0%** on questions computed from record variables but only **61.1%** on those needing a map, where `GPT-6.1 Sol`, `GPT-6 Astra` and `GPT-6.1 Terra` abstain in 46–67% of recognition runs, mostly without viewing an image.
- Giving agents the record lifts every model on computable questions by 4.6 to 60.8 points over the closed-book control, but when one satellite's data are altered with nothing changing on the ground, **53.5%** of previously right answers turn wrong and only **3.5%** of those failed runs blame the instrument.
- Limitations include a sandbox without pretrained vision models, only 22 instrument pairs that test clear-cut breaks instead of subtle drift, and references that rest partly on global products and on 37 AI-drafted, human-reviewed visual interpretations.

papers.title: Train on prefill, monitor at decode: Using sparse autoencoders for topic monitoring
papers.abstract: Topic monitoring is the task of labelling the topic of each token in a model's response during generation. Activation-based monitors that run at generation time have so far been trained to detect harmful content and are limited to two or three classes. We introduce TopicScope, a framework for training causal topic classifiers on SAE features that assign a topic to every token, so that the label can change partway through a response. We train three detector architectures on synthetic multi-topic conversations covering seven topics. Across Gemma-3 1B and 4B, monitors trained on features extracted from prefill hidden states were able to generalise to decoding. We also found that the classifiers are robust to perturbations, losing at most 5 macro-F1 points when off-topic asides are inserted, topics are removed or sections are reordered. Ablations conducted to understand the contribution of the SAE revealed that classifiers reaching baseline performance without it were several times larger. Our findings show that compact topic monitors can be trained inexpensively in prefill and deployed during generation. More broadly, our work shows where SAEs are useful beyond safety classification. Our code, dataset and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/Mercity-AI/SAE-Guardrails and https://huggingface.co/collections/Mercity/online-guardrails-using-sparse-autoencoders-6ac602940468c62fefb2b9e8
papers.summary: Activation-based monitors that run during generation have mostly been limited to detecting harmful content with two or three classes. `TopicScope` trains causal classifiers on sparse autoencoder (SAE) features to assign one of seven topics to every token, so the label can change mid-response, using synthetic multi-topic conversations and three detector architectures. On `Gemma-3` 1B and 4B, monitors trained on prefill hidden states generalised to decoding and **lost at most 5 macro-F1 points** under inserted asides, removed topics, or reordered sections. Ablations found that classifiers matching this performance without the SAE were several times larger.

papers.title: LandslideFM: A Foundation Model Towards Unified Landslide Perception and Understanding
papers.abstract: Intelligent landslide detection is essential for disaster prevention. However, existing models primarily focus on isolated visual tasks, require extensive labeled data, and lack deep analytical and scene-understanding capabilities. To address these limitations, we propose LandslideFM, the first unified foundation model that connects visual perception tasks with contextual interpretation of landslides. Specifically, LandslideFM adapts to multiple visual tasks via a Source-Agreement Graduated Trust semi-supervised learning framework that leverages limited labeled data alongside abundant unlabeled data. Furthermore, predicted landslide regions provide explicit spatial guidance to a Vision-Language Model adapted through parameter-efficient fine-tuning, enabling comprehensive landslide reasoning. To support training and evaluation in this domain, we also present LandslideVL, the first benchmark for intelligent landslide analysis, combining visual imagery and newly introduced textual prompts. Comprehensive experiments across public datasets and LandslideVL demonstrate that LandslideFM achieves superior quantitative and qualitative performance. Most importantly, LandslideFM surpasses general-purpose VLMs in specialized landslide reasoning and scene analysis. Our code is released at https://github.com/wangshanwen001/LandslideFM.
papers.summary: Landslide detection models typically handle isolated visual tasks, need large labeled sets, and offer no scene-level interpretation. `LandslideFM` adapts to multiple visual tasks through a semi-supervised framework called `Source-Agreement Graduated Trust` that combines limited labels with abundant unlabeled data, then passes predicted landslide regions as spatial guidance to a vision-language model (VLM) adapted with parameter-efficient fine-tuning. The authors also introduce `LandslideVL`, a benchmark pairing imagery with textual prompts, and report that the model **surpasses general-purpose VLMs in specialized landslide reasoning and scene analysis**.

papers.title: Tracing Psychometric Inference in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Do large language models represent psychological constructs internally, or do they only generate outputs that resemble psychometric structure? We address this question using a cross-persona paradigm across 14 model variants from two families (Llama 3 and Qwen 2.5, 0.5B-14B, base and instruct). Given responses on one psychological scale from real individuals (N = 272 Taiwanese university students), models predict responses on six other scales. At the behavioral level, larger variants reproduce and amplify human cross-scale correlations; amplification persists after correcting the seven-scale human correlations for measurement attenuation. We then examine whether this structure is reflected internally. Contrastive direction analysis finds geometry aligned with the human matrix in larger instruct variants, but little alignment in base variants under this assay. Across models, geometry strength is associated with behavioral amplification (r = 0.68, p = 0.008; partial r = 0.69 controlling for log size). To relate internal structure to output behavior, a matched activation-probing paradigm shows that probe slopes vary less than behavioral slopes (1.38-1.77 vs 0.52-1.53). A synthetic control shows that ridge probing can inflate these slopes; after subtracting a baseline based on a reliability proxy from another analysis, adjusted slopes remain associated with behavior (r = 0.88). We term the measured probe-behavior gap readout attenuation. These results establish decodability and geometric alignment under the tested assays, without showing that the measured directions mediate the cross-persona answers.
papers.summary: The question is whether language models internally represent psychological constructs or merely produce outputs that resemble psychometric structure. Across 14 variants of `Llama 3` and `Qwen 2.5` (0.5B-14B, base and instruct), models were given one psychological scale's responses from 272 real Taiwanese university students and asked to predict responses on six other scales. Larger variants reproduce and amplify human cross-scale correlations, and the strength of internal geometry aligned with the human correlation matrix is **associated with that behavioral amplification (r = 0.68, p = 0.008)**, mainly in larger instruct variants. The authors state that the results show decodability and geometric alignment, not that the measured directions mediate the answers.

papers.title: Graph Visualizations in Prompts for Knowledge Graph Question Answering
papers.abstract: We study when and how multimodal input improves knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) in large vision--language models. Using a controlled evaluation over 1,500 WebQSP and CWQ questions and six VLMs within a fixed KGQA pipeline, we compare text-only prompting against text-plus-graph visualization at the per-question level and analyze performance changes as a function of reasoning complexity, model size, and image layout. Adding a graph image yields an average gain of 1.85 F1 points, driven by strong precision improvements on low-complexity questions (+4.65 F1). Mixed-effects and regression analyses show that these multimodal gains do not depend strongly on model scale, but are highly sensitive to graph layout: image-only settings sharply degrade performance, hierarchical Graphviz layouts outperform less organized renderings, and decomposing large subgraphs into separated paths yields the largest improvements. Taken together, the results indicate that visual prompting primarily aids KGQA by enhancing prediction precision in low-complexity contexts, provided that visual design respects cognitive and perceptual constraints. To optimize both accuracy and inference efficiency, we argue for adaptive visual prompting policies that selectively append diagrams to small, visually sparse subgraphs with well-structured layouts, avoiding unnecessary visual clutter and token overhead on complex queries. We conclude by relating these findings to a visual notation design theory, outlining how principled diagram encoding can guide future multimodal VLM prompting.
papers.summary: A controlled study examines when adding a rendered graph image to the prompt helps knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) in vision-language models. Over 1,500 `WebQSP` and `CWQ` questions and six models in a fixed pipeline, text-plus-image prompting yields **an average gain of 1.85 F1 points**, driven by precision improvements on low-complexity questions (+4.65 F1). The gains do not depend strongly on model size but are highly sensitive to layout: image-only input sharply degrades performance, hierarchical `Graphviz` layouts beat less organized renderings, and splitting large subgraphs into separated paths helps most. The authors recommend adaptively attaching diagrams only for small, sparse subgraphs.

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning based control of Cancer Chemotherapy treatments
papers.abstract:
Reinforcement Learning has achieved tremendous success in recent years. Extending its scope from the traditional complex games such as Atari, Go, Pokeman, and Chess, reinforcement learning has caught researchers' attention on modelling real-life scenarios. Personalized medicine and the dynamic treatment regimen are two such preliminary research fields; researchers are focusing their mindsets currently. Estimating the optimal dynamic treatment regimens from the observational real clinical data is being popularized among the researchers, widening its scope towards more advanced versions of reinforcement learning algorithms.
  This research is about a research study that focused on reinforcement learning techniques that have been approached in the context of cancer chemotherapy treatments. Primarily this thesis addresses the result of the study by means of the state-of-the-art on reinforcement learning techniques used in generating the optimal policy for sequential treatments, including the existing online reinforcement learning approaches. Thereby a simulation for cancer chemotherapy via traditional Q-learning would be presented. Secondly, the study will extend towards using offline reinforcement learning in the optimal policy generation. Thus, the proposed solution follows a data-driven approach, which works on the real human colon cancer clinical data.
  The novelty of the proposed solution resides in the implementation of an offline reinforcement learning approach by means of a model-based architecture using the conservative Q-learning and the model-based offline policy optimization algorithm. As per the experimental results and the evaluations, it was revealed that the proposed Chemo RL model caters well the problem of cancer chemotherapy treatment scheduling and serves as a supportive model for the junior oncologists in deciding their treatment decisions.
papers.summary: This thesis-style study reviews reinforcement learning methods for scheduling cancer chemotherapy as a dynamic treatment regimen and presents a simulation using traditional Q-learning. It then builds `Chemo RL`, an offline, model-based approach combining conservative Q-learning with the model-based offline policy optimization algorithm, trained on real human colon cancer clinical data. The authors report that the model **handles chemotherapy treatment scheduling well and could serve as a decision-support aid for junior oncologists**.

papers.title: AI Governance Should Prioritize Control and Knowledge Boundaries Over Limiting Intelligence
papers.abstract: The rapid proliferation of autonomously acting AI agents makes the governance of agentic systems urgent. We propose the competence circuit, summarized as IKC + KC + C, that decomposes an agent's real-world impact into three pathways: intelligence-mediated discovery, procedural know-how, and direct control. Using the canonical fast-takeoff debate as a stress test, we formalize the conditions for intelligence-mediated fast takeoff as a conjunction jointly sufficient for fast catastrophic supremacy, showing that most rely on rapid knowledge acquisition or control attainment rather than intelligence alone. We operationalize epistemic intelligence as hypothesis-selection efficiency and validate this framework via stochastic simulation on NK fitness landscapes across six scenarios spanning the conjunctive chain. An analytic bound supported by the simulations shows that intelligence-driven speedup is capped by the ratio of competing intelligence levels regardless of task difficulty. The simulations also expose a fast-takeoff dilemma: a large intelligence-driven speedup multiplier materializes only when the hypothesis space is noisy, but the absolute timescale remains constrained by the time required for capability-critical tests, so a large multiplier need not imply rapid progress. Simulations also indicate that institutional chokepoints disproportionately slow down superintelligent agents when mandatory authorization delays are large relative to the negligible time these agents spend on unproductive search. We argue that the dominant safety levers are restricting control and enforcing knowledge boundaries rather than limiting intelligence alone, and this applies to agentic systems at any capability level. Purely digital domains weaken these bottlenecks, strengthening the case for architectures that intentionally "put physics in the loop."
papers.summary: A position paper proposes the competence circuit, which decomposes an AI agent's real-world impact into intelligence-mediated discovery, procedural know-how, and direct control, and uses it to formalize the conditions required for an intelligence-driven fast takeoff. Treating intelligence as hypothesis-selection efficiency, stochastic simulations on NK fitness landscapes and an analytic bound indicate that **intelligence-driven speedup is capped by the ratio of competing intelligence levels regardless of task difficulty**, while absolute timescales remain limited by the time needed for capability-critical tests. Simulations also suggest mandatory authorization delays disproportionately slow highly intelligent agents. The authors argue that restricting control and enforcing knowledge boundaries are stronger safety levers than limiting intelligence, and note that purely digital domains weaken these bottlenecks.

papers.title: Tabular Foundation Models vs Tuned Gradient Boosting for Telecom Churn: A Profit- and Calibration-Aware Evaluation
papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) predict from a labelled context in a single forward pass. A recent benchmark reported that they decisively outperform tree ensembles for customer churn, but it compared them with untuned gradient-boosted trees (GBDTs) and scored only ranking metrics, while a retention campaign is judged in money. We re-evaluate TabPFN-2.5, TabPFN-3.5, TabPFN-3.5-Fast and TabICL v2 against Optuna-tuned GBDTs on five public telecom churn datasets over 10 seeded splits. We separate three questions: whether a model ranks churners well, whether that ranking earns more expected maximum profit (EMP), and whether its probabilities can drive a threshold policy. With a split-aware test and Holm correction over 20 pre-declared comparisons, TabPFN-3.5 earns significantly more EMP than the best tuned GBDT on Cell2Cell (1.9%) and Iranian (7.6%), and these two gains also hold against each of the three tuned GBDTs separately. On Orange it is ahead in all 10 splits (14.3%), but the gain is not significant after correction (Holm p = 0.155). The splits resample the same datasets, so these results do not stand for independent operators. TabICL v2, the earlier benchmark's leader, beats the best tuned GBDT only on Iranian, not all three of them, and underpredicts Orange churn by 2.1 points on a 7.3% base rate. On the datasets and splits where we tested them, a substantially larger tuning budget and a duplicate-aware split leave the main conclusions unchanged. Retuning the baseline cuts the earlier headline gap from 6.1 to 4.0 PR-AUC points without closing it. The licence of the TabPFN-3.5 weights we used (License v1.0), not scoring cost, is what stands between its gains and production use.
papers.summary: An earlier benchmark claimed tabular foundation models (TFMs) decisively beat tree ensembles for customer churn, but it used untuned gradient-boosted trees (GBDTs) and only ranking metrics. This re-evaluation compares `TabPFN-2.5`, `TabPFN-3.5`, `TabPFN-3.5-Fast`, and `TabICL v2` against `Optuna`-tuned GBDTs on five public telecom churn datasets over 10 seeded splits, separately testing ranking quality, expected maximum profit (EMP), and probability calibration. With Holm correction over 20 pre-declared comparisons, `TabPFN-3.5` earns **significantly more EMP than the best tuned GBDT on `Cell2Cell` (1.9%) and `Iranian` (7.6%)**, while its 14.3% gain on `Orange` is not significant after correction. Retuning the baseline cuts the earlier headline gap from 6.1 to 4.0 PR-AUC points without closing it, and the authors identify the model's weight licence as the main obstacle to production use.

papers.title: When Proofs Are Abundant, What Is a Paper For?
papers.abstract: AI systems now produce formally verified proofs of celebrated open problems, and the cost of obtaining a correct proof is falling toward zero. If correctness becomes cheap, what is left for a research paper to communicate? I argue that a paper is not exhausted by a verified statement. It is a narrative exposed to the criticism of a community, made of an intension (the author's choice of problem and perspective), a scientific chain of thought (the reasoning steps leading to the result), and the arguments supporting each step. Most published mathematics is judged on these two elements rather than on correctness alone, and machine-generated formal scripts convey neither. Borrowing from logic and type theory, I formalise the first as a Derivation-Level Intension and the second as a Directional Extension: a decomposition of a proof into cut-points whose axiomatic footprints reveal its weak links, where the result could be strengthened, and its strong links, which can be transported to other theories. Moreover, I examine five roles AI can play in the research process, including bibliographical search and critical judgment, and show that none of them removes the need to declare these two elements. I mention ways these two concepts could be useful for Journals and for training of young mathematicians in a AI era. If proofs become abundant, the scarce resource is not correctness but a community's shared understanding of why a result matters and how it could be pushed further.
papers.summary: With AI systems producing formally verified proofs at falling cost, this essay asks what a mathematics paper still communicates once correctness is cheap. The author argues that **a paper is a narrative exposed to community criticism, not just a verified statement**, consisting of the author's choice of problem and perspective plus a chain of reasoning, neither of which machine-generated formal scripts convey. Drawing on logic and type theory, these are formalized as a `Derivation-Level Intension` and a `Directional Extension`, the latter decomposing a proof into cut-points whose axiomatic footprints show where a result could be strengthened or transported to other theories. Five roles AI can play in research are examined, and none is found to remove the need to declare these two elements.

papers.title: SetPrint: Black-Box LLM Fingerprinting via Setwise Correspondence of Response Changes
papers.abstract: Black-box LLM fingerprinting aims to determine whether a target model was derived from a source model when only the output responses to input queries are observable. One way to reveal this relationship is to perturb each query and observe the resulting responses of both models, yielding two corresponding sets of response variations. These sets provide two complementary sources of information: the relations among response changes within each set, and the correspondence of response changes between the two sets. Existing approaches, however, have not fully exploited both. We introduce \textbf{SetPrint}, a training-free method that jointly captures both within-set relations and between-set correspondence. SetPrint expresses each response change relative to the mean change of its own set, and then compares changes from the two models that were induced by the same perturbation. On LeaFBench, SetPrint consistently outperforms existing training-free black-box fingerprinting methods. Further analyses attribute these gains to both within-set relations and between-set correspondence.
papers.summary: Black-box fingerprinting of large language models tries to determine whether a target model was derived from a source model using only responses to queries. `SetPrint` is a training-free method that perturbs each query, expresses each resulting response change relative to the mean change of its own model's set, and then compares the changes that the same perturbation induced in the two models. On `LeaFBench` it **consistently outperforms existing training-free black-box fingerprinting methods**, and analyses attribute the gains to using both within-set relations and between-set correspondence.

papers.title: Agent Architecture Cost-Success Trade-offs: A Controlled Evaluation across Enterprise-Style SOPs
papers.abstract: Enterprises increasingly use large language model agents to execute standard operating procedures (SOPs): long, branching, tool-intensive workflows. Yet there is little controlled evidence for choosing among competing agentic architectures. Holding the model, tasks, and tools fixed and varying only the architecture, we compare four designs (a function-calling single agent, a skill-augmented agent, centralized multi-agent orchestration, and a triage swarm; eight arms) across 13 enterprise SOPs, and introduce a skill-definition quality rubric to build matched high and low-quality skill corpora. Three takeaways emerge. (1)~\textbf{There is no universal best architecture; the right choice is SOP-dependent.} On a given SOP, task success ranges from under $10\%$ on the hardest to near $100\%$ on the easiest; no architecture is statistically separable in aggregate, and added structure only plausibly pays off on complex, branching SOPs (a directional, not yet significant, trend). (2)~\textbf{Added architecture cost must be justified by a task-success gain.} Every coordinated arm (multi-agent or skill-augmented) spends $1.4$--$4.7\times$ the tokens and $2.6$--$5.8\times$ the latency of the single agent for gains that are usually small and rarely significant, making the single agent the efficient default; high-quality skills do lift success (to $73.1\%$ from $67.4\%$) while degraded skills fall below it. (3)~\textbf{Implementation quality outweighs the single- versus multi-agent choice.} A plausible multi-agent implementation loses to the single agent, yet a targeted redesign of it becomes the only arm to significantly beat the baseline ($75.6\%$ vs.\ $67.4\%$).
papers.summary: A controlled comparison holds the model, tasks, and tools fixed and varies only the agent architecture across 13 enterprise standard operating procedures (SOPs): a function-calling single agent, a skill-augmented agent, centralized multi-agent orchestration, and a triage swarm, in eight arms. No architecture is statistically separable in aggregate, and every coordinated arm spends **1.4-4.7x the tokens and 2.6-5.8x the latency of the single agent** for gains that are usually small and rarely significant. High-quality skill definitions lift success from 67.4% to 73.1%, while degraded skills fall below the baseline. A plausible multi-agent implementation loses to the single agent, yet a targeted redesign of it becomes the only arm to significantly beat the baseline (75.6% vs. 67.4%).

papers.title: Physics2Weight: Direct Neural Network Architecture and Weight Generation from Physical Laws Using Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled weight-space programming (WSP), which directly generates neural network weights without gradient-based optimization. However, extending WSP to physical problems remains challenging, particularly in achieving both solution accuracy and physical consistency. In this paper, we propose Physics2Weight (PtW), a framework that extends WSP to solving partial differential equations by directly generating neural network weights and editing architectures based on governing equations and initial and boundary conditions. PtW introduces physics-constrained prompting and physics-guided architecture editing, combined with iterative weight refinement from WSP, to improve solution accuracy and physical consistency without gradient-based optimization. Experiments on four PDEs, namely the heat, advection, Burgers', and Allen--Cahn equations, demonstrate lower solution errors than conventional physics-informed neural networks, while revealing limitations in satisfying the governing equations for nonlinear PDEs.
papers.summary: Weight-space programming (WSP) uses large language models to generate neural network weights directly, without gradient-based optimization, but has been hard to apply to physical problems. `Physics2Weight` extends it to partial differential equations (PDEs) by generating weights and editing architectures from the governing equations and initial and boundary conditions, using physics-constrained prompting, physics-guided architecture editing, and iterative weight refinement. On the heat, advection, Burgers', and Allen-Cahn equations it reports **lower solution errors than conventional physics-informed neural networks**, while showing limitations in satisfying the governing equations for nonlinear PDEs.

papers.title: Predictive Surprise as Self-Grounding Concept Bottleneck for Interpretable Time Series
papers.abstract: Time-series classifiers deployed in risk-sensitive domains must be (1) accurate, (2) interpretable, and (3) able to abstain when evidence is weak. Existing methods do not deliver all 3 at once, and the obstacle is structural, rather than logistical. Meaningful temporal patterns cannot be defined without knowing segment boundaries, yet meaningful boundaries cannot be placed without knowing which patterns to expect. Existing approaches break this circularity by using fixed windows or expert-annotated vocabularies, thereby sacrificing at least one of the 3 properties. We introduce ConceptTime, which closes the loop through a single self-supervised signal. A frozen probabilistic forecaster predicts a distribution over the next observation at every timestep of the sequence. We call the mismatch between its prediction and the realized signal the predictive surprise. This signal both locates segment boundaries and characterizes each resulting segment through the forecaster. Segments are thus grounded by how they behaved relative to expectation, not by what they look like. These summaries cluster into a vocabulary of dynamical regimes that we call concepts. A lightweight head classifies from the concept sequence, and the distance to the nearest concept yields reliability by design. Across 17 public benchmarks, ConceptTime is competitive with state-of-the-art black-box accuracy, beats every interpretable baseline, and retains near-98% accuracy on Epilepsy with 1% of labels. It further remains competitive with softmax, prototype-distance, and SHAP/TimeX/TimeX++ on OOD detection and deletion faithfulness, without a single annotation, language model call, or domain expert. Code is available at: https://github.com/Sachithx/ConceptTime.git.
papers.summary: Time-series classifiers in risk-sensitive settings need to be accurate, interpretable, and able to abstain, but defining meaningful patterns requires segment boundaries and vice versa. `ConceptTime` resolves this with a frozen probabilistic forecaster: the mismatch between its prediction and the observed signal, called predictive surprise, both locates segment boundaries and characterizes each segment, and the segment summaries are clustered into a vocabulary of dynamical-regime concepts. A lightweight head classifies from the concept sequence, with distance to the nearest concept serving as a reliability score. Across 17 public benchmarks it is competitive with black-box accuracy, beats every interpretable baseline, and **retains near-98% accuracy on `Epilepsy` with 1% of labels**, without annotations, language model calls, or domain experts.
papers.highlight_summary:
