Concept bottleneck models for time series face a circularity: meaningful concepts need segment boundaries, and meaningful boundaries need concepts. `ConceptTime` breaks it with one frozen probabilistic forecaster whose next-step negative log-likelihood ("predictive surprise") both places the boundaries and describes each segment by how it deviated from expectation, not by its shape.

- A 4-layer causal Transformer (`ARGDM`) is trained once by next-step Gaussian density estimation, its per-timestep surprise drives a length-constrained dynamic program that cuts each series into K patches, and each patch's predictive-statistics signature is clustered by a diagonal `GMM` into 8–32 label-free concepts read by a classifier of only ~10³–10⁴ parameters.
- Across 17 benchmarks it is the strongest interpretable method, and on `Epilepsy` with 1% of labels it reaches **97.91%** against **95.41%** for the best black-box baseline (`TSLANet`), though that low-label advantage does not carry over to `UCI-HAR` (74.60% vs 86.55% for `MiniRocket`) and at full supervision it trails black-box models by roughly 2–8 points outside `Epilepsy`.
- The mean distance from patches to their nearest concept prototype serves as a built-in fidelity score for abstention, reaching OOD-detection AUROC of **0.864 to 0.992** on Gaussian-noise-perturbed `UCI-HAR` while softmax confidence stays near chance, and giving the lowest deletion-faithfulness AUC on `Epilepsy` (0.804) but narrowly losing to `GradientSHAP` on `UCI-HAR` (0.418 vs 0.411).
- On cross-condition fault-diagnosis transfer, keeping the source concept vocabulary and training only a classifier on 5% of target labels with a target-trained density model averages **94.37%** over 12 directed pairs versus 90.76% for fine-tuned `TSLANet`, while zero-shot transfer manages only 67.61%.
- The ablations weaken the single-primitive story: the choice of boundary signal moves accuracy by at most 1.8 points and surprise is not the best signal on `UCI-HAR` or `Sleep-EDF`, a vocabulary of 128 beats the default 32 on all three ablated datasets, and the authors acknowledge that vocabulary size is fixed in advance and that each concept's meaning must be assigned by humans after training.

papers.title: ADIndex: Layer-Adaptive Sparse Attention Indexing via Group-Level Distillation
papers.abstract: DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) reduces the computational cost of attention through token-level selection. However, its indexer still scores the entire causal prefix for each query, making indexing a dominant source of latency in long-context inference. Notably, the indexer alone can account for more than 50% of total prefill GPU time at long context lengths. To address this bottleneck, we propose ADIndex, an Adaptive and Distillation-driven Indexing method for token-level sparse attention. ADIndex integrates three key components: (i) a layer-wise calibration strategy that adaptively accommodates cross-query retrieval overlap, motivated by our observation of pronounced inter-layer heterogeneity; (ii) a group-level distillation scheme that leverages this heterogeneity to efficiently train adaptive layer-wise group indexers, capturing salient retrieval signals from individual queries; and (iii) a low-latency inference strategy that reduces repeated full-prefix scans through token bank sharing within query groups while retaining query-specific refinement. Experiments on DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.1 demonstrate that ADIndex preserves near-lossless task performance on LongBench, LongBench v2, and RULER while delivering substantial efficiency gains over standard DSA, including prefill and decoding kernel speedups of up to 6.22x and 3.40x, respectively, at a context length of 256K across the layer-wise reuse configurations, as well as an end-to-end serving speedup of 1.54x at a context length of 128K.
papers.summary: `DeepSeek Sparse Attention` (DSA) cuts attention cost through token-level selection, but its indexer still scores the entire causal prefix for every query and can exceed 50% of prefill GPU time at long context lengths. `ADIndex` addresses this with layer-wise calibration that exploits differences across layers in how much queries' retrievals overlap, group-level distillation to train layer-adaptive group indexers, and token bank sharing within query groups to avoid repeated full-prefix scans. On `DeepSeek-V3.2` and `GLM-5.1` it keeps near-lossless performance on `LongBench`, `LongBench v2`, and `RULER` while reaching **prefill and decoding kernel speedups of up to 6.22x and 3.40x at 256K context**, plus a 1.54x end-to-end serving speedup at 128K.

papers.title: Embodied Science Agents: Making Embodied Experimental Design Learnable
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large models have accelerated AI for Science toward agentic science, where AI agents autonomously conduct scientific discovery. Realising this vision requires closing the loop between computational reasoning and physical experimentation, positioning self-driving laboratories (SDLs) as critical enablers. However, existing SDLs exhibit a fundamental paradox: foundation model integration has increased linguistic sophistication while severing physical grounding. By treating models as disembodied planners that output symbolic workflows for separate robotic systems, current architectures inherently block the development of embodied experimental intuition. We argue that overcoming this paradox requires embedding \emph{learnability} along three interdependent axes: cognitive learnability (learning what to investigate), experimental learnability (learning where to search), and embodied learnability (learning how to act). Building on this view, we introduce the Embodied Science Agent (ESA), which unifies digital intelligence with physical embodiment through three synergistic components: a Digital Agent that provides cognitive and experimental learnability via memory-based reasoning and Bayesian optimisation, an Embodied Agent that provides embodied learnability via generalisable instrument control, and an Embodied Unified Interface for seamless coordination. We validated ESA in autonomous wastewater treatment experiments, navigating over 200 million possible conditions. Through 15 continuous rounds, ESA raised the final solution transmittance from 82\% to 99.7\%, corresponding to a 98.5\% reduction in residual dye concentration and near-complete decolourisation, while its learned visuomotor policies generalised across varying instrument placements, a promising step toward next-generation SDLs for autonomous scientific discovery.
papers.summary: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) increasingly use foundation models as disembodied planners that emit symbolic workflows for separate robots, which the authors argue blocks learning of physical experimental skill. The `Embodied Science Agent` (`ESA`) combines a Digital Agent using memory-based reasoning and Bayesian optimisation, an Embodied Agent for generalisable instrument control, and a unified interface coordinating the two. In autonomous wastewater treatment experiments spanning over 200 million possible conditions, 15 continuous rounds **raised final solution transmittance from 82% to 99.7%**, a 98.5% reduction in residual dye concentration, and the learned visuomotor policies generalised across different instrument placements.

papers.title: Monitoring One Channel Is Not Communication Control: Causal Evidence for Adaptive Reallocation of Joint Message--Route Codes
papers.abstract: Monitoring a visible channel can change how learned agents communicate without removing why communication is useful. We test this distinction in an end-to-end game where a sender and receiver learn a discrete protocol and route policy without communication supervision. In two independent 20-seed batches, 20/20 and 19/20 protocols form. Online partial coverage increases shadow-route share over no monitoring by .701 [.574,.826] and .575 [.412,.737], while task accuracy remains .905/.913 and signed frozen message contribution remains .592/.563. Complete coverage removes most selective migration without removing communication. Frozen interventions, including a fresh pre-outcome confirmation, show that route is semantic: joint message--route shuffling changes .668 of receiver predictions and route alone retains .388 accuracy versus .25 chance. A corrected explicit-silence cost makes 18/20 policies fully silent and lowers mean sending to .050, but its strict complete-suppression gate fails because two seeds retain communication. Failed semantic-evasion and operational gates further bound the result. The evidence supports adaptive reallocation of a joint message--route code under partial monitoring, not open-world route discovery, emergent encryption, or a universal defense.
papers.summary: The study tests whether monitoring a visible channel actually controls communication between learned agents, using a game where a sender and receiver learn a discrete protocol and a routing policy without communication supervision. In two independent 20-seed batches, partial monitoring **raised the share of traffic on the unmonitored shadow route by .701 and .575** over no monitoring, while task accuracy stayed near .91 and the messages' contribution was preserved. Interventions show the route itself carries meaning: route alone retains .388 accuracy against .25 chance. An explicit cost on sending silenced 18 of 20 policies but failed the strict complete-suppression test, and the authors limit the claim to adaptive reallocation of a joint message-route code, not emergent encryption, open-world route discovery, or a universal defense.

papers.title: IIT Patna at "ICPR 2026 TVRID Competition on Privacy-Preserving Person Re-Identification from Top-View RGB-Depth Camera"
papers.abstract: Privacy-aware person re-identification (Re-ID) from top-view cameras replaces frontal appearance with anthropometric shape, while depth sensing further reduces color-based identity cues. The ICPR 2026 TVRID competition evaluates this setting using 86 identities captured by four synchronized Intel RealSense D455 cameras with RGB and Depth streams across flat, ascent, descent, and oblique viewpoints. Performance is measured using mAP and CMC@1 across within-camera in/out, ascent-descent, and flat-oblique scenarios. The competition had 147 registered participants and 33 final submissions. Three teams from IIT Patna participated: 'abhinavkumar03' and 'sjkdgfhl_' ranked 5th and 7th among 31 ranked participants, and 'vivek katuri' reached 77.67% CMC@1 / 85.20% mAP on the RGB track. This paper presents the methods of the two top-10 teams. Methodology 1 (abhinavkumar03) achieves 93.51% mAP and 90.42% CMC@1 on Depth, ranking 4th of 28, while Methodology 2 (sjkdgfhl_) reaches 99.63%/99.35% on RGB and 86.26%/80.34% on Depth. Both substantially outperform the 57.19% track-average Depth mAP, with Methodology 1 yielding a 7.3-point gain over Methodology 2. These results demonstrate the importance of depth representation and supervision for privacy-preserving Re-ID.
papers.summary: A competition report describes two entries from IIT Patna teams to the `ICPR 2026 TVRID` challenge on privacy-preserving person re-identification (Re-ID) from top-view RGB and depth cameras, a setting with 86 identities captured by four synchronized `Intel RealSense D455` cameras across flat, ascent, descent, and oblique viewpoints. The first method achieves **93.51% mAP and 90.42% CMC@1 on the Depth track**, ranking 4th of 28, while the second reaches 99.63% mAP on RGB and 86.26% on Depth. Both clearly exceed the 57.19% track-average Depth mAP, which the authors attribute to depth representation and supervision choices.

papers.title: RBLA+: Efficient Rank-Specific LoRA Adapter Extraction for Federated Fine-Tuning with Heterogeneous Clients
papers.abstract: Federated fine-tuning with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) reduces communication and computational overhead by training and exchanging compact trainable LoRA factors. Clients may use different LoRA ranks to meet adapter communication budgets and accommodate different local adaptation needs. The server must process these differences during aggregation and construct adapters at each client's rank for local training. We distinguish pre-aggregation alignment, which handles factor dimensions and scaling conventions before aggregation and rank-specific LoRA adapter extraction, which constructs client-sized pairs from the aggregated global model. Two common approaches to rank-specific extraction are direct rank truncation and Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) of the dense update. Direct prefix truncation keeps the leading columns of one aggregated factor and the corresponding rows of the other. It is cheap but can increase reconstruction error. The dense SVD approach first forms the product of aggregated LoRA factors. It then decomposes this matrix and retains the leading singular components to construct adapters at the target rank. This gives the optimal rank-constrained approximation in Frobenius norm but incurs significant computational overhead. To address this trade-off, we propose RBLA+ as an extension of RBLA. It uses established compact QR/core-SVD decomposition to minimize Frobenius error for the extracted LoRA update without forming the dense update. It also accounts for client and server scaling conventions during upload and broadcast. Across vision and language tasks, RBLA+ improves accuracy over RBLA in multiple heterogeneous settings. In CPU benchmarks with synthetic adapters, RBLA+ has lower extraction time than the dense partial-SVD baseline. RBLA+ preserves each client's prescribed adapter size and per-round communication payload.
papers.summary: In federated fine-tuning with low-rank adaptation (LoRA), clients may use different adapter ranks, so the server must extract an adapter at each client's rank from the aggregated model. Simple truncation is cheap but raises reconstruction error, while singular value decomposition (SVD) of the dense update is optimal in Frobenius norm but expensive. `RBLA+`, an extension of `RBLA`, uses a compact QR/core-SVD decomposition to **minimize Frobenius error without forming the dense update**, and also accounts for client and server scaling conventions. It improves accuracy over `RBLA` in multiple heterogeneous settings on vision and language tasks and extracts faster than the dense partial-SVD baseline in CPU benchmarks with synthetic adapters.

papers.title: Exploration via Exploitation: The Blessing of Reward Diversity in Personalized Federated RL
papers.abstract: While federated reinforcement learning (RL) has traditionally guaranteed high efficiency in homogeneous environments, collaboration is often hindered when agents possess distinct goals. In this paper, we flip this paradigm, framing reward heterogeneity not as a hurdle to consensus, but as a structural asset that catalyzes exploration. We first propose Personalized Federated Upper Confidence Bound Value Iteration (PF-UCBVI), which achieves optimal linear speedup by decoupling shared dynamics from personalized objectives. To eliminate the risks of explicit exploration, we then introduce Personalized Federated Exploration-Free Value Iteration (PF-EFVI), a purely greedy algorithm that leverages reward diversity to ensure state-action coverage. We prove that PF-EFVI attains logarithmic regret without explicit exploration bonuses under sufficient reward diversity. Our results reveal that agent disagreement shifts the exploration burden from temporal complexity to spatial diversity, enabling efficient collective learning without explicit exploration.
papers.summary: Federated reinforcement learning usually treats agents with different reward functions as an obstacle to collaboration; this theoretical work treats that heterogeneity as a source of exploration instead. `PF-UCBVI` (Personalized Federated Upper Confidence Bound Value Iteration) achieves optimal linear speedup by separating shared dynamics from personalized objectives. A second, purely greedy algorithm, `PF-EFVI` (Personalized Federated Exploration-Free Value Iteration), relies on reward diversity to cover the state-action space and is proven to **attain logarithmic regret without explicit exploration bonuses** when rewards are sufficiently diverse.

papers.title: BuySideFlow: A Point-in-Time Benchmark for LLM Agents in Investment Research
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate SQL and SQL--Python workflows for investment research, but ensuring point-in-time (PIT) validity remains challenging. Agents must enforce disclosure cutoffs and select the appropriate historical states and record versions throughout data retrieval and financial analysis. We introduce \textsc{BuySideFlow}, a benchmark of 408 practitioner-derived Chinese-language tasks spanning equities, funds, fixed income, and macroeconomics over a fixed snapshot from a licensed production financial database. We provide executable references and a taxonomy of temporal errors, pairing result checks with expert audits of executed workflows. We evaluate nine agent configurations on all tasks, with result accuracy ranging from 16.2\% to 36.8\%. An audit of 900 runs on 100 shared tasks confirms PIT violations in 193 of the 380 runs that pass result checks (50.8\%), showing that output agreement alone does not establish temporal validity.
papers.summary: LLM agents that write SQL and Python workflows for investment research must respect point-in-time (PIT) validity, meaning they may only use data and record versions that were actually disclosed as of the analysis date. `BuySideFlow` is a benchmark of 408 practitioner-derived Chinese-language tasks across equities, funds, fixed income, and macroeconomics, built on a fixed snapshot of a licensed production financial database, with executable references, a taxonomy of temporal errors, and expert audits of executed workflows. Across nine agent configurations, result accuracy ranges from 16.2% to 36.8%, and an audit of 900 runs found PIT violations in **193 of the 380 runs that passed result checks (50.8%)**, so matching the expected output does not establish temporal validity.

papers.title: TrustMod-SM: A Multi-Axis Benchmark for Evaluating Trustworthiness of LLMs in Social Media Content Moderation
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) show strong potential for social media content moderation, but their trustworthiness beyond overall accuracy remains underexplored. We introduce TrustMod-SM, a benchmark of roughly 29,000 instances across eight datasets, to evaluate LLM moderators on five dimensions: trustfulness, fairness, safety, robustness, and context integrity. Evaluating 16 open-weight models (0.5B-284B parameters, spanning text-only and vision-language architectures) and one closed frontier model, we find persistent trustworthiness gaps. Higher detection accuracy often coincides with greater demographic disparity, and models frequently comply with concealment or exaggeration prompts, assign high confidence to wrong predictions, rarely escalate ambiguous cases, and struggle to separate hate speech from counter-speech or reclaimed language (especially below 8B parameters). Scaling does not uniformly resolve these issues, and no single model excels across all five dimensions.
papers.summary: Large language models used as social media content moderators are usually judged on overall accuracy, leaving other aspects of trustworthiness unmeasured. `TrustMod-SM` is a benchmark of roughly 29,000 instances from eight datasets that scores moderators on five dimensions: trustfulness, fairness, safety, robustness, and context integrity. Testing 16 open-weight models from 0.5B to 284B parameters plus one closed frontier model shows that higher detection accuracy often coincides with greater demographic disparity, and that models comply with concealment or exaggeration prompts, are confidently wrong, rarely escalate ambiguous cases, and confuse hate speech with counter-speech or reclaimed language, especially below 8B parameters. Scaling does not uniformly fix these issues, and **no single model excels across all five dimensions**.

papers.title: StatPrompt-LLM: A Lightweight Statistical Refinement for Foundation-Style Time-Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Time-series forecasting has recently seen a paradigm shift with the introduction of foundation-style models that adapt large pretrained language architectures to sequential data. However, effectively exposing fundamental temporal structures, such as trend, scale, and temporal dependence, to these models remains an open challenge, particularly when the available observations are limited. In this paper, we conduct an exploratory empirical study across different generations of forecasting architectures and propose StatPrompt-LLM, a lightweight statistical refinement of Time-LLM. StatPrompt-LLM augments the existing Time-LLM prompting mechanism with dataset-level statistical information and introduces a zero-initialised autoregressive bypass as a complementary linear forecasting pathway. We evaluate our framework on electricity and meteorological time-series benchmarks, including ETTh1, ETTh2, and Weather, under full-prefix and reduced-prefix configurations. Under the 10% reduced-prefix configuration, StatPrompt-LLM achieved lower in-sample prediction errors than Time-LLM, with unweighted average relative reductions across datasets of 40.2% in MSE and 21.4% in MAE. Full-prefix results were more dataset-dependent. Ablation analyses revealed relatively modest and dataset-dependent changes when selected additional statistical descriptor groups were masked within the combined architecture. Computational profiling indicated additional model parameters and runtime overhead relative to Time-LLM.
papers.summary: Forecasting models that adapt pretrained language architectures to time series struggle to pick up basic temporal structure such as trend, scale, and temporal dependence when few observations are available. `StatPrompt-LLM` extends the prompting mechanism of `Time-LLM` with dataset-level statistical information and adds a zero-initialised autoregressive bypass that acts as a complementary linear forecasting pathway. On `ETTh1`, `ETTh2`, and `Weather` with only a 10% prefix of the data, it lowered in-sample error relative to `Time-LLM` by an average of **40.2% in mean squared error** and 21.4% in mean absolute error. Full-prefix results were more dataset-dependent, ablations of the statistical descriptors showed only modest changes, and the method adds parameters and runtime overhead.

papers.title: Attribute-Evidence Learning with Multimodal Prompt for Generalized Category Discovery
papers.abstract: Generalized category discovery (GCD) aims to discover novel categories from unlabeled data by leveraging limited labeled samples from old classes. Existing methods that rely solely on visual cues often neglect the multimodal nature of human perception, prompting recent approaches to incorporate textual information such as category tags and attributes. However, these approaches typically entangle global tags and local attributes within a shared global image representation, rendering attributes unreliable and potentially providing misleading cues that can drive the model toward incorrect predictions. To this end, we propose AptM-GCD, a novel multimodal framework that exploits apt textual guidance through attribute evidence learning and multimodal prompt reasoning. Specifically, we design an Attribute-Evidence Learning (AEL) mechanism that treats attributes as localized visual evidence rather than global category descriptors. By interacting attribute embeddings with patch-level visual tokens, AEL identifies reliable attribute-related regions and extracts discriminative local evidence, thereby reducing the impact of noisy or irrelevant attribute cues. Building upon the extracted evidence, we further develop a Multimodal Prompt Learning (MPL) mechanism to bridge local attribute semantics and global visual understanding. MPL converts fine-grained textual evidence into visual prompts and injects them into a multimodal prompt transformer, enabling attribute information to enhance category discrimination through contextual reasoning without enforcing direct global alignment between modalities. Extensive experiments on six datasets demonstrate that AptM-GCD consistently achieves SoTA performance across both fine-grained and generic benchmarks. Moreover, the proposed framework exhibits strong generalization ability, delivering consistent gains under unimodal and class-imbalanced GCD settings.
papers.summary: Generalized category discovery (GCD) asks a model to find novel categories in unlabeled data using a small set of labeled samples from known classes, and recent multimodal approaches add textual tags and attributes but entangle them in a single global image representation, which makes attribute cues unreliable. `AptM-GCD` introduces Attribute-Evidence Learning, which matches attribute embeddings against patch-level visual tokens to extract localized evidence, and Multimodal Prompt Learning, which converts that evidence into visual prompts fed into a multimodal prompt transformer instead of forcing global alignment between modalities. The authors report **state-of-the-art results on six datasets** covering fine-grained and generic benchmarks, with gains that carry over to unimodal and class-imbalanced settings.

papers.title: Partition, Refine, and Detect: Preserving Novel Category Capacity in Open-Vocabulary Object Detection
papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary object detection (OVD) expects the model trained on base classes to recognize both base and novel classes at inference. Typical methods rely on CLIP-style vision-language embeddings, yet the learned space is often biased toward base categories, with limited effective capacity preserved for novel concepts. Such a base-dominated representation can compress novel semantics, leading to semantic collapse and mis-calibrated confidence at inference. To address this issue, we present PR-OVD, a partition-and-refine framework that explicitly reserves capacity for novel categories and strengthens category separation, while being seamlessly integrated into different detector architectures. Specifically, PR-OVD first performs coarse partitioning to build global divisions for base, novel, and an explicit background partition in both visual and textual modalities, preventing object-irrelevant embeddings from leaking into category-specific representations. It then applies category-level refinement within each partition to sharpen decision boundaries and alleviate the lack of fine-grained region-level pretraining in CLIP. To further provide reliable visual anchors for novel categories, we design a cognitively inspired Structure Prompt (SP) that encodes both egocentric attributes and allocentric context, facilitating stable partition-and-refine learning. Extensive experiments on two OVD benchmarks show that PR-OVD delivers an average 6.5\% proportional improvement on novel categories over the state-of-the-art methods. Notably, PR-OVD also benefits other open-vocabulary tasks, including segmentation and classification, further confirming its effectiveness and generality.
papers.summary: Open-vocabulary object detection (OVD) trains on base classes but must recognize novel ones at inference, and embedding spaces in the style of `CLIP` tend to be dominated by base categories, which compresses novel semantics and miscalibrates confidence. `PR-OVD` first partitions the visual and textual embedding spaces into base, novel, and explicit background regions, then refines category boundaries within each partition, and adds a Structure Prompt that encodes an object's own attributes together with its surrounding context to anchor novel categories. On two OVD benchmarks it yields an average **6.5% proportional improvement on novel categories** over prior state-of-the-art methods, and the approach plugs into different detector architectures and also helps open-vocabulary segmentation and classification.

papers.title: Trajectory-Regularized Distribution Distillation for One-Step Generation
papers.abstract: Distilling flow matching models for one-step generation generally follows two paradigms. Trajectory alignment supervises the student with the teacher's probability flow ODE, but its performance degrades under very small sampling budgets. Distribution matching directly optimizes the generated distribution, but estimating its reverse Kullback-Leibler gradient typically requires a separate network to track the evolving student score. We propose trajectory-regularized distribution distillation (TRD), which combines distribution-level and trajectory-level supervision through a momentum-mixture policy predicted in a single student forward pass. This policy serves simultaneously as a one-step generator, an estimator of the student's marginal velocity that removes the need for a second trainable network in distribution matching, and a closed-form time-dependent velocity field supervised along the teacher ODE trajectory. Experiments on SANA-1.6B and Stable Diffusion 3.5 show that TRD outperforms representative consistency and distribution matching baselines in generation quality and training efficiency for both one-step and few-step generation, with a trade-off in sample diversity.
papers.summary: Distilling flow matching models into one-step generators is usually done either by trajectory alignment, which degrades at very small sampling budgets, or by distribution matching, which typically needs a second network to track the student's evolving score. Trajectory-regularized distribution distillation (`TRD`) combines both forms of supervision through a momentum-mixture policy predicted in a single student forward pass, which serves at once as the one-step generator, as an estimator of the student's marginal velocity, and as a closed-form velocity field supervised along the teacher's trajectory. On `SANA-1.6B` and `Stable Diffusion 3.5`, it **outperforms representative consistency and distribution matching baselines in quality and training efficiency** for one-step and few-step generation, at some cost in sample diversity.

papers.title: MADSNet: A Multi-Scale Axial-Attentive Dense Spiking Network for Spike Camera Image Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Spike cameras encode dynamic scenes into high-temporal-resolution binary spike streams for efficient high-speed vision. Although spiking neural networks (SNNs) can process such signals with sparse and accumulate-only computation, existing SNN-based reconstruction methods are typically shallow and still lag behind ANN-based models in reconstruction fidelity. This paper proposes MADSNet, a Multi-scale Axial-attentive Dense Spiking Network for spike camera image reconstruction. MADSNet adopts a hierarchical spiking encoder--decoder, where a multi-scale spike stem extracts early features, axial spike attention captures long-range dependencies, a dense spiking bottleneck enhances feature reuse, and a spike-to-continuous decoder reconstructs continuous intensity images from spike-domain representations. Experiments on gray-scale and color spike reconstruction show that MADSNet outperforms SSIR by 4.3 dB PSNR and Spk2ImgNet by 1.94 dB on SREDS. Compared with Spk2ImgNet, it achieves about 15$\times$ lower latency and uses only about 1/40 of the estimated energy, demonstrating that carefully designed SNN architectures can improve reconstruction quality while preserving computational efficiency.
papers.summary: Spike cameras record fast scenes as high-temporal-resolution binary spike streams, and spiking neural networks (SNNs) that reconstruct images from them have been shallow and less accurate than conventional artificial neural networks. `MADSNet` is a hierarchical spiking encoder-decoder combining a multi-scale spike stem, axial spike attention for long-range dependencies, a dense spiking bottleneck for feature reuse, and a decoder that converts spike-domain features into continuous intensity images. On the `SREDS` dataset it beats `SSIR` by 4.3 dB PSNR and `Spk2ImgNet` by 1.94 dB, while running at **about 15x lower latency and roughly 1/40 of the estimated energy** of `Spk2ImgNet`.

papers.title: ICLayout-Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Custom Circuit Layout Design
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are being explored for circuit design, but their ability to produce high-quality custom layouts has not been extensively evaluated. ICLayout-Bench is a benchmark in which agents use electronic design automation (EDA) tools to construct and optimize GDSII layouts from transistor-level circuit netlists. These layouts are evaluated using physical verification, parasitic extraction, and post-layout simulation. Layouts that pass the physical and functional checks are scored on electrical performance and area. The benchmark includes 165 tasks across 13 process design kits (PDKs), covering technology nodes from 3 nm to 180 nm. The tasks span analog, mixed-signal, and digital circuits in open-source and commercial EDA flows. The experiments evaluate 22 configurations spanning seven models on 21 public and 19 private tasks. Mean layout scores range from 4.22 to 80.26 on public tasks and from 1.43 to 67.01 on private tasks, on a 100-point scale. Higher reasoning effort does not consistently improve mean scores, and configurations with comparable scores can incur substantially different model costs.
papers.summary: Whether LLM agents can produce high-quality custom integrated circuit layouts has not been systematically tested. `ICLayout-Bench` has agents drive electronic design automation (EDA) tools to build and optimize GDSII layouts from transistor-level netlists, then scores layouts that pass physical verification, parasitic extraction, and post-layout simulation on electrical performance and area; it contains 165 tasks across 13 process design kits (PDKs) from 3 nm to 180 nm, spanning analog, mixed-signal, and digital circuits. Across 22 configurations of seven models, mean layout scores on a 100-point scale range **from 4.22 to 80.26 on public tasks** and from 1.43 to 67.01 on private tasks. Higher reasoning effort does not consistently raise scores, and configurations with similar scores can differ substantially in model cost.

papers.title: Third Eye: Beyond Immediate Gains in Recursive Self-Improvement
papers.abstract: Does a useful self-update remain useful after the model updates again? Third Eye separates immediate performance from the outcome of a further native update. We evaluate five 3-8B backbones on math and code: 64 fresh runs, three candidates per run, and three continuations per candidate. Selection and final scoring use disjoint items. In the balanced Qwen3-4B/Llama-3.2-3B comparison, immediate-selected utility is near zero, but continuation reduces it by 1.78 percentage points (simultaneous 95% interval [0.68, 2.88]). Candidate-averaged immediate utility is already negative: selection partly accounts for the apparently neutral first step. Continuation also lowers utility for SmolLM3-3B and Llama-3.1-8B; Qwen3-8B remains inconclusive. Target and out-of-distribution losses dominate retention changes. Matched recipe and recipient-donor controls identify neither a reliable mitigation nor a single mechanism. The results support evaluating persistent self-updates as adaptation transitions, with independent scoring and a no-update baseline, rather than interpreting immediate performance as their full value.
papers.summary: A model self-update that looks useful immediately may stop being useful once the model updates itself again, and `Third Eye` is an evaluation protocol that separates immediate performance from the outcome after a further update, using disjoint items for selection and final scoring. The study covers five 3-8B backbones on math and code, with 64 fresh runs, three candidates per run, and three continuations per candidate. In the balanced `Qwen3-4B`/`Llama-3.2-3B` comparison, immediately selected utility is near zero but **a further update lowers it by 1.78 percentage points**, with similar declines for `SmolLM3-3B` and `Llama-3.1-8B` and an inconclusive result for `Qwen3-8B`. Controls identified neither a reliable mitigation nor a single mechanism, and the authors argue that persistent self-updates should be evaluated with independent scoring and a no-update baseline.

papers.title: Multimodal Graph Learning: A Survey of Models, Benchmarks, and Frontiers
papers.abstract: Multimodal attributed graphs (MAGs), in which nodes carry text, images, and other modalities while edges encode relations among entities, underlie e-commerce, social media, content platforms, and creative applications. Learning on MAGs has developed along two complementary lines: graph-centric methods redesign how modalities are fused, propagated, and connected within message passing, while foundation-model-centric methods pretrain transferable multimodal graph encoders or bring graph context into multimodal large language models for prediction and generation. In parallel, several benchmarks have appeared with different datasets and evaluation protocols. This survey takes an algorithm-centric and evaluation-grounded view of the field and makes three contributions. Modeling: we introduce a unified message-passing formulation and organize methods into five integration levels (feature, propagation, topology, learning, and foundation model), covering discriminative and graph-conditioned generative models; within this formulation we derive representative methods as special cases, compare their assumptions, expressiveness, and cost, and identify cross-modal sensitivity as a property that separates otherwise similar architectures. Datasets and evaluation: we review recent benchmarks, summarize their datasets and metrics, define model-independent descriptors (label homophily, average degree, clustering, and edge provenance), and map each evaluation protocol to the baselines it uses. Frontiers: we connect multimodal graph learning to AI agents, covering the multimodal graphs that agents perceive and remember and graph engineering, the practice of organizing agent workflows as explicit graphs; we then discuss open problems, concrete efforts for the community, and research directions, including when graph structure helps in the presence of strong multimodal foundation models.
papers.summary: Multimodal attributed graphs (MAGs), where nodes carry text, images, and other modalities and edges encode relations, underlie e-commerce, social media, and content platforms, and methods for learning on them have split into graph-centric and foundation-model-centric lines with inconsistent benchmarks. This survey introduces a unified message-passing formulation that **organizes methods into five integration levels: feature, propagation, topology, learning, and foundation model**, deriving representative methods as special cases and comparing their assumptions, expressiveness, and cost. It also reviews recent benchmarks using model-independent dataset descriptors such as label homophily and average degree, and maps each evaluation protocol to its baselines. A frontiers section connects the field to AI agents, including the graphs agents perceive and remember and the practice of organizing agent workflows as explicit graphs.

papers.title: Specializing Meta Multi-Objectivization as Baseline for Software Engineering Optimization
papers.abstract: Given the discrete nature of many software engineering (SE) optimization problems, trapping at local optima remains a crucial issue in the optimizer designs. Meta Multi-Objectivization (MMO) is an optimization model for overcoming local optima by introducing an extra, auxiliary objective. Yet, MMO is originally designed only for configuration tuning, leaving its suitability for other SE problems in doubt, particularly regarding the choice of the auxiliary objective. In this paper, we study the possibility and resolution for specializing MMO as a general baseline across a range of SE optimization problems, making it a fundamental counterpart for future SE optimizers that seek to mitigate the issue of local optima. We do so by providing both theoretical remit and empirical evidence: we analytically show how the choice of the auxiliary objective is crucial while demonstrating the effectiveness of MMO under nine SE optimization problems comprising 212 cases when the right one can be chosen, i.e., MMO is able to outperform the other state-of-the-art and general-purpose optimizers in 79% and 94% of the cases, respectively. Drawing on the theoretical understanding and empirical findings, we then propose L2RAC, a tool that automatically recommends the best auxiliary objective choice for a given SE problem/case, hence helping to specialize MMO therein. Through extensive experiments, we reveal that, in general, L2RAC can more accurately rank the choice of auxiliary objective for MMO under a case than other guesses by up to 60%, saving as much as 99% of the cost that would otherwise be required to conduct trial-and-error when using MMO.
papers.summary: Many software engineering optimization problems are discrete and prone to trapping optimizers in local optima, and Meta Multi-Objectivization (`MMO`), which escapes them by adding an auxiliary objective, was originally designed only for configuration tuning. The authors analyze theoretically why the choice of auxiliary objective is crucial and test `MMO` on nine software engineering optimization problems comprising 212 cases, where with the right auxiliary objective it **outperforms state-of-the-art optimizers in 79% of cases** and general-purpose optimizers in 94%. They then propose `L2RAC`, a tool that recommends the auxiliary objective for a given problem, ranking choices up to 60% more accurately than other guesses and saving as much as 99% of the trial-and-error cost.

papers.title: ZeroPoint: Lightweight Energy-Based Decision Model
papers.abstract: Energy-based models (EBMs) assign a scalar energy to every joint value of the observed and predicted variables. In decision models, the prediction is chosen from a finite list of options provided with each input. Inference then reduces to comparing the energies of the options, and training lowers the energy of the correct option relative to the others. A complete decision must also account for the possibility that no option is acceptable. However, the energies learned by a standard EBM define only relative compatibility: adding the same input-dependent quantity to all energies leaves the predictions, the Gibbs distribution, and the usual training losses unchanged. The model therefore has no learned reference level against which to decide whether any option fits. We propose ZeroPoint, an EBM that makes the empty answer a state of the model with energy zero for every input. This fixed state provides an explicit reference for the energies of all listed options, whose non-negative depths measure their compatibility with the input relative to the empty answer. The options and the empty answer share one distribution, in which an option at zero depth receives no probability. The decision to select an option or to abstain is thus part of ordinary inference, trained with the negative log-likelihood loss, rather than a separate rejection rule. The energy function is a small multilingual encoder that reads the input together with all the options and is invariant to their order. Ablations show that most of the benefit comes from training with examples in which no option fits. With the same encoder and data, the fixed zero separates inputs with and without an acceptable option slightly better than a learned rejection class and clearly better than a thresholded softmax, while leaving the choice among options unchanged.
papers.summary: Energy-based models (EBMs) that choose among a finite list of options learn only relative energies, so they have no built-in reference level for deciding that none of the options is acceptable. `ZeroPoint` makes the empty answer an explicit state with energy fixed at zero for every input, so each option's non-negative depth measures its fit relative to abstaining, and selection and abstention share one distribution trained with ordinary negative log-likelihood. The energy function is a small multilingual encoder that reads the input with all options and is invariant to their order. Ablations show that **most of the benefit comes from training with examples in which no option fits**, while the fixed zero separates answerable from unanswerable inputs slightly better than a learned rejection class and clearly better than a thresholded softmax.

papers.title: Capacity Allocation at the Source: Sparse Target Optimization for LLM Knowledge Editing
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing has emerged as a promising approach for efficiently updating embedded knowledge in large language models (LLMs). It first computes an ideal target hidden state that steers the LLM toward the new output, and then edits the model parameters so that the original hidden state is mapped to this target. While most existing methods focus on the second stage of parameter editing in preserving other knowledge, we find that the upstream construction of the target hidden state also plays an important role in allocating the model's limited capacity space. We first establish a theoretical connection between interference in the parameter space and interference between target hidden states, showing that the two are positively correlated. Building on this insight, we propose a simple yet effective $\ell_1$ regularization method that prunes away unnecessary ``tentacles'' of each knowledge vector, retaining only the essential components. With fewer extraneous tentacles, each edit affects less other knowledge, enabling better coexistence. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs and benchmark datasets verify the effectiveness of our method. Code: https://github.com/wintersdragon-c/STO.
papers.summary: Knowledge editing in large language models first computes a target hidden state that steers the model toward a new output and then edits parameters to map the original hidden state to that target, and most work focuses on the second step. The authors show theoretically that interference between edits in parameter space is positively correlated with interference between the target hidden states themselves. They propose Sparse Target Optimization (`STO`), an L1 regularization on the target that prunes non-essential components of each knowledge vector, so that **each edit disturbs less unrelated knowledge and more edits can coexist**. Experiments across multiple models and benchmark datasets support the method's effectiveness.

papers.title: TIB: Sample-wise Tempered Information Bottleneck for Multimodal Attribution beyond Alignment Assumption
papers.abstract: Multimodal (e.g. vision-language, in this work) attribution aims to interpret the models without access to ground-truth explanatory supervision. Existing multimodal attribution methods typically rely on paired modalities as proxy supervision, implicitly assuming that image-text pairs are semantically aligned. Information bottleneck (IB)-based attribution methods follow this general paradigm and instantiate it through a global sufficiency-compression objective. In realistic multimodal datasets, however, this assumption is frequently violated due to partial semantic misalignment and unreliable cross-modal correspondences. Through theoretical analysis, we show that, under such misalignment, information-bottleneck-based attribution objectives exhibit a structural limitation: by assuming equal reliability across all proxy supervision signals, they induce posterior over-contraction and forced explanations. To address this issue, we propose TIB, a sample-wise Tempered Information Bottleneck framework that adaptively modulates attribution strength according to cross-modal reliability, without assuming semantic alignment. Extensive experiments on controlled benchmarks and large-scale datasets show the effectiveness of the proposed approach, while also validating the identified failure mode.
papers.summary: Attribution methods for vision-language models typically use paired image-text data as proxy supervision and assume the pairs are semantically aligned, which often fails in real datasets. The authors show theoretically that information bottleneck attribution objectives, by treating all proxy signals as equally reliable, **produce posterior over-contraction and forced explanations under misalignment**. Their sample-wise Tempered Information Bottleneck (`TIB`) adaptively modulates attribution strength according to the estimated cross-modal reliability of each sample, without assuming alignment. Experiments on controlled benchmarks and large-scale datasets support the approach and confirm the identified failure mode.

papers.title: Linear Probes to Bayesian Manifolds: Geometry of Arithmetic in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Linear probes are a standard method to study geometric structures, such as helices and circles, from the activations of large language models (LLMs), and such structure is often taken as evidence that the model computes with it. Probe accuracy alone cannot establish this, because it conflates four separate claims. These are (1) that the concept is decodable from the activations, (2) that they form a specific shape, (3) that the shape belongs to the probed concept rather than to a related concept the model also represents, and (4) that the output of the model depends on the shape. We call these claims decodability, shape, ownership, and causal use, and we test them separately with a four-stage Bayesian pipeline. Stage 2 compares candidate shapes and selects the best one only when its evidence passes a predefined threshold. Stage 3 removes a set of related concepts, specified in advance, and tests whether the shape is owned or inherited. Stage 4 intervenes on the shape to test whether the output of the model depends on it. We apply the pipeline to two-digit addition and multiplication in GPT-J 6B, Llama 3.1 8B, and Pythia 6.9B. Nearly every concept is decodable, but the decoded directions overlap substantially across concepts. Every strongly supported comparison selects a ribbon, which is a helix whose radius changes with the value, or a torus. Of 1,330 cells with an ownership verdict, 19% of shapes are owned and 81% are inherited. Owned and inherited shapes move the output about equally often. Intervening on the shape retains approximately 61% of the effect of intervening on the full probe while using at most five dimensions, against a median of nine for the probe. Our results indicate that a probe verdict alone overstates what a model computes with, and we propose that probe results be reported as verdicts on all four claims rather than as a single accuracy.
papers.summary: Linear probes that find geometric structures such as helices in language model activations are often taken as evidence that the model computes with those structures, but probe accuracy conflates four distinct claims: decodability, shape, ownership by the probed concept, and causal use. A four-stage Bayesian pipeline tests each claim separately and is applied to two-digit addition and multiplication in `GPT-J 6B`, `Llama 3.1 8B`, and `Pythia 6.9B`. Nearly every concept is decodable, and the well-supported shapes are ribbons (helices whose radius varies with the value) or tori, but of 1,330 cells with an ownership verdict **only 19% of shapes are owned by the probed concept while 81% are inherited** from related concepts. Intervening on the shape retains about 61% of the effect of intervening on the full probe while using at most five dimensions, and the authors propose reporting probe results as verdicts on all four claims.

papers.title: PhysMoE: Fast Spatial Grounding with Single-Token Coordinate Representation in Modality-Decoupled VLMs
papers.abstract: Embodied Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are backbones for robotic planning and manipulation. However, for coordinate prediction in grounding tasks, existing architectures suffer from two distinct bottlenecks: discrete tokenization disrupts spatial continuity with high decoding latency, while standard point regression fails on multi-contact affordances and irregularly shaped targets. To resolve these challenges, we propose PhysMoE, introducing three core contributions: (1) sharing lower layers for multimodal context while routing upper layers to specialized spatial (pixel) and linguistic (text) experts by physical modality, eliminating gradient interference; (2) encoding each coordinate as a single token by reusing the visual encoder's learned positional embeddings, injecting 2D spatial priors to natively align coordinates with visual features and ease training; and (3) differentiable Signed Distance Field (SDF) supervision on pointing, accommodating affordances and irregular geometries without costly mask decoders. Compared to the base model, PhysMoE achieves a 15.7% average gain and an 8.31x throughput speedup across 9 coordinate-based grounding benchmarks (trajectory, affordance, and localization), while preserving multimodal understanding and reasoning across 11 text-based embodied benchmarks.
papers.summary: Embodied vision-language models used for robotic planning predict coordinates either as discrete tokens, which breaks spatial continuity and is slow to decode, or by point regression, which fails on multi-contact affordances and irregular shapes. `PhysMoE` shares lower layers for multimodal context and routes upper layers to separate spatial and linguistic experts, encodes each coordinate as a single token by reusing the visual encoder's positional embeddings, and supervises pointing with a differentiable Signed Distance Field (SDF) loss instead of a mask decoder. Compared with its base model it achieves a **15.7% average gain and an 8.31x throughput speedup** across 9 coordinate-based grounding benchmarks, while preserving performance on 11 text-based embodied benchmarks.

papers.title: One Table, Many Queries: Benchmarking Generalist Tabular Models Across Generation, Imputation, and Prediction
papers.abstract: Generation, imputation, and prediction query different aspects of the same tabular distribution, but are usually evaluated separately. This leaves unclear which capabilities they share, how their training objectives interact, and whether one model can perform all three well. We introduce the One Table Benchmark (\ours{}), spanning 56 datasets, 46 registered methods, and 20 capability axes under aligned data splits and explicit task contracts. We compare task ranks on aligned support, train five backbones under all seven non-empty objective combinations on five datasets with three seeds, and contrast fixed-model profiles with specialist portfolios. Rank comparisons connect imputation and prediction through numerical recovery and dependence preservation, and link generation to both through predictive utility; distributional fidelity follows different, sometimes opposing, rankings. Objective interventions show the largest pooled gains from including the recipient's own objective. Generation has the broadest coverage of positive pooled auxiliary effects, while prediction shows potential to improve imputation and synthetic-data utility, with responses that vary across backbones. Cross-addition effects reveal that objective benefits need not add and depend on the objectives already present. Fixed-model comparisons expose corresponding utility--fidelity trade-offs: some generalists surpass specialist portfolios on utility, while fidelity continues to favor specialization. Frozen foundation models show strong prediction and numerical point imputation, together with promising synthetic-data utility, highlighting their potential across all three tasks. These findings motivate unified tabular models that share useful conditional information while improving categorical reconstruction and faithful joint sampling.
papers.summary: Generation, imputation, and prediction all query the same underlying tabular distribution but are usually evaluated separately, leaving it unclear what they share and whether one model can do all three well. The `One Table Benchmark` covers 56 datasets, 46 methods, and 20 capability axes under aligned splits, and additionally trains five backbones under all seven combinations of the three objectives. Rankings link imputation and prediction, and connect generation to both through predictive utility, while distributional fidelity follows different and sometimes opposing rankings; objective benefits are not additive and depend on which objectives are already present. In fixed-model comparisons, **some generalists surpass specialist portfolios on utility, while fidelity still favors specialization**, and frozen tabular foundation models show strong prediction and numerical imputation.

papers.title: Branch-and-Commit for Frozen RL Agents: When and Where to Spend Test-Time Compute
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning agents are often deployed with policies that cannot be retrained or modified. In digital environments whose states can be copied and resumed, an operator has another option: sample several continuations from the current state, evaluate them, and continue from the endpoint of the selected branch. We call this procedure branch-and-commit. We study when it improves return, what produces the improvement, and where its computational budget should be spent. Across four environments, two frozen policies, five continuation verifiers, and a model-free selection rule, we find that the benefit of branching depends on dispersion: the difference between the best candidate return and the mean candidate return. Branching provides no benefit in low-dispersion settings, while increasing return by 12.8% in our main Craftax-Medium setting. Most of this gain comes not from selecting better actions, but from selecting among different stochastic realizations of the same action. Several competent verifiers achieve similar episode returns, suggesting that verifier quality is not the main constraint at our operating budget. Instead, computation is better allocated to states where useful dispersion is likely. On held-out seeds, gating branching using predicted dispersion retains 69% of the improvement from uniform branching while using 48% as many branching calls. These results characterize when branch-and-commit is useful and clarify what its gains represent.
papers.summary: When a reinforcement learning policy cannot be retrained but its environment state can be copied and resumed, an operator can sample several continuations, evaluate them, and continue from the chosen one, a procedure the authors call branch-and-commit. Experiments across four environments, two frozen policies, and five continuation verifiers show the benefit depends on dispersion, the gap between the best and mean candidate return: branching does nothing in low-dispersion settings but **raises return by 12.8% in the main `Craftax-Medium` setting**. Most of that gain comes from selecting among different stochastic realizations of the same action instead of choosing better actions, and verifier quality is not the main constraint. Gating branching on predicted dispersion keeps 69% of the improvement with 48% as many branching calls on held-out seeds.

papers.title: The Shape of a Program: Path Signatures for Trace-to-Program Induction
papers.abstract: Synthesizing programs from execution traces is a fundamental challenge in algorithmic interpretability and the reverse engineering of complex systems. We bring a rough-path-theoretic perspective to program induction, treating execution traces as high-dimensional rough paths and encoding them with the path signature transform, a tool from stochastic analysis whose expectation provably characterizes the distribution of traces a program induces. On three program-induction domains, Karel, List, and RASP, our log-signature trace encoder outperforms LSTM, Transformer, and Fourier baselines in almost every setting, with its largest margins when training data is scarce. We further observe that the trace-to-program pipeline is naturally contractive: it often produces valid programs that are shorter than the ground truth. We turn this into a bootstrapping procedure that exposes redundancy in the ground-truth supervision without any external oracle, which we demonstrate on redundancy-injected versions of our datasets. Finally, the log-signature encoder induces a markedly more interpretable latent geometry than the baselines, in which the nearest neighbors of every state lie on its own execution trace.
papers.summary: Synthesizing a program from its execution traces is treated here through rough path theory: traces are viewed as high-dimensional paths and encoded with the path signature transform, a tool from stochastic analysis whose expectation provably characterizes the distribution of traces a program induces. On the `Karel`, `List`, and `RASP` program-induction domains, the log-signature trace encoder **outperforms LSTM, Transformer, and Fourier baselines in almost every setting**, with the largest margins when training data is scarce. The pipeline also tends to output valid programs shorter than the ground truth, which the authors turn into a bootstrapping procedure for exposing redundancy in the supervision without an external oracle. The encoder's latent space is also more interpretable, with each state's nearest neighbors lying on its own execution trace.

papers.title: Seeing Is Not Believing: Counterfactual Lesion Erasure Teaches a Small Medical Vision-Language Agent to Report Only What the Image Shows
papers.abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) often report a finding because the question names it; standard benchmarks miss this. From public segmentation datasets we build counterfactual views without manual annotation: the lesion erased by inpainting, a same-shape control edit elsewhere, and unedited lesion-free images. The evidence sensitivity gap (ESG) is the rate of absent-or-refer answers after erasure minus the rate after the control edit; it is zero for a model that ignores the image or reacts to both edits alike. MedScope-4B (Qwen3.5-4B, LoRA, image tools) was trained on label-derived trajectories, selected by a pre-registered rule and tested once against nine frontier and six open VLMs; four pre-registered checks then probed the mechanism. On 507 internal cases across five imaging types, MedScope-4B reached ESG 0.758 and claimed an erased lesion in 9.6% of cases, against 0.27-0.47 and 41-62% for the frontier models (all p<0.001), without significant loss of accuracy on real lesions. Without counterfactual views ESG fell to 0.279+-0.107 (three seeds); the effect replicated on MedGemma 1.5 4B and two unseen inpainting tools. At four external centres the advantage held but frontier models detected more real lesions; on a fresh external test MedScope-4B detected 0 of 48 pneumothorax films, with net utility below gemini-4-argon's (-0.36 [-0.50, -0.23]). Matching the control edit was not shown to matter; over three seeds no fresh-external ESG advantage over removal-based DPO was established; a paired-view consistency objective did not beat a matched-compute control, while that continuation alone cut erased-lesion claims on unseen tools at every seed, at a cost in sensitivity at one. Training on erased and edited images gives a small model an evidence-gated disposition that prompting does not give frontier models; it does not improve perception, and rare critical findings need coverage.
papers.summary: Medical vision-language models often report a finding simply because the question names it, so the authors build counterfactual views from public segmentation datasets, including images with the lesion erased by inpainting and a same-shape control edit elsewhere, and define the evidence sensitivity gap (ESG) as the rate of absent-or-refer answers after erasure minus the rate after the control edit. `MedScope-4B`, a `Qwen3.5-4B` model fine-tuned with LoRA and image tools on these views, reached an ESG of 0.758 on 507 internal cases and **claimed an erased lesion in 9.6% of cases versus 41-62% for frontier models**, without significant loss of accuracy on real lesions. The limits are substantial: at external centres frontier models detected more real lesions, and on a fresh external test the model detected 0 of 48 pneumothorax films. The authors conclude that counterfactual training gives a small model an evidence-gated disposition that prompting does not give frontier models, but does not improve perception.

papers.title: Just AI Governance and the Forbidden-Boundary Principle
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes consequential decisions, yet predictive accuracy is not a sufficient justification for delegated authority. This conceptual study develops an integrated framework for assessing just AI across normative, data, model, and governance layers. Drawing on plural theories of justice, sociotechnical fairness research, and publicly available governance standards, it maps six justice requirements to observable evidence, decision rights, and remedies. It proposes a two-stage evaluation rule: exclude uses that fail independently justified minimum rights constraints, then compare eligible alternatives across multiple performance and governance criteria. As an explicitly limited normative analogy, Genesis chapter 2 motivates a Forbidden-Boundary Principle (FBP), under which an AI agent must not execute externally consequential actions outside pre-authorized boundaries. The resulting First-Principle Safe-Stop Protocol (FPSSP) comprises an independently governed policy monitor, a mandatory execution gate, a restricted or alternative safe-state controller, immutable-oriented audit trails, and accountable human authorization for recovery. We distinguish this normative and traceability contribution from existing Simplex and runtime assurance architectures; we do not claim a novel safety switch or formal proof of universal ethical compliance. A policy schema, threat model, test matrix, outcome definitions, and a prospective comparison design make the proposal falsifiable. No FPSSP implementation, experimental dataset, numerical improvement, or verified latency bound is reported. The framework supports future evaluation rather than constituting evidence of operational safety.
papers.summary: Predictive accuracy alone does not justify delegating consequential decisions to AI, so this conceptual study builds a framework for assessing just AI across normative, data, model, and governance layers, mapping six justice requirements to observable evidence, decision rights, and remedies. It proposes a two-stage rule (exclude uses that violate minimum rights constraints, then compare the remaining alternatives on multiple criteria) and a Forbidden-Boundary Principle (FBP), under which an agent must not execute externally consequential actions outside pre-authorized boundaries. The accompanying First-Principle Safe-Stop Protocol (`FPSSP`) combines an independent policy monitor, a mandatory execution gate, a safe-state controller, audit trails, and human authorization for recovery. The authors state that **no implementation, dataset, or numerical result is reported**, and position the work as a falsifiable design for future evaluation.

papers.title: An Open Implementation Flow for the Xilinx Spartan-3E and Spartan-6 that Runs in the Browser, Checked Byte for Byte Against ISE
papers.abstract: The author describes an open implementation flow, from HDL to a programmable bitstream, for the Xilinx Spartan-3E (XC3S100E to XC3S1200E) and Spartan-6 (XC6SLX16, XC6SLX45), devices that only the discontinued ISE 14.7 supports. The flow runs unchanged in a web browser or in Node.js: Yosys and nextpnr compiled to WebAssembly, with nextpnr's Himbaechel framework given Spartan-3E and Spartan-6 architectures generated from Silinx's own device descriptions, bit database and timing model, and Silinx's own bitstream writer. The bit database was built by black-box observation of ISE's documented XDL and bitgen tools, using codeword-batched experiments; the router is given only switches whose bits were measured, and the writer refuses a feature it has not measured. ISE is the oracle: for the same placed and routed design, the bitstream is byte-identical to the one bitgen writes and ISE's DRC is clean. Placement and routing were first done by an in-house annealer and PathFinder router, which nextpnr replaced once it matched them. On 67 open-source designs for the XC3S1200E, compared with ISE at the same optimisation goal (45 designs built by both), the flow uses 15% fewer slices and has 14% shorter critical paths at goal Area, 21% fewer slices and 8% shorter paths at Speed, and 20% fewer slices but 12% longer paths at Fast (geometric means). XST cannot read 15 of the designs. The flow is published as the npm package silinx-fpga (Apache-2.0).
papers.summary: Xilinx Spartan-3E and Spartan-6 FPGAs are supported only by the discontinued `ISE 14.7` toolchain, so the author builds an open flow from hardware description language to bitstream that runs unchanged in a web browser or Node.js. It compiles `Yosys` and `nextpnr` to WebAssembly and adds device descriptions, a bit database, a timing model, and a bitstream writer under the name `Silinx`, with the bit database derived by black-box observation of ISE's documented tools. For the same placed and routed design, **the output bitstream is byte-identical to the one ISE's bitgen writes**. On 45 open-source designs built by both flows for the XC3S1200E, it uses 15% fewer slices with 14% shorter critical paths at the Area goal, though paths are 12% longer at the Fast goal.

papers.title: Compile-Gated Lean Proof Refactoring with Enterprise Agent Practices: A Model per Step under a US\$3 Cap, Followed by Programmatic Rewrite Rules
papers.abstract: Our closed-track entry (Arena username Vexorium-Agent) scored 86.31 points on the final board (L = 77.07, H = 81.86, Z = 100) over the 60 final problems, against 33.33 for the reference proofs, 8th at the deadline (top: 92.57), for US\$166.33 at list prices with every call counted (per problem: mean US\$2.772, at most US\$2.874; US\$3 cap). Three practices carry the entry. First, each paid stage runs the model that measured best per dollar for it among the 9 we tested in our own harness: GPT-6.1 Sol the early sessions, GPT-6.1 Terra the later ones and the tail at 70% of Sol's cost per turn, and Gemini 4 Argon the review and repair; Sol also runs the style rewrite. Second, what our development and research runs learned ships as compiler-checked programmatic rewrite rules rather than prompt text (+0.93 points from rules fixed before the release; +0.26 and +0.30, in sample, from passes built or switched on after the release). Third, every call is recorded and reviewed before each change (all 9 board scores came within -0.063 to +0.015 points of our meter's prediction). The harness, gate and many of these rules also serve our open-track entry. We report the full bill and the spread of three runs.
papers.summary: A competition entry for refactoring Lean proofs under a US$3 per-problem cost cap is described, in which every candidate rewrite must pass the compiler before it is accepted. Each paid stage uses whichever of nine tested models measured best per dollar (`GPT-6.1 Sol`, `GPT-6.1 Terra`, and `Gemini 4 Argon` for different steps), lessons from development runs are shipped as compiler-checked programmatic rewrite rules instead of prompt text, and every call is logged and reviewed before changes. The entry scored **86.31 points on the 60 final problems versus 33.33 for the reference proofs**, placing 8th (top score 92.57) at a total cost of US$166.33. The rewrite rules contributed roughly 0.3 to 0.9 points each, and the team's internal meter predicted board scores to within about 0.06 points.

papers.title: khammoon: From a Linguistic Guideline to a Thai Morpheme Segmenter
papers.abstract: Thai is written without spaces between words, making segmentation a foundational step in most Thai NLP pipelines. Existing tools primarily reproduce the word-level conventions of corpora such as BEST; however, because the notion of a "word" in Thai lacks a unified linguistic consensus, these conventions struggle with productive compounding, leading to arbitrary boundaries and ambiguity in downstream representations. Instead, we propose operating at the morphological level, focusing on khammoon, the smallest atomic unit that carries meaning. Segmenting at the morphemic level provides an explicit, consistent morphological representation that eliminates compounding ambiguity. Crucially, this representation benefits downstream learning: models trained on morphemes perform on par with or exceed word-level baselines across part-of-speech tagging, named-entity recognition, and sentiment classification, demonstrating that linguistic consistency improves representation quality without downstream performance penalty. To operationalize this representation, we translate linguistic principles into a formal decision guideline with near-perfect human agreement ($\kappa \approx 0.99$), scale annotation with an LLM, and correct systematic errors with human labels. Finally, we train khammoon, a lightweight 1M-parameter convolutional BiLSTM segmenter designed for efficient CPU inference, achieving a boundary F1 of 0.992 on out-of-domain text. The guideline, datasets, model, and library are all publicly released.
papers.summary: Thai is written without spaces, and existing segmenters reproduce word-level corpus conventions that handle productive compounding inconsistently because there is no agreed definition of a Thai word. The authors instead segment into morphemes, turning linguistic principles into a formal decision guideline with near-perfect human agreement (kappa of about 0.99), scaling annotation with a large language model, and correcting systematic errors with human labels. Models trained on morphemes match or exceed word-level baselines on part-of-speech tagging, named-entity recognition, and sentiment classification. The resulting `khammoon` segmenter, a 1M-parameter convolutional BiLSTM built for CPU inference, reaches **a boundary F1 of 0.992 on out-of-domain text**.

papers.title: FaST: Factored Synthesis of Transitions for Offline Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Synthetic data augmentation promises to scale offline reinforcement learning beyond fixed logged datasets, but leading diffusion-based generators model the transition tuple (state, action, next state, reward, terminal) as a monolith: no single factor can be natively redrawn in isolation. We present FaST (Factored Synthesis of Transitions), which factors transitions via the chain rule into state, action, dynamics, reward, and terminal stages, fitting each with an estimator matched to its statistical properties. Across twelve D4RL locomotion and maze benchmarks, TD3+BC and IQL agents trained on FaST transitions match the SynthER diffusion baseline while generating transitions over 90x faster. The explicit action-given-state conditional can also be re-queried for a fixed state, enabling targeted action synthesis: drawing N candidate actions per generated state and keeping the highest-advantage one under a value function fit to the same data, thereby synthesizing improved behavior during generation rather than filtering for it post-hoc. Best-of-10 synthesis beats training on real data on 11 of 12 medium and medium-replay settings (+8.9 D4RL points on average, up to +28.4), and is competitive with advantage-filtered SynthER at a fraction of its generation cost. On expert mixtures both mechanisms degrade identically, tracing the failure to the advantage estimate itself rather than to either targeting mechanism.
papers.summary: Diffusion-based data generators for offline reinforcement learning model each transition (state, action, next state, reward, terminal) as a single block, so no one factor can be redrawn on its own. `FaST` (Factored Synthesis of Transitions) splits the transition by the chain rule into state, action, dynamics, reward, and terminal stages, each fit with an estimator suited to it. On twelve `D4RL` locomotion and maze benchmarks, `TD3+BC` and `IQL` agents trained on its data match the `SynthER` baseline while generating transitions over 90x faster. Drawing ten candidate actions per generated state and keeping the highest-advantage one **beats training on real data in 11 of 12 medium and medium-replay settings, by 8.9 D4RL points on average**, though the approach degrades on expert mixtures because of the advantage estimate.

papers.title: From Questions to Decisions: Benchmarking How LLM Agents Acquire Decision-Relevant Information from Human Beings
papers.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly asked to make plans for people, such as scheduling drivers or assigning nurses. However, people's requests are often incomplete, and the supporting information for decision-making may be outdated, requiring agents to ask for clarification. Existing benchmarks typically provide fully specified problems or rely on uncalibrated LLM-simulated users, leaving this ability insufficiently tested. We introduce Ask2Decide, a benchmark of 43 planning tasks that evaluates whether agents ask for missing information that matters for their decisions. An operator holds facts absent from the agent's request and records, and optimization solvers determine which facts change the optimal plan. We also include similarly worded facts that leave the optimal plan unchanged to test whether agents distinguish useful information from irrelevant details. We collect 79 interaction sessions from 19 participants and find that, after an incorrect plan, human replies omit the correcting fact far more often than replies from an uncalibrated simulated user (43% versus 7%). Using these interactions, we calibrate a simulated operator that more closely matches human reply patterns. Evaluating four frontier LLMs, we find that their initial plans are infeasible on 58-98% of tasks when information is missing, compared with 5-28% when all facts are provided upfront. Agents uncover facts that change the optimal plan only slightly more often than facts that leave it unchanged (39-52% versus 32-41%). These results show that obtaining decision-relevant information through interaction remains a major bottleneck for LLM planning. This is ongoing work and will be updated. The date of this version is shown on the first page.
papers.summary: Agents asked to plan for people often receive incomplete requests and stale records, yet benchmarks usually supply fully specified problems or rely on uncalibrated simulated users. `Ask2Decide` is a benchmark of 43 planning tasks in which an operator holds missing facts, optimization solvers determine which facts change the optimal plan, and similarly worded irrelevant facts act as distractors. Using 79 sessions from 19 human participants, the authors calibrate a simulated operator after finding that humans omit the correcting fact far more often than an uncalibrated simulator (43% versus 7%).
