Across four frontier models, **initial plans are infeasible on 58-98% of tasks when information is missing, versus 5-28% when all facts are given upfront**, and agents uncover plan-changing facts only slightly more often than irrelevant ones (39-52% versus 32-41%).

papers.title: Permutation-Based Pre-trained Model Merging via Reciprocal Orthogonality
papers.abstract: Ito et al. (2026) showed that sufficiently wide, independently trained neural networks can exhibit linear mode connectivity (LMC) with softmax temperature calibration, even without permutation. LMC means that a low-loss linear path connects the models' parameters. This behavior is explained by layerwise exponentially weighted connectivity (LEWC), whereby each merged layer outputs an exponentially weighted sum of the original models' corresponding representations, yielding ensemble-like predictions. However, prior work observed LEWC with substantial widening, such as 8192 units per hidden layer for MLPs and $16\times$ width for VGG-11, raising the question of whether such widths are necessary. We therefore search for permutations that encourage reciprocal orthogonality (RO), which suppresses interference between each model's weights and the other model's representations. This allows both models' computations to coexist in the merged network, promoting LEWC at smaller widths. We formulate the search as independent layerwise quadratic assignment problems and approximately solve their continuous relaxations using Frank--Wolfe. Experiments show that our method facilitates LMC with less width expansion. It also merges models trained on different data distributions, where weight matching, which maximizes weight similarity through permutations, struggles. The merged predictions approximate those of a logit ensemble of the original models.
papers.summary: Earlier work showed that very wide, independently trained networks can be linearly interpolated at low loss, known as linear mode connectivity (LMC), because each merged layer outputs an exponentially weighted sum of the two models' representations, termed layerwise exponentially weighted connectivity (LEWC); that result required extreme widening. This work searches for neuron permutations that promote reciprocal orthogonality (RO), which suppresses interference between one model's weights and the other's representations, by solving relaxed layerwise quadratic assignment problems with `Frank-Wolfe`. Experiments show the method **achieves linear mode connectivity with less width expansion**. It also merges models trained on different data distributions where `weight matching` struggles, with merged predictions approximating a logit ensemble of the originals.

papers.title: Multi-Future Drafting: Mixture Block Drafters for Tree-Verified Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Block drafters such as DFlash draft a block of future tokens in one forward pass, and draft trees such as DDTree verify the prefixes ranked highest by the product of the drafter's per-position distributions. Under tree verification, the expected number of accepted tokens is the probability mass the tree covers. We show that a product misallocates it: when the continuation can follow several futures, it splices them into chimeras, prefixes stitched together from different futures that the target never produces, and gives them as much budget as the futures themselves. Barring ties, no product-ranked tree can hold two futures that disagree in $m$ positions without $2^{m-1}-1$ chimeras, however well the drafter is trained, and in practice chimeras make up 27-33% of a 64-node tree. We propose Multi-Future Drafting (MFD), which restores the coupling with a latent variable instead of the chain rule: $K$ learned mode embeddings at the drafter's input draft $K$ coherent blocks in the same pass, and a mixture DDTree lets the verifier pick the future the target takes, losslessly and with $K+1$ extra vectors. On four Qwen targets from 4B to 27B parameters, at batch size 1, MFD reaches up to 7.8$\times$ speedup, 5-8% faster than the best single-mode tree trained identically and, on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, 9-16% faster than the released DARTree trained on the same prompts.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding with block drafters such as `DFlash` and draft trees such as `DDTree` ranks candidate prefixes by the product of per-position distributions, which the authors show wastes verification budget on chimeras: prefixes spliced from different plausible continuations that the target model never produces, making up 27-33% of a 64-node tree. Multi-Future Drafting (`MFD`) adds K learned mode embeddings at the drafter's input so that K coherent blocks are drafted in one pass, and a mixture tree lets the verifier follow whichever future the target takes, losslessly and with only K+1 extra vectors. On four `Qwen` targets from 4B to 27B parameters at batch size 1, it reaches **up to 7.8x speedup**, 5-8% faster than the best identically trained single-mode tree and 9-16% faster than the released `DARTree` on the two smaller models.

papers.title: ChipOmni: A General-Purpose AI Agent for Electronic Design Automation
papers.abstract: Electronic design automation (EDA) workflows remain highly fragmented, requiring engineers to coordinate heterogeneous representations, specialised software tools, and iterative verification across multiple design stages. Although large language models have brought more general reasoning and code-generation capabilities to EDA, many existing approaches remain focused on isolated tasks and struggle to plan, verify, and repair designs autonomously within executable engineering environments. Here we introduce ChipOmni, a knowledge-enhanced, context-evolving AI agent framework for EDA. ChipOmni integrates multimodal understanding, dynamic planning, multi-agent collaboration, and verification-driven tool interaction into a unified autonomous system. By continually incorporating feedback from external engineering tools, the framework maintains an evolving task context, integrates domain knowledge, and iteratively refines intermediate designs. Across benchmarks for analog circuit, RTL, testbench, and formal-assertion generation, ChipOmni improves multiple task-specific measures over the evaluated baselines and solves all 30 AnalogCoder-Pro tasks. In a long-horizon case study, ChipOmni advances a natural-language RISC-V specification through three design levels to a micro-SoC GDSII layout that passes physical sign-off, without human intervention after initialization. Together, these results show that ChipOmni can coordinate verification-driven design across heterogeneous tasks and sustain long-horizon engineering workflows, advancing a shift from fragmented, tool-centred processes towards agent-centred, closed-loop systems.
papers.summary: Electronic design automation (EDA) workflows are fragmented across representations, tools, and verification stages, and existing language-model approaches mostly address isolated tasks. `ChipOmni` is an agent framework that combines multimodal understanding, dynamic planning, multi-agent collaboration, and verification-driven tool use, maintaining an evolving task context from engineering tool feedback. It improves task-specific measures over the evaluated baselines on analog circuit, RTL, testbench, and formal-assertion generation, and solves all 30 `AnalogCoder-Pro` tasks. In a long-horizon case study it takes **a natural-language RISC-V specification to a micro-SoC GDSII layout that passes physical sign-off without human intervention after initialization**.

papers.title: Understanding-First AI Engineering: Purposes, Reference Architecture, and Architectural Patterns for Human Understanding
papers.abstract: AI systems can produce reliable results without developing human understanding. However, human understanding remains valuable for shaping subsequent AI-supported work, forming preferences, governing collective choices and satisfying curiosity, even when human participation is unnecessary for correcting errors. We propose understanding-first AI engineering, which treats purpose-specific human understanding as a first-class design principle guiding requirements, design and operation. The purposes of understanding are organised into four complementary rationales: reflective agency, effective action, collective governance and epistemic value. A reference architecture connects production, verification, use, and learning and exploration through shared records, supporting understanding through explanation and participation. Five candidate architectural patterns guide choices about parallel learning, explanatory models, goal exploration, audience-specific views and distributed expertise. Qualitative scenario analysis of two hypothetical use cases demonstrates how the purpose classification, reference architecture and selected patterns guide investigation, participation and decision processes while retaining operational controls. The cases illustrate design consequences and limitations rather than establish empirical effectiveness. The approach makes human understanding an explicit engineering commitment whose justification need not depend on improving the original AI task.
papers.summary: AI systems can deliver reliable results without the people involved understanding them, yet that understanding still matters for shaping later work, forming preferences, governing collective choices, and satisfying curiosity. The authors propose treating purpose-specific human understanding as a first-class engineering requirement, organised under four rationales: reflective agency, effective action, collective governance, and epistemic value. They give a reference architecture linking production, verification, use, and learning through shared records, plus five candidate architectural patterns. The approach is illustrated through qualitative analysis of two hypothetical use cases, which the authors say **show design consequences and limitations without establishing empirical effectiveness**.

papers.title: GRAP: Gender Rubric-Aware Probing for Analyzing Gender Bias in LLMs
papers.abstract: As LLMs increasingly mediate everyday interactions, subtle gender biases in open-ended responses pose growing societal risks. Existing probing methods have two key limitations: they rely on fixed-format tasks, such as pronoun resolution or occupation association, that alignment-tuned models can easily handle; and they compare raw group-level rubric scores, ignoring per-dimension variance and obscuring which bias dimensions reliably distinguish gender groups. We introduce GRAP (Gender Rubric-Aware Probing), a framework that uses a lightweight logistic probe to identify the most discriminative bias dimensions from responses scored across 10 rubric dimensions, operating task-agnostically on open-ended instruction following.
papers.summary: Gender bias in open-ended responses from large language models is hard to detect with existing probes, which rely on fixed-format tasks such as pronoun resolution that alignment-tuned models handle easily, and which compare raw group-level rubric scores without accounting for per-dimension variance. `GRAP` (Gender Rubric-Aware Probing) scores responses to open-ended instructions across 10 rubric dimensions and then fits **a lightweight logistic probe to identify which bias dimensions most reliably distinguish gender groups**, independent of task format. The abstract describes the framework only and reports no experimental results.

papers.title: Repository-Context-Guided Image Understanding for Agentic Software Development
papers.abstract: Coding agents increasingly receive UI screenshots as part of bug reports, yet degraded image quality - caused by low resolution, compression artifacts, or small rendered text - can prevent them from identifying the relevant UI elements and source files. Vision-language models become less reliable as image quality deteriorates, while OCR-assisted approaches may propagate recognition errors from degraded inputs. Both approaches are limited when the visual evidence required for localization is no longer clearly observable in the query screenshot. We propose augmenting coding agents with repository-rendered reference images: crisp screenshots generated from the same codebase that the agent is tasked with modifying. These references provide readable visual evidence of the application's UI while preserving the current, potentially bug-containing implementation state. Because they are generated from the available repository rather than requiring a known bug-free version, they can be produced automatically for reproducible application states without manual image annotation. We evaluate the approach on a controlled benchmark derived from SWE-bench Multimodal by injecting visual UI bugs into a real web application. We vary screenshot degradation and reference-image provision and measure whether the coding agent identifies the correct source file. The results show that reference images improve file localization especially for degraded image quality, increasing the gold file match rate under fourfold downsampling with JPEG compression. We confirmed with further analysis that the proposed approach recognizes text approximately 12 percentage points better than language biased OCR under the same degradation.
papers.summary: Coding agents often receive UI screenshots in bug reports, but low resolution, compression artifacts, and small text can prevent them from identifying the relevant UI elements and source files, and OCR-based workarounds propagate recognition errors. The proposed fix is to give the agent crisp reference screenshots rendered from the same repository it is modifying, which show the current, possibly buggy UI and need no known-good version or manual annotation. On a controlled benchmark built by injecting visual UI bugs into a web application from `SWE-bench Multimodal`, reference images improve identification of the correct source file, particularly under fourfold downsampling with JPEG compression. The approach also recognizes text **about 12 percentage points better than language-biased OCR** under the same degradation.

papers.title: GTAGym: Real AAA Game Tasks Environment for Evaluation and Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: AAA games offer a rich testbed for evaluating agent perception, reasoning, and control. However, evaluating whether agents can complete tasks in AAA games is challenging and often human-annotated because task outcomes are often difficult to verify automatically, let alone applying it for Reinforcement Learning (RL). We introduce GTAGym, an environment and framework for evaluation and RL on GTA V tasks. Its evaluation benchmark, GTAVBench, derived from GTA V main-story missions, contains 103 online tasks reconstructed across nine task families, alongside 47 image-based shooting and sniping tasks using GTA V imagery. A web server provides access to the online environment and evaluation interface, supporting parallel testing through screenshots and keyboard-mouse actions with automatic engine-state outcome checks. We evaluate six frontier LLMs on GTAVBench with textual task instructions and on its GTAVBench-AGI branch, where instructions appear only in the first screenshot and a harness automatically compresses interaction history. The best configuration achieves 70.9% overall accuracy in GTAVBench-AGI, yet aerial navigation, evasion and interception remain difficult. GTAGym also provides a scalable generator that samples task parameters within user-specified ranges and option sets under fixed templates, creating batches of 3D and image-based shooting environments for RL with automatic reward and termination signals. LoRA RL of Qwen3.8-27B on generated on-foot navigation tasks improves the in-domain performance and transfers to out-of-domain task categories, and native GTA V tasks from 15% to 23%.
papers.summary: Checking whether an agent completed a task in a AAA game usually needs human annotation, which blocks both scalable evaluation and reinforcement learning (RL). `GTAGym` is an environment for GTA V that exposes screenshots and keyboard-mouse actions through a web server with automatic engine-state outcome checks; its benchmark `GTAVBench` has 103 online tasks across nine families drawn from main-story missions plus 47 image-based shooting tasks. Among six frontier models, the best configuration reaches **70.9% overall accuracy on the `GTAVBench-AGI` variant**, where instructions appear only in the first screenshot, while aerial navigation, evasion, and interception remain difficult. A task generator supplies automatic rewards for RL, and LoRA RL of `Qwen3.8-27B` on generated on-foot navigation tasks transfers to other categories and raises native GTA V task success from 15% to 23%.

papers.title: APS-VLA: Action-Guided and Future-Aware Token Pruning for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies have demonstrated strong generalization in robotic manipulation, yet processing dense visual tokens often incurs high inference latency. Visual token pruning offers a practical way to reduce this cost, but identifying a compact set of tokens that preserves reliable action generation remains challenging. Existing methods largely rely on static or immediate heuristic cues to estimate token importance. We introduce APS-VLA, a framework that learns visual token selection from robot demonstrations while keeping the pretrained VLA backbone frozen. A lightweight Decision Influence Estimator scores tokens conditioned on current visual observations, language instructions, and robot proprioception. Its training combines two complementary signals: action supervision matches both the full-input policy predictions and demonstrated actions, while an auxiliary visual transition objective uses demonstrated actions to predict subsequent visual features from the selected representation. At deployment, the estimator performs a single hard selection and packing step before the policy's native action-generation procedure; the auxiliary predictor is removed. Experiments with OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO and with $\pi_{0.5}$ and XR-1 on RoboCasa365 demonstrate inference acceleration with modest changes in task success. Across five real-world tasks on two dual-arm platforms, APS-VLA reduces mean policy inference latency from 137.25 to 93.25 ms, achieving a $1.47\times$ speedup with an average success rate of 61%, compared with 60% for the unpruned baseline. Together, these results support APS-VLA as a modular, plug-in framework for efficient robotic control across VLA architectures, preserving the underlying policy parameters and native action-generation procedure.
papers.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) robot policies are slowed by dense visual tokens, and existing pruning methods rank tokens using static or immediate heuristics. `APS-VLA` keeps the pretrained backbone frozen and trains a lightweight estimator that scores tokens from the visual observation, language instruction, and proprioception, supervised by matching both full-input policy predictions and demonstrated actions, with an auxiliary objective that predicts future visual features and is dropped at deployment. Tests with `OpenVLA-OFT` on `LIBERO` and with `pi0.5` and `XR-1` on `RoboCasa365` show faster inference with modest changes in task success. On five real-world tasks across two dual-arm platforms, mean inference latency falls from 137.25 ms to 93.25 ms, **a 1.47x speedup with 61% average success versus 60% unpruned**.

papers.title: Code-Grounded Agentic Explanations for Static Analysis Vulnerability Findings
papers.abstract: Static application security testing (SAST) tools surface vulnerabilities early and their verdicts are rule-based and auditable. Yet developers routinely dismiss findings they cannot interpret. Large language models can supply the missing explanation, but designs that also hand the model the detection give up the auditability that makes static analysis defensible. We keep detection with the analyser and give the model only the explaining. A preliminary user study with 20 participants and a workshop with 19 practitioners yielded five requirements. Guided by these we redesigned SAFE, an open-source IntelliJ IDEA plugin that explains findings from any analyser reporting in the Static Analysis Results Interchange Format. It tiers explanations by demand, ties them to the reported data flow, and replaces the single-prompt backend with an agent that must consult the repository and the rule that fired before answering. A within-subjects crossover experiment with 24 participants compared the redesign against its predecessor. Perceived usability rose from 77.3 to 85.0 on the System Usability Scale. Actionability gained most among the explanation-quality items, the aspect both earlier studies flagged as weakest, and the odds of a correct remediation were 2.6 times higher. Triage accuracy and time per finding were indistinguishable, which we read as uninformative rather than as equivalence. Trust was the one measure that did not move, and the closing interviews indicate that grounding made findings easier to understand rather than easier to believe. Participants also drew a boundary no requirement anticipated, wanting the tool to find and explain while they judge and apply.
papers.summary: Developers often dismiss findings from static application security testing (SAST) tools because they cannot interpret them, while handing detection itself to a language model sacrifices the auditability of rule-based analysis. The authors keep detection in the analyser and redesign `SAFE`, an open-source IntelliJ IDEA plugin, so that explanations are tiered by demand, tied to the reported data flow, and produced by an agent that must consult the repository and the triggering rule before answering. In a within-subjects crossover experiment with 24 participants, System Usability Scale scores rose from 77.3 to 85.0 and **the odds of a correct remediation were 2.6 times higher** than with the single-prompt predecessor. Triage accuracy and time per finding were indistinguishable, and trust did not change; participants wanted the tool to find and explain while they judge and apply fixes.

papers.title: Trust, but verify, audit and attribute: a human-in-the-loop framework for checking AI-produced research results
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems now produce research results in bulk: in October 2026 a single laboratory released more than 700 AI-generated mathematics manuscripts, only part of them with machine-checked proofs. Such volumes will be checked mostly by AI agents that call specialised software. A passing check certifies only the artefact that was checked. For proofs translated into the proof assistant Lean, it has been shown that this artefact may state something other than the author's text, and that deciding whether a translation is faithful is undecidable in general. The human researcher therefore stays in the loop, and human and AI contributions must be recorded. We propose a domain-independent, human-in-the-loop framework for checking AI-produced results. Validated, agent-usable tools with different grounds of trust check the results; a fidelity audit asks whether each check addressed the claim as stated; the human decides at fixed points; and a dialog report attributes the work to the human and to the AI. We describe two automatic implementations of the tool layer, for mathematics (Wolfram Language, MATLAB, Lean) and statistics (Python and R), and run the mathematical one on a two-claim example. An ambiguous claim was split into two readings, one refuted and one proved.
papers.summary: AI systems now generate research results in bulk, and a passing machine check certifies only the artefact that was checked, which for proofs translated into Lean may state something different from the author's text. The proposed human-in-the-loop framework has validated, agent-usable tools with different grounds of trust check each result, a fidelity audit ask whether each check addressed the claim as stated, a human decide at fixed points, and a dialog report attribute work to human and AI. Tool layers are implemented for mathematics (`Wolfram Language`, `MATLAB`, `Lean`) and statistics (Python and R). The mathematical one is demonstrated on a two-claim example, in which **an ambiguous claim was split into two readings, one refuted and one proved**.

papers.title: Explanation-Aware Fairness Beyond Output Parity: Joint Output-Attribution Regularization for Medical Image Classification
papers.abstract: Output-level fairness does not constrain whether demographic groups rely on similar predictive contributions in representation space. For a nonlinear encoder with a linear head, we show that outcome-conditioned output score disparity equals the signed sum of feature attribution differences across subgroups by allowing small prediction gaps to arise through cancellation effect. We test whether an attribution disparity penalty complements output-level equalized odds based fairness surrogates. Across 960 DINOv2-LoRA models on HAM10000 and Harvard-GF datasets for gender and race fairness, attribution augmentation increases utility-fairness trade-off performance for hypervolume in six different settings with paired 95% confidence intervals and relative gains of 1.49-10.57%. Under a predefined utility constraint, augmented model families also achieve 9.0-38.7% lower equalized odds difference, lower attribution disparity, and reduced cancellation ratio while preserving predictive utility. These results support attribution fairness as a complementary explanation-aware constraint on output fairness.
papers.summary: Fairness constraints on model outputs do not ensure that demographic groups rely on similar feature contributions, and the authors show that for a nonlinear encoder with a linear head, small output gaps between subgroups can arise from attribution differences cancelling out. They add an attribution disparity penalty to equalized-odds fairness surrogates and test it across 960 `DINOv2`-LoRA models on the `HAM10000` and `Harvard-GF` medical imaging datasets for gender and race. The penalty improves the utility-fairness trade-off hypervolume in six settings by 1.49-10.57%, and under a fixed utility constraint yields **9.0-38.7% lower equalized odds difference** along with lower attribution disparity and less cancellation.

papers.title: Beyond the Document: Compiled Context and Governed Agents for Any Work Product
papers.abstract: A document preserves the visible result of professional work but often discards the research, calculations, assumptions, evidence, and authorization boundaries behind it. We study a different unit of delivery: a Portable Agent Format (PAF) package that carries a work product together with compiled context, evidence, provenance, and rules for subsequent interaction. To test whether this context remains useful beyond the process that produced it, we evaluate four new packages, created after the hosted and offline readers were fixed: an investment proposal, fund research, financial-statement analysis, and an engineering incident review. Two packages were produced by specialized agents and two through a general-purpose assistant's packaging skill. Across 400 frozen questions and 12,000 evaluated responses, a hosted governed reader succeeds on 96% of questions versus 86% with instructions plus raw-file retrieval (Holm-adjusted p < 10^-7). On the 260 answerable questions per condition, success is 94% versus 79%; the gap varies by package. Source-material chat and instructions alone reach 48% and 74% overall. A separate 0.8-billion-parameter offline reader succeeds on 69% overall, but 54% on answerable questions. Its -1 response rate is 2.9%, combining materially wrong and unauthorized answers, versus 56% with the source and instructions alone. Ablations suggest advantages for the integrated selector and package-adapted writer, without isolating representation from training effects. The same run exposes a failure: offline retrieval resolves none of the 40 historical-record questions in one financial-data package. These findings support treating compiled knowledge as part of the delivered work product, while leaving independent standards interoperability and end-to-end governance conformance unproven.
papers.summary: Documents preserve the visible result of professional work but drop the research, calculations, assumptions, evidence, and authorization boundaries behind it. The authors study a Portable Agent Format (`PAF`) package that ships a work product with compiled context, provenance, and interaction rules, and evaluate four packages in finance and engineering over 400 frozen questions and 12,000 responses. A hosted governed reader **succeeds on 96% of questions versus 86% for instructions plus raw-file retrieval**, while source-material chat and instructions alone reach 48% and 74%. A separate 0.8-billion-parameter offline reader reaches 69% overall with a 2.9% rate of materially wrong or unauthorized answers, but its retrieval resolves none of 40 historical-record questions in one package, and standards interoperability and end-to-end governance conformance remain unproven.

papers.title: Continuous-Time Set-Transformers for Asynchronous WiFi-IMU Indoor Localization
papers.abstract: Indoor localization commonly combines WiFi received signal strength indicator (RSSI) fingerprints with inertial measurements. However, these sensor streams are sampled asynchronously at different rates; therefore, observations rarely align in time and may be missing or stale. Most existing methods resample the data onto a shared clock and process each modality using a separate branch. We instead present a continuous-time transformer that represents observations as an unordered set of timestamped tokens. Each token encodes its measurement, modality, and elapsed time since acquisition. A single attention block jointly fuses information across modalities and time, avoiding both resampling and modality-specific branches while remaining invariant to token order. During training, we randomly mask entire modalities and individual observations, enabling the model to operate under missing or outdated inputs. We validate the modality-specific encoders on their respective benchmarks and evaluate the fused model on both simulated and real datasets, including a crosssession dataset collected on unseen days. The proposed approach improves upon an open WiFi fingerprinting baseline under cross-session drift, remains competitive with learned fusion and dead-reckoning baselines, and degrades gracefully as observations become missing or stale. These results suggest that a single continuoustime transformer provides a practical framework for indoor localization from asynchronous sensors.
papers.summary: Indoor localization fuses WiFi received signal strength indicator (RSSI) fingerprints with inertial measurements, but the two streams arrive asynchronously at different rates, and most methods resample them onto a shared clock with separate per-modality branches. The proposed continuous-time transformer treats observations as an unordered set of timestamped tokens encoding measurement, modality, and elapsed time, fused by a single attention block, with entire modalities and individual observations randomly masked during training. On simulated and real data, including a cross-session dataset collected on unseen days, it **improves on an open WiFi fingerprinting baseline under cross-session drift**, stays competitive with learned fusion and dead-reckoning baselines, and degrades gracefully as inputs go missing or stale.

papers.title: The Indic Token Tax in 2026: Measuring Tokenizer. Disparity and Its Cost for the Languages of India
papers.abstract: Commercial language model APIs bill per token, so a tokenizer that needs more tokens for the same content in one language makes that language more expensive, slower, and able to fit less text in a fixed context window. We measure this disparity for nine public tokenizers, including those of GPT-4, GPT-4o, Qwen2.5, DeepSeek-V3, Mistral-Nemo and four Sarvam models, on all 25 languages of India available in FLORES-200 (2,009 professionally translated sentences aligned with English) and on 13,732 human-translated Hinglish-English social media pairs from PHINC. On GPT-4o's tokenizer the same content needs between 1.57 times (Hindi) and 5.01 times (Odia) the tokens of English, and 13.7 times for Santali in Ol Chiki script; GPT-4's tokenizer needs up to 12.8 times. Sarvam-30B/105B is the only third-party tokenizer that stays below 2.6 times on every language (median 1.53). In an illustrative scenario using official list prices accessed on 5 November 2026 and stated assumptions, a support bot handling 100,000 chats a month on GPT-4o would cost about INR 56,640 in English and INR 102,829 in Marathi; these are estimates, not measured production costs. Against an openly licensed Hindi and Marathi morphological segmentation set, no tokenizer places more than 35% of its word-internal boundaries on morpheme boundaries (boundary F1 at most 0.48). In a companion paper we present a tokenizer that reduces this tax. Code, pinned artifacts and raw token counts are available at https://github.com/HavonAI/indic-token-tax.
papers.summary: Because commercial language model APIs bill per token, a tokenizer that needs more tokens for the same content makes a language costlier, slower, and less able to fit in a context window. The study measures this for nine public tokenizers, including those of `GPT-4`, `GPT-4o`, `Qwen2.5`, `DeepSeek-V3`, `Mistral-Nemo`, and four `Sarvam` models, on all 25 languages of India in `FLORES-200` and on 13,732 Hinglish-English pairs from `PHINC`. On the `GPT-4o` tokenizer, **the same content needs 1.57 times (Hindi) to 5.01 times (Odia) the tokens of English, and 13.7 times for Santali in Ol Chiki script**; the `Sarvam-30B/105B` tokenizer is the only third-party one staying below 2.6 times on every language. No tokenizer places more than 35% of its word-internal boundaries on morpheme boundaries in Hindi and Marathi, and an illustrative price scenario puts a support bot at about INR 56,640 per month in English versus INR 102,829 in Marathi.

papers.title: A Multi-Word Tokenizer for 204 Languages That Needs Fewer Tokens Than GPT-4o's, Including on English
papers.abstract: Languages of India need 1.6 to 14 times as many tokens as English on GPT-4o's tokenizer for the same content, which makes them more expensive and slower to serve. We train tokenizers from scratch on human-written text in about 200 languages. Havon v3 is a byte-level BPE tokenizer with 262,144 tokens and a pre-tokenizer that keeps combining marks with their letters and chunks scripts written without spaces. On FLORES-200 devtest it needs fewer tokens than GPT-4o's o200k_base on all 25 languages of India (median 0.74 of GPT-4o's count) and on 172 of 204 languages, but 7% more on English. Havon v4 adds a second, multi-word training stage (SuperBPE) to v3. At exactly GPT-4o's vocabulary size of 200,019 tokens, v4 needs 6.1% fewer tokens than GPT-4o on English and fewer on 161 of 204 languages and all 25 languages of India (median 0.74); at the same size, v3 needs 9.4% more on English and wins on 133. With 262,144 tokens, v4 needs 9.6% fewer tokens on English and fewer on 182 of 204 languages, and with 524,288 tokens it needs fewer on 203 of 204. The gains are largest for English, Hindi and the Romance languages; scripts without spaces, such as Khmer, Burmese and Tibetan, gain little and lose subword merges. Havon v5 replaces v4's Python-only code sample with permissively licensed code in 15 languages: on code it needs 1.03 to 1.22 times GPT-4o's tokens, against 1.11 to 1.29 for v4, while keeping all 25 languages of India (median 0.74, all significant under a sentence-level bootstrap) and English (0.94). These are compression results only: we have not yet evaluated a model trained with v4 or v5.
papers.summary: Indian languages need 1.6 to 14 times as many tokens as English under GPT-4o's tokenizer, raising serving cost and latency. The authors train byte-level byte-pair encoding (BPE) tokenizers from scratch on roughly 200 languages: `Havon v3` uses a pre-tokenizer that keeps combining marks with their letters and chunks scripts written without spaces, `Havon v4` adds a multi-word `SuperBPE` training stage, and `Havon v5` broadens the code sample to 15 programming languages. On `FLORES-200` devtest, **`v4` at exactly GPT-4o's vocabulary size of 200,019 tokens needs 6.1% fewer tokens than `o200k_base` on English and fewer on 161 of 204 languages, including all 25 languages of India**, whereas `v3` needs more tokens on English. These are compression results only; no model has yet been trained with `v4` or `v5`.

papers.title: The Left Ripple of Byte-Pair Encoding: Certified Lookbehind for Every Dictionary
papers.abstract: Berglund and van der Merwe formalized byte-pair encoding and bounded how far an appended string can change a tokenization, leaving the converse open: how far can a string prepended on the left change it, which dictionaries make that ripple infinite, and can it be computed efficiently when finite? We answer all three for every dictionary. The origin radius, how far a prepend can change covering spans, is decided with radius certificates by a product of two runs of the automaton that guesses the final tokens, in time polynomial in the dictionary written out, and it is infinite exactly when one periodic word has two canonical tilings with no common boundary. Under their ordering condition it is infinite exactly when some rule (t, t) finds its two copies adjacent at its own stage, and such a rule makes any dictionary infinite. A finite radius makes every window of a width read off the radii have a cut, and the radius is finite exactly when such cuts are dense. The token machine completes for every dictionary, and the tokenization is subsequential, extending what Berglund, Martens and van der Merwe proved for proper ones under one pass per rule. A streaming tokenizer emits after every symbol exactly the tokens that no continuation changes, in polynomial time, answering a question of Dalirrooyfard and Ye. Boundedness of the label measure, the edit distance of the token sequences, is decided for every dictionary in polynomial time as well, and under the ordering condition the largest distance one edit causes over dictionaries of m rules lies asymptotically between m^2/10 and m^2/2. GPT-2's merge table carries 244 effective self-pairs, so its origin radius is infinite from the forty-second merge on, and that of cl100k, o200k and Llama 3 from their first. Every measured number is its program's output, and what is not executed is named.
papers.summary: Earlier formal work on byte-pair encoding (BPE) bounded how far an appended string can change a tokenization but left open how far a string prepended on the left can do so. The authors answer this for every dictionary, giving a polynomial-time procedure that decides and certifies this "origin radius", a characterization of when it is infinite, and a streaming tokenizer that emits after each symbol exactly the tokens no continuation can change. Applied to real merge tables, **the radius is infinite for `GPT-2` from its forty-second merge on, and for `cl100k`, `o200k` and `Llama 3` from their first merge**. They also show that boundedness of the edit distance between token sequences is decidable in polynomial time.

papers.title: Elicitation of the parameters of a multi-criteria sorting model
papers.abstract: Multiple-criteria decision aiding (MCDA) proposes models and methods for different types of decision problems such as choice, ranking or sorting. Such models involve various parameters that must be elicited. In the elicitation process, all necessary information has to be taken from the decision-maker. For this, several direct and indirect elicitation methods are suggested in the literature. In this work, we concentrate on direct elicitation: we aim at providing a rigorous elicitation procedure for the parameters of the Non-Compensatory Sorting model (NCS), which has been characterized by an axiomatic analysis. A basic version of the NCS model is considered, i.e., a model with two categories and no vetoes. The parameters are the set of sufficient coalitions of criteria and the profile separating the two categories. Regarding the sufficient coalitions, we propose several questioning algorithms that engraft questions on classical graph exploration algorithms such as depth-first search. Such algorithms are implemented and evaluated by simulation. For eliciting the limit profile, we design a questioning algorithm using dichotomy. Questioning algorithms can be optimal in the worst case or on average. An optimal algorithm in the worst case has been proposed by Hansel in the framework of monotone Boolean functions. We implement and evaluate this algorithm as a variant of the depth-first search approaches. Regarding optimal questioning strategies on average, we evaluate decision trees for up to four criteria. On the other hand, we assess how more general is NCS as compared to MR-Sort, a particular case of the NCS model in which sufficient coalitions can be represented by additive weights.
papers.summary: Multiple-criteria decision aiding (MCDA) models have parameters that must be elicited from a decision-maker, and this work designs a direct questioning procedure for the Non-Compensatory Sorting (`NCS`) model in its basic form with two categories and no vetoes. **The set of sufficient coalitions of criteria is elicited by questioning algorithms grafted onto graph exploration such as depth-first search, including Hansel's worst-case-optimal algorithm for monotone Boolean functions**, while the profile separating the two categories is found by dichotomy. The algorithms are evaluated by simulation, with average-case-optimal decision trees studied for up to four criteria. The authors also assess how much more general `NCS` is than `MR-Sort`, the special case in which coalitions are represented by additive weights.

papers.title: INTENT: Out-of-Sample, Out-of-Time, and Cold-Start Evaluation on User Event Sequences
papers.abstract: Banks now train foundation models on ordered sequences of customer events such as transactions, app sessions, and authorizations. Deployed, such a model predicts forward in time, often for customers and merchants absent from training, yet each is evaluated on private data, so no two can be compared. Public benchmarks for such sequences rarely test a period the model has not seen; recommendation studies usually hold out each user's last events instead. We present INTENT (INTEraction, Novelty, and Transfer evaluation for next-action prediction), a public benchmark that scores a model in seven cells defined by whether the user, the period, and the target item appeared in training. An audit of 59 public dataset families retains five datasets; the most common defect is the lack of a calendar timestamp that orders events. No date lies within the time span of all five datasets, so each is split at its own cutoff, chosen by one rule fixed before any model is evaluated. Summed over the datasets, every cell holds at least 111,769 users. In reference results the cell determines the best model: a transformer leads on seen items after the cutoff but scores zero on new items, a variant that embeds item metadata helps mainly on MicroLens, and repeating the user's last item leads on new items in four of five datasets. This parameter-free control also shows that on three datasets most of the score lost after the cutoff reflects changed behavior rather than the model. The pipeline, the cutoff rule, and the per-cell user counts are publicly available.
papers.summary: Foundation models trained on sequences of customer events such as transactions and app sessions are usually evaluated on private data and rarely on a time period the model has not seen. `INTENT` (INTEraction, Novelty, and Transfer evaluation for next-action prediction) is a public benchmark that scores a model in seven cells defined by whether the user, the period, and the target item appeared in training, built from five datasets retained after auditing 59 public dataset families. In reference results the best model depends on the cell: **a transformer leads on seen items after the cutoff but scores zero on new items, where simply repeating the user's last item leads in four of five datasets**. That parameter-free control also indicates that on three datasets most of the score lost after the cutoff comes from changed user behavior, not from the model.

papers.title: IC-GNN: Modeling Individualized Brain Community Organization for Disease Prediction
papers.abstract: Brain networks exhibit modular organization, where community structures vary substantially across individuals and diseases. Understanding these individual differences is crucial for advancing both basic neuroscience research and precision medicine. However, widely used predefined group-level brain atlases often overlook this heterogeneity. While individualized functional parcellations capture subject-specific variability in community boundaries, they often require lengthy scan times to achieve fine-grained resolution and complicate cross-subject comparisons. To address this trade-off and investigate how individualized community organization captures disease-associated changes across individuals, we propose IC-GNN, an atlas-anchored model that forms distinct, individualized functional communities directly over atlas-defined brain regions. IC-GNN derives discrete, individualized multiscale communities from resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data, refines community-guided connections, and adapts shared regional weights to each subject's community context to enable both individualized modeling and group-level comparisons. Across more than 30,000 participants from ABIDE (autism spectrum disorder), ADNI (Alzheimer's disease), and the UK Biobank (depression), IC-GNN achieves the highest performance compared with 15 baseline methods. We further demonstrate that these individualized communities are reproducible within scans and across sessions, and carry predictive power on their own. Furthermore, IC-GNN identifies disease-related shifts in community organization that align with established literature, highlighting a promising approach for modeling individualized community structure for disease prediction and biomarker discovery.
authors: for the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative
papers.summary: Group-level brain atlases ignore individual differences in how brain regions organize into communities, while fully individualized parcellations need long scans and make subjects hard to compare. `IC-GNN` is a graph neural network that derives discrete, multiscale, subject-specific communities over atlas-defined regions from resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), refines community-guided connections, and adapts shared regional weights to each subject's community context. Across **more than 30,000 participants from `ABIDE` (autism), `ADNI` (Alzheimer's disease), and the `UK Biobank` (depression), it outperforms 15 baseline methods**. The learned communities are reported to be reproducible within scans and across sessions, to be predictive on their own, and to shift with disease in ways consistent with prior literature.

papers.title: One Temperature to Rule Them All?
papers.abstract: Inference-time sampling is a central mechanism for improving large language models, with temperature controlling the tradeoff between reliability and diversity. While recent work suggests that varying temperature across samples can improve multi-sample inference, simple fixed-temperature schemes remain the standard in practice. We investigate this discrepancy in the canonical pass@K setting, asking when temperature diversity is useful, and when a single tuned temperature suffices. To this end, we analyze per-question success probabilities across multiple models and datasets, tracking how they vary with sampling temperature. We identify several consistent properties of these profiles, including that harder questions are less likely to share efficient sampling temperatures, although this trend is only logarithmic in hardness. We then derive an efficient method for evaluating the theoretically optimal multi-temperature allocation scheme, and show that although such a scheme improves performance, its gains over single-temperature baselines are typically modest when temperature is tuned as a function of the sampling budget K. We explain this phenomenon through mathematical mechanisms that we call dulling effects, and show how they ensure the robustness of temperature choices across different question distributions. Our results clarify when multi-temperature sampling is useful, and how temperatures should ideally be chosen.
authors: Aviv Orly (School of Physics and Astronomy
Ori Shem-Ur (School of Physics and Astronomy
Yaron Oz (School of Physics and Astronomy
papers.summary: Varying sampling temperature across samples has been proposed for multi-sample large language model inference, yet fixed-temperature schemes remain standard; the authors ask when temperature diversity actually helps in the pass@K setting. They analyze how per-question success probabilities change with temperature across several models and datasets, and derive an efficient way to evaluate the theoretically optimal multi-temperature allocation. **The optimal multi-temperature scheme yields only modest gains over a single temperature once that temperature is tuned as a function of the sampling budget K**. They attribute this to mathematical mechanisms they call dulling effects, which also make temperature choices robust across question distributions, and note that harder questions are less likely to share efficient temperatures, though only logarithmically in hardness.

papers.title: Catch It Where It Happens: Real Time Error Correction During LLM Reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly trusted with mathematical, scientific and engineering work, yet their mistakes are often confidently written and hard to spot. A single wrong step tends to propagate, making the model waste inference tokens following a false premise. Existing safeguards either check only the final answer and restart from scratch, or rely on a verifier LLM that competes for GPU capacity and slows down response time. We propose online, deterministic verification: many kinds of reasoning steps can be validated by code, so a step can be verified in real time, as it is written, without any model call or GPU use. Whenever a check fails, we point out the mistake and let the model continue from the same spot. We demonstrate this approach on symbolic mathematics, where derivations already contain explicit expressions that a computer algebra system can check in milliseconds. Tested on the ASyMoB benchmark with three open-weights models, our online validation improves accuracy by 1.4-5.6 percentage points, corresponding to a 1.8-14.9% net reduction in incorrect answers, while increasing token usage by only 6-7%. Because the verifier is independent of the model, the approach complements progress in LLMs rather than competing with it: every new model can benefit immediately, and the benefit grows as deterministic checkers extend to more kinds of reasoning steps.
papers.summary: A single wrong step in a large language model's (LLM's) reasoning tends to propagate, and existing safeguards either check only the final answer or call a second verifier model that costs GPU time. The authors instead verify reasoning steps deterministically with code as they are written, flagging a failed check and letting the model continue from the same spot, and demonstrate this on symbolic mathematics using a computer algebra system that checks expressions in milliseconds. On the `ASyMoB` benchmark with three open-weights models, **accuracy improves by 1.4 to 5.6 percentage points, a 1.8 to 14.9% net reduction in incorrect answers, for only 6 to 7% more tokens**. Because the verifier needs no model call, it can be attached to any model.

papers.title: Building World Models from Intrinsic Motivation
papers.abstract: In the absence of extrinsic rewards or task supervision, human behavior is guided by intrinsic motivation---neural signals that drive curiosity, creativity, play, and other essential facets of intelligence. Intrinsic motivation plays an important developmental role in building robust world models that enable generalization and adaptation. Yet existing studies leave open how a broad range of intrinsic motivations interacts with world-model representation learning to support downstream control. This limits our understanding of which intrinsically collected experiences build reusable models. To address these gaps, we integrate 24 intrinsic objectives, including established methods and explicit variants spanning curiosity, entropy, and competency, into a common model-based reinforcement learning framework. We evaluate the world models they build through zero-shot, few-shot, and multi-task control in locomotion, manipulation, and open-ended gaming environments, using three representation-learning strategies: observation reconstruction, latent prediction, and redundancy reduction. Curiosity-driven exploration with observation reconstruction yields the strongest aggregate family profile, although the best individual pairing depends on the experiment. In compositional vision-based tasks, intrinsic motivation derived from both episodic and lifelong novelty---providing a complementary memory to the world model's generic recurrent state---achieves the best zero-shot transfer and few-shot adaptation. These findings motivate designing intrinsic motivation and representation learning jointly. Our results demonstrate world models as a powerful tool for measuring the quality of intrinsically motivated experience, and positions intrinsic motivation as a key ingredient for building world models autonomously.
papers.summary: How different forms of intrinsic motivation interact with world-model representation learning to support downstream control has not been compared systematically. The authors place 24 intrinsic objectives spanning curiosity, entropy, and competency in one model-based reinforcement learning framework and evaluate the resulting world models on zero-shot, few-shot, and multi-task control in locomotion, manipulation, and open-ended game environments under three representation-learning strategies: observation reconstruction, latent prediction, and redundancy reduction. **Curiosity-driven exploration combined with observation reconstruction gives the strongest aggregate results**, though the best individual pairing varies by experiment. On compositional vision-based tasks, motivation that combines episodic and lifelong novelty achieves the best zero-shot transfer and few-shot adaptation.

papers.title: ASPIRE: An Agentic System-Identification Platform for Iterative Reasoning and Exploration
papers.abstract: System identification requires expert decisions on the identification method, incorporation of prior physical knowledge, and model validation. We propose ASPIRE, a framework for nonlinear system identification in which a large language model agent selects and executes the identification method. ASPIRE constructs closed-form, nonlinear static or dynamic models from measured data, optionally supplemented by a system description, the intended use of the model, and physical requirements expressed formally or in natural language. Each model includes its parameters, an estimation record, an interpretation of its terms, and an error evaluated on test data inaccessible to the agent. Formal physical requirements are verified independently. ASPIRE operates autonomously or interactively, allowing the agent to ask questions and the user to request further analyses and identification rounds. We evaluate ASPIRE on three measured systems: a mobile robot, a rotational system with dry friction, and a laboratory fermenter. Each system is tested with and without a description, in five runs per task. All 30 runs delivered valid models, at a cost of 0.96 to 3.38 US dollars per run. An assessment by the authors found that, for the 30 models recommended by the agent, one per run, the interpretation of the model and the documentation of its structure selection and parameter estimation fully satisfied 132 of 150 assessed items and partly satisfied 18. The most frequent discrepancy, found in nine models, concerned inaccurate or unsupported claims about model structure selection.
papers.summary: Nonlinear system identification depends on expert choices about the method, the use of prior physical knowledge, and validation. `ASPIRE` hands these choices to a large language model agent that selects and runs the identification method, producing closed-form static or dynamic models from measured data with documented parameters, term interpretations, independently verified physical requirements, and an error computed on test data the agent cannot access. On three measured systems (a mobile robot, a rotational system with dry friction, and a laboratory fermenter), **all 30 runs delivered valid models at a cost of 0.96 to 3.38 US dollars per run**. In the authors' own assessment of the recommended models, 132 of 150 documentation and interpretation items were fully satisfied and 18 partly, the most frequent problem being inaccurate or unsupported claims about model structure selection.

papers.title: Just Image Transformers with Late-Stage Pixel Refinement
papers.abstract: Recent work on latent-free diffusion transformers has demonstrated the feasibility of training image generators without a latent VAE. This avoids compression artifacts from the VAE and simplifies the training pipeline. In particular, JiT showed that even a standard transformer can be trained to generate images when the model is trained to predict the final image ($x$-prediction). Even though JiT unlocks training efficiency comparable to latent models, it still suffers from reduced image quality likely arising from modeling the image as a collection of large patches. In this work, we revisit JiT and show that adding simple convolutional pixel-pathway layers in a post-training phase significantly improves generation quality. Moreover, we show that the added pixel-pathway does not need to be active in the early denoising stages, and can be activated as late as in the last $20\%$ of the denoising process. Our experiments on ImageNet@256 show improvements compared to the original JiT results, achieving an FID of $1.78$ (from $2.34$ with corrected sampling), without using additional losses.
papers.summary: Diffusion transformers that work directly on pixels avoid the compression artifacts of a latent variational autoencoder, but `JiT`, which trains a standard transformer to predict the final image, loses quality by modeling images as large patches. The authors add simple convolutional pixel-pathway layers to `JiT` in a post-training phase and find the pathway only needs to be active late in sampling, as late as the last 20% of the denoising process. On `ImageNet` at 256x256, **FID improves to 1.78 from 2.34 (the original result with corrected sampling)** without any additional losses.

papers.title: Activation-Guided Graph Retrieval for Cognitive Memory Reconstruction in Language Model Systems
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented language model systems generally select context by query-conditioned relevance. We argue that long-lived AI systems require a second operator: activation-conditioned memory availability. We specify an architecture in which request and goal cues seed an authorized memory graph, activation and fan attenuation allocate a bounded traversal frontier, retrieved entities recursively emit cues, and a typed evidence graph is reconstructed before generation. The specification yields five architectural consequences about candidate selection, traversal control, graph regularization, evidence reconstruction, and reinforcement. We derive implementation-level cost estimates and define ablations, failure conditions, and a reproducible evaluation protocol. The central claim is narrowed or falsified if a simpler graph reranker matches full traversal on causal and temporal recovery under equal budgets. This architecture-and-analysis preprint reports no benchmark measurements. If the claim holds, retrieval returns the evidence path that makes a memory available, not only a ranked list.
papers.summary: Retrieval-augmented language model systems usually select context by relevance to the query; the authors argue that long-lived systems also need memory availability conditioned on activation. They specify an architecture in which request and goal cues seed a memory graph, activation with fan attenuation bounds the traversal frontier, retrieved entities recursively emit new cues, and a typed evidence graph is reconstructed before generation. The preprint derives cost estimates and defines ablations, failure conditions, and an evaluation protocol, but **reports no benchmark measurements**. The authors state that the central claim is narrowed or falsified if a simpler graph reranker matches full traversal on causal and temporal recovery under equal budgets.

papers.title: Which Successes Make Good References? Action-Sequence Alignment for Multi-Turn On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) reduces train-inference distribution mismatch by supervising a student on its own trajectories. For multi-turn tool-use agents, conditioning the teacher on a validated same-task successful trajectory as a reference can provide useful hindsight, but different successes may reach incompatible interaction states and offer misleading supervision. We cast successful-reference selection as a free-target optimal transport problem, which reduces to assigning each failed trajectory its most compatible successful reference. Because latent state paths are hidden, we use action-sequence alignment as an observable proxy for compatibility and instantiate it with longest common subsequence (LCS), which identifies a shared ordered backbone of actions while allowing recoverable detours. This perspective makes trajectory compatibility the central criterion for reference selection in multi-turn OPD. Experiments on ALFWorld and the airline domain of $\tau^3$-bench show that LCS is the only evaluated reference selector to improve over reference-free OPD on both ALFWorld overall scores and all three airline metrics. Without further optimization, the airline-trained models also transfer to the retail domain, where LCS improves all three metrics.
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) supervises a student on its own trajectories, and for multi-turn tool-use agents the teacher can be conditioned on a successful trajectory for the same task, but a success that passed through incompatible interaction states can give misleading supervision. The authors frame reference selection as a free-target optimal transport problem that reduces to assigning each failed trajectory its most compatible success, and use longest common subsequence (LCS) alignment over action sequences as an observable proxy for compatibility. On `ALFWorld` and the airline domain of `tau^3-bench`, **LCS is the only evaluated reference selector that improves over reference-free OPD on both `ALFWorld` overall scores and all three airline metrics**. The airline-trained models also transfer to the retail domain without further optimization, where LCS again improves all three metrics.

papers.title: Byzantine-Robust Muon: Resilient Momentum Orthogonalization for Distributed Learning
papers.abstract: Optimization methods, including the Muon optimizer based on the Linear Minimization Oracle (LMO) and momentum orthogonalization, have shown strong empirical performance in large-scale and distributed learning, yet their robustness to adversarial behavior and data heterogeneity is not well understood. We study these methods within a unified first-order trust-region framework and analyze Muon-based updates with robust aggregation for Byzantine-robust distributed and federated learning. Our analysis does not rely on the i.i.d. assumption and introduces a non-Euclidean notion of heterogeneity consistent with the trust-region geometry. Under this framework, we establish convergence guarantees for both general non-convex and star-convex objectives. Our results provide a theoretical characterization of Byzantine-robust Muon-based optimization, with an additive heterogeneity error floor consistent with known impossibility results, under explicit aggregation assumptions. Under an explicit additive oracle-error condition, the guarantees also cover inexact orthogonalization, with the non-convex Byzantine terms in the bound's numerator unchanged but a smaller progress denominator. In simulated federated training with ResNet-18 and ViT-Tiny on CIFAR-10, additional image benchmarks, and a 38M-parameter byte-level language model on TinyStories, the tested Muon configuration attains higher attacked accuracy (lower perplexity) than the tested SGD and normalized-SGD configurations, and than sign updates on CIFAR-10. Fixed-honest controls further show a substantial RFA advantage over averaging under a bounded RFA-query attack, higher attacked accuracy for Muon-NS than tensorwise Euclidean normalization from shared checkpoints, and lower held-out TinyStories perplexity than a tuned AdamW baseline.
papers.summary: The `Muon` optimizer, built on momentum orthogonalization and a Linear Minimization Oracle (LMO), performs well in large-scale training, but its robustness to adversarial (Byzantine) workers and heterogeneous data has not been characterized. The authors analyze `Muon`-style updates with robust aggregation in a first-order trust-region framework using a non-Euclidean notion of heterogeneity and no i.i.d. assumption, and **prove convergence guarantees for non-convex and star-convex objectives with an additive heterogeneity error floor consistent with known impossibility results**; the guarantees extend to inexact orthogonalization. In simulated federated training of `ResNet-18` and `ViT-Tiny` on `CIFAR-10`, and of a 38M-parameter byte-level language model on `TinyStories`, the tested `Muon` configuration holds up better under attack than the tested SGD and normalized-SGD configurations.

papers.title: Agreeing on the Answer but Not the Reason: Measurement Limits of LLM Reasoning Failure Taxonomies
papers.abstract: Failure taxonomies for LLM reasoning are increasingly reported as measurements: papers state what fraction of a model's errors fall into named categories, then compare those fractions across models. We show that for one such category the reported fraction is largely a property of the measurement procedure. We defined Compositional Collapse (a model notices a required sub-part of a problem, then drops or misapplies it) and measured it across twelve models and eleven languages on a public multilingual math benchmark (2,316 graded records). First, 50.1% of failures carry evidence for more than one category, so the reported plurality depends on the order in which the classifier tests them: reversing two tests moves it in eleven of twelve models, and across all six orderings Collapse's share spans 26.4% to 76.4%. Second, agreement collapses for the category but not for the task. Native speakers of all eleven languages judged 179 transcripts, agreeing with our inspector at kappa = 0.932 on answer correctness but only kappa = 0.093 on Collapse. A second native speaker per language re-rated 142 items; on 121 determinate pairs the two humans agree with each other at kappa = 0.659, while each agrees with the inspector at kappa <= 0.094. Re-running the same inspector model with the human instructions verbatim raises kappa against Human 2 from 0.147 to 0.636, so the gap is largely attributable to the prompt, not the model. Third, the inspector labels Collapse 1.81 times as often as native speakers, but only 1.17 times once a defective benchmark item (a deleted clause in the Bengali and Chinese translations) is excluded. We recommend four cheap checks before comparing failure-mode rates across models: report label co-occurrence, permute the tie-break, validate on a shared independent sample, and audit systematic disagreements.
papers.summary: Papers on large language model (LLM) reasoning often report what fraction of errors fall into named failure categories and compare those fractions across models. The authors test how stable such numbers are by defining one category, Compositional Collapse (a model notices a required sub-part of a problem, then drops or misapplies it), and measuring it across twelve models and eleven languages on a multilingual math benchmark. Half of all failures carry evidence for more than one category, so the category's share ranges from 26.4% to 76.4% depending on the order in which the classifier tests them, and **native speakers agree with the automated inspector at kappa = 0.932 on answer correctness but only kappa = 0.093 on the category**, a gap largely attributable to the inspector's prompt. They recommend four checks before comparing failure rates: report label co-occurrence, permute the tie-break order, validate on a shared independent sample, and audit systematic disagreements.

papers.title: DOBB: Dynamic Oriented Bounding Boxes for Multi-Agent Collision Avoidance under State Uncertainty and Heterogeneous Dynamics
papers.abstract: Learning-based decentralized collision avoidance must remain reliable under state-estimation uncertainty and heterogeneous agent dynamics. Existing methods typically address these factors through training-domain variation or by exposing uncertainty and capability estimates to the policy at runtime. However, both leave the policy to infer how these quantities should alter the physical separation required for safe interaction, which can couple collision-avoidance behavior to relationships learned from the training distribution. We introduce the Dynamic Oriented Bounding Box (DOBB), an online geometric representation that maps the current state estimate, uncertainty, and agent-specific response characteristics into a dynamic, direction-dependent safety margin. We derive geometric features that jointly characterize the relative configuration and severity of interactions between agents' DOBBs, along with a reward function that preserves the physical interpretation of those interactions. Across four evaluation environments, DOBB achieves the lowest mean total failure rate of 2.6%. This performance persists under out-of-distribution shifts in actuation dynamics and state-estimation uncertainty, with collision-based failure remaining at or below 2.3% in every tested condition. We attribute this robustness to the geometric abstraction of the safety margin, which is less coupled to the specific uncertainty and actuation regimes encountered during training.
papers.summary: Learned decentralized collision-avoidance policies must stay reliable when state estimates are uncertain and agents have different dynamics, and existing methods leave the policy to infer how those factors should change the required separation. The Dynamic Oriented Bounding Box (`DOBB`) is an online geometric representation that converts the current state estimate, its uncertainty, and each agent's response characteristics into a direction-dependent safety margin, paired with geometric features and a reward function defined on interactions between agents' boxes. Across four evaluation environments it achieves **the lowest mean total failure rate, 2.6%**. Collision-based failures stay at or below 2.3% under out-of-distribution shifts in actuation dynamics and state-estimation uncertainty.

papers.title: Autonomous Optimization of Numerical Algorithms by an AI Agent: Application to Atomistic Simulation
papers.abstract: Coding agents built on large language models, run in automated improvement loops, can discover more efficient algorithms. We present AIOA, a framework that brings this approach to the numerical algorithms of atomistic simulation: an agent improves an algorithm against a pre-specified metric in a loop guarded by verifiers it cannot alter. Applied to ASE, a widely used atomistic simulation library, AIOA targets two facets of an algorithm: its implementation, rewritten to run faster with unchanged results, and the method itself, redesigned to converge with fewer force evaluations. Agents made six kernels 22-24 times faster on average in Python with NumPy and SciPy. On unseen problems, optimizers from the best configuration needed 3.1-3.4 times fewer force evaluations than L-BFGS for structure relaxation and 4.6-17 times fewer than standard climbing-image nudged elastic band calculations for reaction paths. The agents' optimizers also contain two algorithmic components we did not find in the literature.
papers.summary: `AIOA` is a framework in which a large language model coding agent improves numerical algorithms for atomistic simulation against a pre-specified metric, inside a loop guarded by verifiers the agent cannot alter. Applied to `ASE`, a widely used atomistic simulation library, it targets both implementations (faster code with unchanged results) and the methods themselves (convergence in fewer force evaluations). **Agents made six kernels 22 to 24 times faster on average in Python with NumPy and SciPy**. On unseen problems, the best agent-designed optimizers needed 3.1 to 3.4 times fewer force evaluations than `L-BFGS` for structure relaxation and 4.6 to 17 times fewer than standard climbing-image nudged elastic band calculations for reaction paths, and contain two algorithmic components the authors did not find in the literature.

papers.title: Teaching the Harness: Student-Aware Skill Transfer for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Effective teaching requires reasoning about the learner as well as the task, a capacity that Theory of Mind describes as inferring another agent's latent state from its behavior. We ask whether a stronger LLM teaches a fixed student better when it applies this principle. The student is an LLM agent acting through a harness that fixes its tools, context, and action budget, so a procedure that helps one model can exhaust the budget of another. We introduce Student-Aware Teaching (SAT). The teacher builds a learner model that pairs an empirical profile with hypotheses about the student's limitations, tests these hypotheses with diagnostic probes, and writes reusable skills for the diagnosed failures. A skill enters the library only after it raises success on matched development tasks. With Claude-Sonnet-5 teaching DeepSeek-V4-Flash, SAT reaches 86.46% task success across four primary runs, leading both a profile-free teacher with the same framework (81.04%) and the untaught student (75.00%) in each run. Removing the analytical learner model lowers both prediction and success, and under misleading learner profiles none of the 48 candidate skills passes admission. When DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Gemini-3.8-Flash exchange libraries, each performs better with its own. Saved libraries keep average gains of up to 11.1 points after the teacher leaves. The benefit depends on a student that can follow instructions and a deployment route that delivers them.
papers.summary: A procedure that helps one large language model (LLM) agent can exhaust the action budget of another running in the same harness, so the authors ask whether a stronger model teaches a fixed student better when it explicitly models that student. In Student-Aware Teaching (`SAT`), the teacher builds a learner model from an empirical profile and hypotheses about the student's limitations, tests them with diagnostic probes, and writes reusable skills that enter the library only if they raise success on matched development tasks. With `Claude-Sonnet-5` teaching `DeepSeek-V4-Flash`, **`SAT` reaches 86.46% task success, against 81.04% for a profile-free teacher and 75.00% for the untaught student**. Skill libraries work better for the student they were written for than when swapped between `DeepSeek-V4-Flash` and `Gemini-3.8-Flash`, and saved libraries keep average gains of up to 11.1 points after the teacher is removed.

papers.title: Everything in its right place: attention is a radio head
papers.abstract: Attention, the core of language models, is a digital calculation over tokens: an exponential selects them, a division normalizes and a positional code sets the order. We show that attention can instead emerge from the synchronization of a receiver with its context tokens. Each past token is an oscillator whose state carries its content and whose frequency drifts with its age. The present token selects them by content, aligning an antenna with its query, and by position, setting the frequency of a receiver with its dial. Solving Kuramoto's problem for this receiver yields an attention layer in closed form with two phases: above a critical coupling set by the context, the receiver locks and its weights normalize; below it, it stays silent and its weights sum to less than one. Trained networks use both phases to select, abstain and count, fail where the theory predicts and keep reading far beyond the training length. Each part of attention finds its place in one device, a radio head: it tunes in to what to hear and when, and stays silent when nothing relevant is on air.
papers.summary: Attention is recast as a physical synchronization process instead of a digital computation with an exponential, a normalization, and a positional code. Each past token is modeled as an oscillator whose state carries its content and whose frequency drifts with its age, and the current token acts as a receiver that selects by content and by position. Solving the Kuramoto synchronization problem for this receiver gives **a closed-form attention layer with two phases: above a critical coupling it locks and its weights normalize, and below it stays silent with weights summing to less than one**. Trained networks use both phases to select, abstain, and count, fail where the theory predicts, and keep reading well beyond the training length.

papers.title: VIGOR: Benchmarking Visual Rationale Correctness in Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are typically evaluated by whether they produce correct answers, but correctness alone does not reveal whether their outputs are supported by the right visual evidence. We introduce VIGOR, a benchmark for evaluating VIsually GrOunded Rationales in MLLMs. VIGOR represents visual rationales as explicit concepts paired with pixel-level groundings, covering multiple abstraction levels including low-level visual properties, intermediate structures, objects, parts and high-level motion, relations. To construct VIGOR at scale, we develop an automatic annotation framework that reuses existing dense supervision when available and generates missing concept groundings through proposal-based annotation followed by conservative multimodal verification. Using VIGOR, we evaluate whether MLLMs "look at what they say" by comparing model-derived visual evidence for each expressed concept against annotated ground-truth rationales.
