Our results show that current MLLMs exhibit limited visual rationale correctness and reveal distinct grounding failures across concept levels. VIGOR provides a benchmark and scalable data construction pipeline for studying whether MLLM outputs are supported by appropriate visual evidence. Code is available at https://github.com/deep-real/VIGOR
papers.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are usually scored on answer correctness, which does not show whether an answer rests on the right visual evidence. `VIGOR` is a benchmark of visually grounded rationales, represented as explicit concepts paired with pixel-level groundings across abstraction levels from low-level visual properties to objects, parts, motion, and relations, and built with an automatic annotation pipeline that reuses existing dense supervision and verifies newly generated groundings conservatively. Comparing the visual evidence a model uses for each concept it mentions against the annotations, the authors find that **current MLLMs show limited visual rationale correctness**, with distinct grounding failures at different concept levels.

papers.title: How Much of Your VLA Is kNN
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models now exceed 95% success on the LIBERO simulation benchmark, yet it remains unclear how much of this performance requires generalization beyond the training demonstrations. In this work, we show that retrieving nearby demonstrations and reusing their action chunks achieves a success rate of 91.7 % on LIBERO without policy training. Under LIBERO-Plus perturbations, retrieval shows the smallest drop of all evaluated policies. Across nine publicly available VLAs, fine-tuning mostly makes the vision-language backbone a better retrieval key, and the actions of the VLAs remain close to the demonstrations. In addition, we introduce Local Action Consistency (LAC), an offline metric that measures whether nearby observations in representation space are also associated with similar future actions. We show that LAC tracks the success rate of retrieval and can guide the training of a retrieval key. Our evaluation and source code are available at https://github.com/sereact/lerobot_knn.
papers.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models now exceed 95% success on the `LIBERO` simulation benchmark, and the authors ask how much of that requires generalizing beyond the training demonstrations. **Retrieving nearby demonstrations and replaying their action chunks reaches 91.7% success on `LIBERO` with no policy training**, and shows the smallest drop of all evaluated policies under `LIBERO-Plus` perturbations. Across nine public VLAs, fine-tuning mostly turns the vision-language backbone into a better retrieval key while the predicted actions stay close to the demonstrations. They also introduce Local Action Consistency (`LAC`), an offline metric of whether observations that are close in representation space lead to similar future actions, which tracks retrieval success and can guide training of a retrieval key.

papers.title: Cognitive Multi-Agent Search and Rescue: Language-Grounded Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning for Collaborative Robotics
papers.abstract: Effective search and rescue (SAR) operations require autonomous systems capable of coordinating multiple heterogeneous agents, adapting to dynamic hazards, and aligning with human mission intent. Existing language-guided reinforcement learning (RL) methods primarily focus on single-agent instruction following and lack mechanisms for team-level coordination in complex, partially observable environments. This paper presents a Cognitive Multi-Agent Framework based on Language-Grounded Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (LG-HRL) that integrates natural-language understanding, hierarchical policy decomposition, and a shared cognitive workspace to achieve cohesive multi-agent behavior in SAR scenarios. Human instructions are interpreted by a large language model (LLM) and transformed into structured semantic cues that guide high-level strategy selection and role assignment across UAV and UGV agents. A formal Language-Grounded Multi-Agent Hierarchical Decision Process (LG-MAHDP) is introduced to model the interplay between semantic grounding, hierarchical control, and distributed coordination. Comprehensive experiments in a simulated disaster environment show that LG-HRL improves learning speed by 2.3 times, increases coordination coherence by 37%, and enhances subgoal accuracy and hazard avoidance by 46% and 31%, respectively. The system achieves 20-30% higher victim rescue rates, demonstrates emergent role specialization, and adapts immediately to human verbal updates. Ablation studies confirm that both the shared cognitive workspace and language grounding are critical to overall system performance. Overall, this work establishes a new paradigm for language-guided multi-agent SAR robotics, demonstrating that semantic grounding combined with hierarchical reasoning enables safer, more efficient, and more interpretable autonomous rescue operations.
papers.summary: Language-guided reinforcement learning has mostly targeted single-agent instruction following, leaving team coordination in partially observable search and rescue (SAR) settings unaddressed. The proposed `LG-HRL` (Language-Grounded Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning) framework uses a large language model to turn human instructions into structured semantic cues that drive high-level strategy selection and role assignment across aerial and ground robots, which coordinate through a shared cognitive workspace. In a simulated disaster environment the authors report 2.3 times faster learning and **20-30% higher victim rescue rates**, along with emergent role specialization and immediate adaptation to verbal updates. Ablations indicate that both the shared workspace and the language grounding are needed for these gains.

papers.title: High Probability Risk Control for Online Policy Learning
papers.abstract: We study risk control for online policy learning, where an agent adaptively collects data and aims to learn a new policy whose risk stays below a tolerance threshold at every round with high probability. Such policy updates and data collection induce feedback covariate shift (FCS): observed data depend on history through evolving policies and the data-collection process. FCS brings two substantive problems for risk control: 1) efficient risk evaluation for each candidate policy and 2) valid policy selection with high-probability risk control. To address these, we propose a permutation-based weighted risk evaluator with weights efficiently approximated by the Sinkhorn algorithm and select policies whose estimated risk upper confidence bounds (UCB) fall below the target threshold, with the UCB obtained through a proposed Gaussian bootstrap method. Theoretically, we prove that our risk evaluator has a no-larger variance upper bound than that of the standard importance-weighted evaluator. Our policy control method also yields an asymptotically valid simultaneous risk bound and provides asymptotic high-probability risk control for the selected policy. Empirically, we evaluate our method on the online contextual bandit problem, safe question answering benchmark, and Medical Claim Filtering tasks. Our method maintains the target risk level, achieves lower risk than baseline methods, has lower variance in risk estimation, and achieves reliable policy selection with high-probability risk control. Further ablation studies support our theoretical claims.
papers.summary: When an agent updates its policy while collecting data, the observed data depend on past policies, a situation called feedback covariate shift that complicates keeping a new policy's risk below a threshold at every round. The authors propose a permutation-based weighted risk evaluator whose weights are approximated with the `Sinkhorn` algorithm, and select policies whose upper confidence bound on risk, obtained from a Gaussian bootstrap, falls under the target. They prove the evaluator's **variance upper bound is no larger than that of the standard importance-weighted evaluator** and that the selection procedure gives asymptotic high-probability risk control. Experiments on contextual bandits, a safe question answering benchmark, and medical claim filtering show the target risk level is maintained with lower estimation variance than baselines.

papers.title: AI Alignment Is Neither Solvable nor Sufficient
papers.abstract: Humans and AI systems increasingly act within the same social and economic environments. Alignment, the goal of ensuring that AI systems act in accordance with human values, is widely regarded as a central challenge for ensuring that AI benefits society while avoiding harm. We argue that this endeavor is misguided. First, alignment is not well defined, as it presumes a sufficiently stable and identifiable set of human intentions or values. Second, where a concrete notion of alignment can be specified, it is not solvable. Third, where alignment appears solvable, solving it would not necessarily mitigate the negative consequences of AI. A key reason is that alignment is typically framed as a property of individual AI systems, while the resulting hybrid societies of humans and machines are complex systems shaped by interactions and feedback loops. Emergent risks, and not only those posed by individual misaligned systems, are therefore likely to become a major source of harm. We conclude that AI safety is an ongoing challenge and not a problem that can be solved once and for all by verifying a particular model property.
papers.summary: A position piece arguing that the goal of aligning AI systems with human values is misguided as a route to safe AI. The authors make three claims: alignment is not well defined because it presumes a stable, identifiable set of human values; where a concrete notion can be specified, it is not solvable; and where it appears solvable, solving it would not necessarily prevent harm. Their central reason is that alignment is framed as a property of individual systems, whereas **emergent risks from interactions and feedback loops in hybrid human-machine societies** are likely to become a major source of harm. They conclude that AI safety is an ongoing challenge and not something settled by verifying a single model property.

papers.title: RadRef: A Reference-Free Metric for Radiology Report Generation
papers.abstract: AI-generated radiology reports are usually evaluated by comparison with a radiologist-authored reference, leaving no way to score them when no reference exists. We introduce RadRef, a reference-free metric that scores report claims against image-derived beliefs over a clinical finding vocabulary, weighted by relevance to the clinical indication. On ReXVal, RadRef achieves 73.1% agreement on non-tied same-radiograph report pairs with radiologist rankings, comparable to leading reference-based metrics overall. It is also competitive on false findings and has its clearest relative result on omissions (missed findings). We further evaluate 100 model-generated and 100 radiologist-authored reports from 100 MIMIC-CXR studies, all independently annotated by two board-certified radiologists. On omissions, RadRef attains Kendall's tau-b = 0.295, against 0.386 between the two readers themselves, and no compared metric differs significantly from RadRef on this target. The same image-grounded representation provides a false-finding readout, RadRef-FF, with tau-b = 0.32 on ReXVal and 0.29 in the reader study, without requiring a reference. Controlled perturbations confirm that RadRef depends on the radiograph, report, and clinical indication. RadRef enables image-grounded evaluation before a radiologist-authored reference exists, supporting quality monitoring of report-generation systems in clinical settings, and complements reference-based metrics when one is available.
papers.summary: AI-generated radiology reports are normally scored against a radiologist-written reference, so they cannot be evaluated when none exists. `RadRef` is a reference-free metric that checks a report's claims against beliefs derived from the image over a vocabulary of clinical findings, weighted by relevance to the clinical indication. On `ReXVal` it reaches **73.1% agreement with radiologist rankings** on non-tied report pairs, comparable to leading reference-based metrics, with its clearest relative result on missed findings. In a reader study on 100 `MIMIC-CXR` studies it attains a Kendall's tau-b of 0.295 on omissions, against 0.386 between the two radiologists themselves.

papers.title: Making Strides in Symbolic Imitation Learning: Offline Demonstrations, Online Tuning
papers.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) methods have been the dominant paradigm in continuous control tasks due to their efficacy in function approximation, while interpretable evolutionary methods have lagged largely behind for the opposite reason. In this work, we introduce Symbolic Imitation Learning, a framework for distilling an oracle policy through an offline dataset into a decision list with linear model motion primitives. We show that this, in conjunction, with online Augmented-Random Search (ARS) tuning of the constants and motion primitives approximates the performance of the oracle across 20 benchmark RL tasks and exceeds the oracle in 11 of those 20 tasks while simultaneously producing parsimonious, interpretable policies that domain experts can better understand.
papers.summary: Deep reinforcement learning dominates continuous control but yields opaque policies, while interpretable alternatives have lagged in performance. `Symbolic Imitation Learning` distills an oracle policy from an offline dataset into a decision list whose leaves are linear-model motion primitives, then tunes the constants and primitives online with `Augmented Random Search` (`ARS`). Across 20 benchmark reinforcement learning tasks the resulting policies approximate the oracle and **exceed it on 11 of the 20 tasks**, while staying compact enough for domain experts to read.

papers.title: AgentScript-Eval: Benchmarking LLMs and Agents for Code Generation in an Enterprise DSL
papers.abstract: Domain-specific languages (DSLs) are widely used in enterprise software, giving a compact interface to complex tasks, from data access to infrastructure automation. Platforms increasingly extend them to agents, where a developer declares the topics, permitted actions, and guardrails of an agent rather than writing general-purpose code. Large language models (LLMs) write general-purpose code well, but that ability has been measured almost entirely on languages abundant in public pretraining data, and enterprise DSLs are neither abundant nor public. We introduce AgentScript-Eval, an execution-graded benchmark of 100 real tasks for AgentScript, the declarative DSL that Salesforce uses in Agentforce to build conversational agents. Tasks span authoring an agent from a specification, debugging a broken definition, and optimizing a working one. Evaluating five models zero-shot, we find that the regime is hard: the best model reaches only 25.0% pass@3, and every model scores 0% on authoring from scratch. We further find that model scale and price are weak predictors of success -- a 31B open-weight model attains the highest compilation rate of any model tested (48.0%) and matches the strongest frontier model on partial-credit accuracy at the lowest token cost. Adding an agentic compile-and-edit loop is the single largest lever, roughly doubling partial-credit accuracy. Beyond that gain, the wording of domain guidance matters more than its packaging. The same skill pack scores 28% as plain documentation but only 14% as a live plugin. Rewriting one skill inside that plugin then raises it to 37%, our best result, with catalog and tooling untouched. Larger models did not reliably outperform smaller ones; what mattered was the harness surrounding the model and the guidance supplied to it.
papers.summary: Code generation ability of large language models (LLMs) has been measured mostly on languages abundant in public training data, which enterprise domain-specific languages (DSLs) are not. `AgentScript-Eval` is an execution-graded benchmark of 100 real tasks in `AgentScript`, the declarative DSL Salesforce uses in `Agentforce`, covering authoring, debugging, and optimizing agent definitions. Zero-shot, **the best of five models reaches only 25.0% pass@3 and every model scores 0% on authoring from scratch**, with a 31B open-weight model achieving the highest compilation rate at the lowest token cost. An agentic compile-and-edit loop roughly doubles partial-credit accuracy, and the wording of domain guidance matters more than its packaging: the same skill pack scores 28% as plain documentation, 14% as a live plugin, and 37% after rewriting one skill.

papers.title: Prediction-Powered LLM Ranking with Adaptively Collected Human Feedback
papers.abstract: Ranking large language models (LLMs) through human evaluations is essential for downstream decision-making. Because human feedback is expensive, evaluation platforms often collect it adaptively, prioritizing informative model comparisons using previously observed feedback. To further improve precision with limited human feedback, evaluators can draw on abundant unrated responses and relatively inexpensive LLM judges; however, judge bias and adaptive dependence challenge standard i.i.d. inference frameworks. We propose Prediction-Powered Ranking (PP-Rank), a framework that combines LLM-judge predictions with human feedback to improve precision while providing valid inference under adaptive sampling. Data-driven prediction weights minimize the asymptotic covariance trace within the proposed class. In theory, we establish asymptotic normality for general evaluation targets and simultaneous ranking inference. A joint martingale analysis handles dependence between adaptive human feedback and auxiliary data. We further derive a rule for reducing exploration that prioritizes lower-cost comparisons while matching a conservative variance bound, and characterize allocation limits for regular $\sqrt{T}$-rate estimation of pairwise means. Semi-synthetic experiments on UltraFeedback-Extended show improvements over human-only baselines in score estimation, confidence interval width, and ranking certification. Synthetic experiments demonstrate robustness to judge quality and adaptive allocation, while showing that PP-Rank can substantially reduce evaluation costs without sacrificing precision.
papers.summary: Ranking large language models (LLMs) by human evaluation is expensive, and platforms often collect feedback adaptively, which breaks the independence assumptions behind standard statistical inference. `PP-Rank` (Prediction-Powered Ranking) combines cheap LLM-judge predictions on unrated responses with adaptively collected human feedback, using data-driven weights that minimize asymptotic covariance while correcting for judge bias. The authors establish **asymptotic normality and simultaneous ranking inference that remain valid under adaptive sampling**, and derive a rule for reducing exploration that favors lower-cost comparisons. Semi-synthetic experiments on `UltraFeedback-Extended` show narrower confidence intervals and better ranking certification than human-only baselines.

papers.title: One-Sided Expert-Parallel All-to-All for Mixture-of-Experts Inference over NVLink
papers.abstract: Expert parallelism (EP) shards the experts of a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layer across GPUs, so every MoE layer requires two all-to-all communications, namely dispatch and combine. Compared with training, inference processes relatively few tokens per GPU at a time, and at small batch sizes fixed costs that do not grow with the number of tokens, rather than data movement, dominate the latency. We present NVLinkOneSided, a one-sided EP all-to-all for GPUs within a single NVLink domain. Each source rank pushes its tokens, without first exchanging metadata, into rank-major buffers on the target GPUs, and the grouped GEMMs read them in place instead of from a per-expert copy. We provide two protocols for the synchronization that the communication requires, namely Fence and Sentinel, for high-throughput and low-latency scenarios respectively. On Blackwell GPUs, NVLinkOneSided completes dispatch and combine 1.2-3.0$\times$ faster than DeepEP, with the largest speedups at small batch sizes. The resulting MoE layer is up to 2.4$\times$ faster than DeepEP with DeepGEMM. It even outperforms the fused DeepGEMM MegaMoE at up to 128 tokens per GPU, making it still competitive for decoding. We expose NVLinkOneSided through a modular interface, so that it is agnostic to the activation quantization format, decoupled from the MoE compute backend and easy to integrate into inference frameworks.
papers.summary: Expert parallelism spreads the experts of a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layer across GPUs, so each layer needs two all-to-all exchanges, and at the small batch sizes typical of inference fixed overheads dominate latency more than data movement does. `NVLinkOneSided` has each source GPU push tokens directly into buffers on the target GPUs within a single NVLink domain without first exchanging metadata, with the matrix multiplications reading them in place; two synchronization protocols, `Fence` and `Sentinel`, target high-throughput and low-latency use respectively. On Blackwell GPUs, dispatch and combine run **1.2-3.0x faster than `DeepEP`**, with the largest gains at small batches, and the full MoE layer is up to 2.4x faster than `DeepEP` with `DeepGEMM`. It also outperforms the fused `DeepGEMM MegaMoE` at up to 128 tokens per GPU.

papers.title: EvoSurv: Evolution-Aware Multimodal Survival Modeling Reveals Complementary Prognostic Signals
papers.abstract: Accurate cancer survival prediction remains challenging due to tumor heterogeneity. Although multimodal survival models integrate clinical and molecular data, they often overlook evolutionary information encoded in genomic alterations. To address this gap, we developed eTime, a 38-dimensional evolutionary representation comprising eight feature groups that characterize clonal and subclonal mutation burden, mutational spectra, functional consequences, copy-number alterations, and anoikis-related genomic changes. We further developed EvoSurv, a multimodal survival framework integrating eTime with clinical variables and RNA expression. Across six TCGA cancer cohorts comprising 2,782 patients, EvoSurv achieved the highest mean concordance index (C-index) in all six cancers, averaging 0.663 and outperforming three state-of-the-art survival prediction methods. More importantly, we assessed whether evolutionary features provide additional prognostic information beyond clinical and transcriptomic predictors. eTime remained significantly associated with survival in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSC) and liver hepatocellular carcinoma (LIHC) after adjustment for clinical variables and RNA-derived risk scores. Feature-group analyses further revealed cancer-specific prognostic patterns. In HNSC, T>G substitutions were associated with increased mortality risk after clinical and molecular adjustment, including in HPV-negative patients, with supporting evidence from an independent CPTAC-HNSCC cohort. Overall, these findings demonstrate that eTime captures survival-associated evolutionary information and highlight its potential to provide prognostic value beyond clinical and transcriptomic predictors.
papers.summary: Multimodal cancer survival models combine clinical and molecular data but usually ignore the evolutionary information encoded in a tumor's genomic alterations. The authors build `eTime`, a 38-dimensional representation covering clonal and subclonal mutation burden, mutational spectra, copy-number changes, and related features, and integrate it with clinical variables and RNA expression in a framework called `EvoSurv`. Across six `TCGA` cohorts totalling 2,782 patients, `EvoSurv` achieves **the highest mean concordance index in all six cancers, averaging 0.663**, ahead of three existing survival methods. `eTime` stays significantly associated with survival in head and neck and liver cancers after adjusting for clinical and transcriptomic predictors.

papers.title: Multimodal Road Closure Mapping via Cross-Modal Graph Attention
papers.abstract: Accurate and timely identification of road closures is critical for large-scale navigation and logistics systems, yet remains challenging due to the need to jointly reason over visual evidence, spatial context, and road network topology. Existing approaches either rely on manual map updates or focus on detecting closure-related objects without resolving which road segment is affected. In this work, we introduce a unified multimodal and multitask framework that jointly performs road closure classification (no, partial, complete) and road segment association within a single learning architecture. Our model integrates graph-structured map data, satellite imagery augmented with projected street-level detections, and street-view images using modality-specific encoders and cross-modal transformer attention, enabling explicit reasoning over visual cues and network topology. Evaluated on nearly 20K real-world scenarios collected from a large-scale commercial vehicle fleet, our approach achieves 72.7% closure classification accuracy and 60% road segment association accuracy, outperforming frontier vision-language models by over 28 percentage points on closure classification while being over 4,000x smaller and 100x faster at inference. Extensive ablations demonstrate the importance of cross-modal attention, edge-aware pooling, and graph message passing for accurate geospatial reasoning. This work establishes the first benchmark for joint road closure classification and segment-level attribution, and shows that task-specific architectural inductive biases substantially outperform general-purpose multimodal models for structured geospatial understanding.
papers.summary: Detecting road closures for navigation systems requires deciding both whether a closure exists and which road segment it affects, which object-detection approaches do not resolve. The proposed model jointly classifies closures as none, partial, or complete and associates them with a segment, fusing graph-structured map data, satellite imagery with projected street-level detections, and street-view images through cross-modal transformer attention. On nearly 20K real-world scenarios from a commercial vehicle fleet it reaches 72.7% classification accuracy and 60% segment association accuracy, **beating frontier vision-language models by over 28 percentage points on classification while being over 4,000x smaller and 100x faster**. Ablations attribute the gains to cross-modal attention, edge-aware pooling, and graph message passing.

papers.title: From Process Models to Composable Agentic Workflows: Combining BPMN, Agents and Enterprise Knowledge
papers.abstract:
LLM-based agents can reason, use tools and collaborate. However, coordinating increasingly complex agentic applications becomes difficult to understand, monitor and improve. Decisions distributed across prompts, tool calls and application logic make workflows implicit. We introduce **Recursive Capability Composition**, enabling agents to execute business processes and expose them as reusable Agentic Tools.
  This paper presents a BPMN-based approach to Agentic Workflows, combining explicit orchestration with autonomous reasoning. SemTalk BPMN models are transformed into executable workflows using a LangGraph/Pregel runtime. Agentic Tasks introduce LLM reasoning at selected activities, while conventional BPMN controls process flows, deterministic decisions, system interactions and human approvals. Agentic Participants provide reusable interfaces for agent behavior or other executable processes.
  BPMN orchestration makes multi-agent systems more understandable and manageable. Explicit process models provide developers and operators with a shared view of workflow structures and execution progress, facilitating debugging, monitoring and optimization.
  Enterprise agents also need organization-specific context. Process Models and Knowledge Graphs describe activities, participants, information objects, decisions and relationships between processes. They provide structured knowledge of how an organization operates, supporting informed agent decisions and actions.
  Our contributions are threefold: 1. **Model-Driven Execution:** Transforming BPMN models into executable Agentic Workflows. 2. **Recursive Capability Composition:** Exposing agents and executable business processes as reusable tools for other agents. 3. **Enterprise Context:** Using Process Models and Ontologies to provide organization-specific knowledge for agent reasoning.
papers.summary: Complex LLM agent applications scatter their decisions across prompts, tool calls, and application logic, which makes workflows implicit and hard to monitor or debug. The authors convert Business Process Model and Notation (`BPMN`) models authored in `SemTalk` into executable workflows on a `LangGraph`/`Pregel` runtime, where selected activities invoke LLM reasoning while conventional BPMN constructs handle control flow, deterministic decisions, system calls, and human approvals. Their central idea, **`Recursive Capability Composition`, exposes agents and whole executable business processes as reusable tools for other agents**. Process models and knowledge graphs additionally supply organization-specific context for agent decisions; the work describes the approach and reports no quantitative evaluation in the abstract.

papers.title: Structured Kernel Surrogate Models for Multimodal Attribution
papers.abstract: We study the problem of cross-sample modality attribution, which involves measuring how one modality in one sample affects the learning outcome in other multimodal samples. This problem is crucial in a multimodal system because a data modality (such as a text description) may be redundant for one sample (a self-explanatory image), but the same data modality would otherwise be uniquely informative for another sample, or informative when combined with other modalities. Prior work focuses on influence estimation at the level of one sample, and it remains an open question how one should capture the interactions across both samples and modalities. To capture scenarios like the above, we propose structured kernel surrogate models, which are surrogate mappings from both samples and modalities to the prediction outcome when they are trained together. We design an algorithm, SKS, which applies kernel ridge regression with a structured, compositional kernel on the selection states of individual samples and modalities. Specifically, the kernel function multiplies kernel-based similarity scores between every pair of data modalities for one sample and a pair of two samples. Additionally, we design a gradient-based estimation algorithm to efficiently estimate the structured kernel surrogate model. We evaluate our approach on two multimodal benchmarks, spanning a range of data modalities including satellite images, road networks, text, audio, and tabular data. We find that SKS achieves $57.8$% higher correlation with the true prediction outcomes than existing methods. In downstream data selection, SKS improves the average accuracy by $1.93$% over baselines. Models with data selected by SKS have lower Hessian traces, indicating a flatter loss surface. Using SKS to select satellite images identifies road segments, where accident scenes commonly occur, as opposed to background images.
papers.summary: Cross-sample modality attribution asks how one modality of one training sample affects learning outcomes on other multimodal samples, a question that sample-level influence methods do not capture. The `SKS` algorithm fits a structured kernel surrogate model using kernel ridge regression with a compositional kernel over which samples and modalities are included in training, estimated efficiently with a gradient-based procedure. On two multimodal benchmarks spanning satellite images, road networks, text, audio, and tabular data, `SKS` achieves **57.8% higher correlation with true prediction outcomes than existing methods**. Using it for data selection improves average accuracy by 1.93% over baselines and yields models with lower Hessian traces.

papers.title: XAI-Driven Confidence Estimation for OOD-Resilient Runtime Prediction
papers.abstract: Machine learning-based resource management (RM) models degrade under out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs at runtime, yet existing approaches in the literature rely on a single global error margin that is overly conservative and fails to distinguish reliablepredictions from catastrophic failures. We propose Lightweight Runtime EXplainability (LEX), the first post-hoc XAI framework for input-specific runtime confidence estimation in ML-based RM. LEX clusters the embeddings of the training input space using a Gaussian Mixture Model and associates per-cluster prediction error bounds to input samples, enabling fine-grained runtime confidence signals without retraining. Evaluated on a state-of-the-art LSTM-based IPS forecasting model on Intel Alder Lake, across 34 benchmark applications, LEX achieves ~94% containment on unseen workloads and produces ~17% tighter per-input confidence bounds than global baselines. With its negligible runtime overhead, LEX advances the field by providing explainable and reliable input-specific confidence signals of ML predictions, thereby making ML-based resource management resilient to OOD at runtime.
papers.summary: Machine learning models used for system resource management degrade on out-of-distribution inputs at runtime, and existing approaches apply one global error margin that is overly conservative. `LEX` (Lightweight Runtime EXplainability) clusters embeddings of the training inputs with a Gaussian Mixture Model and attaches a prediction error bound to each cluster, giving input-specific confidence signals without retraining. Evaluated on an LSTM-based instructions-per-second forecasting model on Intel Alder Lake across 34 benchmark applications, it achieves **about 94% containment on unseen workloads with roughly 17% tighter bounds than global baselines**, at negligible runtime overhead.

papers.title: Audited Gradients, Anchored Policies: Model-Based Reinforcement Learning for Efficient Flow Control
papers.abstract: Feedback controllers for flows are expensive to design, since each candidate must be evaluated with a high-fidelity solver. Differentiable surrogates reduce that cost, but they also introduce a failure mode that prediction error cannot detect. Policy optimization uses the derivative of the objective with respect to the action, which we call the action gradient and which can be computed either through the surrogate or through the high-fidelity solver. Optimization through the surrogate uses only its action gradient, and a surrogate can follow the flow trajectory closely while misestimating this derivative. The surrogate action gradient is compared against a central finite-difference estimate from the high-fidelity solver on held-out states, under acceptance criteria fixed before the comparison, and we call that comparison an audit. A low-dimensional feedback law is then fitted to the surrogate action gradient when the surrogate passes the audit, and to the solver estimate when it does not. This law initializes a neural policy, and a quadratic penalty holds the policy near it during optimization. The proposed approach is validated on four test cases. The resulting controllers outperform or match a model-free baseline, while using 3 to 156 times fewer high-fidelity solver interactions across the four test cases. One surrogate predicts the objective at correlation 0.9996 but its action gradient at only 0.459, so prediction accuracy does not identify a usable surrogate. Another surrogate, whose action gradient agrees with the solver estimate at correlation 0.996, makes the objective 0.52% worse when the policy is optimized through it without the anchor penalty, so an accurate gradient alone does not provide a working controller. Finally, a surrogate that passes the audit at one fixed action fails it around the actions the deployed controller applies, so a pass is local.
papers.summary: Designing feedback controllers for fluid flows is costly because each candidate needs a high-fidelity solver, and differentiable surrogates can track the flow accurately while getting the derivative of the objective with respect to the action wrong. The method audits the surrogate's action gradient against finite-difference estimates from the solver on held-out states, fits a low-dimensional feedback law to whichever gradient source passes, and uses that law to initialize and anchor a neural policy via a quadratic penalty. Across four test cases the controllers match or beat a model-free baseline using **3 to 156 times fewer high-fidelity solver interactions**. One surrogate predicted the objective at correlation 0.9996 but its action gradient at only 0.459, showing that prediction accuracy does not identify a usable surrogate, and audit passes were found to hold only locally.

papers.title: HiCAP: Hierarchical Cultural Adaptation via Personality for Dialogue Generation
papers.abstract: Cultural adaptation in dialogue systems refers to the ability to generate responses that conform to linguistic norms and social expectations across different cultures. However, existing dialogue generation approaches pay limited attention to the role of personality in shaping cultural expression and communication style. We therefore propose HiCAP, a novel framework that integrates personality traits into culturally adaptive dialogue generation. HiCAP employs a personality-conditioned control mechanism that hierarchically modulates response style by first aligning it with the cultural tone and then refining linguistic expression and content according to individual personality attributes. To embed these factors, the model combines supervised fine-tuning and instruction-based tuning, supported by dynamic instruction templates and multi-agent demonstrations to capture diverse combinations of culture and personality. Experiments on CulturalPersonas and CPED show that HiCAP achieves the strongest overall performance across various dialogue generation metrics, demonstrating effective cultural adaptability and personality modelling.
papers.summary: Culturally adaptive dialogue systems aim to match the linguistic norms and social expectations of different cultures, but existing approaches give little attention to how personality shapes cultural expression. `HiCAP` conditions generation hierarchically, first aligning a response with cultural tone and then refining wording and content according to individual personality traits. It is trained with a mix of supervised fine-tuning and instruction-based tuning, supported by dynamic instruction templates and multi-agent demonstrations. On `CulturalPersonas` and `CPED`, the authors report **the strongest overall performance across dialogue generation metrics**.

papers.title: Near-Optimal Sample Complexity of Deterministic Agnostic PAC Learning
papers.abstract: We study the problem of agnostic PAC learning under deterministic labels, where the examples are labeled by an arbitrary deterministic function, which need not belong to the concept class $C$. This model captures misspecification without stochastic label noise and lies between the realizable and fully agnostic settings. Prior work showed that, when $C$ has finite diameter $K$ and VC dimension $d$, deterministic labels can improve the sample complexity upper bound from the classical agnostic guarantee $O(d/\varepsilon^2)$ to $\widetilde{O}(K/\varepsilon)$, but left a large gap between upper and lower bounds. Our main result sharpens this picture. We prove that every class of VC dimension $d$ and finite diameter $K$ is learnable with sample complexity $\widetilde{O}\left( \frac{K^{1/3} \, d^{2/3}}{\varepsilon} \right)$, and we construct classes for which this bound is tight up to logarithmic factors. We also study the online analogue of this problem and show that the minimax regret is again partly controlled by the diameter of the class. Technically, our upper bounds are obtained via memorization-based learning algorithms that exploit the deterministic label structure.
papers.summary: Agnostic PAC learning with deterministic labels covers the case where examples are labeled by an arbitrary deterministic function outside the concept class, sitting between the realizable and fully agnostic settings. Prior work gave an upper bound of roughly K/ε for classes of diameter K and VC dimension d but left a large gap to the lower bound. The authors prove that every such class is learnable with **sample complexity of order K^(1/3) d^(2/3) / ε up to logarithmic factors, and construct classes for which this is tight**. The upper bounds come from memorization-based algorithms, and an online analogue shows minimax regret is also partly controlled by the class diameter.

papers.title: Before Words, Beyond Speech: Evaluating Nonverbal Social Reasoning in Early Childhood
papers.abstract: Children's earliest years are a period of intense social learning, during which meaning is built through gaze, gesture, and physical contact. Yet, this critical aspect of social interaction remains under-evaluated in multimodal video understanding, as existing benchmarks prioritize the conversation-driven interactions of adults. We address this gap with \bench ($\textbf{N}$aturalistic $\textbf{E}$arly-childhood $\textbf{S}$ocial in$\textbf{T}$eractions), the first child-centric benchmark for nonverbal social reasoning. \bench comprises \totalvids manually annotated clips ($\sim$12s) curated for diversity across naturalistic settings, cultural contexts, and developmental stages. Beyond a lack of data, targeted model improvement in this domain is hindered by coarse evaluation schemas that conflate basic perception with higher-order reasoning. To resolve this, \bench introduces a compositional schema that builds atomic interaction cues into progressive levels of social reasoning: contextual, behavioral, interpersonal, and open-ended descriptions. Extensive analysis of state-of-the-art Vision-Language Models (VLMs) reveals a stark performance collapse: despite strong contextual recognition, models exhibit substantial gaps in decoding precise behavioral and interpersonal cues. We trace these failures to specific biases, including poor consequence grounding and temporal sensitivity. Finally, we ground \bench in real-world applications by evaluating VLMs using domain adaptation strategies. Ultimately, \bench provides a rigorous testbed for advancing socially grounded artificial intelligence in early childhood. Project page: https://laubravo.github.io/nest_website/.
papers.summary: Video understanding benchmarks focus on adult, conversation-driven interaction and overlook the gaze, gesture, and physical contact through which young children communicate. `NEST` (Naturalistic Early-childhood Social Interactions) is a child-centric benchmark of manually annotated clips of about 12 seconds, with a compositional schema that builds atomic cues into contextual, behavioral, interpersonal, and open-ended levels of social reasoning. State-of-the-art vision-language models show **strong contextual recognition but a sharp drop on precise behavioral and interpersonal cues**, which the authors trace to biases including poor consequence grounding and temporal sensitivity. They also evaluate domain adaptation strategies on the benchmark.

papers.title: Counting Under Disagreement: Dollar-Weighted Measurement, Selective Machine Labelling and Budgeted Human Review from Disagreeing AI Readers of Administrative Text
papers.abstract: We study AI-assisted measurement when one text label applies to many administrative records, the target is a monetary total, and the human readings that anchor the machines disagree. The testbed is 121,070 grant-purpose texts from US tax filings (799,675 records, \$126.4B), labelled by a rule-based classifier and three language models, with a designed sample of 651 texts read independently by three people under one codebook. We state exact conditions for a fixed-predictor difference estimator and for a cross-fitted predictor whose folds are assigned to the whole frame before sampling, under Poisson sampling, and assess the implemented fixed-size procedures by simulation: 8 predictors whose own totals span \$11.2-15.0B agree to within \$0.4B once rectified. Two rules that accept machine labels at a stated dollar-weighted error, weighted conformal p-values under a dollar measure and Learn-then-Test on the design estimate of the error, are evaluated on nested held-out folds and on re-draws of the design with synthetic truths; their error control in deployment is not established, and the count-based rule accepts no text under a dollar-drawn sample. In a replay that charges every human label, a two-phase review policy whose calibrator is fitted on its own first phase reduces the RMSE of the total by 28% at a budget of 100 texts relative to dollar-proportional sampling, while pure Neyman allocation fails with an uncalibrated predictor. Independent readers shift the estimated total by \$3.93B, 2.2 times the within-reader sampling interval, and institution-level intervals under-cover at every size. Every headline result is re-run under each reader. The results identify both the benefits and the limits of using learned predictions to decide what a person should verify.
papers.summary: The study examines AI-assisted measurement when one text label applies to many administrative records, the target is a dollar total, and the human readers used as ground truth disagree with each other. The testbed is 121,070 grant-purpose texts from US tax filings covering $126.4B, labelled by a rule-based classifier and three language models, with 651 texts read independently by three people. After statistical rectification against the human sample, eight predictors whose raw totals span $11.2-15.0B agree to within $0.4B, and a two-phase human review policy cuts error in the total by 28% at a budget of 100 texts. However, **switching between independent human readers shifts the estimated total by $3.93B, 2.2 times the within-reader sampling interval**, and the error control of the rules for accepting machine labels is not established in deployment.

papers.title: Latin American Studies since the 1980s: From Apocalyptic Dreams to Assimilationist Consolidation
papers.abstract: We investigate how Latin American Studies (LAS) has evolved since 1982 in three leading LAS journals. Using network analysis, text mining, and bibliometrics, we trace transformations in disciplinary positioning, authorship, and citation patterns. Our main claim is that LAS has undergone an assimilationist consolidation. The field is now institutionally recognisable, with core LAS journals occupying central positions in disciplinary networks and acting as bridges across fields. Yet this consolidation has reinforced hierarchies privileging Anglophone academic norms. Journals based in Latin America, once central, have been marginalised. The share of Latin American authors has grown, but their profiles converge towards Northern standards.
papers.summary: A bibliometric study of how Latin American Studies has evolved since 1982, based on network analysis, text mining, and citation analysis of three leading journals in the field. The authors argue the field has undergone an **"assimilationist consolidation"**: its core journals now occupy central, bridging positions in disciplinary networks, but this has reinforced hierarchies favoring Anglophone academic norms. Journals based in Latin America have been marginalised, and although the share of Latin American authors has grown, their profiles converge toward Northern standards.

papers.title: Reliability of Claude Code as an Agentic AI Grading System for Handwritten University Exams
papers.abstract: This study examines the reliability of Claude Code, an agentic deployment of the Claude Opus 4.6 large language model, as a grading system for handwritten university exams. Four research questions addressed agreement with expert human grading on total scores (RQ1), agreement across five question types from multiple choice to evaluative judgement (RQ2), consistency across two independent grading sessions one week apart (RQ3), and the accuracy of AI-generated feedback (RQ4). Claude Code graded the 20-mark mid-term papers of 60 consenting students in a Saudi computer graphics course in a single agentic session, guided by three rubric files. Reliability was estimated on disjoint samples: 20 papers for RQ1, RQ2 and RQ4, and 15 papers for RQ3. Analyses used Pearson correlation, mean absolute error, Bland-Altman analysis, weighted Cohen kappa, intraclass correlation, and a four-category coding scheme separating diagnostic from confirmation feedback. The author, as the sole subject-matter expert for the course, provided the human benchmark, so the design assesses agreement with a domain-expert reference rather than inter-rater reliability. AI grading agreed strongly with human grading on totals (r = 0.97; MAE = 0.85 marks) with a small but significant AI-positive bias of 0.68 marks, showed excellent test-retest consistency (ICC = 0.96), and produced accurate feedback (92.8% diagnostic; 97.8% confirmation). Drawing items were the outlier on three of four measures. Three failure modes recurred: keyword matching without conceptual depth, selection-state ambiguity on corrected multiple-choice answers, and region-of-attention drift on hand-drawn diagrams. The findings suggest that AI grading at this capability level can assist instructors on objective and short-form items under structural safeguards but is not yet ready to replace instructor judgement at boundary cases or on drawing items.
papers.summary: The study tests how reliably `Claude Code`, running `Claude Opus 4.6` as an agent guided by three rubric files, grades handwritten mid-term exams from 60 students in a university computer graphics course. Against a single expert human grader, AI totals **correlated at r = 0.97 with a mean absolute error of 0.85 marks out of 20** and a small AI-positive bias of 0.68 marks, with test-retest consistency of ICC = 0.96 across sessions a week apart and feedback accuracy above 92%. Drawing questions were the outlier, and three failure modes recurred: keyword matching without conceptual depth, ambiguity on corrected multiple-choice answers, and attention drift on hand-drawn diagrams. The author concludes the system can assist on objective and short-form items under safeguards but not replace instructor judgement on boundary cases or drawings.

papers.title: Wrong the Same Way: Cross-Prompt Sharing Both Suppresses and Amplifies Reward Hacking in RLVR
papers.abstract: Two accounts of how reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) interacts with an imperfect verifier coexist: in one, reward hacking is inherited from the base model; in the other, RL amplifies it. We study both in a controlled environment small enough to compute the entire response distribution exactly. We vary the universality of a leak, or the fraction of prompts that accept the same wrong response, and the verifier's static false-positive rate. At its KL-regularized optimum, RLVR acts as a filter that reweights the accepted set without altering its composition, so the hack rate is inherited exactly. Taking that as a null model, a known decomposition writes the drift from it as a sum over prompts of covariances between reward and the empirical tangent kernel. The terms from other prompts vanish without parameter sharing. With sharing, every prompt that accepts a wrong answer pushes it up and every prompt that rejects it pushes it down through the baseline, in proportion to the model's probability of producing it there. A shared-parameter policy thus drives a leak that few prompts accept below the base rate and amplifies one that most prompts accept. At every convergent learning rate under Adam, SGD, and sampled GRPO, hacking ends higher at high universality than at low, but whether either end crosses the base rate depends on the step size. Independent per-prompt copies remove the dependence. The direction of this push depends on neither the verifier's error rate nor universality alone, but on how much of the model's kernel-weighted probability of a wrong answer falls on prompts that accept it, which frozen base model controls support. Verifier fixes should target the mistakes the model repeats across prompts: two patches that remove equally many errors differ by up to 38 points of true accuracy. We propose this alignment as a hypothesis for why earlier studies disagree.
papers.summary: Two competing accounts of reward hacking in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (`RLVR`) — that it is inherited from the base model, or that RL amplifies it — are studied in an environment small enough to compute the full response distribution exactly. At the KL-regularized optimum the hack rate is inherited unchanged, but with shared parameters a wrong answer accepted on few prompts is pushed below the base rate while one accepted on most prompts is amplified, a pattern that holds under `Adam`, `SGD`, and sampled `GRPO`. The practical implication is that verifier fixes should target mistakes the model repeats across prompts: **two patches removing equally many verifier errors can differ by up to 38 points of true accuracy**.

papers.title: MediPFN: Amortized In-Context Nuisance Learning and Inference for Causal Mediation Analysis
papers.abstract: Causal mediation analysis decomposes a treatment effect into indirect pathways through mediators and direct pathways through other processes. Tabular foundation models perform classification and regression through in-context learning, providing estimates of conditional means and propensity scores used in causal mediation analysis. Constructing confidence intervals from these estimates requires accounting for uncertainty introduced by fitting and combining several nuisance functions. We introduce MediPFN, an amortized inference framework that adapts a pretrained tabular foundation model to nuisance prediction and combines its predictions through a cross-fitted influence-function estimator. A separate head learns quantiles of the estimator's standardized error from simulated tables with known indirect effects. Supervised fine-tuning, symmetrization, and independent calibration then produce a confidence interval. We establish coverage bounds for the resulting intervals under standard assumptions. Across experiments, MediPFN attains coverage closer to the nominal level than several comparators. It also reduces the computational cost of uncertainty quantification, running 59.1 times faster than bootstrap in matched comparisons.
papers.summary: Causal mediation analysis splits a treatment effect into indirect paths through mediators and direct paths, and building valid confidence intervals requires accounting for uncertainty from several fitted nuisance functions. `MediPFN` adapts a pretrained tabular foundation model to predict those nuisance functions in-context, combines them with a cross-fitted influence-function estimator, and trains a separate head on simulated tables to learn quantiles of the estimator's standardized error. The authors prove coverage bounds under standard assumptions and report coverage closer to nominal than several comparators while running **59.1 times faster than bootstrap**.

papers.title: Deletion Sensitivity Is a Property of the Model: A Three-Condition Measurement across Seven Open Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Reasoning models write a reasoning trace at every turn of a multi-turn tool session, and later turns read this history. Across 94k ShareGPT conversations, 73 percent of user interactions span multiple turns. Upstream providers bind each trace to its issuer, so a request forwarded across issuers arrives with its history deleted, and the task cost of this stripping remains unmeasured. To the best of our knowledge, this paper presents the first direct, blind, multi-seed measurement of full reasoning-history deletion in multi-turn tool calling, through three rendering conditions, seven open-weight reasoning models, three seeds, 794 tasks, and the official checker. The same deletion spans -4.4 to +51.3 points with both ends excluding zero, and for the one model re-dosed from 0 to 100 percent deletion, the reading varies by at most 1.5 points. Deletion sensitivity is a model-level property. The reading follows the model itself and stays constant across deployments, and a retrained or re-released model is a new model that a two-cell screen, one retention run and one deletion run, re-reads for the cost of two runs. Deletion sensitivity is thus a measurable property of the model, and the reading must enter routing and aggregation as prior information rather than persist as an invisible default cost.
papers.summary: Reasoning models write a reasoning trace on every turn of a multi-turn tool session, but providers bind traces to their issuer, so requests forwarded across providers arrive with that history stripped. A blind measurement across three rendering conditions, seven open-weight reasoning models, three seeds, and 794 tool-calling tasks finds that **the same deletion changes task scores by anywhere from -4.4 to +51.3 points depending on the model**, while for the one model tested at varying deletion levels the reading moved by at most 1.5 points. The authors conclude that deletion sensitivity is a stable per-model property that can be screened with two runs and should inform routing decisions.

papers.title: Continuous Horizon Forecasting
papers.abstract: Multi-horizon forecasting has been dominated by discrete forecast strategies that treat model outputs as fixed-vectors or recurrently create them. In this paper, we introduce the Continuous Horizon (CH) strategy that generalizes upon recursive, direct, and multi-step strategies by redefining forecasts as a continuous operator and the forecast horizon as a query variable rather than an index. We present the theoretical foundations for the CH strategy, a Universal Operator Approximation Theorem, and a continuous-horizon bias-variance decomposition that formally proves the estimation variance improvements of CH over the discrete strategies. We validate the CH strategy empirically through a simulation study, and on 16 large-scale datasets from the M-series benchmark, showing how CH achieves competitive RMSE accuracy, while uniquely enabling parallel inference, targeted horizon querying, and interpolation and extrapolation across unseen horizons.
papers.summary: Multi-horizon time-series forecasting usually emits a fixed-length vector or builds forecasts recursively. The `Continuous Horizon` (`CH`) strategy instead treats the forecast as a continuous operator and the horizon as a query variable, generalizing recursive, direct, and multi-step strategies, with a universal operator approximation theorem and a bias-variance decomposition proving lower estimation variance than discrete strategies. On a simulation study and 16 datasets from the `M-series` benchmark, **`CH` reaches competitive RMSE while enabling parallel inference, querying of specific horizons, and interpolation or extrapolation to unseen horizons**.

papers.title: Block-Sparse Gauss-Newton Optimization of Finite Basis Physics-Informed Neural Networks: Sparse Automatic Differentiation Approach
papers.abstract: In this work, we develop an efficient Gauss-Newton optimization approach for finite basis physics-informed neural networks (FBPINNs). The key ingredient is the overlapping domain decomposition architecture of FBPINNs, which localizes the influence of each subnetwork and induces block sparsity in both the residual Jacobian and the corresponding Gauss-Newton matrix. We characterize this structure and exploit it through sparse automatic differentiation, using graph coloring to partition structurally orthogonal Jacobian columns or rows. This reduces differentiation costs and memory requirements while preserving all structurally nonzero derivative information. The resulting compressed Jacobian representations allow us to assemble the Gauss-Newton system directly in block-sparse form, enabling the use of sparse direct solvers and preconditioned iterative methods. In this way, the otherwise expensive second-order optimization problem is reduced to scalable sparse linear algebra. We demonstrate the approach on multiscale PDEs, where accurate approximation requires rich neural network parametrizations and large numbers of collocation points. Numerical experiments show that our block-sparse Gauss-Newton method attains high accuracy and substantially accelerates optimization relative to first-order baselines while remaining computationally tractable for large problem sizes.
papers.summary: Second-order optimization is expensive for finite basis physics-informed neural networks (`FBPINNs`), which solve partial differential equations with overlapping subdomain networks. Because each subnetwork only influences its own region, the residual Jacobian and Gauss-Newton matrix are block-sparse, and the authors exploit this with sparse automatic differentiation based on graph coloring, assembling the system directly in sparse form for direct or preconditioned iterative solvers. On multiscale PDEs, the **block-sparse Gauss-Newton method reaches high accuracy and substantially accelerates optimization relative to first-order baselines** while staying tractable at large problem sizes.

papers.title: W-ISA: Transactional Execution of Weight-Space Intervention Programs
papers.abstract: We present W-ISA, a software instruction set and transactional runtime for executing weight-space intervention programs on pretrained language models. Shape-checked instructions express parameter updates, projections, ablations, and rank-one transformations. The runtime applies these programs within request-scoped execution contexts and restores saved parameters after completion or interruption. Activation-based match-action rules connect measured model states to intervention selection. We evaluate restoration and replay on SmolLM-135M-Instruct and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, and compare materialized rank-one updates with equivalent PyTorch hooks on the latter. In 45 timed requests, both intervention implementations produce identical greedy sequences at 32, 128, and 512 tokens; their maximum prompt-logit difference is 0.000184. On the complete WikiText-2 raw test split, the combined SmolLM attention-head ablation and MLP projection changes perplexity from 22.2353 to 22.3188, a relative increase of 0.3754%. W-ISA separates intervention specification, execution, and measurement, making parameter-level experiments reproducible and composable.
papers.summary: `W-ISA` is a software instruction set and transactional runtime for applying temporary edits to a pretrained language model's weights: shape-checked instructions express updates, projections, ablations, and rank-one transformations, which run inside request-scoped contexts and are rolled back afterward, even on interruption. Activation-based match-action rules choose which interventions to apply. Tested on `SmolLM-135M-Instruct` and `Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct`, materialized rank-one updates and equivalent PyTorch hooks **produced identical greedy outputs across 45 timed requests, with a maximum prompt-logit difference of 0.000184**, and a combined head ablation plus MLP projection raised `WikiText-2` perplexity by 0.3754%.

papers.title: Decisions by Discrimination: Differential Evidence for Medical Reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly studied for clinical decision support, and medical question answering provides a testbed for evaluating this capability. In particular, medical multiple-choice questions (MCQs) reflect a core challenge in clinical decision-making: plausible options often share overlapping evidence, while only a few decisive factors distinguish the correct option from incorrect ones. However, existing retrieval-based and reasoning-oriented methods mainly focus on supplying broadly relevant knowledge or eliciting reasoning paths, rather than identifying the compact differential evidence that separates confusing alternatives. In this work, we present a retrieval-grounded differential evidence framework for medical MCQs. Our method extracts option-specific pieces of differential evidence and organizes them into concise evidence prompts for answer selection. This design better aligns external knowledge with differential reasoning while reducing irrelevant context. Experiments show consistent accuracy gains across multiple datasets and target LLMs. Ablation studies further show that our framework outperforms both directly using retrieved evidence chunks and closed-source LLM-generated general hints, and that its improvements are not solely explained by answer-proximal guidance, but are consistent with differential evidence serving as a compact aid for reasoning over competing alternatives. Our findings also offer insights for medical reasoning and other decision-making settings with multiple possible choices.
papers.summary: Medical multiple-choice questions are hard for large language models (LLMs) because plausible options share overlapping evidence and only a few decisive factors separate the right answer from the wrong ones. Rather than supplying broadly relevant retrieved knowledge or eliciting reasoning chains, this retrieval-grounded framework extracts option-specific differential evidence and organizes it into concise prompts for answer selection. Experiments show **consistent accuracy gains across multiple datasets and target LLMs**, and ablations find it beats both raw retrieved chunks and general hints generated by closed-source LLMs.

papers.title: NCP: Verifier-Guided Optimization of Weight-Space Control Policies
papers.abstract: We present the Neural Control Plane (NCP), a closed-loop system that observes language-model execution, synthesizes candidate weight-space intervention rules, evaluates them, and maintains a versioned table of admitted policies. NCP separates a pretrained model's inference data plane from the control policy that selects temporary parameter interventions. W-ISA supplies transactional execution and parameter restoration; NCP supplies telemetry, candidate synthesis, admission criteria, priorities, and rule lifetime management. The optimization state consists of active rules and an archive of evaluated candidates, while base-model parameters are restored after each request. In a local SmolLM-135M-Instruct experiment, NCP generated three candidates from development telemetry and evaluated them on separate task examples and a 4,095-target WikiText-2 slice. One projection reduced validation token repetition from 0.4133 to 0.2191, with a perplexity change of -0.0574%. All candidates produced zero newly correct exact answers, so the configured admission gate archived all three and retained the original active policy. Fresh-process repetition and saved-table resumption reproduced the measured outcomes. NCP provides an executable framework for studying recursive self-improvement at the control-policy level through explicit synthesis, verification, and state transitions.
papers.summary: The Neural Control Plane (`NCP`) is a closed-loop system that observes a language model's execution, synthesizes candidate rules for temporary weight-space interventions, evaluates them, and keeps a versioned table of admitted policies, building on `W-ISA` for transactional execution and restoration of base weights. In a local experiment on `SmolLM-135M-Instruct`, one candidate projection cut validation token repetition from 0.4133 to 0.2191 with negligible perplexity change. However, **all three generated candidates produced zero newly correct answers, so the admission gate rejected them all** and kept the original policy; the authors present the system as a framework for studying recursive self-improvement at the control-policy level.

papers.title: STAR: Semantic-Criticality Tiered Allocation of Radio Resources via Zero-Shot Learning
papers.abstract: In remote inference, edge devices transmit high-resolution images over wireless links to a receiver, where an artificial intelligence (AI) model answers task-specific questions about these images to enable reliable decisions. These answers are often determined by a small set of task-causal pixels, such as those of text, whose corruption changes the answer, so these pixels must be delivered with high fidelity. Conventional transmission protects every pixel equally, so it either consumes many resource elements (REs) or corrupts these regions at low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). To overcome these limitations, in this paper, a zero-shot, domain-agnostic framework, termed semantic-criticality tiered allocation of resources (STAR), is proposed. In particular, a per-pixel semantic-criticality indicator (SCI) is derived from the attention of a frozen vision-language model, so new tasks and domains are handled by changing only the prompt, without retraining. The resulting task causality-aware resource allocation problem over protection tiers is solved exactly by a threshold rule on the SCI, realized by a coded tier for the task-causal pixels and an uncoded, downsampled base layer for the full image. Simulations over a 5G New Radio link demonstrate that STAR attains a semantic accuracy of at least 0.98 for $E_s/N_0 \geq -4$ dB and, at comparable semantic reliability, reduces the REs of robust coded transmission by 59.5% and 91.5% on factory- and vehicle-monitoring datasets, respectively, the latter without any change to the models. Although a deep joint source-channel coding baseline uses fewer REs at comparable semantic accuracy, it must be retrained with labeled data for every new task or domain.
papers.summary: In remote inference, edge devices send images over wireless links for an AI model to answer questions about, and the answer often hinges on a small set of pixels such as text. `STAR` (semantic-criticality tiered allocation of resources) derives a per-pixel criticality score from the attention of a frozen vision-language model, so new tasks need only a new prompt, then sends critical pixels in a coded tier and the full image as an uncoded, downsampled base layer. In 5G New Radio simulations it reaches semantic accuracy of at least 0.98 at low signal-to-noise ratios and **cuts resource elements by 59.5% and 91.5% versus robust coded transmission** on factory- and vehicle-monitoring datasets, though a trained joint source-channel coding baseline uses fewer still at the cost of per-task retraining.

papers.title: GigaEdge Spench: An SDK for Practical Streaming Speech Enhancement
papers.abstract: We present GigaEdge Spench, an open-source SDK for streaming speech enhancement on CPU servers, mobile devices, and in browsers. Applications can build enhancement channels from neural denoising, normalization and dynamics blocks, sample-rate conversion, and acoustic echo cancellation where supported. These stages can be combined, while normalization can also run without a neural model. The release includes an 8 kHz INT8 denoiser and discriminative and hybrid 48 kHz FP32 models. A shared C++ core supports ONNX Runtime and TensorFlow Lite through native interfaces, Android and iOS SDKs, and WebAssembly integration. Independent stream contexts share model resources, and consecutive frames from one stream can be processed in a single inference call. We evaluate the released models on EARS-WHAM v2 and compare their quality and processing costs with RNNoise and DPDFNet2. All tested native and Web configurations process files faster than real time, although larger chunks require more time to collect input. We also measure how many streams a shared model can process on a CPU. Our contribution is a configurable deployment system and an experimental study of how model choice, chunk size, and execution environment affect its use. All reported SDK timing uses ONNX Runtime. Index Terms: speech enhancement, streaming inference, cross-platform deployment, temporal frame grouping, computational efficiency
papers.summary: `GigaEdge Spench` is an open-source SDK for streaming speech enhancement on CPU servers, mobile devices, and browsers, letting applications compose neural denoising, normalization, dynamics processing, sample-rate conversion, and echo cancellation. A shared C++ core supports `ONNX Runtime` and `TensorFlow Lite` with Android, iOS, and WebAssembly bindings, and ships an 8 kHz INT8 denoiser plus 48 kHz FP32 models. Evaluated on `EARS-WHAM v2` against `RNNoise` and `DPDFNet2`, **every tested native and Web configuration runs faster than real time**, with further measurements of how chunk size and execution environment affect cost and how many streams one shared model can serve.

papers.title: ExpertCrowd-SWE: Measuring Frontier Coding Agents on Expert-Authored Engineering Tasks in Unfamiliar Codebases
papers.abstract: ExpertCrowd-SWE (EC-SWE) is a benchmark of 100 expert-authored, multi-file software engineering tasks for evaluating autonomous coding agents in large, unfamiliar codebases. Each task is a change request written by a practising engineer against a pinned commit of a real repository, paired with a sealed reference solution and a task-specific grader whose weighted, mostly executable criteria award partial credit; must-pass blockers and pass/fail gates encode what a maintainer would refuse to merge. The tasks span 87 open-source projects and 11 languages. The median ticket is 148 words, while the median reference solution changes 471 lines. Every task image is calibrated before release so that the reference solution scores 1.0 and both the untouched repository and an inert change score 0; nearly half of the tasks also ship alternative, lazy and adversarial control patches that the grader must classify correctly. The final 100 tasks were selected for difficulty against current frontier models. We evaluate seven frontier models, five runs each (3,495 scored runs), in a single platform harness that gives each model its provider-native tool interface. Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3%) and GPT-6 Astra (63.7%) lead without a statistically significant gap, followed by Claude Fable 5.1 (46.5%), Gemini 3.8 Flash (40.0%), and a statistically indistinguishable group of Qwen 3.8 Max, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Grok 4.6 (32-34%). No task is fully solved by every model, and on 80 tasks no model earns full credit on all five runs. Scores span 35 points. Depending on the model, agents take a median of 33 to 166 steps per run, with little relation to score. We release 24 tasks with their environments, graders and results, and hold out 76 to limit contamination.
papers.summary: `ExpertCrowd-SWE` (`EC-SWE`) is a benchmark of 100 multi-file software engineering tasks written by practising engineers against pinned commits of real repositories, spanning 87 open-source projects and 11 languages, with sealed reference solutions and executable graders that award partial credit and enforce merge-blocking criteria. Each grader is calibrated so the reference scores 1.0 and no-op changes score 0, and many tasks include lazy and adversarial control patches. Across seven frontier models with five runs each, **`Claude Opus 5.5` (67.3%) and `GPT-6 Astra` (63.7%) lead without a statistically significant gap**, the rest score between 32% and 46.5%, and step counts per run show little relation to score. Twenty-four tasks are released publicly and 76 are held out to limit contamination.

papers.title: Domain-Routed Delta Optimization for Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation assigns each sample a domain teacher but typically updates shared student parameters. We introduce Domain-Routed Delta Optimization (DRD-MOPD), which specifies which parameter components each domain's samples update. The student is the sum of a frozen base and trainable components initialized from expert-minus-base weights. All components participate in every forward pass; four update modes define the correspondence between sample domains and components, each with independent optimizer states. We analyze these update rules and measure retention of the original expert geometry through angles, projection coefficients, and energy. Prior work such as Open-MOPD distills directly from the base model; 97.02% of its released final checkpoint's increment energy lies outside the span of the original expert directions. In comparison, our Own checkpoint after 20 updates retains coefficients near one along each component's original direction and pairwise angles ranging from 88.04 to 92.41 degrees; its exported BF16 student's increment has 4.90% outside energy, versus 10.52% for the sum of saved FP32 components. The same checkpoint achieves a 32.72% macro score across six benchmarks, compared with 32.44% for its initial task-arithmetic merge. These measurements describe geometry and capability at the evaluated training stages and settings.
papers.summary: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation assigns each training sample a domain teacher but normally updates shared student parameters. Domain-Routed Delta Optimization (`DRD-MOPD`) instead builds the student as a frozen base plus trainable components initialized from expert-minus-base weights, and controls which components each domain's samples update, with separate optimizer states. Geometric measurements show the approach preserves the original expert directions far better than `Open-MOPD`, whose final checkpoint has 97.02% of its increment energy outside the expert span versus 4.90% here, though capability barely moves: **a 32.72% macro score across six benchmarks versus 32.44% for the initial task-arithmetic merge**.

papers.title: Curie's Jarvis: Autonomous Robotic Chemistry Experiments from Printed Protocols
papers.abstract: A person running a bench experiment works from a printed instruction sheet, tells identical containers apart by the labels written on them, and looks at the bench again before each step. Lab automation usually works the other way around: the procedure is written as a script, and containers stand at fixed positions or carry fiducial markers. We present Curie's Jarvis, a system that lets a robot arm carry out a chemistry experiment on a bench set up for people. It reads the steps from a photo of the printed sheet, finds containers on an ordinary bench with no fixed positions or markers, tells identical-looking containers apart by reading their labels in four camera views, locates its target again before every step, and sets how each step is carried out, including its speed, from what is being handled. On a Franka Panda arm, Curie's Jarvis completed 5 of 5 runs of one protocol from a children's chemistry kit and 4 of 5 runs of another, with no human intervention, and in 160 locates on printed and handwritten labels it identified every container correctly. This brings robots a step closer to doing bench chemistry the way people do.
