papers.summary: Lab automation usually relies on scripted procedures and containers at fixed positions or with fiducial markers, unlike a human who works from a printed sheet and reads labels. `Curie's Jarvis` lets a robot arm run chemistry experiments on a bench set up for people: it reads the steps from a photo of the printed protocol, finds unmarked containers, distinguishes identical ones by reading their labels from four camera views, re-locates its target before each step, and adapts motion speed to what it is handling. On a `Franka Panda` arm it **completed 5 of 5 runs of one children's chemistry kit protocol and 4 of 5 of another without human intervention**, and identified the container correctly in all 160 label-reading trials.

papers.title: Dependable Long-Horizon LLM Agents: A Trajectory-Centered Empirical Study of Where Errors Enter and Which Controls Reach Them
papers.abstract: When an LLM agent fails part-way through a long task, the usual analysis records a symptom: a failure-mode label, or the agent and step judged responsible. It does not say where the error entered, which state carried it to the symptom, whether anything in the trajectory contradicted it, or which control could have caught it. We define an episode record that ties a candidate fault to its origin, propagation, detection, response and consequence, located by operational phase and state domain, and that names the control families whose observation and reach cover it. We turned the record into a written annotation protocol and applied it to 95 failed runs of six multi-agent systems from the public Who&When and MAD corpora, reading each trajectory in full. Faults enter early (median at 0.18 of the run), mostly as wrong decisions or fabrications over task state, and in 37 of 88 Who&When runs before the step the corpus' human labels mark as decisive. In 72% of failed runs the trajectory already contained evidence against the error before the failure; in 88% of those no agent acted on it. Something flagged a deviation in 31% of runs, but no response removed the deviated state. Independent judges reading the unused evidence, task contracts fixed at admission, and re-checking beliefs against the environment reach most episodes; restoring the agent's own state would have sufficed in 35 of 95 runs. A text scan of the raw corpus also shows that 45% of the hand-crafted Who&When failures ended with a provider content-filter crash after which the harness emitted a final answer no agent produced, a failure class that neither symptom taxonomies nor responsible-agent labels represent. Protocol, records and scripts are included.
papers.summary: Failure analyses of long-running LLM agents usually record a symptom or a responsible step rather than where the error entered, how it propagated, and which control could have caught it. The authors define an episode record linking a fault's origin, propagation, detection, response, and consequence, and apply it by fully reading 95 failed runs of six multi-agent systems from the `Who&When` and `MAD` corpora. Faults enter early (median 18% into the run), and **in 72% of failed runs the trajectory already contained evidence against the error, yet in 88% of those no agent acted on it**; independent judges, task contracts fixed up front, and re-checking beliefs against the environment would reach most episodes. They also find that 45% of hand-crafted `Who&When` failures ended in a provider content-filter crash, after which the harness emitted an answer no agent produced.

papers.title: Which Acoustic Features Survive Compression? Tracker-Estimated First-Formant Statistics for Codec-Robust Audio DeepfakeDetection
papers.abstract: Audio deepfake detectors that work well on clean lab recordings often degrade after telephone or platform compression. This paper asks a specific question: which low-dimensional acoustic descriptors stay informative after codec degradation? We screen 36 utterance-level features(formants, PNCCs, LFCCs, prosody) on ASVspoof 2019 data and test on the official ASVspoof 2021 LA set across seven codec conditions. Of 33 statistically significant descriptors, only four show large practical separation (|r| >0.5, bootstrap 95% CIs), all first-formant (F1) measures, highly redundant (PC1: 79% variance). The payoff is stability: the 36-feature SVM degrades 14 pp under codec mismatch (9.5%-23.5% EER), while the four-feature RBF-SVM degrades only 5.9 pp (17.0%-22.9%). The F1 subset varies 3.4 pp across conditions versus 13.1 pp for the full set. F1 differences persist after controlling for speaker identity (p greater than 10^10, mixed-effects model). The results suggest that physically interpretable F1 statistics offer a compact, codec-stable diagnostic signal that may complement higher accuracy neural detectors.
authors: Yash Sukhdeve (Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering
Masudul H. Imtiaz (Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering
papers.summary: Audio deepfake detectors often degrade after telephone or platform compression, so the authors ask which low-dimensional acoustic features remain informative across codecs. Screening 36 utterance-level features on `ASVspoof 2019` and testing on `ASVspoof 2021 LA` under seven codec conditions, they find only four with large practical separation, all statistics of the first formant (F1) and highly redundant with each other. A four-feature RBF-SVM is less accurate on clean audio but far more stable: **its equal error rate degrades 5.9 points under codec mismatch versus 14 points for the full 36-feature SVM**, suggesting F1 statistics as a compact complement to neural detectors.

papers.title: Adaptive Residual Quantization for Memory-Efficient Temporal Action Segmentation
papers.abstract: Temporal action segmentation (TAS) is commonly trained on large banks of pre-extracted frame features, but storing and replaying those features becomes a practical bottleneck for long-form video, especially in incremental TAS where past-task data must remain available to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. Recent TAS replay and condensation methods reduce this burden, but they rely on dense frame-wise annotations and allocate storage through fixed segment-level structures, limiting their flexibility for long procedural videos whose frame complexity varies substantially over time. We introduce Adaptive Residual-Quantized Variational AutoEncoder (ARQ-VAE), a compact and label-free memory representation for TAS features that learns a discrete residual quantization of frame-level video features and then adaptively truncates the residual chain on a per-frame basis, retaining only the residual prefix that best reconstructs each frame feature. This yields a practical compact feature memory that does not depend on frame-wise labels and can therefore support multiple TAS settings with the same stored representation, while a lightweight fine-tuning stage further improves reconstruction quality for the truncated codes that are actually retained. Across standard TAS benchmarks, ARQ-VAE achieves a substantially improved storage-performance trade-off over prior replay and condensation baselines. On Breakfast, our final representation reduces training-set storage from 28 GB for the original I3D feature bank to 10 MB while retaining strong downstream segmentation performance; with ASFormer, it achieves 71.5 Edit and 51.2 F1@50 in the supervised setting. We further show that the same label-free memory remains effective for incremental and unsupervised TAS. We position ARQ-VAE as a practical memory representation for TAS and a promising direction for broader dataset condensation applications.
papers.summary: Temporal action segmentation (TAS) trains on large banks of pre-extracted frame features, and storing them is a bottleneck for long videos and for incremental learning, where past data must be replayed. `ARQ-VAE` (Adaptive Residual-Quantized Variational AutoEncoder) learns a discrete residual quantization of frame features and truncates the residual chain per frame, keeping only the prefix that best reconstructs each frame, with no dependence on frame-wise labels. On `Breakfast` it **shrinks training-set storage from 28 GB of `I3D` features to 10 MB** while reaching 71.5 Edit and 51.2 F1@50 with `ASFormer`, and the same memory works for incremental and unsupervised settings.

papers.title: What drives the emergence of symbolic mechanisms in large language models?
papers.abstract: Recent work has identified a set of emergent symbolic mechanisms that support abstract reasoning in large language models, but it remains unclear what factors drive the emergence of these mechanisms. To address this question, we trained neural networks from scratch on abstract sequence tasks, varying both architectural and data distributional factors, and investigated the effects of these factors on the emergence of symbolic mechanisms. Using representational, attentional, and causal mediation analyses, we first confirmed that transformer-based language models trained from scratch on our task developed symbolic mechanisms. We then found that, across multiple axes of data diversity, greater diversity produced stronger symbolic signatures. Surprisingly, the same signatures emerged in modified transformer architectures and even multilayer perceptrons, indicating that architectural inductive biases are not necessary for the development of symbolic mechanisms. We also observed consistent patterns in an entity-attribute binding task. Together, these findings identify data diversity, not architecture, as the primary driver of emergent symbolic computation in neural networks.
papers.summary: Prior work found emergent symbolic mechanisms supporting abstract reasoning in large language models, but not what causes them to form. Training networks from scratch on abstract sequence tasks while varying architecture and data distribution, and probing them with representational, attentional, and causal mediation analyses, the authors find that greater data diversity yields stronger symbolic signatures. The same signatures appear in modified transformers and even multilayer perceptrons, leading to the conclusion that **data diversity, not architecture, is the primary driver of emergent symbolic computation**; an entity-attribute binding task shows consistent patterns.

papers.title: Off-policy Learning with Excursion Policies
papers.abstract: Off-policy reinforcement learning (RL) tries to learn the value of a target policy while data comes from a different behavior policy. This often requires trading off bias for variance or stability. One way to trade these off is to linearly interpolate between the behavior and target policies, but this represents only one point in a broader space of interpolation mechanisms. We introduce excursion policies--a structured alternative where the agent follows the target policy for a multi-step "excursion" before reverting to the behavior policy. We derive dynamic programming results for these policies, establishing the theoretical basis for their use in RL. We further develop provably sound off-policy temporal-difference (TD) algorithms for excursion value estimation. We find that excursion policies provide an efficiency-stability trade-off comparable to mixture policies in continuous control benchmarks, and our analysis illustrates conceptual differences in their behavior.
papers.summary: Off-policy reinforcement learning evaluates a target policy from data generated by a different behavior policy, typically trading bias against variance or stability by linearly mixing the two. Excursion policies offer a structured alternative in which the agent follows the target policy for a multi-step excursion before reverting to the behavior policy. The authors derive dynamic programming results and provably sound off-policy temporal-difference algorithms for them, and find on continuous control benchmarks that **excursion policies give an efficiency-stability trade-off comparable to mixture policies**, while behaving differently in concept.

papers.title: An Analytical Model of Compute-limited Multistage Training Pipelines
papers.abstract: Modern foundation models are trained through multiple stages, yet how these stages interact and how compute should be allocated across them remain poorly understood. We introduce an analytically tractable high-dimensional model combining unsupervised pretraining with a linear autoencoder, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with noisy stepwise labels, and reinforcement learning (RL) with sparse episodic rewards. Using random matrix theory and an operator-projection closure, we derive approximate low-dimensional learning dynamics that closely match simulations. We show that finite pretraining data imposes a representation-dependent performance limit, with Bayes classification error scaling as the inverse square root of the pretraining sample ratio, and observe the same exponent in asymptotic SFT and RL errors. Better pretraining also reduces sensitivity to noisy supervision. SFT initialization shortens the initial RL plateau induced by sparse rewards, an effect we also observe in OLMo-2 1B on GSM8K. Longer SFT warm starts additionally improve asymptotic RL performance. Optimizing compute across all three stages reveals that the optimal allocation depends on supervision quality and total budget, with a non-monotonic dependence of the RL compute share on budget. Finally, a complementary compositional model shows how RL selectively strengthens task-relevant pretrained skills while largely preserving unused skills. Together, these results identify mechanisms linking representation quality, feedback structure, and compute allocation in multistage training.
papers.summary: How pretraining, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL) interact, and how compute should be split among them, is studied through an analytically tractable high-dimensional model combining a linear autoencoder, noisy stepwise labels, and sparse episodic rewards. Using random matrix theory, the authors derive low-dimensional dynamics matching simulations and show that finite pretraining data caps performance, with **error scaling as the inverse square root of the pretraining sample ratio** across stages. SFT warm starts shorten the initial RL plateau caused by sparse rewards, an effect also observed in `OLMo-2 1B` on `GSM8K`, and the optimal compute allocation depends on supervision quality and budget, with the RL share varying non-monotonically.

papers.title: MRFoundry: Knowledge-guided agent loops for end-to-end MRI research
papers.abstract: AI agents can write code, use scientific software, and revise computational workflows, opening new possibilities for MRI research. Effective assistance requires connecting acquisition physics, data conventions, specialized tools, and scientific validation. We present MRFoundry, an open-source, extensible package that connects MRI knowledge to agent actions and output checks. Project-local memory preserves decisions and evidence, while reviewed contributions allow researchers to improve shared guidance. Researcher-supervised examples demonstrate skill-guided sequence auditing and acquired-data reconstruction, connecting tool use, output checks, and documented decisions. Alongside MRFoundry, we introduce MRI Agent Bench to compare agents with and without the package across models and MRI task domains. Across 240 paired Core evaluations spanning 24 task types and ten models, all-checks-passed completion increased from 67.5% without MRFoundry to 78.3% with it. Across 134 Hard pairs, completion increased from 36.6% to 44.8%. MRFoundry makes MRI workflow expertise available as reusable guidance that researchers can inspect, adapt, and extend within existing agent and scientific software environments. MRFoundry is openly available at https://github.com/KeWang0622/MRFoundry.
papers.summary: `MRFoundry` is an open-source package that connects magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) domain knowledge — acquisition physics, data conventions, specialized tools, and validation checks — to the actions of AI coding agents, with project-local memory for decisions and evidence and a review process for shared guidance. The authors also introduce `MRI Agent Bench` to compare agents with and without the package across models and task domains. Across 240 paired core evaluations spanning 24 task types and ten models, **all-checks-passed completion rose from 67.5% to 78.3% with the package**, and on 134 hard pairs from 36.6% to 44.8%.

papers.title: Decode Token Parallelism: Memory-Efficient Distributed Attention Parallelism for Scalable LLM Decoding
papers.abstract: Serving large language models at high concurrency with long contexts requires KV-cache capacity and attention bandwidth that grow with the decode pool. Existing parallelization strategies trade one against the other: data parallelism replicates model weights, limiting KV capacity; tensor parallelism stops scaling attention at the model's KV-head count and pushes dense collectives across nodes; and decode context parallelism (DCP) recovers capacity by sharding the sequence but adds cross-node aggregation of partial attention results. We observe that during decode, dense layers and attention scale differently: dense layers amortize weight reads across the batch and run efficiently within a single NVLink domain, whereas attention cost grows with every active request's KV cache. We present Decode Token Parallelism (TKNP), a decode-pool architecture that decouples weight placement from attention ownership. TKNP distributes a single model copy across nodes in balanced layer blocks. The active node holding a block executes its projections and MLP for the full batch using intra-node tensor parallelism, while every node computes attention for its own requests against locally resident KV cache. This extends request-local attention across nodes without replicating weights: only current-token activations cross the network, dense all-reduces remain within NVLink, and attention requires no cross-node merging of partial results. Implemented in vLLM and evaluated on Llama 3.1 405B and Nemotron-4 340B on up to 64 H100 GPUs, TKNP improves completion throughput for long-context, high-concurrency workloads by up to 1.7$\times$ over DCP and by up to 2.06$\times$ over data parallelism at matched GPU count.
papers.summary: Serving large language models at high concurrency with long contexts forces a trade-off between KV-cache capacity and attention scaling under data parallelism, tensor parallelism, and decode context parallelism (DCP). `TKNP` (Decode Token Parallelism) spreads a single model copy across nodes in balanced layer blocks: the node holding a block runs its dense layers for the full batch, while every node computes attention for its own requests against its locally stored KV cache, so only current-token activations cross the network. Implemented in `vLLM` and tested on `Llama 3.1 405B` and `Nemotron-4 340B` on up to 64 H100 GPUs, it improves completion throughput on long-context, high-concurrency workloads by **up to 1.7x over DCP and up to 2.06x over data parallelism** at matched GPU count.

papers.title: Time Series Change Point Detection with Gaussian Processes
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a novel general Gaussian process framework for change point detection in time series. A change is defined as an alteration of the hyperparameters of the Gaussian process prior. We formulate the problem in the context of statistical hypothesis testing and demonstrate its performance over both offline and online multiple change points detection. The approach provides theoretical guaranties of its performance. An important advantage of the developed framework is that it does not need a detailed specification of the time series function before and after a change. The hyperparameter values are learned from the data. Comprehensive evaluation of the proposed framework is provided both on synthetic and real data and its efficiency is demonstrated.
papers.summary: Change points in a time series are defined here as alterations in the hyperparameters of a Gaussian process prior, and detecting them is framed as a statistical hypothesis test. The framework covers both offline and online detection of multiple change points and comes with theoretical performance guarantees. Its main stated advantage is that **it needs no detailed specification of the series before and after a change**, because hyperparameter values are learned from the data; evaluation uses synthetic and real data.

papers.title: Neural Network-Assisted CLEAN for Efficient Multipath Parameter Estimation in MIMO Systems
papers.abstract: High-resolution multipath estimation in wideband multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) channels requires repeated searches over angle of arrival, angle of departure, and propagation distance. This paper presents neural network-assisted CLEAN (NN-CLEAN), which replaces the multidimensional search at each extraction step with a multi-head classifier while retaining least-squares (LS) estimation of the complex path gain, parametric reconstruction, and residual cancellation. The same classifier is applied to successive residuals, allowing the extraction depth to vary without changing its output structure. With the number of iterations prescribed by the reference multipath-component (MPC) count, off-grid synthetic tests show that NN-CLEAN slightly exceeds grid-search CLEAN (GS-CLEAN) in path accuracy for one and two MPCs, although its accuracy declines more rapidly at larger path counts. For complete three-MPC extraction at a batch size of eight, NN-CLEAN achieves an approximately $27\times$ speedup and a $52$-fold reduction in peak GPU memory relative to GS-CLEAN. Applied without retraining to two-MPC line-of-sight (LOS) and non-line-of-sight (NLOS) Sionna ray-tracing channels within a coded MIMO link, NN-CLEAN substantially reduces channel-reconstruction mean-squared error (MSE) and bit error rate (BER) relative to interpolated LS channel estimation. GS-CLEAN retains an accuracy advantage on these channels, indicating the estimation cost associated with the computational savings.
papers.summary: Estimating multipath components in wideband multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) channels normally requires repeated grid searches over angle of arrival, angle of departure, and propagation distance. `NN-CLEAN` replaces that search at each extraction step with a multi-head classifier, while keeping least-squares estimation of path gain, parametric reconstruction, and residual cancellation. For three-path extraction it is **about 27x faster with 52-fold lower peak GPU memory** than grid-search `GS-CLEAN`, and it slightly exceeds it in accuracy for one and two paths but degrades faster at larger path counts. Applied without retraining to `Sionna` ray-traced channels, it reduces channel-reconstruction error and bit error rate relative to interpolated least-squares estimation, though `GS-CLEAN` remains more accurate there.

papers.title: DUO: Dual Readouts of Diffusion Models for OOD Detection
papers.abstract: Diffusion models are powerful generative methods for learning and sampling from complex data distributions. Safely deploying these models requires detecting inputs that fall outside their training distribution. Because diffusion models recover clean samples from noisy inputs, reconstruction error is often used for out-of-distribution (OOD) detection. This approach assumes that in-distribution (ID) inputs are reconstructed more accurately than OOD inputs. However, OOD inputs may be reconstructed equally well or even better, making this score unreliable. We therefore propose the leading sensitivity spectrum of intermediate denoising features as a complementary OOD signal and demonstrate that it remains informative when reconstruction error is misleading. We introduce DUal-readout of diffusion models for OOD detection (DUO), a fully unsupervised, training-free OOD detector that combines reconstruction error and feature sensitivity. DUO improves average AUROC by approximately 6% points over the strongest baselines while substantially reducing inference cost, and achieves SOTA on near-OOD and high-resolution benchmarks.
papers.summary: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection with diffusion models usually relies on reconstruction error, which fails when OOD inputs are reconstructed as well as or better than in-distribution ones. `DUO` adds a second signal, the leading sensitivity spectrum of intermediate denoising features, and combines it with reconstruction error in a fully unsupervised, training-free detector. It improves average AUROC by **about 6 percentage points over the strongest baselines** while substantially reducing inference cost, and reports state-of-the-art results on near-OOD and high-resolution benchmarks.

papers.title: Train High, Ship Low: Efficient LoRA Synchronization for Distributed On-Policy Post-Training
papers.abstract: Transmitting LoRA adapters to rollout workers can bottleneck distributed on-policy post-training over bandwidth-constrained networks. Lowering the training rank may limit the capacity a workload needs, while adaptive optimizer updates are difficult to compress. Rollout workers can instead reconstruct updates from gradients by maintaining replicated optimizer states. We introduce HiLo, a compressor-agnostic framework that replaces parameter transmission with compressed gradient dissemination and local optimizer replay. By applying the same decoded gradients, the learner and workers maintain consistent policy states at the same version under reproducible execution. We further develop Spar, a budget-aware gradient compressor that combines spectral truncation, adaptive rank allocation and error feedback to decouple training rank from communication cost. Experiments across on-policy distillation and reward-guided post-training show that HiLo with Spar maintains learning quality close to full synchronization while transmitting as little as 1.6% of the adapter bytes, and accelerates end-to-end updates by up to $2.2\times$ under bandwidth constraints.
papers.summary: Sending LoRA adapters to rollout workers can bottleneck distributed on-policy post-training when bandwidth is limited. `HiLo` instead transmits compressed gradients and has each worker replay the optimizer locally from replicated optimizer state, so learner and workers stay at the same policy version under reproducible execution. Its companion compressor `Spar` combines spectral truncation, adaptive rank allocation, and error feedback to decouple training rank from communication cost. Across on-policy distillation and reward-guided post-training, learning quality stays close to full synchronization while transmitting **as little as 1.6% of the adapter bytes**, with end-to-end updates up to 2.2x faster under bandwidth constraints.

papers.title: PegasusAI Studio: Legible Cyberinfrastructure and Accountable AI Agents for Scientific Workflows
papers.abstract: AI coding agents can now construct scientific workflows, but operating them on shared cyberinfrastructure (CI) raises problems that code generation does not solve. Agents need current knowledge of the workflow system and its execution sites and access to the runtime state of distributed executions, while facilities need to attribute every agent action to a user and bound it by that user's privileges. We present PegasusAI Studio, an AI-assisted science gateway built on the Pegasus and HTCondor stack. Studio makes CI legible to agents by projecting one facility-curated knowledge base into the native configuration of several coding agents, by introspecting workflow interfaces and execution sites, and by grounding diagnosis in workflow and scheduler telemetry. Agent actions operate within a trust envelope that combines federated authentication, per-user execution environments and scheduler credentials, provider-neutral model access, observability, and approval controls for state-changing actions. The same application runs as a JupyterHub-based gateway on a research cloud and as an Open OnDemand application on HPC systems. We evaluate Studio through case studies of legacy CASA weather workflow modernization, a gravitational-wave reanalysis, an EEG analysis built with an open-weight model, and an Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) M87 image reconstruction that recovered from two failed runs to a zero-failure execution. The evaluation establishes that these mechanisms operate as designed.
papers.summary: Running AI coding agents on shared scientific cyberinfrastructure requires that agents know the current workflow system and execution sites, and that facilities can attribute every agent action to a user and bound it by that user's privileges. `PegasusAI Studio`, a science gateway built on the `Pegasus` and `HTCondor` stack, projects one facility-curated knowledge base into the native configuration of several coding agents, introspects workflow interfaces and sites, and grounds diagnosis in workflow and scheduler telemetry. Agent actions run inside a trust envelope of federated authentication, per-user execution environments and credentials, observability, and approval controls for state-changing actions. Evaluation is by case study only, including weather workflow modernization, a gravitational-wave reanalysis, and an Event Horizon Telescope image reconstruction that **recovered from two failed runs to a zero-failure execution**.

papers.title: One Trajectory, Two Requirements: Accuracy and Local Stability in Euler Sampling for Flow Matching Policies
papers.abstract: Flow matching robot policies commonly use a fixed Euler step count selected from offline accuracy sweeps. At inference time, however, each policy input (visual observation, robot state, and language instruction) together with a source-noise draw defines a different ODE trajectory and sequence of local Jacobians. We ask whether a step count that accurately follows the nominal noise-to-action trajectory can still be too coarse for strongly contracting directions around it. An exact two-coordinate system and a controlled augmentation of six trained flow models show that trajectory accuracy and local Euler stability can impose different step requirements even when the original learned transport is unchanged. We then study a frozen $\pi_{0.5}$-LIBERO checkpoint without modifying its weights or action dynamics. Across 30 policy inputs from 10 LIBERO-10 tasks, the Jacobian exhibits strong contracting directions near the action endpoint, yet no sampled mode violates the Euler non-expansion condition. On five of those inputs, accuracy sweeps require 4--9 Euler steps at 5% terminal error and 87--112 at 1%. These five paired cases are therefore consistent with accuracy-limited rather than stability-limited sampling under this local criterion, while the controlled experiments show why endpoint accuracy alone cannot rule out a separate stability requirement.
papers.summary: Flow matching robot policies typically use a fixed Euler step count chosen from offline accuracy sweeps, which raises the question of whether a count that tracks the nominal trajectory accurately can still be too coarse for strongly contracting directions around it. An exact two-coordinate system and a controlled augmentation of six trained flow models show that trajectory accuracy and local Euler stability can impose different step requirements. On a frozen `π0.5`-`LIBERO` checkpoint across 30 inputs from 10 `LIBERO-10` tasks, the Jacobian shows strong contraction near the action endpoint but **no sampled mode violates the Euler non-expansion condition**. Five of those inputs need 4-9 steps for 5% terminal error and 87-112 for 1%, consistent with sampling that is limited by accuracy and not by stability.

papers.title: Towards Scalable Network-Based Interventions for HIV Treatment and Prevention via R2C-Agent
papers.abstract: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) remains a pressing public health challenge worldwide. Targeting limited HIV prevention and treatment resources effectively with network-based algorithms is a long-standing problem with a rich history at AAMAS and other computational venues. However, optimizing targeted biomedical interventions for minimizing spread of HIV often requires observability of the contact network of HIV transmission risk behavior among individuals, which is prohibitively expensive to collect at scale. Peer referral networks, i.e., networks collected through a recursive peer referral process, are an alternative network class often used to study HIV in hidden populations that can be collected digitally at scale, but they deviate from the underlying contact network: referrals can follow non-risk social ties and participants accept only one referral, hiding contacts among already-recruited individuals. In this work, we first formalize the novel problem of planning network-based interventions to minimize HIV spread in the hidden contact network while observing only the peer referral network. Second, we implement R2C-Agent, a decision making agent for interventions that is designed around our new conditional graph diffusion model called Referral-to-Contact Diffusion (R2C-Diff). R2C-Diff positions the peer referral process as incremental corruption of the underlying contact network and learns to reverse it. R2C-Agent plans its interventions over contact networks sampled from R2C-Diff, so its decisions account for uncertainty about the hidden contact network. Finally, we conduct simulated experiments using real-world HIV network data that demonstrate that R2C-Agent empirically plans more effective interventions than baselines from interdisciplinary literature and highlight key tradeoffs and assumptions driving performance.
papers.summary: Planning network-based HIV prevention and treatment interventions usually assumes the contact network of transmission risk is observable, but only peer referral networks can be collected at scale, and these omit or distort contacts. The authors formalize intervention planning on the hidden contact network given only the referral network, and introduce `R2C-Diff` (Referral-to-Contact Diffusion), a conditional graph diffusion model that treats peer referral as incremental corruption of the contact network and learns to reverse it. `R2C-Agent` plans over contact networks sampled from that model so its decisions account for uncertainty. In simulations on real-world HIV network data, it **plans more effective interventions than baselines** drawn from the interdisciplinary literature.

papers.title: MicroLens: Read, Trace, and Rewire the Residual Stream with Two Lenses
papers.abstract: Lenses that decode hidden states into words are a popular way to look inside language models, but a heatmap of decoded words only shows what a vector reads as and cannot distinguish whether, or how much, the model uses the information. We present an interactive viewer that puts reading, tracing and editing on the same layers-by-tokens grid of the residual stream. In the viewer, every cell can be decoded with two lenses, the logit lens and the Jacobian lens (J-lens), traced back to the tokens it drew from, and edited, with the rest of the model rerun on the spot. We demonstrate three usage scenarios on Gemma-3-4B-it, backed by sweeps over a few hundred prompts, to show what this tool can discover. First, the two lenses give different directions to write with, each suiting a different edit: the logit lens's word direction sets what a token outputs, while the J-lens's direction changes what later tokens read. Second, in two-hop trivia questions (the capital of the state or country containing a given city), the state or country is readable at the city token from as early as layer 7, and swapping it there can redirect the answer 92-98% of the time; however, at the answer position, the state or country information is not used. Third, when a chat model answers questions with a step-by-step reasoning prompt, the correct answer is often already the top word in the residual stream before any reasoning is written: for 89-92% of retrieval questions and 39-63% of multi-hop and serial ones, far above their respective distractors (at most 5%). However, ordering puzzles are an exception, as the model works them out only once it writes its final reasoning steps. Furthermore, for answers that are visible in the residual stream, the J-lens reads them a layer or two earlier than the logit lens across the different types of question.
papers.summary: Lenses that decode hidden states into words show what a vector reads as, but not whether the model uses that information. `MicroLens` is an interactive viewer over the layers-by-tokens grid of the residual stream in which each cell can be decoded with the `logit lens` or a Jacobian lens (`J-lens`), traced back to source tokens, and edited with the model rerun on the spot. On `Gemma-3-4B-it`, swapping the state or country readable at the city token from layer 7 redirects two-hop trivia answers 92-98% of the time, even though that information is not used at the answer position. Under step-by-step reasoning prompts, the correct answer is **already the top residual-stream word before any reasoning is written for 89-92% of retrieval questions** and 39-63% of multi-hop and serial ones, with ordering puzzles as the exception.

papers.title: Robust Flow Matching under Target Corruption and Label Noise
papers.abstract: Flow Matching (FM) is a strong framework for generative modeling due to its stable training and efficient sampling. However, FM assumes clean target data and labels, an assumption often violated in practice. We formulate FM training as a time-dependent regression problem over conditional vector fields and analyze how the two corruption types affect the objective: i) target corruption adds a time-dependent residual term that grows with time, ii) label noise causes updates to the wrong class-conditional vector field. Based on this analysis, we propose to improve FM robustness by mapping corruption-specific residual scores to sample weights. For target corruption, we propose the Temporal Residual Score (TRS), which emphasizes residual magnitudes at intermediate-to-late FM times, where clean and corrupted samples are more separable. For label noise, we propose the Comparative Conditional Score (CCS), which compares the residual of the observed class-conditional vector field against alternative class-conditional vector fields for the same trajectory and velocity target. Experiments across controlled corruption settings and real-world noisy labels show that the proposed methods improve robustness over standard FM and robust-training baselines, supporting corruption-specific residual structure as a practical basis for robust FM.
papers.summary: Flow Matching (FM) training assumes clean target data and labels, which often does not hold in practice. Treating FM as a time-dependent regression over conditional vector fields, the analysis shows that target corruption adds a residual term that grows with time, while label noise sends updates to the wrong class-conditional vector field. Two sample-weighting scores follow: the `Temporal Residual Score` (TRS), which emphasizes residuals at intermediate-to-late times where clean and corrupted samples separate, and the `Comparative Conditional Score` (CCS), which compares the residual under the observed class against alternative classes. Across controlled corruption settings and real-world noisy labels, the methods **improve robustness over standard FM and robust-training baselines**.

papers.title: F3-AGI v4.0: Bioenergetically-Gated Active Inference, Metaplastic Preconditioning, and Residual Program Synthesis for Sample-Efficient Abstract Reasoning
papers.abstract: Few-shot abstract reasoning on ARC-AGI requires inducing algorithmic transformations from 2 to 5 demonstration pairs without task-specific pretraining. Because few-shot demonstrations under-constrain the hypothesis space, program synthesis suffers from the Rashomon effect (predictive multiplicity): heuristic search finds spurious programs with low training error that fail on test inputs, while unconstrained library growth degrades latency. We introduce F3-AGI v4.0, a CPU-native neuro-symbolic and active inference architecture comprising three mechanisms: (1) F3-Metabolic-Optim, combining mistake-gated plasticity, Fisher-EMA preconditioning, and virtual ATP gating; (2) Adaptive Complexity-Guided Program Synthesis (AACR) with a Cycle-3 ResidualPatchSynthesizer and smallest-pair early rejection; and (3) a 512D L2-normalized random projection driving Expected Free Energy (EFE) exploration with dead-signature pruning. Across three empirical studies: (i) on a synthetic 5-task class-incremental stream without replay, F3-Metabolic-Optim achieves 91.67% final accuracy with 9.17% forgetting, skipping 93.47% of updates, cutting L1 plasticity cost by 65.7%, and running 2.19x faster than EWC; (ii) on the 400-task ARC-AGI-1 public evaluation set (offline CPU, zero LLM calls), F3-AGI v4.0 solves 57/400 tasks (14.25% pass@2; 56/400 pass@1) with a mean latency of 1.62 s/task, decomposed into 19/50 (38.00%, 1.19 s/task, a 42.5x paired speedup over Horizon 2) on the 50-task calibration slice and 38/350 (10.86%) on the 350 strictly uninspected hold-out tasks (with 7 autonomous Cycle-3 patch solutions); and (iii) in a local 5-game (15-level) ARC-AGI-3-inspired interactive suite, our agent completes 15/15 levels with 89.44% level-weighted RHAE (90.72% unweighted).
papers.summary: Few-shot abstract reasoning on `ARC-AGI` is under-constrained by its 2 to 5 demonstration pairs, so program search tends to find spurious programs that fit the examples but fail on test inputs. `F3-AGI v4.0` is a CPU-only neuro-symbolic and active inference architecture combining a gated-plasticity optimizer (`F3-Metabolic-Optim`), complexity-guided program synthesis with residual patching, and exploration driven by Expected Free Energy. On the 400-task `ARC-AGI-1` public evaluation set, run offline on CPU with no LLM calls, it solves **57/400 tasks (14.25% pass@2) at a mean 1.62 s per task**, of which 38/350 (10.86%) are on tasks the authors did not inspect. It also reports 91.67% final accuracy on a synthetic 5-task continual learning stream and completion of 15/15 levels in a local `ARC-AGI-3`-inspired interactive suite.

papers.title: Agent-Guided Discovery of Exchange-Correlation Functionals with Physics-based Validation
papers.abstract: Accurate, compact exchange--correlation functionals are central to predictive density functional theory. Symbolic search and language-model agents can propose new functional forms, but it remains unclear whether their gains survive self-consistency and external evaluation, whether the new terms carry physical content, whether agents outperform evolutionary search, and how language-model backbones compare. We connect frontier LLM agents to a GPU evaluator through the Model Context Protocol, with training-only fitting, persistent memory, and self-consistent and external evaluation. Opus-5.5 agents passed the screening gate with about 40-fold fewer tokens than Codex (GPT-6-Astra) agents and found a candidate with lower validation and held-out errors; only this candidate advanced to self-consistent evaluation. The resulting 13-parameter functional, O159, multiplies same-spin correlation by a smooth density window. Refitted controls favor a window that scales the entire same-spin factor, reducing it by 15--30\% at its peak, and that acts on reaction energies mainly in near-iso-orbital regions; against a refitted no-window control, it lowers heavy-atom total-energy errors on GSCDB137 by 29\%. With about 400 fits each, SyFES evolution did not improve on its GAS22 seed, whereas the agents found forms 0.10--0.13 \kcal\ lower in validation error by adding an explicit density scale. Self-consistent O159 lowers the held-out MGCDB84 test error of $\omega$B97M-V by 11.7\%, and its mean normalized error ratio on 36 GSCDB137 datasets (1.139) is comparable to $\omega$B97M-V (1.144) and below GAS22 (1.190). Frontier-LLM agents thus produced O159, a compact functional whose improvement over $\omega$B97M-V survives self-consistent, physics-based validation.
papers.summary: Whether language-model agents can discover exchange-correlation functionals for density functional theory whose gains survive self-consistent and external evaluation is tested by connecting frontier LLM agents to a GPU evaluator through the Model Context Protocol, with training-only fitting and persistent memory. `Opus-5.5` agents passed the screening gate with about 40-fold fewer tokens than `Codex` (`GPT-6-Astra`) agents and found the better candidate, while `SyFES` evolutionary search did not improve on its `GAS22` seed in about 400 fits. The resulting 13-parameter functional, `O159`, multiplies same-spin correlation by a smooth density window. Evaluated self-consistently, it **lowers the held-out `MGCDB84` test error of `ωB97M-V` by 11.7%** and is comparable to it on 36 `GSCDB137` datasets.

papers.title: Stochastic Projections and Rank-Aware Learning Rates for Federated LoRA
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large-scale foundation models across resource-constrained, distributed clients presents significant computational and communication challenges. While merging Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) with Federated Learning (FL) enables rank-based flexibility, the interdependence of the adaptation matrices ($\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$) often complicates optimization. In this work, we theoretically demonstrate that LoRA fine-tuning with Gaussian initialization and a frozen $\mathbf{A}$ matrix acts as a stochastic approximation of full fine-tuning, where batch gradients are subject to a random, rank-dependent perturbation. Motivated by this insight, we propose freezing and periodically resampling $\mathbf{A}$ matrices at the client level. This strategy decouples the $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ gradients, diminishes LoRA low-rank constraints and reduces both computational and uplink communication overheads by 50\%, allowing for the reallocation of resources toward higher adaptation ranks. Furthermore, we show that in this frozen-$\mathbf{A}$ regime, the adaptation rank $r$ directly governs the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the perturbed gradients. Specifically, we find that the SNR increases linearly with $r$, implying that clients' learning rates must be dynamically scaled with their adaptation ranks for higher utility. Building on these foundations, we introduce SPRA-LoRA (Stochastic Projection Rank-Aware LoRA), a federated rank-aware fine-tuning strategy that utilizes frozen, resampled $\mathbf{A}$ matrices and rank-dependent learning rates for clients. We also prove its convergence with heterogeneous client resources. Our experiments across benchmark datasets demonstrate that SPRA-LoRA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines with half the overhead on clients.
papers.summary: Combining Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) with Federated Learning is complicated by the interdependence of the two adaptation matrices A and B. The authors show theoretically that LoRA with Gaussian initialization and a frozen A acts as a stochastic approximation of full fine-tuning, with a gradient signal-to-noise ratio that increases linearly with rank. `SPRA-LoRA` (Stochastic Projection Rank-Aware LoRA) therefore freezes and periodically resamples A on each client and scales client learning rates with rank, **cutting client computation and uplink communication by 50%**. A convergence proof covers heterogeneous client resources, and experiments report consistent gains over state-of-the-art baselines.

papers.title: Do AI Agents need Preventive Care? An Epidemiologic Cohort Design for Agentic AI
papers.abstract: As AI agents increasingly perform tasks autonomously across sectors, including healthcare and biomedical research, understanding how their behaviors develop and influence outcomes over time becomes increasingly important. Existing evaluations largely focus on model capabilities and performance on predefined tasks. Here, we propose an epidemiologic cohort design for studying agentic AI, drawing on principles established in human population studies. The framework treats individual agents as members of a cohort, their underlying model as genetic makeup, accumulated work as their time scale, and naturally occurring behaviors as exposures that may influence subsequent outcomes. By following agents longitudinally, this approach enables investigation of behavioral determinants of adverse events, estimation of their potential preventable burden under causal assumptions, and characterization of behavioral changes over an agent's work life. We illustrate the design through two prospective observational cohorts examining curiosity and probing as a safety question, and data checking and analytical accuracy as a reliability question. Together, the framework and illustrative studies provide a generalizable blueprint for designing epidemiologic cohorts of AI agents.
papers.summary: Evaluations of AI agents mostly measure capability on predefined tasks and say little about how behaviors develop and affect outcomes over time. The proposal is an epidemiologic cohort design that **treats individual agents as cohort members followed longitudinally**, with the underlying model as genetic makeup, accumulated work as the time scale, and naturally occurring behaviors as exposures. This allows study of behavioral determinants of adverse events and estimation of preventable burden under causal assumptions. Two prospective observational cohorts illustrate it: one on curiosity and probing as a safety question, and one on data checking and analytical accuracy as a reliability question.

papers.title: Disentangling Multimodal Rotary Positional Embedding in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language models widely adopt Multimodal Rotary Position Embedding (MRoPE), an extension of Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) that incorporates temporal, height, and width axes to encode the spatial structure of visual tokens. However, MRoPE also assigns height and width coordinates to text tokens that lack inherent spatial structure, introducing spatial positional effects into text-vision attention. Existing MRoPE variants explore different frequency allocations and coordinate layouts, with their designs suggesting different intuitions about these cross-modal effects: they may provide useful spatial references for associating language with visual regions, or introduce unnecessary positional preferences that hinder text-vision interactions. In this work, we disentangle intra-visual spatial structure from cross-modal spatial effects to investigate this question. We identify a constraint of shared coordinate layouts that prevents eliminating cross-modal spatial effects while preserving intra-visual spatial encoding, and develop controlled experiments to isolate their respective contributions. Our results across multiple model scales, MRoPE variants, and benchmarks show that cross-modal spatial effects provide little additional benefit as spatial references and can even impair model performance, while intra-visual spatial encoding remains useful for fine-grained grounding.
papers.summary: Multimodal Rotary Position Embedding (`MRoPE`) gives visual tokens temporal, height, and width coordinates, but also assigns height and width to text tokens, which introduces spatial positional effects into text-vision attention. The authors identify a constraint of shared coordinate layouts that prevents removing these cross-modal effects while keeping spatial encoding among visual tokens, and design controlled experiments to separate the two contributions. Across model scales, `MRoPE` variants, and benchmarks, **cross-modal spatial effects add little as spatial references and can impair performance**, while intra-visual spatial encoding remains useful for fine-grained grounding.

papers.title: Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks
papers.abstract: The effectiveness of a self-improving system relies heavily on the quality of its verifier, which judges the outcome of each improvement round. However, the verifiers of most tasks are written by hand, which is expensive and does not scale to tasks that come without one. We propose Veritas, a harness that generates verifiers automatically. Unlike general-purpose agent harnesses, Veritas adds three mechanisms for verifier generation: an evidence header stating what the verifier will observe, a library of domain rules that tasks leave unstated, and authoring principles, partly refined by a self-improvement loop. We evaluate on six benchmarks: four scored by execution, whose official verifiers we first certify, and two that compare pairs of responses. With the model fixed, the verifiers Veritas generates agree better with the official verdicts than those of seven other harnesses on all four execution-scored benchmarks. On the two pairwise benchmarks they are at or near the best. They also agree better than those of the vendor's own harness for two of three other model families. Its mechanisms also improve 9 of 12 harness-benchmark pairs scored by execution across three harnesses.
papers.summary: Self-improving agent systems depend on a verifier to judge each round, and those verifiers are mostly written by hand. `Veritas` is a harness that generates verifiers automatically using an evidence header stating what the verifier will observe, a library of domain rules that tasks leave unstated, and authoring principles partly refined by a self-improvement loop. With the model held fixed, its verifiers **agree with official verdicts better than those of seven other harnesses on all four execution-scored benchmarks** and are at or near the best on two pairwise-comparison benchmarks. Adding its mechanisms to three other harnesses improves 9 of 12 harness-benchmark pairs scored by execution.

papers.title: VC-Dimension and Generalization in Geometric Machine Learning with Applications to Active Learning
papers.abstract: We compute the VC-dimension of metric ball classifiers in the model spaces of Riemannian geometry (Euclidean, spherical, hyperbolic) and present upper and lower bounds on the VC-dimension of metric balls in several other situations, including general normed vector spaces (potentially infinite VC-dimension), vector spaces with $\ell^p$-norms (VC-dimension grows at least linearly in the dimension, faster than Euclidean for $p=1$), flat tori, and general Riemannian manifolds (arbitrarily large VC-dimension after a conformal change). In several situations where the VC-dimension is large or even infinite, we prove generalization bounds under additional assumptions on the data distribution using covering arguments. Both in the VC-dimension and covering setting, we consider data on low-dimensional subsets of high-dimensional Euclidean spaces. As an application, we consider coverage-based algorithms in active learning.
papers.summary: The VC-dimension of metric ball classifiers is computed exactly for the Euclidean, spherical, and hyperbolic model spaces of Riemannian geometry, with upper and lower bounds given for several other settings. Those settings show it can be **infinite in general normed vector spaces** and arbitrarily large on Riemannian manifolds after a conformal change, and that it grows at least linearly with dimension under lp norms. Where the VC-dimension is large or infinite, generalization bounds are proved via covering arguments under additional assumptions on the data distribution, including data on low-dimensional subsets of high-dimensional Euclidean space. The results are applied to coverage-based active learning algorithms.

papers.title: Measuring Definition Sensitivity in LLM Annotation of Social Science Concepts
papers.abstract: In social science research, text annotation is a fundamental task that is traditionally a costly, hard-to-scale manual process. Researchers have used large language models (LLMs) to perform annotation by writing a definition of a concept into a prompt - a rule that determines whether a label should be attributed to a text depending on its content. However, concepts such as hate speech, fake news, and terrorism typically have several theoretically defensible competing definitions. It is also unknown whether the model actually applied the definition to provide the label or the label was based on the model's pretrained notion of the concept. To test this, we have the model annotate the same texts twice, each time with a different definition. We call the disagreement between the two sets of annotations definition sensitivity. As a control, we paraphrase one definition but leave its requirements unchanged - the disagreement between the annotations with the two wordings becomes the paraphrase floor. Across six concepts and three LLMs, a swap of competing definitions always changes more annotations, on average, than a paraphrase. This shows that the annotations depend on the prompted definition, so any set of annotations should be interpreted together with the definition that produced it. The LLM annotator's definition sensitivity and its paraphrase floor should both be reported in such work.
papers.summary: When large language models (LLMs) annotate text for contested social science concepts such as hate speech or fake news, it is unclear whether labels follow the definition written in the prompt or the model's pretrained notion of the concept. The test has a model annotate the same texts under two competing definitions and measures the disagreement, called definition sensitivity, against a paraphrase floor obtained by rewording one definition without changing its requirements. Across six concepts and three LLMs, **swapping definitions always changes more annotations on average than paraphrasing**, indicating that the labels depend on the prompted definition. The authors recommend reporting both quantities alongside any LLM-produced annotations.

papers.title: Advancing Mass-Conserving Deep Learning for Distributed Hydrologic Modeling: A Case Study in a Snow-Dominated Watershed
papers.abstract: Recent progress in physics-aware deep learning (DL) has embedded mass conservation within Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) architecture for hydrologic modeling, improving physical consistency and enabling diagnostics of internal states. However, existing mass-conserving neural networks are primarily developed in lumped formulations. Consequently, previous studies provide only fragmented and often indirect evidence of when and why imposed physical constraints may lead to unrealistic hydrologic behavior. To address this limitation, we propose Physics-Enhanced Conservation-Augmented Net (PECAN), a mass-conserving convolutional LSTM-based framework for distributed hydrologic modeling and diagnosing structural limitations of physics-aware DL models. PECAN is implemented in two variants: (1) PECAN-MC with a strict precipitation-based conservation constraint and (2) PECAN-MCR with a relaxed conservation constraint allowing additional water inputs beyond precipitation. Both variants are trained solely on gauge streamflow and evaluated in a snow-dominated watershed in Colorado. We benchmark PECAN against lumped DL baselines and the distributed process-based Variable Infiltration Capacity (VIC) model. Results show that PECAN achieves competitive outlet streamflow simulation accuracy while producing spatially explicit latent states for interpretation. Comparisons with reference soil moisture indicate that PECAN cell states resemble meaningful temporal soil moisture dynamics. However, analyses also reveal that PECAN misrepresents snow processes by prematurely removing winter snow water storage from the system rather than retaining it for spring release. PECAN demonstrates accurate streamflow simulation at gauges and shows diagnostic potential to expose structural limitations in hydrologic process representation, thereby informing future physics-aware neural network development for hydrology.
papers.summary: Mass-conserving neural networks for hydrology have mostly been lumped models, which limits evidence about when imposed physical constraints produce unrealistic behavior. `PECAN` (Physics-Enhanced Conservation-Augmented Net) is a mass-conserving convolutional Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) framework for distributed modeling, with a strict precipitation-based variant and a relaxed variant that allows additional water inputs, both trained only on gauge streamflow in a snow-dominated Colorado watershed. It reaches streamflow accuracy competitive with lumped deep learning baselines and the process-based Variable Infiltration Capacity (`VIC`) model, and its cell states resemble soil moisture dynamics. The analysis also shows that it **misrepresents snow processes by removing winter snow water storage prematurely** instead of retaining it for spring release.

papers.title: ProTEUS: A mutation-resolved world model for closed-loop protein evolution
papers.abstract: Protein engineering requires navigating rugged fitness landscapes, where small sequence changes can produce large functional differences, but experimental screening can only sample a small fraction of sequence space. Thus, a central challenge is to efficiently traverse the large combinatorial space of mutations in silico. We introduce ProTEUS, a mutation-resolved world model for closed-loop protein evolution. Pretrained on deep mutational scanning assays, ProTEUS learns a joint representation of sequence, evolutionary, and structural information using MutationFormer, a mutation-biased attention architecture. Variants are represented as states in this joint latent space, and mutations define actions whose functional consequences are predicted. To support exploration of many mutants, we developed a fast, physics-constrained all-atom predictor that utilizes explicit geometric constraint enforcement to achieve >10 fold increase in speed than AlphaFold3 with guaranteed physical validity. Lastly, ProTEUS refines its prediction and understanding of protein activity through closed loop experimental feedback to guide evolution toward a desired phenotype. ProTEUS surpasses established models in both zero-shot and supervised fine-tuning mutation prediction tasks. We experimentally demonstrate its utility in two closed-loop multi-objective engineering campaigns on aldehyde dehydrogenase and levansucrase, yielding variants with >10 fold higher activity than wild type. ProTEUS provides a world-model framework that connects virtual evaluation of mutational outcomes with experimental learning for efficient protein evolution.
papers.summary: Protein engineering must search a huge combinatorial mutation space while experiments can sample only a small fraction of it. `ProTEUS` is a world model pretrained on deep mutational scanning assays that uses a mutation-biased attention architecture, `MutationFormer`, to represent variants as states and mutations as actions with predicted functional consequences, and it is refined through closed-loop experimental feedback. It includes a physics-constrained all-atom structure predictor reported as more than 10 times faster than `AlphaFold3` with guaranteed physical validity. Beyond surpassing established models on zero-shot and fine-tuned mutation prediction, two closed-loop campaigns on aldehyde dehydrogenase and levansucrase yielded **variants with more than 10-fold higher activity than wild type**.
papers.highlight_summary:
Protein engineering has to search a combinatorial mutation space that wet-lab screening can only sample sparsely, so the bottleneck is deciding which variants are worth making. `ProTEUS` casts this as a world model: variants are states in a joint sequence-evolution-structure latent space, mutations are actions, and the model predicts their functional consequences, then updates itself on experimental feedback from each design round.

- The backbone is `MutationFormer`, a mutation-biased attention architecture pretrained on deep mutational scanning assays, which fuses sequence, evolutionary, and structural signal into a per-variant state representation rather than scoring mutations in isolation.
- To make in-silico exploration of many mutants tractable, the authors pair it with an all-atom structure predictor that enforces geometric constraints explicitly, reporting a **>10-fold speedup over `AlphaFold3`** with guaranteed physical validity of the output coordinates.
- On mutation-effect prediction the model reportedly beats established baselines in both **zero-shot** and **supervised fine-tuning** settings, though the abstract gives no benchmark numbers, so the size of the margin and the choice of comparators remain to be checked in the paper itself.
- Two closed-loop, multi-objective campaigns — on `aldehyde dehydrogenase` and `levansucrase` — produced variants with **>10-fold higher activity than wild type**, which is the strongest evidence here because it is wet-lab rather than retrospective.
- The main caveats are scope and dependency: only two enzymes were engineered experimentally, the pretraining signal is deep mutational scanning data that is itself biased toward shallow, single-mutant coverage, and the closed-loop gains require real assay rounds, so the framework is not a drop-in replacement for screening so much as a way to aim it.

papers.title: Multi-Stage Phase-Aware Self-Supervised Reconstruction for Multi-Echo Gradient-Echo MRI
papers.abstract: Purpose: To develop a phase-aware self-supervised framework for accelerated high-resolution multi-echo gradient-echo (mGRE) MRI that preserves anatomical detail and complex echo information for quantitative mapping. Methods: We developed multi-stage phase-aware self-supervised reconstruction (MSPR-GRE), integrating progressive k-space expansion with phase estimation and refinement. Sequential unrolled networks reconstruct complex multi-echo images and update echo-dependent phase priors. A relaxation-informed temporal subspace is used for acquisitions with at least four echoes, while shorter echo trains are reconstructed in the image domain. Training uses held-out acquired k-space samples without fully sampled targets. Evaluation included 9.4 T ex vivo mouse-brain data 30um eight-echo and 18um dual-echo) and retrospectively undersampled 7 T AHEAD human-brain data, with supervised ablations. Results:MSPR-GRE reduced artifacts in regions of rapid phase variation and preserved fine mouse-brain anatomy. Across five AHEAD test datasets at R = 4, 8, and 12, it generally improved magnitude-image, T2* map, and QSM metrics, particularly at higher acceleration. At R = 12, fourth-echo magnitude NRMSE was 12.09$\pm$0.60% versus 21.55$\pm$1.12% for SSDU. Ablations indicated benefits of phase refinement, while supervised experiments supported multi-stage phase-aware reconstruction. Conclusion: MSPR-GRE improves accelerated mGRE reconstruction and quantitative-map agreement without fully sampled training targets. Further validation of generalizability and phase-estimation accuracy is needed.
papers.summary: Accelerated high-resolution multi-echo gradient-echo (mGRE) MRI needs reconstructions that keep both anatomical detail and the complex phase information used for quantitative mapping, without fully sampled training targets. `MSPR-GRE` chains unrolled networks that progressively expand k-space coverage while estimating and refining echo-dependent phase priors, training only on held-out acquired k-space samples. On 9.4 T ex vivo mouse-brain data and retrospectively undersampled 7 T `AHEAD` human-brain data it reduced artifacts in regions of rapid phase variation, and at 12-fold acceleration the fourth-echo magnitude error was **12.09% versus 21.55% for the self-supervised baseline `SSDU`**. The authors note that generalizability and phase-estimation accuracy still need validation.

papers.title: DEPUTYBENCH: Evaluating Contextual Safety in Enterprise Agents
papers.abstract: Enterprise agents must determine whether ordinary requests are permitted by organizational records and policies while continuing legitimate work. We introduce DEPUTYBENCH, an executable benchmark with 79 base items, 375 instances, paired permission contexts, and graded evidence requirements. Across 12 models, revised audits give 88.0% pooled safety and 79.1% paired success. A controlled study of 28 derived tasks and six models tests authorization-fact flips, evidence masking, and irrelevant rewrites. Outcomes track backend permissions, yet restricted execution is more frequent with missing evidence than explicit non-permission: 10.3% versus 3.5% on 27 matched tasks, a 6.8-percentage-point difference (95% interval: 1.9-13.0; secondary analysis). A post-hoc analysis locates 61 of 100 masked-condition executions in four privacy tasks requiring complete cumulative counts or person-specific consent. The difference persists when the most error-prone model or the largest contributing task is excluded, but is much smaller outside those four tasks. Thus high safety with available evidence does not establish reliable stopping when permission cannot be verified. Mean paired success is equivalent within a prespecified five-point margin under irrelevant rewrites, while strong-model safety remains near ceiling. Scorer validation improves from 178 to 266 correctly scored cases out of 284 held-out counterexamples. Two security experts manually verified task ground truth over a two-week period; stage labels remain LLM-generated. The concentration analysis describes task structure and audited outcomes, not an identified internal mechanism.
papers.summary: Enterprise agents have to decide whether an ordinary-looking request is actually permitted by organizational records and policies, while still completing legitimate work. `DEPUTYBENCH` is an executable benchmark of 79 base items and 375 instances with paired permission contexts and graded evidence requirements; across 12 models it yields 88.0% pooled safety and 79.1% paired success. In a controlled study on six models, agents carried out restricted actions more often when authorization evidence was missing than when permission was explicitly denied, **10.3% versus 3.5% on 27 matched tasks**, a secondary-analysis gap concentrated in four privacy tasks. The authors conclude that high safety when evidence is available does not establish reliable stopping when permission cannot be verified.

papers.title: When Are Predictions Enough? An Evaluation Protocol for Frozen Expert Composition
papers.abstract: Practitioners often combine independently trained models while keeping their weights frozen. These experts are commonly combined through their final predictions, although their internal features may retain useful information that those predictions omit. We ask when combining features improves on combining predictions, and how to make that comparison fair. We introduce a reusable evaluation protocol, apply it to 21 frozen deepfake detectors from DF40 (Yan et al., 2024), and audit how evaluation choices change the conclusions. The protocol uses strong prediction baselines, compares simple and larger feature combiners, varies architecture and training data separately, and reports results by held-out generator with train/test overlap controls. Under leave-one-generator-out evaluation, logistic regression on the features of six architecture-diverse experts improves macro AUROC by 0.081 over the best tested prediction combiner in each fold, with gains on seven of eight generators. The larger network shows no clear improvement over the linear model (approximately 3.5M versus 10K parameters), suggesting that access to richer information matters more than additional combiner capacity on this pool. Features may help when they retain information that the predictions omit and that transfers to new generators. Predictions may be enough when the strongest prediction baseline already performs well, while neither approach reliably compensates for poor expert transfer. Weakening prediction baselines on the overlap-affected standard split inflates the apparent feature advantage by up to 0.172 AUROC. Overlap-aware evaluation also changes the estimated gain, though the contrast does not isolate overlap. Results by generator and expert pool show where the advantage holds, weakens, or reverses. Without these controls, the same benchmark can support different conclusions.
papers.summary: Independently trained frozen models are usually combined through their final predictions, even though their internal features may hold information those predictions discard. The authors define a reusable evaluation protocol with strong prediction baselines, simple and larger feature combiners, and train/test overlap controls, and apply it to 21 frozen deepfake detectors from `DF40`. Under leave-one-generator-out evaluation, logistic regression on the features of six architecture-diverse experts **improves macro AUROC by 0.081 over the best prediction combiner**, while a combiner with roughly 350 times more parameters shows no clear further gain. Weakening the prediction baselines on the overlap-affected standard split inflates the apparent feature advantage by up to 0.172 AUROC, so the same benchmark can support different conclusions depending on evaluation choices.

papers.title: Understanding Students' Rationales for AI-Mediated Cheating: An Instructor Perspective from Online Forums Analysis
papers.abstract: The extensive adoption of AI has precipitated a crisis in academic integrity. While studies attempt to quantify cheating, less is known about the motivations instructors believe students have for using AI in prohibited ways. We analyze 2.01 million posts on r/Professors to understand how instructors perceive students' justifications for AI-mediated cheating. Our qualitative analyses reveal four primary themes: (1) Academic System Gaming, (2) Digital-Academic Literacy Gap, (3) Performance Anxiety, and (4) Normalization of Dishonesty.
papers.summary: Less is known about why students use AI in prohibited ways than about how often they do, particularly from the viewpoint of those who teach them. A qualitative analysis of 2.01 million posts on the `r/Professors` subreddit examines how instructors perceive students' justifications. It identifies **four primary themes: academic system gaming, a digital-academic literacy gap, performance anxiety, and normalization of dishonesty**.

papers.title: Reconstructing Boundary Layer Wind Profiles with Machine Learning: A Comparative Study on IGRA Radiosonde Data
papers.abstract: Wind profiles in the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) drive short-range forecasting and wind-energy siting, yet sparse radiosonde coverage forces practitioners to interpolate them from a handful of physical predictors. We benchmark modern tabular learners against analytical parameterizations on 158,097 IGRA soundings. CatBoost, TabM, and FT-Transformer reduce RMSE to 1.3-1.6 m/s, against approximately 3 m/s for power-law and Monin-Obukhov fits; once the predictor set is fixed the three architectures differ by less than 0.05 m/s, so accuracy is driven by predictors rather than architecture. A cohort analysis of within-bin profile dispersion places an empirical floor of approximately 1.77 m/s on any point-wise predictor that uses standard radiosonde features, consistent with prior eddy-viscosity inversions. A one-dimensional Fourier Neural Operator applied as a post-hoc corrector to frozen tabular predictions reduces near-surface RMSE on U.S. stations from 1.5 to 1.2 m/s, while leaving upper-layer error unchanged. Further gains should come from new predictors rather than larger models.
papers.summary: Wind profiles in the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) matter for short-range forecasting and wind-energy siting, but sparse radiosonde coverage means they are usually interpolated from a few physical predictors. A benchmark on 158,097 `IGRA` soundings compares the tabular learners `CatBoost`, `TabM`, and `FT-Transformer` with analytical power-law and Monin-Obukhov fits. The learned models **cut root-mean-square error to 1.3-1.6 m/s from about 3 m/s**, and differ from each other by less than 0.05 m/s once the predictor set is fixed, so accuracy depends on predictors rather than architecture. A one-dimensional `Fourier Neural Operator` used as a post-hoc corrector lowers near-surface error on U.S. stations from 1.5 to 1.2 m/s without changing upper-layer error.

papers.title: A Technique to Model Product Information and User Reviews (MPIUR)
papers.abstract: Modern e-commerce platforms naturally provide three complementary modalities: textual item descriptions, item images, and user reviews. However, existing multimodal recommendation methods often omit reviews or do not integrate all three modalities within a unified framework. In this paper, we propose MPIUR, a multimodal graph-based recommendation model that encodes reviews in heterogeneous graphs, aligns image and text representations, and adapts collaborative--semantic alignment to item interaction density. Experiments on the Amazon Reviews 2023 Musical Instruments and Baby categories show that MPIUR achieves the best global nDCG@10 and Recall@10 among the evaluated methods on both datasets. It also obtains the best nDCG@10 and Recall@10 on sparse items, indicating that jointly exploiting reviews and multimodal item content is particularly useful when interaction histories are limited.
papers.summary: E-commerce platforms offer item descriptions, item images, and user reviews, but multimodal recommenders often leave out reviews or fail to combine all three in one framework. `MPIUR` is a graph-based recommendation model that encodes reviews in heterogeneous graphs, aligns image and text representations, and adapts the alignment between collaborative and semantic signals to how densely an item has been interacted with. On the Musical Instruments and Baby categories of `Amazon Reviews 2023`, it achieves **the best nDCG@10 and Recall@10 among the evaluated methods, both overall and on sparse items**.

papers.title: Mapping Instructors' Attitudes Towards Cheating with AI: An Exploratory Analysis Using Forum Analysis
papers.abstract: In teaching and learning environments, cheating and the violation of academic integrity have always been one of the challenges, involving different levels of concerns such as administrative, personal knowledge, learning, and equity. The introduction of large language models has brought cheating in dialogue to the forefront, given the apparent capabilities of these models to complete students' academic assignments. This study aims to leverage recent dialogues among university professors about cheating with Generative AI to better understand their beliefs about academic honesty. In doing so, we analyze a corpus of 2.01 million posts (threads and comments) in the r/Professors subreddit discussing cheating after the release of ChatGPT, providing a better understanding of teachers' motivations to discourage cheating and the strategies they use to do so. We synthesize the why and how of addressing cheating to identify caveats about the future of AI and academic integration.
papers.summary: Large language models that can complete student assignments have pushed cheating to the centre of discussion among university teachers. An exploratory analysis of 2.01 million threads and comments on the `r/Professors` subreddit, posted after the release of `ChatGPT`, examines instructors' beliefs about academic honesty.
