The study synthesizes **why instructors want to discourage AI-assisted cheating and the strategies they use to do so**, and draws out caveats about the future of AI in academic settings.

papers.title: No finite rulebook can certify every safe program: an impossibility theorem for gatekeeping AI agents
papers.abstract: An AI assistant writes small programs, and a gatekeeper must decide, from the code alone, whether each one may run. Suppose the rules are fixed: never perform a forbidden action, never let the output depend on a secret, always answer eventually. Can two rulebooks, one listing what is allowed and one listing what is not, both be complete, if every rule must be backed by evidence that a machine can check in finite time? We prove that they cannot. Checkable evidence can only establish what a finite record settles, and ``never'' and ``eventually'' are never settled by a finite record. For prohibitions the failure is one-sided: every violation can be caught by watching, but no safe program can be cleared for good. For confidentiality and responsiveness, neither side can be. We characterise exactly which rules about visible behaviour evidence can confirm, and we show that any sound rulebook of $n$ bits omits a compliant program of about $n$ bits. A time limit makes everything checkable, but only by running the program for essentially the whole limit, so a finite machine is not a feasible one. Finally, we show what a gatekeeper can still guarantee: not a verdict on every program, but a checkable list that contains everything it must allow and nothing it must refuse. Simulations on 2.2 million random programs and on self-referential adversaries show that the obstruction is adversarial rather than typical, and that the one error a longer test never removes is the liveness part of confidentiality.
papers.summary: A gatekeeper that must decide from code alone whether an AI-written program may run would ideally have complete lists of what is allowed and what is not, each rule backed by evidence a machine can check in finite time. The authors prove this is impossible: **no finite, machine-checkable rulebook can certify every safe program**, because properties phrased as never or eventually are not settled by any finite record. For prohibitions every violation can be caught by observation but no safe program can be cleared permanently, while for confidentiality and responsiveness neither side can be settled, and any sound rulebook of n bits omits a compliant program of about n bits. A gatekeeper can still guarantee a checkable list containing everything it must allow and nothing it must refuse, and simulations on 2.2 million random programs indicate the obstruction is adversarial rather than typical.

papers.title: Enforcing Axioms for AI Alignment under Loss-Based Rules
papers.abstract: Many alignment methods, most notably reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), train reward models by minimizing a loss on pairwise comparisons of model responses. Inspired by principle-guided methods such as Constitutional AI, we treat each principle as a voter that compares responses according to that principle, for example, preferring the more helpful or less toxic response. We represent these voters as linear directions in a fixed embedding space, a simplifying assumption motivated by the Linear Representation Hypothesis. In this linear social choice model, Ge et al. (2024) showed that an optimal linear reward model can violate Pareto optimality (PO): From the principles-as-voters lens, this means a response A can be less helpful and more toxic than B, yet still receive a higher reward. We ask whether richer reward models or changes to comparison data can recover PO within loss-based training. We show that PO can still fail for polynomials of any fixed degree and one-hidden-layer ReLU multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) of any fixed width $ d\ge 2 $ with suitable finite parameter bounds. We then recover PO for loss-based training of linear rewards under suitable assumptions in an idealized setting with uniform comparison directions and equal comparison lengths. These results motivate dataset design as an approach to recovering PO in constitutional-style alignment while retaining loss-based training.
papers.summary: Reward models for alignment methods such as reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) are trained by minimizing a loss on pairwise comparisons, and earlier work showed that an optimal linear reward model can violate Pareto optimality (PO), rewarding a response that is worse on every principle. Treating each principle as a voter represented by a linear direction in a fixed embedding space, the authors ask whether richer reward models or different comparison data can restore the property. They show that **Pareto optimality can still fail for polynomials of any fixed degree and for one-hidden-layer ReLU networks of any fixed width of at least two**, under suitable finite parameter bounds. It is recovered for linear rewards in an idealized setting with uniform comparison directions and equal comparison lengths, which the authors take as motivation for dataset design.

papers.title: Looping Deeper Without Growing the KV Cache: Recurrent Depth for Causal Encoder-Decoders
papers.abstract: Looped language models deepen computation without adding parameters, yet caching full-context key-value (KV) states across layers and rounds severely bounds serving batch size. We design a looped causal encoder-decoder (CED) that achieves recurrent depth with zero round-wise KV growth, addressing where and how to loop an asymmetric stack in which only sparse encoder layers generate global KV. We find that recurrence must be placed in the encoder to iteratively refine global KV representations rather than re-reading static decoder projections, which both drives language-modeling gains and preserves long-context scaling. Furthermore, training the encoder loop under stochastic recurrence depth induces a fixed-point equilibrium where every round losslessly shares the last round's KV cache. Compounding cross-layer and cross-round KV sharing, the resulting Looped CED matches an unlooped CED's minimal memory footprint and recovers 86-93% of a looped Transformer's gain with 1/6 of its global KV. To test serving at production scale, we loop the 552B-parameter DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash for 8 rounds on one 4xGB200 node: with per-layer and per-round KV the loop cannot fit a single 128K-token request, whereas Looped CED holds 36.8x less KV per token, fits 38 such requests (as many as the unlooped model), and serves 3.6x higher throughput on 8K-token prompts.
papers.summary: Looped language models add computational depth without adding parameters, but caching key-value (KV) states for every layer and every round sharply limits serving batch size. The authors design a looped causal encoder-decoder (CED) in which recurrence sits in the encoder and is trained with stochastic recurrence depth, producing a fixed point where every round can share the last round's cache. The resulting `Looped CED` matches the memory footprint of an unlooped model and recovers 86-93% of a looped Transformer's gain with one sixth of its global KV. Looping the 552B-parameter `DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash` for 8 rounds on one 4xGB200 node, it **holds 36.8x less KV per token**, fits 38 requests of 128K tokens where the naive loop fits none, and serves 3.6x higher throughput on 8K-token prompts.

papers.title: Discrete Model-Based Diffusion for Combinatorial Optimization in Multi-Robot Task Allocation
papers.abstract: Decision making in multi-agent and multi-robot systems often involves discrete decision variables, leading to NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems that must be solved within seconds for near real-time implementation. Denoising diffusion has emerged as a powerful tool for such problems, but existing approaches face a trade-off: Model-Based Diffusion (MBD) incorporates diffusion in sampling-based optimization (SBO) without training but only over continuous spaces, while existing diffusion-based combinatorial solvers operate over discrete spaces but require offline training. To this end, we propose Discrete Model-Based Diffusion (Discrete MBD), a training-free SBO method that directly optimizes discrete variables by approximating categorical reverse transition distributions through Monte Carlo sampling. We establish a finite-step lower bound on the probability of finding a global minimizer and show that this bound converges to one as the number of denoising steps increases. Extensive experiments on generic integer programs and heterogeneous multi-robot coalition formation and scheduling demonstrate that Discrete MBD outperforms SBO baselines in nearly all settings while achieving solution quality competitive with that of mixed-integer programming and reinforcement learning methods at a fraction of their computational cost.
papers.summary: Task allocation in multi-robot systems leads to NP-hard problems over discrete variables that must be solved within seconds, and existing diffusion-based solvers either work only in continuous spaces or need offline training. `Discrete MBD` extends Model-Based Diffusion (MBD), a training-free form of sampling-based optimization (SBO), to discrete variables by approximating the categorical reverse transition distributions with Monte Carlo sampling. The authors prove a finite-step lower bound on the probability of finding a global minimizer that converges to one as denoising steps increase. On generic integer programs and heterogeneous multi-robot coalition formation and scheduling, it beats sampling-based baselines in nearly all settings and is **competitive with mixed-integer programming and reinforcement learning methods at a fraction of their computational cost**.

papers.title: Settling the Burn-in Gap: Sharp Risk Bounds for Tail-Averaged SGD in Linear Regression
papers.abstract: We study the excess risk of constant-stepsize online stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with tail-averaging for high-dimensional linear regression. Building on the instance-dependent spectral framework of Zou et al. (2021), we establish matching initialization-explicit upper and lower bounds on the total excess risk of tail-averaged SGD in terms of the population covariance spectrum $\mathbf{H}$ and initialization $\mathbf{w}_0-\mathbf{w}^*$ whenever a trajectory spectral feedback condition holds. Existing analyses exhibit a fundamental gap in the effective variance: the upper bound of Zou et al. (2021) retains an undamped contribution from the initial error in the head eigenspace $\mathbf{I}_{0:k^\dagger}$, whereas their lower bound omits the variance induced by the head initialization altogether. We show that both the existing upper and lower bounds are loose: the single-hop fast-mode variance contribution from the head initialization is exponentially damped during the burn-in phase, whereas fourth-moment energy scattered from the head initialization into slow spectral modes during the early burn-in steps survives undamped into the averaging window. We prove that our spectral feedback condition is satisfied in two concrete constant-stepsize regimes: (i) for arbitrary covariance spectra $\mathbf{H}$ and any finite horizon, under an explicit horizon-dependent stepsize chosen prior to execution; and (ii) for polynomially decaying spectra $\lambda_i\asymp i^{-a}$ ($a>1$), under a single horizon-independent positive stepsize. Finally, we complement these positive results with explicit one- and two-dimensional separation constructions proving an exponential-versus-polynomial gap in the lower bound of Zou et al. (2021) and showing why fourth-moment assumptions alone cannot determine the asymptotic exponential decay rate without additional structural conditions.
papers.summary: Existing analyses of constant-stepsize online stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with tail-averaging for high-dimensional linear regression leave a gap between upper and lower bounds on how the initial error contributes to variance. The authors establish **matching upper and lower bounds on the total excess risk** in terms of the covariance spectrum and the initialization, whenever a trajectory spectral feedback condition holds. They show both earlier bounds are loose: the fast-mode variance from the head initialization is exponentially damped during burn-in, while fourth-moment energy scattered into slow spectral modes survives undamped into the averaging window. The condition is verified for arbitrary spectra with a horizon-dependent stepsize and for polynomially decaying spectra with a single horizon-independent stepsize.

papers.title: How Hyperbolic Are Hyperbolic Vision-Language Models?
papers.abstract: Hyperbolic vision-language models (VLMs) have emerged as a rapidly growing area of research, reporting strong zero-shot performance alongside an interpretable embedding space in which radius orders representations by generality. But how hyperbolic are hyperbolic VLMs in practice? We investigate this at the exponential map, the single operation through which curvature enters an otherwise Euclidean network. We show that across MERU, HyCoCLIP, ARGENT, and PHyCLIP, the exponential map is well approximated by the identity function, i.e., pairwise distances and angles in the pre-map Euclidean space barely change under projection, and removing the map at inference leaves evaluation scores unchanged. Motivated by this observation, we train Euclidean VLMs on CC3M from scratch under the same hierarchy losses. Over roughly the final 90% of the training steps, the training statistics are nearly indistinguishable from those of their hyperbolic counterparts, and the resulting models match the evaluation scores and recover the same radial distributions. Our findings establish Euclidean space as a sufficient substrate for hierarchical vision-language learning as it is currently practiced, and motivate new paradigms in which hyperbolic geometry can deliver on its theoretical promise. Code is available at https://github.com/fbyrman/hyperbolic-vlms.
papers.summary: Hyperbolic vision-language models (VLMs) report strong zero-shot results and an embedding space in which radius orders representations by generality, but it is unclear how much the hyperbolic geometry is actually used. Examining the exponential map through which curvature enters these otherwise Euclidean networks, the authors find that in `MERU`, `HyCoCLIP`, `ARGENT`, and `PHyCLIP` it is well approximated by the identity function, and **removing it at inference leaves evaluation scores unchanged**. Euclidean models trained from scratch on `CC3M` with the same hierarchy losses match the hyperbolic versions in training statistics, evaluation scores, and radial distributions. The authors conclude that Euclidean space is sufficient for hierarchical vision-language learning as currently practiced.

papers.title: Online-Adaptive Fuzzy Cognitive Maps for Neuro-symbolic Financial Forecasting
papers.abstract: We present a neuro-symbolic framework that pairs online-adaptive Fuzzy Cognitive Maps (FCMs) with long short-term memory (LSTM) networks for financial forecasting. Financial markets exhibit regime shifts and nonlinear dynamics. Existing models often trade off one of these key properties: these models capture temporal patterns but hide causal drivers, or they recover causal graphs that cannot adapt post-training. We close this gap with two frameworks. Framework I constructs an FCM from live dual-source price series and macroeconomic indicators, and adapts its edges online through an error-driven Hebbian rule. We introduce the Asymmetric Additive Residual Fusion method to seamlessly combine the FCM and LSTM predictions under Framework I. Framework II constructs a literature-grounded, LLM-augmented FCM where every edge carries a verifiable citation that gives an auditable map of factor interactions. On NASDAQ Composite data, Framework I matched the performance of the LSTM baseline on state-directional accuracy and outperformed LSTM by 7.6 percentage points on the return-sign accuracy. Framework I outperformed standalone FCM models across both evaluation metrics. The adaptive maps converged to new regimes within 10-15 trading days, and Framework II center-node FCMs scored 68.9% to 85.7% on the state-directional accuracy.
papers.summary: Financial forecasting models tend either to capture temporal patterns while hiding causal drivers or to recover causal graphs that cannot adapt after training. The authors pair Fuzzy Cognitive Maps (FCMs) with long short-term memory (LSTM) networks in two frameworks: one builds a map from live price series and macroeconomic indicators and updates its edges online with an error-driven Hebbian rule, fused with LSTM predictions through `Asymmetric Additive Residual Fusion`; the other builds a literature-grounded map, augmented by a large language model, in which every edge carries a citation. On NASDAQ Composite data the first framework matched the LSTM baseline on state-directional accuracy and **outperformed it by 7.6 percentage points on return-sign accuracy**. The adaptive maps converged to new regimes within 10-15 trading days, and the second framework scored 68.9% to 85.7% on state-directional accuracy.

papers.title: AdjointFlow: Accelerating Scientific Inverse Problems with Physics-Based Transport
papers.abstract: Inverse problems are ubiquitous across scientific applications ranging from seismic imaging to astrophysics to nondestructive testing, yet classical solvers often struggle with nonconvexity and repeated evaluations of expensive physical models. Diffusion models can amortize this computation offline, but largely data-driven conditional models underutilize known physics and suffer from ill-conditioned transport maps when the target distribution is concentrated. Plug-and-play (PnP) methods explicitly leverage the physical model to guide a learned prior, improving data consistency but reintroducing costly iterative computations. We instead propose AdjointFlow, a framework built on stochastic interpolants that injects the known physics into the generative transport itself. We design a data-dependent, adjoint-based initialization to reduce transport distance to the target, modify the transport velocity to remain regular as the endpoint distributions concentrate, and parameterize the network to build the initialization directly into the learned velocity. Together, these enable accurate reconstruction at substantially lower cost than generative models starting from Gaussian noise. Experiments on inverse scattering, seismic imaging, and black hole imaging show that AdjointFlow consistently produces more accurate reconstructions than conditional diffusion models while being up to five orders of magnitude faster at inference than PnP methods. Optional inference-time refinement that queries the physical model can further improve data consistency, matching or exceeding the accuracy of PnP methods without retraining.
papers.summary: Scientific inverse problems such as seismic imaging are costly for classical solvers, while conditional diffusion models underuse known physics and plug-and-play (PnP) methods reintroduce expensive iterative computation. `AdjointFlow` builds the physics into the generative transport itself using stochastic interpolants: it starts from a data-dependent, adjoint-based initialization instead of Gaussian noise, modifies the transport velocity to stay regular as the endpoint distributions concentrate, and parameterizes the network around that initialization. On inverse scattering, seismic imaging, and black hole imaging it reconstructs more accurately than conditional diffusion models while being **up to five orders of magnitude faster at inference than PnP methods**. An optional refinement step that queries the physical model matches or exceeds PnP accuracy without retraining.

papers.title: Plumbline: When the Loss Lies, Validating LLM Training Correctly
papers.abstract: Correctness is a prerequisite for training large language models (LLMs) at scale, yet it is hard to ensure: a fault can sit in any part of a run, and how it shows differs across frameworks and the libraries they depend on. Some failures are loud and some are silent, and both take time to detect and trace. A single fault can waste a long run: the run crashes late, or the model scores lower only at the final evaluation. We present Plumbline, a correctness validation system for LLM training, used in production at Amazon. Plumbline checks each part of the training lifecycle, from the data a run trains on to the model it serves, down to the new layers each model brings and up to whole runs. Its diagnosis reuses these checks to trace failures to their root causes. Both rest on a systematic correctness methodology designed to carry across models and frameworks. Plumbline supports two agentic use cases: Day-0 onboarding, which validates the training of a newly released model before teams rely on it, and root-cause tracing of training failures. Across 3 frameworks and 5 models, it found 61 problems, 32 of them silent. Of these, 42 are fixed or reported upstream, 8 of them first raised by us. We further group the 61 into seven failure patterns that show where training breaks, and report how problems recur across frameworks and models.
papers.summary: Faults in large language model (LLM) training can sit anywhere in a run and are often silent, surfacing only as a late crash or a lower score at final evaluation. `Plumbline`, a correctness validation system used in production at Amazon, checks each part of the training lifecycle from data through new model layers to whole runs, and reuses those checks to trace failures to root causes. It supports two agentic use cases: validating the training of a newly released model before teams rely on it, and root-cause tracing of training failures. Across 3 frameworks and 5 models it **found 61 problems, 32 of them silent**, of which 42 are fixed or reported upstream, and the authors group them into seven recurring failure patterns.

papers.title: The AI Era's Lines of Code? A Case Study on What an Engineer's Token Spend Measures
papers.abstract: Organizations use engineers' token spend to monitor AI adoption, set budgets, and measure productivity, but the metric's relationship with engineering output is unclear. We link five weeks of token usage in coding agents to the commits of 404 engineers at JetBrains, and analyze a company survey of 412 employees. We find that token spend varied mostly between engineers, and which engineers spent the most stayed largely the same over the five weeks. Among weeks with similar commit counts, the 90th percentile of spend was 39 to 240 times the 10th. Within an engineer, doubling spend was associated with about 10% more commits. Available work metrics explained 38% of the variation in spend between engineers and 13% of the week-to-week variation within an engineer. In the survey, respondents in technical roles reported in nearly nine of ten agent evaluations using agents for tasks beyond coding, such as analysis, research, and planning. Token spend therefore measures how much engineers use agents across many kinds of work and not the outcome and value of that work. We recommend using token spend at most for resource accounting, and evaluating agent-assisted work with evidence about tasks and outcomes.
papers.summary: Organizations track engineers' token spend to monitor AI adoption and productivity, though its relationship to engineering output is unclear. The authors link five weeks of coding-agent token usage to the commits of 404 engineers at JetBrains and analyze a survey of 412 employees. Spend varied mostly between engineers; among weeks with similar commit counts the 90th percentile of spend was 39 to 240 times the 10th, and within an engineer **doubling spend was associated with only about 10% more commits**. Technical respondents reported using agents for non-coding work such as analysis, research, and planning in nearly nine of ten evaluations, so the authors recommend using token spend at most for resource accounting.

papers.title: The Dose Makes the Poison: Exposure-Aware Evaluation of Generative Drug Design
papers.abstract: Generative models are increasingly used to propose molecules for drug discovery. They can produce far more candidates than can be experimentally tested, making computational selection essential. Most selection methods rely on predicted molecular properties, such as potency and toxicity, but overlook how these properties translate into drug exposure at a given dose. As a result, molecules that appear promising on paper may require impractical doses or raise safety concerns. We investigate this gap by using physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) simulations to re-evaluate molecules selected from three PARP1-targeted generative pipelines. Of 60 shortlisted molecules, seven fail to achieve sufficient target exposure, while 28% of the remaining candidates show predicted safety risks at their required dose. Moreover, 85% of candidates with an achievable dose are outperformed by molecules overlooked during static selection. These findings suggest that accounting for dose and exposure can substantially change which generated molecules are considered promising for drug development.
papers.summary: Generative models for drug discovery propose far more molecules than can be tested, and selection usually relies on predicted properties such as potency and toxicity without considering the drug exposure achieved at a given dose. The authors re-evaluate molecules shortlisted from three PARP1-targeted generative pipelines using physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) simulations. Of 60 shortlisted molecules, seven fail to reach sufficient target exposure and 28% of the rest show predicted safety risks at their required dose. In addition, **85% of candidates with an achievable dose are outperformed by molecules overlooked during static selection**.

papers.title: Orthographic depth at two scales, with English also matched for lexicon size
papers.abstract: A reader can struggle to read in only one of their languages, and one proposed reason is how predictably spelling maps to sound. We measure that predictability as conditional entropy, the pronunciation uncertainty left once the spelling is seen, at two grain sizes (unit sizes): the alignment unit, an aligned spelling-sound chunk, and the syllable, bounded in the pronunciation. We analyse word lists in twelve alphabetic orthographies and report five in full, with English pronunciations from a dictionary and the rest from the synthesizer eSpeak-ng, length marks removed. Among the five, English has the most uncertainty and Finnish the least at both grains. Across all twelve, Portuguese and Danish exceed English per alignment unit, and German and Italian order differently by grain and transcription. These orders hold when English is transcribed by eSpeak-ng with u allowed to spell /j/ plus a vowel. Uncertainty per unit has no shared direction as units grow: it falls in Spanish and, less securely, German, is level in Finnish, depends on transcription in Italian and on the word list in English, and rises in Norwegian and Swedish. Summed uncertainty per word falls in all twelve, but that score is handed the pronunciation's boundaries and mixes context with in-sample memorisation, so it is no evidence of what a reader computes. An exact identity states when discarded spelling boundaries could reverse that fall. A uniform 20,000-word English sample holds 35% of the dictionary's syllable spellings and has syllable entropy 0.098 bits lower, so lexicons must be matched in size. In an exploratory check over eleven languages, syllable-scale entropy tracked first-year reading accuracy (rho = -0.74, falling to -0.25 if English is given the lowest entropy instead), without separating the syllable scale from the alignment unit. These estimates describe sampled writing systems, not readers.
papers.summary: How predictably spelling maps to sound is one proposed reason a reader can struggle in only one of their languages. The authors measure this as conditional entropy, the pronunciation uncertainty remaining once the spelling is seen, at the level of aligned spelling-sound chunks and of syllables, across word lists in twelve alphabetic orthographies with most pronunciations from the synthesizer `eSpeak-ng`. Among the five languages reported in full, **English has the most uncertainty and Finnish the least at both grain sizes**, though Portuguese and Danish exceed English per alignment unit across all twelve. A uniform 20,000-word English sample has lower syllable entropy than the full dictionary, so lexicons must be matched in size, and an exploratory correlation between syllable-scale entropy and first-year reading accuracy (rho = -0.74) weakens sharply depending on how English is treated.

papers.title: Living constitutions: Participatory alignment for sovereign foundation models
papers.abstract: In Constitutional AI, a plain-text "constitution" encodes values and gets incorporated into a model via post-training. However, the procedure for creating such a constitution poses significant challenges: who contributes, who decides which norms are included, and to what extent must the process be participatory or democratic? These challenges can be paralyzing. Yet, we argue that taking action is essential: without a deliberate constitution, sovereign models would risk misalignment or default to norms set by frontier model providers. We propose treating the development of a constitution as an evolving, participatory process akin to citizen science, iteratively drafted, tested, and refined. We therefore formulate five desirable principles: iterative, modular, justifiable, positional, and legitimate. We further argue that such a document must remain responsive not only over time but across the people it governs, and propose that provisions be marked as settled, contested, or underdetermined, so that durable disagreement is recorded in the constitution rather than resolved away. Empirically, we show via agent-based modelling that proposed process for maintaining living constitutions is robust against 50% bad actors among citizens - assuming a share of 75% participants with good intent in the deliberative body. This indicates that the proposed process tolerates a substantial share of adversarial participants.
papers.summary: In `Constitutional AI`, a plain-text constitution encodes values that are trained into a model, which raises the question of who contributes to and decides on those norms, particularly for sovereign foundation models that would otherwise default to the norms of frontier providers. The authors propose treating the constitution as an evolving, participatory process akin to citizen science, guided by five principles: iterative, modular, justifiable, positional, and legitimate. Provisions would be marked as settled, contested, or underdetermined so that durable disagreement is recorded instead of resolved away. Agent-based modelling suggests the process is **robust against 50% bad actors among citizens, assuming 75% of the deliberative body has good intent**.

papers.title: Stinging the Swarm: Extracting Attacker Intelligence from a Twin-Controller OT Honeypot
papers.abstract: Autonomous language-model agents can drive industrial controllers over fieldbus protocols, probing a plant at machine speed and in coordinated swarms. We present Talos, an inline gate that judges every agent request to a controller in milliseconds and routes agents it flags as hostile to a device-faithful decoy -- a mirror twin of the real plant -- where their attack continues harmlessly and is read for intelligence. We evaluate the full pipeline (detect -> quarantine -> mirror -> extract) against 2,400 autonomous attacker agents, 600 in each of four tiers that escalate the attacker's effort to stay hidden, from no concealment to an explicit non-disclosure rule and a trained cover story. No write reached the real plant in any tier: the gate denies the damage path and a device-level envelope check backstops it, while unmapped registers are denied without exception and the gate still permits safe-direction stop commands. Decisions are model-driven in every tier with no inference timeouts, closing a common objection to small on-device judges. Beyond blocking, the pipeline reads the attacker. We find a behavioral structure along two axes -- how persistently an agent attacks and how much it discloses -- and show that the system has a capture channel for three of the four resulting regions: hardened, silent attackers escalate most and are read on the mirror; compliant, talkative attackers volunteer their identity to a diagnostic form before they are ever quarantined; only the paranoid, low-yield region resists both. Attacker identity fields are self-authored cover stories, but involuntary tells -- the self-reported toolchain fingerprint and the attacker's own list of targeted registers -- accumulate across the swarm into a high-confidence profile drawn from agents under explicit orders to stay silent. The gate, mirror, and harness are released under Apache 2.0 with a synthetic device family.
papers.summary: Autonomous language-model agents can drive industrial controllers over fieldbus protocols and probe a plant at machine speed, so `Talos` places an inline gate in front of the controller that judges each request in milliseconds and reroutes agents flagged as hostile to a device-faithful mirror twin of the plant. The detect, quarantine, mirror and extract pipeline was tested against 2,400 attacker agents across four tiers of increasing concealment effort, and **no write reached the real plant in any tier**, with no inference timeouts from the small on-device judge. Attackers fall along two axes, persistence and disclosure, and the system captures intelligence from three of the four resulting regions, with only paranoid, low-yield agents resisting. Self-reported toolchain fingerprints and targeted-register lists accumulate across the swarm into a profile even from agents ordered to stay silent.

papers.title: SteerDistill: Quantizing LLM Agents via Closed-Loop Teacher Steering
papers.abstract: Low-bit quantization reduces the inference cost of LLM agents but can compromise task success. Examining failed rollouts, we find that quantized agents overlook task requirements or environmental conditions, producing environment transitions that diverge from successful full-precision references. Correcting these behavioral divergences remains difficult: offline data may miss the student's failure contexts, while its own rollouts may provide few correct responses in those contexts. We introduce SteerDistill, a quantization-aware distillation method in which a full-precision teacher guides the student to revise failed responses and iteratively refines its guidance using feedback from student execution. This closed-loop teacher steering produces locally verified behavioral corrections. We internalize these corrections by training the student without guidance to match the steered student's predictions at corrected turns and the full-precision teacher's at other turns, enabling unassisted inference. Across five agentic benchmarks and three models, SteerDistill exceeds the strongest quantized baseline by 1.67--2.18 points in average score under W4A16 and stays within one point of BF16. On $\tau^2$-Bench, it outperforms QeRL by 1.84 percentage points in success rate using 67% fewer training GPU hours and produces shorter successful trajectories than the quantized baselines.
papers.summary: Low-bit quantized LLM agents fail tasks by overlooking requirements or environment conditions, and neither offline data nor the student's own rollouts supply enough correct responses in those failure contexts. `SteerDistill` has a full-precision teacher guide the quantized student to revise failed responses, refining the guidance from the student's execution feedback, then trains the student to reproduce the corrected behavior without guidance. Across five agentic benchmarks and three models it beats the strongest quantized baseline by 1.67 to 2.18 points under `W4A16` and **stays within one point of the full-precision `BF16` model**. On `τ²-Bench` it outperforms `QeRL` by 1.84 percentage points in success rate with 67% fewer training GPU hours.

papers.title: Bursts That Outlast Themselves: Persistent Degradation in Prefix-Cached Agent Serving
papers.abstract: LLM agents drive inference engines with closed-loop sessions whose context grows every turn, and serving them economically depends on prefix caching: a hit costs an incremental prefill of about a thousand tokens, a miss recomputes a 10--40K-token context. We show that this makes prefix-cached agent serving metastable. With an identical base workload, a few minutes of extra arrivals leaves a vLLM server in a degraded regime--a ~10% hit ratio, about half the throughput, and a backlog that grows for the remaining 70 minutes--while its no-burst twin stays healthy (9 of 12 pairs; none in the reverse direction). The regime appears at loads the cache-warm server sustains, is absent without prefix caching, and also appears with Qwen3-32B on SWE-bench agent trace shapes and on SGLang, which tolerates larger triggers. Slower service keeps more sessions in the system, their working set outgrows the KV pool, and every turn becomes a recomputation; a first-order workload-balance condition, calibrated independently, brackets when the regime can drain. Getting out is the harder problem: throttling new admissions recovered 1 of 7 matched collapsed runs, while suspending admitted sessions against a capacity-based limit recovered all of them within minutes. A CPU offload tier delays the collapse but does not prevent it. A budgeter that bounds the resident KV demand of active sessions to the pool, with thresholds that need no per-workload tuning, prevented the failure in every run we tested.
papers.summary: Agent sessions have contexts that grow every turn, so serving them cheaply relies on prefix caching, where a hit costs about a thousand tokens of prefill and a miss recomputes 10K to 40K tokens. Experiments show this makes serving metastable: **a few minutes of extra arrivals left a `vLLM` server stuck at roughly a 10% hit ratio and half its throughput for the remaining 70 minutes** in 9 of 12 paired runs, while the no-burst twin stayed healthy. The regime also appears with `Qwen3-32B` on `SWE-bench` agent trace shapes and on `SGLang`, and arises because slower service keeps more sessions resident until their working set outgrows the key-value cache pool. Throttling new admissions recovered 1 of 7 collapsed runs, suspending admitted sessions recovered all of them, and a budgeter bounding resident cache demand prevented the failure in every tested run.

papers.title: Placing LLM Lookup Tables by Per-Layer Prefetch Deadlines
papers.abstract: DeepSeek-V4.1's 203 GB of Engram n-gram tables sit in host DRAM today, taking 190 of the 223 GiB a 4-GPU serving process uses. Row indices depend only on input tokens, so reads can start with each step and overlap earlier layers. V4.1's two Engram layers have windows that differ by 30x (0.3 vs. 9.3 ms). We show that this deadline, together with session reuse and contention on a shared device, decides which tier each table can use and which layers need cache, and we give a model that predicts the resulting slowdown from measured read times. Agent and chat traffic reuse rows within sessions, and static hot sets transfer poorly. We build SlackTier, a table tier for SGLang that issues all lookups at step start. It reads the short-window layer first and splits a small GPU row cache across layers. The path runs inside the decode CUDA graph and is bit-exact with the original gather. Layer 14's table can go to NVMe uncached with no measurable decode cost. With both tables on four NVMe disks, mean time per output token on agent and chat replays rises at most 1.4% over unmodified SGLang, and host memory falls from 212 to 34 GiB. Both tables need no cache when read over RDMA (remote direct memory access) from another node's memory; one copy serves two instances. On a KV-constrained agent workload, using the freed memory as host KV cache at the same memory budget raises median throughput by 36% and cuts median p90 time to first token from 38 to 24 s.
papers.summary: `DeepSeek-V4.1` keeps 203 GB of `Engram` n-gram lookup tables in host memory, which dominates the footprint of a 4-GPU serving process. Because row indices depend only on input tokens, reads can start at the beginning of each decode step, and each table's layer sets a prefetch deadline (0.3 versus 9.3 ms) that determines which storage tier it can live on. `SlackTier`, built for `SGLang`, issues all lookups at step start, prioritizes the short-deadline layer and shares a small GPU row cache, staying bit-exact with the original gather. With both tables on four NVMe disks, **time per output token rises at most 1.4% while host memory falls from 212 to 34 GiB**, and reusing the freed memory as key-value cache raises median throughput by 36% on a constrained agent workload.

papers.title: Free Lunch Uncertainty: Sequence-Level R\'enyi Entropy from Particle Decoding for Adaptive LLM Reasoning
papers.abstract: Quantifying uncertainty over an entire LLM completion is critical for selective prediction and adaptive compute. Zero-cost signals such as mean token entropy and log-probability are local to tokens or to one completion, and self-consistency needs many extra completions. We show that Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) decoding for power sampling already estimates the normalizing constant of the power distribution, which gives the sequence-level R'enyi entropy (SRE) of the model's completion distribution at zero marginal cost, with a guarantee at every particle budget. A R'enyi chain rule extends this readout to a family of stepwise entropies of any order. We prove that orders above one are tied to the most likely token of each step, which explains why they track log-probability, while the order-1/2 member accumulates the log of per-step search effort. This member is the best zero-cost selective-prediction signal in 10 of 13 settings. On MATH500 its AUROC is 0.022 to 0.044 above log-probability with all four models and within length quartiles, and the same order is selected when each setting is held out. An 8-particle probe identifies the problems that benefit from more particles, and a two-pass policy matches 64-particle accuracy on MATH500 with 34.2% fewer particles over three seeds.
papers.summary: Estimating uncertainty over a whole LLM completion usually means choosing between cheap token-local signals and costly self-consistency sampling. Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) decoding for power sampling already estimates the normalizing constant of the power distribution, which yields the sequence-level Rényi entropy (SRE) of the completion distribution at no extra cost, and a chain rule extends this to stepwise entropies of any order. The order-1/2 variant is the best zero-cost selective-prediction signal in 10 of 13 settings and beats log-probability on `MATH500` by 0.022 to 0.044 AUROC across four models. An 8-particle probe identifies problems that benefit from more compute, and a two-pass policy **matches 64-particle accuracy on `MATH500` with 34.2% fewer particles**.

papers.title: BioMem: Agentic Memory for Biomedical LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated considerable potential in biomedical applications, while agentic memory systems have emerged as a promising approach to preserving and utilizing information across tasks and interactions. However, a fundamental question remains: how effectively and reliably do these systems retain, retrieve, update, and utilize biomedical information? In this study, we systematically investigate agentic memory in the biomedical domain, focusing on task effectiveness, retrieval quality, information fidelity, and long-term robustness. We evaluate five memory approaches across four LLMs in three representative settings: biomedical knowledge reasoning, clinical prediction, and long-term conversational memory. Our analyses reveal how memory construction, evidence relevance, and conversational history shape downstream biomedical performance, highlighting the distinct challenges of retrieving relevant information, preserving its fidelity, and effectively utilizing it for reasoning. Building on these findings, we introduce Hybrid Memory Retrieval and Utilization (HMRU), a training-free framework that jointly enhances evidence accessibility and task-aware utilization to improve biomedical reasoning and long-term conversational memory. HMRU achieves an average relative improvement of 8.6% across biomedical question-answering and conversational memory benchmarks, with additional gains in selected clinical prediction tasks. It further reduces conversational answer errors by 24.9% and closes 48.0% of the performance gap to full-context inference. Our findings provide a systematic characterization of biomedical agentic memory and practical insights into developing more effective and reliable memory-augmented LLM systems.
papers.summary: How reliably agentic memory systems retain, retrieve, update and use biomedical information is evaluated across five memory approaches and four LLMs, in knowledge reasoning, clinical prediction and long-term conversational settings. The analysis separates the challenges of retrieving relevant evidence, preserving its fidelity and using it in reasoning. Building on those findings, Hybrid Memory Retrieval and Utilization (`HMRU`) is a training-free framework that improves both evidence accessibility and task-aware use. It yields **an average relative improvement of 8.6%** on biomedical question-answering and conversational memory benchmarks, cuts conversational answer errors by 24.9% and closes 48.0% of the gap to full-context inference.

papers.title: Off-target posterior mass: A training-free diagnostic for fine-tuning spoken language diarization probes
papers.abstract: Spoken Language Diarization (SLD) models provide frame-level language information of a speech recording. SLD modeling pipeline includes feature extraction from pre-trained speech models followed by clustering. Fine-tuning pre-trained speech models has shown performance gains for SLD with its magnitude being dataset dependent. Off-target Posterior Mass (OTPM), computed based on posterior language identification probabilities is proposed as a diagnostic metric to forecast performance gains from SLD fine-tuning. OTPM obtains positive correlation with probe gains, 0.56 on unseen synthetic bilingual data and 0.23 on real-world corpora. These results indicate promising potential of OTPM as a diagnostic metric for SLD.
papers.summary: Spoken language diarization (SLD) labels the language of each frame in a recording, and fine-tuning the underlying pre-trained speech model helps by an amount that varies across datasets. Off-target Posterior Mass (`OTPM`), computed from language-identification posterior probabilities without any training, is proposed as a way to forecast how much fine-tuning will help. Its correlation with the observed probe gains is **0.56 on unseen synthetic bilingual data and 0.23 on real-world corpora**.

papers.title: You Don't Need Feature Learning to Do In-Context Learning
papers.abstract:
How should we understand memorization vs. generalization in in-context learning (ICL) tasks, and when does one happen vs. the other? To investigate, we study how rotation-invariant kernel machines learn the ICL linear regression task proposed by Raventos et al. (2023). By decomposing the task in the kernel eigenbasis, we obtain a spectral picture of learning in this ICL setting. This picture reveals that as sample size grows, kernel machines learn successively-higher-degree components of the memorizing solution, which depend upon successively-higher-degree statistics of the training task set. The generalizing solution is approximately a low-degree truncation of the memorizing solution, and so the model first generalizes, then degrades into memorization as training proceeds.
  The takeaways are threefold. First, if this case is indicative, learning a "generalizing" solution on an ICL task is really just underfitting the memorizing solution! Second, the fact that kernel machines can generalize on this task means that feature learning is inessential to ICL. Third, transformers empirically trained to do ICL are shown to memorize tasks through the higher-order statistics of the training tasks that the kernel-based theory predicts, suggesting it applies even to models capable of feature learning.
papers.summary: To understand memorization versus generalization in in-context learning (ICL), rotation-invariant kernel machines are analyzed on the ICL linear regression task of Raventos et al., with the task decomposed in the kernel eigenbasis. As sample size grows, the kernel machine learns successively higher-degree components of the memorizing solution, and the generalizing solution is approximately a low-degree truncation of it, so the model generalizes first and then degrades into memorization. The authors conclude that **generalizing on this task amounts to underfitting the memorizing solution and that feature learning is not needed for ICL**. Trained transformers are shown to memorize through the same higher-order task statistics the kernel theory predicts.

papers.title: Inherited Weights: Measuring the Tokenization Premium and the Sovereignty Cost of Language Models for the Global South
papers.abstract: Most language models deployed outside the United States and China are fine-tuned descendants of a small number of pretrained families. We argue that fine-tuning leaves the decisive properties of a model inherited from its base: vocabulary, knowledge, cultural alignment, memorized data and license. We contribute (i) an updated, reproducible measurement of the tokenization premium across 31 languages and 7 tokenizers released in 2023-2024, on 27 articles of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, with explicit correction for unknown-token collapse. Premiums reach 10x for Amharic in older tokenizers and remain at 6.8x in the newest commercial one; Indigenous South American languages pay between 1.6x and 2.7x under global tokenizers. A vocabulary built from Portuguese lowers the premium for 11 of 13 Latin-script Global South languages relative to every global tokenizer tested, by about 24% for Guarani and Quechua. (ii) An eight-test black-box sovereignty audit that a buyer can run without access to weights. (iii) A regime argument: under energy and liability constraints, accuracy per joule, calibration and selective risk should replace raw accuracy as design objectives, with metrics that abstention cannot inflate. We close with preliminary internal measurements from a proprietary architecture built around these objectives, reported with their limitations. Data and measurement code are included.
papers.summary: Most language models deployed outside the United States and China are fine-tunes of a few pretrained families, and the argument here is that vocabulary, knowledge, cultural alignment, memorized data and license are all inherited from the base model. A reproducible measurement of the tokenization premium covers 31 languages and 7 tokenizers on Universal Declaration of Human Rights text: **premiums reach 10x for Amharic in older tokenizers and remain 6.8x in the newest commercial one**, while Indigenous South American languages pay 1.6x to 2.7x. A Portuguese-built vocabulary lowers the premium for 11 of 13 Latin-script Global South languages. The work also offers an eight-test black-box audit runnable without weight access and argues for accuracy per joule, calibration and selective risk as design objectives.

papers.title: ForeSpark: Joint Draft and Verification Budget Scheduling for Parallel Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Parallel drafters accelerate LLM decoding by proposing a whole block of draft tokens in a single forward pass, making them attractive for LLM serving. Recent systems optimize goodput (i.e., accepted tokens per second) because rejected drafts steal compute from other requests. However, these systems control only how many tokens are verified, so every request still drafts a full block. At high serving load, we find that drafting consumes up to 40% of step time, of which a majority is discarded because it is never verified. Yet, draft-length control from autoregressive drafters does not carry over, because a parallel drafter commits to its length before its single pass. Moreover, draft and verification lengths are coupled across the batch, so they must be selected jointly for every request while keeping the decision computationally cheap at every step. In this paper, we propose work-conserving speculation (WCS), a design that jointly allocates draft and verification budgets per request in LLM serving, and present ForeSpark as its prototype. ForeSpark realizes WCS with (i) a context-aware pre-draft estimator that predicts acceptance for every candidate length from the target model's context features, (ii) a lightweight joint draft-verify scheduler that selects both lengths through a global sort, and (iii) a post-draft budget distribution that spends verification on the most promising tokens. Implemented on vLLM, ForeSpark improves throughput by up to 1.77x over the state-of-the-art DSpark and by 2.49x over autoregressive decoding at a matched per-request generation rate, without changing the output distribution. It also tolerates higher load, sustaining up to 1.51x the request rate of DSpark under latency service level objectives (SLOs).
papers.summary: Parallel drafters speed up LLM decoding by proposing a block of draft tokens in one forward pass, but existing serving systems only control how many tokens are verified, so at high load drafting takes up to 40% of step time and most of it is discarded. Work-conserving speculation (WCS) jointly allocates draft and verification budgets per request, and its prototype `ForeSpark` combines a pre-draft acceptance estimator, a joint scheduler based on a global sort and a post-draft verification budget distribution. Implemented on `vLLM`, it **improves throughput by up to 1.77x over `DSpark`** and 2.49x over autoregressive decoding without changing the output distribution. It also sustains up to 1.51x the request rate of `DSpark` under latency service level objectives (SLOs).

papers.title: Fermat ProbCover: Coverage-Based Active Learning on Fermat Distance Graphs
papers.abstract: Active learning aims to reduce annotation cost by selecting the most informative examples for labeling. In the low-budget regime, where uncertainty-based methods often fail, coverage-based active learning methods such as ProbCover have been shown to be effective. However, these methods typically rely on Euclidean distance, which may not adequately capture the underlying geometry of data. In this article, we propose PC-Fermat, a coverage-based active learning method that replaces Euclidean coverage neighborhoods with neighborhoods defined by a Fermat distance, i.e., a data-adaptive distance that reflects the underlying distribution of the data points. To facilitate computation, we construct a weighted Euclidean neighborhood graph and use a truncated shortest-path algorithm to compute the Fermat coverage graph. We also establish sufficient conditions under which this construction exactly preserves the Fermat coverage computed on the complete graph. Finally, we evaluate PC-Fermat on eight classification datasets across varying labeling budgets, with particular emphasis on the very low-budget regime. Our experimental results demonstrate that PC-Fermat outperforms several existing active learning methods on the majority of the datasets.
papers.summary: Coverage-based active learning methods such as `ProbCover` work well at low labeling budgets but define coverage neighborhoods with Euclidean distance, which can misrepresent the data's geometry. `PC-Fermat` substitutes a Fermat distance, a data-adaptive metric reflecting the underlying density, computed with a truncated shortest-path algorithm on a weighted neighborhood graph, with sufficient conditions given for exactly matching the complete-graph result. On eight classification datasets, with emphasis on very low budgets, it **outperforms several existing active learning methods on the majority of datasets**.

papers.title: SLIC: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning Small LMs for Multi-Turn Analog Circuit Optimization
papers.abstract: Analog integrated circuit (IC) design is a multi-turn, simulator-grounded engineering task that demands iterative reasoning over coupled performance tradeoffs, yet proprietary process design kits (PDKs) make hosted large language model workflows difficult to deploy in practical design settings. We present SLIC (Small LM Iterating on Circuits), a reinforcement fine-tuning framework that trains a 4B-scale, locally deployable language model for closed-loop analog circuit optimization. SLIC pairs structured circuit representations with discretized relative-update actions, domain- and success-gated multiobjective rewards, and Reward-Guided Rollout Steering (RGRS), which turns per-step simulator feedback into signals for both policy learning and online rollout construction in this sparse, highly constrained domain. We further release an open, goal-conditioned benchmark of 41 amplifier topologies with standardized protocols for in-distribution validation, held-out topology evaluation, and cross-technology-node transfer. Trained solely with open source 65 nm CMOS predictive technology models (PTM), SLIC-Random achieves 87.1% in-distribution four-specification Pass@1 within eight turns, surpassing the 763B DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash Think by 48.5 percentage points. Beyond the training distribution, SLIC-Softmax reaches 72.6% Pass@1 on held-out topologies, and the trained policies consistently transfer across five unseen technology nodes without additional fine-tuning. This transfer extends to a commercial TSMC 65 nm CMOS PDK, where SLIC-Random achieves 49.9% held-out-topology Pass@1, demonstrating practical deployment through local inference without transmitting proprietary data to external LLM services. Performance further scales with test-time simulator interactions, reaching up to 83.2% held-out-topology Pass@1 at a 32-turn budget.
papers.summary: Analog integrated circuit sizing is a multi-turn, simulator-in-the-loop task, and proprietary process design kits (PDKs) make hosted LLMs hard to use for it. `SLIC` applies reinforcement fine-tuning to a 4B-scale, locally deployable language model using structured circuit representations, discretized relative-update actions, gated multiobjective rewards and Reward-Guided Rollout Steering (`RGRS`), and comes with an open benchmark of 41 amplifier topologies. Trained only on open 65 nm predictive technology models, it reaches **87.1% in-distribution Pass@1 within eight turns, 48.5 percentage points above the 763B `DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash Think`**. It reaches 72.6% on held-out topologies and transfers without further tuning to five unseen technology nodes and a commercial TSMC 65 nm PDK.

papers.title: SafeRoute-MAS: Coverage-Aware and Risk-Calibrated Message Routing for Multi-Agent Scientific Reasoning
papers.abstract: We introduce SafeRoute-MAS, a coverage-aware, risk-calibrated procedure that keeps all specialist messages or removes one using only pre-integration information. On a sealed cache of 5,328 committees, its source-compatible operating point gains +1.80 percentage points (95% CI [+1.13, +2.52]) while removing 12.76% of message tokens. We also run 4,580 controlled integrations over a stratified 458-committee sample on a public gpt-oss-120b endpoint. The sample estimate is -0.09 points; design weighting to the original workload gives +0.94 points (95% CI [-1.31, +3.50]) and 18.72% acted-input reduction. A weighted token-matched comparison likewise does not establish a selector advantage (+1.68 points, CI [-1.27, +5.10]). Only 13 of 88 cached non-neutral labels (14.8%) retain direction by repeated-call majority. Expected-corruption UCL is 4.60% after weighting, but only 2 of 11 prespecified marginals pass the support/risk rule. We therefore propose a numerical qualification with Keep-All fallback, applied here retrospectively rather than validated prospectively.
papers.summary: `SafeRoute-MAS` decides, using only pre-integration information, whether a multi-agent scientific reasoning committee should keep all specialist messages or drop one. On a sealed cache of 5,328 committees it gains 1.80 percentage points while removing 12.76% of message tokens, but **4,580 controlled live integrations on a `gpt-oss-120b` endpoint do not establish an advantage**, with a weighted estimate of +0.94 points and a confidence interval spanning zero. Only 14.8% of cached non-neutral labels keep their direction under repeated calls, and 2 of 11 prespecified marginals pass the support and risk rule. The authors therefore propose a numerical qualification with a keep-all fallback, applied retrospectively rather than validated prospectively.

papers.title: When Reasoning looks like Hidden Understanding: How Chain-of-Thought Fosters Anthropomorphism, Perceptions of Epistemic Superiority, and Cognitive Deference
papers.abstract: As AI-based products permeate society, specifically systems using generative models, a belief system is emerging about what these products are and what they can and cannot do. One common belief concerns the perception of the form of language as evidence of 'understanding' language. As these generative models reproduce linguistic patterns rather than understand meaning, interpreting these patterns as evidence of understanding is a misattribution. This misconception is extended by the notion that generative models can 'explain their reasoning.' Anecdotally, these misconceptions which mistake the form of language for its meaning are driving cognitive deference to AI systems in a way that displaces human agency. Such mistakes involve attributions of cognitive properties to the system, allowing them to be treated like intentional 'minds'. Importantly, perceived epistemic authority and superiority make that 'mind' worth deferring to. Anthropomorphism in tandem with epistemic authority and superiority, we argue, increases the risk that users generalise from narrow task performance to broader competencies, committing the "fallacy of composition". This paper explores misconceptions of Chain of Thought (CoT) reasoning as sufficient transparent 'explanation'. We explore how anthropomorphism acts as a vehicle for cognitive deference of decision-making and perceptions of epistemic superiority in AI systems. Finally, we explore CoT's ramifications using medicine as an example. Taken together, we conclude that explainability operationalised through CoT is highly problematic and undercuts the very ethical principles it is intended to serve. While CoT may be valuable for improving output accuracy and moderation, we suggest that the practice of asking models to provide user facing reasons for their outputs should be actively discouraged, and AI literacy training should explicitly caution against its use.
papers.summary: A position piece argues that users mistake the fluent form of chain-of-thought (CoT) output for evidence of understanding and for a transparent explanation of how a model reached its answer. The authors contend that this fosters anthropomorphism and a perception of epistemic authority, which together drive cognitive deference and lead users to generalize from narrow task performance to broad competence, with medicine used as the worked example. They conclude that **explainability operationalised through CoT undercuts the ethical principles it is meant to serve**, and recommend discouraging user-facing reasoning while granting that CoT may still help accuracy and moderation.

papers.title: Deep Personalization: Continuous Context Observation for Local Proactive Agents
papers.abstract: As AI agents become increasingly capable, users must still recognize when and how to ask for help, leaving many opportunities for useful support unrealized. Proactive agents hold the promise to close this gap, but effective proactivity requires understanding users' real-time activities and personalizing intervention timing so that assistance is offered when it is likely to be helpful rather than disruptive. We introduce deep personalization, a closed-loop process that connects continuous context observation with continual agent adaptation: an agent observes user activity, selectively retains long-term context, and adapts intervention decisions from implicit feedback. We initiate deep personalization in Coco, a proactive desktop agent, by having a separate Observer Agent that monitors desktop activity, maintains compact long-term user modeling context, and learns when assistance is desirable from implicit signals such as engagement, dismissal, explicit requests, and repeated work patterns. We further develop efficient on-device strategies to enable the Observer Agent to run on local AI compute platforms without streaming raw activity data off-device. For evaluation at scale without collecting sensitive real-user activity, we introduce a data-synthesis pipeline that transforms existing computer-use trajectories into OSWorld-Persona, a benchmark with persona-conditioned intervention labels. On OSWorld-Persona, deep personalization improves macro F1 across three model backbones from 0.12-0.19 under direct prompting to 0.35-0.48 after adaptation, a 2.4-3.0x relative gain. In a week-long user study, we observe that Coco improves its macro-averaged F1 score from 0.199 to 0.515. These results suggest that on-device deep personalization can make proactive agents more timely and increasingly aligned with each user's everyday work.
papers.summary: Proactive agents need to know when an intervention will help rather than disrupt, which requires understanding a user's ongoing activity. `Coco`, a proactive desktop agent, uses a separate Observer Agent that monitors desktop activity on-device, keeps compact long-term user context and learns intervention timing from implicit signals such as engagement, dismissal and repeated work patterns. For evaluation without real user data, a synthesis pipeline converts computer-use trajectories into `OSWorld-Persona`, a benchmark with persona-conditioned intervention labels. Adaptation **raises macro F1 from 0.12-0.19 under direct prompting to 0.35-0.48** across three model backbones, and a week-long user study saw it rise from 0.199 to 0.515.

papers.title: Leveraging Psychophysical Attentional Distribution for Gaze-Augmented Reward Modeling
papers.abstract: Integrating human feedback into language models has gained increasing attention as a means to align model outputs with human preferences, with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) serving as a prominent framework for preference-based alignment. Recent studies have incorporated eye-tracking (ET) data as an additional supervisory signal for reward model training, grounding reward learning in human reading behavior. Building on this approach, we extend prior fixation-centric models by leveraging established findings from cognitive psychology on human letter recognition. Specifically, we model visual attention as a spatially graded distribution centered on the current gaze location and incorporate this representation into reward model training. Our results show that the reward model trained with the proposed gaze distribution achieves higher preference prediction accuracy than a baseline model. Moreover, some results from our experiments are qualitatively consistent with established findings on human attention during reading, suggesting that they potentially capture cognitively meaningful aspects of human attention allocation.
papers.summary: Eye-tracking data has been used as an extra supervisory signal when training reward models for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), typically through fixation-centric features. Drawing on cognitive psychology findings about human letter recognition, this work instead models visual attention as a spatially graded distribution centered on the current gaze location and feeds that into reward model training. The resulting reward model **achieves higher preference prediction accuracy than a baseline model**, and some results are qualitatively consistent with known patterns of attention during reading.

papers.title: Sharp Sample Complexity of KL-Regularized Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: KL-regularized reinforcement learning, the objective behind maximum-entropy RL and RL from human feedback, is variational inference in the graphical model of "control as inference": the regularized optimal policy is a posterior over trajectories, and the suboptimality of a policy is $\beta$ times a KL divergence between path measures. However, it is not known how many samples it takes to learn this posterior, even with a generative model. Earlier $1/\epsilon$ guarantees scale with $H^5$ in the effective horizon $H$, and no lower bound for MDPs depends on the temperature $\beta$. In this work, we show that for a discounted MDP with $K$ state-action pairs, the plug-in estimator finds a policy that is $\epsilon$-optimal from every initial state with $\widetilde{O}(KH^3/(\epsilon\max\{\epsilon,\beta\}) + KH)$ samples, and that no algorithm, even one that chooses where to sample, can do with fewer when $\epsilon \lesssim \min\{H, H^2/\beta\}$. For $\epsilon < \beta$ this is a $1/\epsilon$ rate with the same horizon dependence as unregularized RL. We also find the exact asymptotic constant of the plug-in estimator, a Fisher-weighted variance of the estimated soft Q-function. The estimator is locally asymptotically minimax among methods that sample every pair equally often, and we give the allocation of samples that is optimal among adaptive designs. Simulations on small MDPs match the rates and the constants.
papers.summary: The number of samples needed to learn the optimal policy in KL-regularized reinforcement learning, the objective behind maximum-entropy RL, was not known even with a generative model. For a discounted Markov decision process with K state-action pairs and effective horizon H, the plug-in estimator is shown to find an ε-optimal policy with **on the order of KH³/(ε·max{ε,β}) + KH samples, matched by a lower bound** that holds even for adaptive sampling in the stated regime. When ε is below the temperature β this gives a 1/ε rate with the same horizon dependence as unregularized RL. The exact asymptotic constant and the optimal adaptive sample allocation are also derived, and simulations on small problems match the rates.

papers.title: Differentially Private Statistical Inference for Rankings from Pairwise Comparisons
papers.abstract: Reliable inference for rankings of large language models based on human pairwise comparisons must preserve the privacy of individual preference records. To meet this need, we develop methods for score and rank inference under the Bradley-Terry model with edge differential privacy. For an objective-perturbed estimator, a new leave-one-out analysis establishes finite-sample bounds on Euclidean and entrywise estimation errors. For sufficiently dense comparison graphs, the error bounds extend to smaller privacy budgets, including regimes in which its privacy term dominates its statistical term. A uniform asymptotic expansion yields asymptotically valid confidence intervals for individual scores and pairwise score differences. To improve finite-sample performance, we account for both regularization bias and privacy-induced randomness by combining a plug-in ridge-bias correction with Gaussian-Laplace calibration. We further establish a bootstrap procedure for simultaneous rank inference, providing asymptotically valid confidence sets for individual ranks and tests of top-$K$ membership. When the comparison probability is public and known, all proposed inferential procedures require no additional privacy budget. We evaluate finite-sample performance through simulations and apply the proposed methods to rank large language models for creative writing.
papers.summary: Ranking LLMs from human pairwise comparisons exposes individual preference records, so methods are developed for score and rank inference under the Bradley-Terry model with edge differential privacy. A leave-one-out analysis of an objective-perturbed estimator gives finite-sample error bounds, and an asymptotic expansion yields **valid confidence intervals for scores and score differences, with a bootstrap procedure for simultaneous rank inference and top-K membership tests**. Finite-sample accuracy is improved by a ridge-bias correction combined with Gaussian-Laplace calibration. The methods are evaluated in simulation and applied to ranking LLMs for creative writing.

papers.title: The WoW: A Large-Scale World Knowledge Corpus for Full-Lifecycle LLM Training
papers.abstract: Existing Chinese educational corpora often suffer from fragmented coverage and a lack of systematic organization. In this paper, we propose WoW (\textbf{Wo}rld Kno\textbf{w}ledge), a large-scale dataset designed for the full-cycle training of foundation models. The construction of this dataset is driven by an Educational Knowledge Graph, which serves as a taxonomic backbone for the systematic collection and completion of missing educational modules across all levels. Compared to previous versions, this iteration provides enhanced systematicity, superior quality, and a larger scale, while incorporating multimodal signals and supporting every stage of model development. Experiments demonstrate that WoW significantly improves model performance across diverse benchmarks. To facilitate community research, we further provide an interactive platform for graph-based data selection and retrieval.
papers.summary: Chinese educational corpora tend to have fragmented coverage and little systematic organization. `WoW` is a large-scale dataset for all stages of foundation model training, built around an Educational Knowledge Graph that serves as a taxonomy for collecting material and filling missing modules across education levels, and it includes multimodal signals. The authors report that training with it **improves model performance across diverse benchmarks**, and they provide an interactive platform for graph-based data selection and retrieval.

papers.title: Simultaneous Near-Optimal Region Identification in Continuous Simulation Optimization: Minimax Complexity and Adaptive Sampling
papers.abstract:
Simulation optimization typically returns a single estimated optimal point. When decisions also depend on criteria evaluated independently of simulation, such as resource cost, the decision maker instead needs the set of designs whose expected performance lies within a tolerance of the optimum, often choosing the tolerance only after seeing the tradeoffs. We study how to identify these near-optimal regions on a continuous design space, simultaneously for all tolerances up to a prescribed maximum $T$, with region estimation error at most $\eta$. We show that region identification is not a by-product of optimization. Specifically, when $\alpha>
u$, any procedure, even one given the optimal design in advance, needs at least $\Omega igl(\eta^{-(2+d/
u)}\min\{1,KT^{d/\alpha}\} igr)$ simulation evaluations, where $d$ is the dimension, $
u$ the smoothness, and $(K,\alpha)$ the covering parameters that describe the geometry of the near-optimal designs. We propose SASORI, which returns an estimated optimal point and the regions for all tolerances from the same evaluations, matching this lower bound up to logarithmic factors. SASORI also achieves the optimal tradeoff between region estimation error and cumulative regret, and reduces to a minimax-optimal simulation optimization procedure at zero tolerance. Numerical experiments illustrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.
papers.summary: Simulation optimization usually returns a single estimated optimum, but decision makers weighing outside criteria need the whole set of designs within a tolerance of optimal, for every tolerance up to a maximum. The analysis shows that identifying these regions on a continuous design space is not a by-product of optimization, deriving a minimax lower bound on simulation evaluations that holds even when the optimal design is known in advance. The proposed `SASORI` procedure returns the optimum and all regions from the same evaluations and **matches the lower bound up to logarithmic factors**, while achieving the optimal tradeoff between region estimation error and cumulative regret.

papers.title: Reasoning-Aware Relational Representation Learning for Open-Vocabulary Scene Graph Generation
papers.abstract: Open-Vocabulary Scene Graph Generation (OV-SGG) requires models to recognize visual relationships beyond the training vocabulary, yet existing methods often rely on dataset-specific object--predicate co-occurrence patterns. Under long-tailed distributions and noisy object localization, such reliance leads to biased, entangled relation representations, limiting both rare-relation recognition and generalization to unseen predicates. To address these challenges, we propose RaRe, a reasoning-aware relational representation learning framework that transforms MLLM-generated chain-of-thought (CoT) rationales into structured relation embeddings. Rather than using CoT only as an intermediate reasoning trace for final prediction, RaRe directly optimizes the rationale-derived representation space to improve inter-relation discriminability. Specifically, RaRe first aligns rationale embeddings with textualized relation descriptions through self-supervised contrastive learning, and then refines rationale generation with a specificity-oriented reinforcement learning objective that encourages semantically object-pair-specific relational evidence. Experiments on VG150 and PSG demonstrate improved category-balanced recognition over existing baselines, while the additional gains from learning vary across datasets and proposal settings. Code available at: https://artanic30.github.io/project_pages/RaRe.
papers.summary: Open-vocabulary scene graph generation models tend to lean on dataset-specific object–predicate co-occurrence patterns, which hurts rare relations and unseen predicates. `RaRe` turns chain-of-thought (CoT) rationales generated by a multimodal large language model into structured relation embeddings, aligning them with textual relation descriptions through self-supervised contrastive learning and then refining rationale generation with a reinforcement learning objective that rewards object-pair-specific evidence. On `VG150` and `PSG` it reports **improved category-balanced recognition over existing baselines**, though the extra gains from the learning stages vary across datasets and proposal settings.

papers.title: Evaluating Compositional Generalization in Transformers: The Role of Composition Equivalence and Module Coverage
