papers.abstract: Compositional generalization is an important form of out-of-distribution generalization, defined as the ability to train on some combinations of modules (e.g., functions such as sort, filter) and then generalize to unseen combinations. Despite substantial empirical work evaluating compositional generalization in transformers, findings have been inconsistent because evaluations were often conducted on a limited set of train-test splits, defined in an ad hoc manner. Through a systematic evaluation, we identify two key aspects of the train-test distribution that strongly affect performance: composition equivalence and module coverage. We show that the apparent performance of direct models (trained only on final outputs) results primarily from exploiting composition equivalences, meaning different sequences of modules that reduce to identical end-to-end functions. When benchmarks eliminate these equivalences, performance drops significantly, showing their inability to generalize to compositions of known modules that produce novel end-to-end functions. We further demonstrate that performance degrades monotonically as module coverage shifts increase (when modules appear in different contexts between train and test), affecting both direct and step-by-step models (trained on intermediate and final outputs). These findings have concrete implications for benchmark design: benchmarks that include compositional equivalences can lead to significant overestimation of the generalization abilities of direct models, and benchmarks that include both module coverage violations and compositional equivalences can exacerbate shortcut learning. As a case study, we demonstrate the role of compositional equivalence on the generalization performance of the pre-trained model Llama3-8B on the code-output prediction task in the coding benchmark LiveCodeBench.
papers.summary: Results on whether transformers generalize to unseen combinations of known modules (such as sort and filter) have been inconsistent, largely because train-test splits were chosen ad hoc. A systematic evaluation isolates two factors: composition equivalence, where different module sequences reduce to the same end-to-end function, and module coverage, where modules appear in different contexts at train and test time. **Models trained only on final outputs owe most of their apparent success to exploiting composition equivalences, and their performance drops significantly once those are removed**, while accuracy degrades monotonically with coverage shift for both direct and step-by-step models. A case study with `Llama3-8B` on the code-output prediction task of `LiveCodeBench` shows the same equivalence effect.

papers.title: Dark Matters: VAE-Aware HDR Encoding for SDR-to-HDR Video Reconstruction
papers.abstract: SDR-to-HDR reconstruction is an ill-posed problem in which clipped highlights, crushed shadows, and quantization artifacts must be recovered while preserving the original content. Latent diffusion models provide powerful generative priors for restoring missing detail, but their effectiveness is constrained by how HDR signals pass through the pretrained VAE. We find that common log-like encodings suppress low-luminance chromatic differences before generation, producing a dark-side collapse in the frozen-VAE latent. We introduce EquivFlow, a compact, invertible exposure-equivariant encoding that maps exposure changes to additive shifts while retaining a scale-independent chromatic component, without modifying the VAE. Encoding-level tests across pretrained image and video VAEs show that its exposure structure and deep-dark chroma transport persist across the tested hosts. Integrated into SDR-to-HDR video diffusion, EquivFlow delivers consistent chromatic-fidelity gains across the tested settings while retaining competitive reconstruction fidelity.
papers.summary: Reconstructing high dynamic range (HDR) video from standard dynamic range (SDR) input with latent diffusion is limited by how HDR signals pass through the pretrained variational autoencoder (VAE). The authors find that common log-like encodings suppress low-luminance color differences, producing a **dark-side collapse in the frozen-VAE latent**. Their `EquivFlow` encoding is compact and invertible, maps exposure changes to additive shifts, and keeps a scale-independent chromatic component without modifying the VAE. Integrated into SDR-to-HDR video diffusion, it yields consistent chromatic-fidelity gains across the tested settings with competitive reconstruction fidelity.

papers.title: Mobile AI Factory: Building Specialized Language Models for Your Mobile Device
papers.abstract: Small language models (SLMs) running on mobile devices can keep user data private and work without connectivity. But they perform well only when fine-tuned for the target task and sized for the target device, a process that today requires repeated expert tuning. We present {\it Mobile AI Factory}, an agentic system that builds a fine-tuned, quantized SLM for a given task and phone. Given a task specification and a target phone, an orchestrator LLM chooses whether to tune hyperparameters, mine real data, or generate synthetic examples, while fixed rules roll back changes that hurt accuracy. The factory searches from small to large models across base models and quantizations, adapts its accuracy goal as it searches, and uses real measurements of the target phone across inference engines and backends. We evaluate Mobile AI Factory on ten tasks and four Android phones. On an unseen testset, its on-device models outperform two five-shot frontier models on five tasks, by up to 0.34, and match them on three more. Its search comes within 0.03 of exhaustively training all 27 model variants on an entity extraction task, while using 19$\times$ less GPU time. Phone measurements also matter: the best configuration changes across phones. Without phone measurements, Claude Opus 5.5, given the full hardware and model specifications, misses the app's requirements in 25\% of easy and moderate cases and in 60\% of hard ones. Code is available at: https://github.com/evanly-gh/SLM_Factory.
papers.summary: Small language models (SLMs) on phones only perform well when fine-tuned for the task and sized for the device, which currently takes repeated expert tuning. `Mobile AI Factory` is an agentic system in which an orchestrator LLM decides whether to tune hyperparameters, mine real data, or generate synthetic examples, while fixed rules roll back harmful changes and the search uses real measurements from the target phone across inference engines and backends. Across ten tasks and four Android phones, its on-device models beat two five-shot frontier models on five tasks and match them on three more, and its search comes **within 0.03 of exhaustively training all 27 model variants while using 19× less GPU time**. The best configuration differs across phones, and without phone measurements `Claude Opus 5.5` misses the app's requirements in 25% of easy and moderate cases and 60% of hard ones.

papers.title: Distribution Shift Detection in Remote Sensing Imagery using Machine Learning Models
papers.abstract: Remote sensing imagery acquired by Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) supports wide range of applications; however, deploying machine learning (ML) models on resource-constrained aerial platforms introduces challenges beyond predictive accuracy, particularly when deployment data differ from the distributions observed during training. Such shifts are common in remote sensing due to geographic, sensor, seasonal, and other visual variations. A practical solution is to equip deployed models with mechanisms that detect emerging distribution shifts and support subsequent responsive actions. This paper presents an empirical case study of three open-source detection tools: (i) Alibi-Detect; (ii) NannyML; and (iii) PyTorch-OOD. Using cross-dataset remote-sensing shifts, we evaluate both detection effectiveness and computational latency of these tools. Our results reveal differences in detection behavior and processing cost across methods and implementations, highlighting trade-offs between detection capability and response-time. These findings motivate further work toward lightweight, and latency-aware monitoring mechanisms for resource-constrained systems.
papers.summary: Machine learning models deployed on unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) often face imagery that differs from training data because of geographic, sensor, and seasonal variation. This empirical case study compares three open-source shift-detection tools, `Alibi-Detect`, `NannyML`, and `PyTorch-OOD`, on cross-dataset remote-sensing shifts, measuring both detection effectiveness and computational latency. The results show **trade-offs between detection capability and response time** across methods and implementations, which the authors use to argue for lightweight, latency-aware monitoring on resource-constrained platforms.

papers.title: Nepali-English Code-Mixed Speech Recognition: Data Preparation and Adaptation of a Speech Foundation Model
papers.abstract: Nepali speakers regularly mix English words into conversation, but multilingual speech recognisers often struggle with language switches and the writing script used for English words. We study how to adapt SraVaani, a 449M-parameter hybrid TDT-CTC model, using a 172.8-hour corpus covering six Nepali speech domains. Its pretrained tokenizer does not support digits and several common symbols. Rather than replace it or discard these recordings, we generate Nepali and English readings for numbers and use zero-shot ASR output to select a plausible form. Full fine-tuning reduces test word error rate (WER) from 48.6% to 17.1%; a 12-epoch run reaches 16.3%, compared with 16.4% for fine-tuned Whisper large-v3-turbo. Freezing the encoder increases WER to 25.5%, while excluding numeric clips raises WER on numeric test speech from 14.3% to 21.3%. We also evaluate on FLEURS using both its original references and mixed-script alternatives. The comparison shows that transcription conventions explain part, but not all, of the out-of-domain performance loss.
papers.summary: Nepali speakers routinely mix English words into speech, which multilingual recognizers handle poorly, both at language switches and in the script used for English words. The authors adapt `SraVaani`, a 449M-parameter hybrid TDT-CTC model, on a 172.8-hour corpus spanning six Nepali speech domains, working around a tokenizer that lacks digits by generating Nepali and English readings for numbers and using zero-shot recognition output to pick a plausible one. **Full fine-tuning cuts test word error rate (WER) from 48.6% to 17.1%**, with a 12-epoch run reaching 16.3% against 16.4% for fine-tuned `Whisper large-v3-turbo`; freezing the encoder raises WER to 25.5%. Evaluation on `FLEURS` with alternative mixed-script references shows that transcription conventions explain part, but not all, of the out-of-domain loss.

papers.title: Evidential Deep Learning with conditional entropy for glaucoma detection
papers.abstract: We propose a novel conditional entropy function as a basis for quantifying predictive uncertainty in Evidential Deep Learning (EDL) for glaucoma detection from retinal fundus images. Using the EyePACS-AIROGS-light-V2 and RIM-ONE-DL datasets for validation, we found that our proposed EDL model regularized by conditional entropy function produced uncertainty estimates with substantially lower calibration errors than Deep Ensembles, MC Dropout, post-hoc calibration and the conventional EDL framework based on Dempster uncertainty. To further probe our models' interpretability, we analyzed Grad-CAM heatmaps using a focus index representing spatial concentration. Compared with the other uncertainty quantification methods, EDL models exhibited greater separation between the index distributions of correctly and incorrectly classified fundus images. In particular, false negatives were associated with localized Grad-CAM activations that were displaced from the optic disc, consistent with its established clinical importance in glaucoma assessment. Overall, our findings suggest that our proposed EDL framework for glaucoma detection provides not only enhanced uncertainty calibration but also admits a more physiologically consistent interpretability.
papers.summary: Uncertainty estimates for glaucoma detection from retinal fundus images are addressed with a new conditional entropy function used to regularize Evidential Deep Learning (EDL). On the `EyePACS-AIROGS-light-V2` and `RIM-ONE-DL` datasets, the resulting model shows **substantially lower calibration error than Deep Ensembles, MC Dropout, post-hoc calibration, and conventional EDL based on Dempster uncertainty**. A focus index computed over `Grad-CAM` heatmaps separates correctly and incorrectly classified images more clearly for EDL models, and false negatives tend to show activations displaced from the optic disc.

papers.title: Seeing the Small: Deformable Duality Mamba for Retinal Lesion Segmentation
papers.abstract: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) lesions vary widely in shape, and microaneurysms (MAs) span only a few pixels. We hypothesize that modeling the spatial organization of lesion regions, with global context and shape-adaptive scanning, improves the segmentation of such small and irregular lesions. To test this, we propose D$^2$Mamba, which couples non-causal state space duality with deformable Mamba scanning. We evaluate it with five-fold cross-validation on the DDR dataset, comparing against representative segmentation baselines under an identical training protocol, and conduct ablations on each component. D$^2$Mamba achieved the best overall performance, with 33.87% mIoU, 2.99 percentage points above the strongest baseline. The largest gain appeared on MAs, the smallest and most easily missed lesions, where Dice improved by 10.06 percentage points. These results confirm our hypothesis that spatially adaptive state space modeling benefits tiny-lesion segmentation. Code and pretrained weights are available at https://github.com/PUREPANEL1/D2Mamba.
papers.summary: Diabetic retinopathy lesions vary widely in shape, and microaneurysms cover only a few pixels, making them easy to miss in segmentation. `D²Mamba` combines non-causal state space duality with deformable Mamba scanning to model the spatial organization of lesion regions with global context and shape-adaptive scan paths. In five-fold cross-validation on the `DDR` dataset under an identical training protocol, it reaches 33.87% mean intersection-over-union, 2.99 points above the strongest baseline, with the largest gain on microaneurysms, where **Dice improves by 10.06 percentage points**.

papers.title: Differentiable Filtering for Inertial Odometry
papers.abstract: Accurate inertial odometry is critical for autonomous systems but suffers from unbounded drift caused by the integration of sensor noise and biases. In approaches such as TLIO, neural pseudo-measurements are trained independently of their downstream filter. This paper introduces Differentiable Filtering for Inertial Odometry (DFIO), a learning framework that embeds the update stages of an error-state Kalman filter directly into a computational graph. Following standalone pre-training, DFIO jointly optimizes the displacement and covariance output heads using posterior-position supervision through differentiable measurement updates. The proposed system is validated on public pedestrian motion datasets featuring both calibrated and uncalibrated inertial measurements. Experimental results on a pedestrian dataset demonstrate that DFIO reduces mean absolute and one-second relative translation errors by 13.2% and 39.6% relative to the TLIO baseline, and by 7.7% and 17.4% relative to its pre-trained counterpart. Furthermore, evaluations on uncalibrated smartphone inertial data indicate that the proposed method effectively mitigates translational drift and maintains trajectory alignment under highly noisy sensor conditions. Source code will be made publicly available.
papers.summary: Inertial odometry drifts without bound as sensor noise and bias are integrated, and in approaches such as `TLIO` the neural pseudo-measurements are trained separately from the filter that consumes them. Differentiable Filtering for Inertial Odometry (`DFIO`) embeds the update stages of an error-state Kalman filter in the computational graph and, after standalone pre-training, jointly optimizes the displacement and covariance heads with supervision on the posterior position. On a pedestrian dataset it **reduces mean absolute and one-second relative translation errors by 13.2% and 39.6% relative to `TLIO`**, and by 7.7% and 17.4% relative to its own pre-trained version. Tests on uncalibrated smartphone inertial data indicate reduced translational drift under highly noisy sensing.

papers.title: Developing an Operational Model for an Internet of Data Based Trusted Data Space for Vocational Education
papers.abstract: Data circulation in vocational education has long been constrained by unclear ownership, a lack of trust, and insufficient incentives. The Internet of Data provides a new underlying technology for enabling trusted cross-domain data circulation. Building on an Internet of Data based trusted data space for vocational education, this paper develops a multi-stakeholder operational model encompassing a value network, a product portfolio, revenue allocation, and governance rules. Emphasizing data sovereignty protection and incentive compatibility, the model provides a reference for the sustainable operation of regional vocational education data ecosystems.
papers.summary: Sharing data across vocational education institutions has been held back by unclear ownership, lack of trust, and weak incentives. Building on a trusted data space based on the Internet of Data, the authors design a **multi-stakeholder operational model covering a value network, a product portfolio, revenue allocation, and governance rules**. The model emphasizes data sovereignty protection and incentive compatibility and is offered as a reference for operating regional vocational education data ecosystems; no empirical evaluation is reported in the abstract.

papers.title: Parallel Broyden Methods for Efficiently Evaluating Nonlinear State Space Models
papers.abstract: Nonlinear state space models are typically evaluated sequentially, limiting their ability to exploit modern parallel hardware. Recent work has shown that state space models can be evaluated in parallel by reformulating evaluation as a root-finding problem, which can be solved with a parallel form of Newton's method. However, exact Newton methods require expensive multiplication of dense Jacobian matrices, and quasi-Newton methods based on diagonal approximations, while more scalable, are often slow to converge because they neglect interactions across state dimensions. We introduce a novel quasi-Newton approach based on Broyden's method, which captures coupling terms with diagonal-plus-low-rank approximations to blocks of the Jacobian. We construct the approximations from trajectory secants, avoiding automatic differentiation while retaining the favorable scaling of diagonal approximations and remaining compatible with parallel scan through rank compression. We prove finite-step recovery of the exact trajectory under the compressed scan, and show that convergence is tracked by the compression error and by the block approximation error along the current trajectory error, rather than in spectral norm. Empirically, we show that our method is advantageous when interactions are approximately low rank or when Jacobian evaluation is expensive: on low-rank RNNs, parallel MCMC algorithms, and denoising diffusion models, it converges in fewer iterations than other quasi-Newton methods and is the fastest parallel method when Jacobian evaluation is expensive or state dimensions are large.
papers.summary: Nonlinear state space models are usually evaluated step by step, and existing parallel alternatives either need costly dense Jacobian products (exact Newton) or converge slowly because diagonal approximations ignore coupling between state dimensions. The proposed quasi-Newton method uses Broyden's method to build diagonal-plus-low-rank approximations of Jacobian blocks from trajectory secants, avoiding automatic differentiation and staying compatible with parallel scan through rank compression. The authors prove finite-step recovery of the exact trajectory under the compressed scan and characterize convergence in terms of compression and block approximation error. On low-rank RNNs, parallel MCMC algorithms, and denoising diffusion models it converges in fewer iterations than other quasi-Newton methods and is **the fastest parallel method when Jacobian evaluation is expensive or state dimensions are large**.

papers.title: The RSI Tax: When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost
papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) seeks to improve an agent using its own task experience. Its practical value depends on whether performance gains justify the full cost of self-improvement and task execution. We evaluate this trade-off on continual task streams, scoring each task before its feedback is used for subsequent updates. We define the \emph{RSI Tax} as the token cost of the self-improvement process and include it alongside task-execution costs in end-to-end evaluation. Across six methods and two language models, a bounded-note baseline matches or exceeds the observed accuracy of Meta-Harness, EvoSkill, and RRSI, with mean total-token savings of 65.6-71.0\%. We decompose the RSI Tax into verification, exploration, and writing costs, and track subsequent use of the associated state or artifact. For these three RSI methods, verification accounts for 74.8--93.6% of the aggregate RSI Tax. A substantial share of the RSI Tax is also associated with states or artifacts that are not used later in the evaluated streams. These results expose a practical limitation of costly RSI procedures: improvements in the deployed agent need not justify the expense of the improvement process. They motivate RSI objectives that jointly optimize the RSI Tax and expected task-execution cost while ensuring continued growth in agent capabilities across the task stream.
papers.summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI), where an agent improves itself from its own task experience, is only worthwhile if the gains justify the cost of the improvement process. The authors define the `RSI Tax` as the token cost of self-improvement and include it alongside task-execution cost when evaluating six methods and two language models on continual task streams. A simple bounded-note baseline **matches or exceeds the accuracy of `Meta-Harness`, `EvoSkill`, and `RRSI` while using 65.6–71.0% fewer total tokens on average**. For those three methods, verification makes up 74.8–93.6% of the tax, and a substantial share of the spend goes to states or artifacts never used later in the stream.

papers.title: EJAI: Judgment-Preserving Civic AI for Data Center Environmental Justice
papers.abstract: Communities in the United States and around the world are contesting data centers, the physical infrastructure of AI. These disputes pose environmental justice issues: residents must weigh unevenly distributed burdens using evidence scattered across metrics, corporate claims, policy documents, and public testimony. A formative study with 10 users showed that dashboards and single-agent AI can settle questions before people examine that evidence. Here we present EJAI, a source-grounded system that links an interactive map, retrieved evidence, missing-data statements, and two stakeholder personas that allow people to inspect evidence and form their own policy recommendations. In a small functional benchmark of 21 queries, retrieved evidence supported 98.4% of factual claims and the system acknowledged missing evidence in 32 of 33 cases. Persona alignment carried a grounding cost: the Corporate Executive omitted some evidence that conflicted with its assigned priorities. In a within-subjects study, 15 participants acting as residents prepared for a simulated town hall. Some checked cited AI claims while treating map metrics as official, some made conditional recommendations with safeguards such as water-use disclosure, and some found the personas simplified or biased. Our results suggest that civic AI can support preparation for public reasoning when it makes evidence, gaps, and disagreement open to inspection, and that corpus imbalance and two-sided personas remain open justice concerns.
papers.summary: Residents contesting data center projects must weigh environmental burdens using evidence scattered across metrics, corporate claims, policy documents, and public testimony, and a formative study with 10 users found that dashboards and single-agent AI can settle questions before people examine that evidence. `EJAI` is a source-grounded system linking an interactive map, retrieved evidence, explicit missing-data statements, and two stakeholder personas so that users form their own policy recommendations. In a 21-query benchmark, **retrieved evidence supported 98.4% of factual claims** and missing evidence was acknowledged in 32 of 33 cases, though the Corporate Executive persona omitted some evidence that conflicted with its priorities. In a within-subjects study with 15 participants preparing for a simulated town hall, some verified cited claims and made conditional recommendations, while others found the personas simplified or biased.

papers.title: Framing-Induced Vulnerability in Large Language Models: Evidence from Chinese News Headlines
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly evaluate, route, and moderate news, so a model's judgment of a headline has become a gatekeeping decision. We ask whether that judgment follows the fact being reported or the way the fact is framed. We combine an ecological audit of 63,926 Chinese news headlines with a controlled experiment. The experiment covers 30 real events, 30 synthetic events, and 29 natural headline pairs, tested on four Chinese models. Changing only the headline frame shifted both perceived misleadingness and event severity, and the direction and ordering of the shifts were the same for DeepSeek, MiMo, Dots, and LongCat. Emotionally intensified headlines raised severity ratings by 0.65 to 0.88 points, whereas positively reframed headlines lowered them by 0.34 to 0.52 points. Supplying the article body reduced this severity bias by 54 to 80 percent, and all four reductions were significant at p < .01. A small human reference study showed the same direction of effect. Headline-only LLM evaluation therefore carries a measurable robustness gap, and framing sensitivity belongs among the reliability properties that deployment and governance check.
papers.summary: When language models evaluate, route, or moderate news, the question is whether their judgment tracks the reported fact or the way a headline frames it. An audit of 63,926 Chinese news headlines is combined with a controlled experiment over 30 real events, 30 synthetic events, and 29 natural headline pairs on four Chinese models: `DeepSeek`, `MiMo`, `Dots`, and `LongCat`. Changing only the frame shifted perceived misleadingness and severity in the same direction for all four, with emotionally intensified headlines raising severity ratings by 0.65 to 0.88 points and positive reframing lowering them by 0.34 to 0.52. **Supplying the article body reduced the severity bias by 54 to 80 percent**, and a small human reference study showed the same direction of effect.

papers.title: Beyond the Log-Linear Frontier: Pre-Asymptotic Analysis of Finite-Budget Neural Scaling Laws
papers.abstract: Classical neural scaling laws model excess risk as a separable power law in model capacity $N$ and dataset size $D$. At finite budgets, however, empirical learning curves and compute-optimal allocations depart from this log-linear frontier. This paper analyzes how spectral and domain heterogeneity govern these finite-scale departures. Along the capacity axis, Mellin--Barnes analysis of covariance resolvents yields a three-term expansion where competing spectral and regularization modes produce finite-scale curvature and logarithmic transitions. Because fitting multiple power laws on narrow pilot grids is ill-conditioned, we eliminate the loss floor via first-order Aitken differencing to obtain a well-conditioned closed-form initializer. Along the data axis, KKT duality reduces $K$-domain mixing to scalar water-filling, yielding finite-budget bottleneck bounds, an online sampling curriculum, and a simplex Hessian metric for cross-domain transfer. Along the iso-compute frontier $C=6ND$, we prove that the optimal allocation exponent drifts in proportion to capacity and data exponent variances, while Schur-complement reduction separates intrinsic drift from frozen-hyperparameter bias. Across 45 operator spectra, Pythia (70M--12B), Chinchilla (245 runs), and RegMix (17 domains), our estimators achieve $5.89\%$ holdout MAPE, cut high-compute allocation regret by up to $76.4\%$, and reduce cross-scale mixture RMSE by $59.4\%$ with zero selection regret.
papers.summary: Classical neural scaling laws treat excess risk as a separable power law in model capacity and dataset size, but real learning curves and compute-optimal allocations deviate from this at finite budgets. The analysis attributes these deviations to spectral and domain heterogeneity, deriving a three-term expansion along the capacity axis, a water-filling solution for mixing data across domains, and a proof that the optimal allocation exponent drifts along the iso-compute frontier in proportion to the variances of the capacity and data exponents. It also supplies a well-conditioned closed-form initializer for fitting on narrow pilot grids. Across 45 operator spectra, `Pythia`, `Chinchilla`, and `RegMix` data, the estimators reach 5.89% holdout mean absolute percentage error and **cut high-compute allocation regret by up to 76.4%**.

papers.title: Adaptive catalyst discovery emerges from composable scientific intelligence
papers.abstract: Catalysis underpins chemical manufacturing, yet knowledge for catalyst design remains dispersed across experimental observations, computational data and catalysis subdisciplines. To overcome this challenge, we present Composable Catalytic Intelligence (CatAI), a physics-grounded modular AI framework that learns 1.8 million structure-property relations and organizes them into 30 physicochemical encoders. This reusable intermediate layer enables task-specific models to guide catalyst discovery for targeted reactions and objectives. Across benchmark tasks, CatAI achieves a 7.8% lower task-averaged prediction error than the next-best models. In experimental validation, CatAI identified a new confined-passable pocket catalyst applicable in industrial homogeneous polymer synthesis with 9 times the activity of the commercial benchmark. In parallel, it guided autonomous closed-loop optimization of a highly active Cu-based geminal-atom photocatalyst for C-O coupling reactions surpassing the traditional Ni-based systems. This approach connects property-level data to catalytic objectives, supporting physicochemical knowledge reuse across mechanistically distinct systems through computational screening and iterative model-experiment feedback.
papers.summary: Knowledge for catalyst design is scattered across experiments, computational data, and catalysis subfields. Composable Catalytic Intelligence (`CatAI`) is a physics-grounded modular framework that learns 1.8 million structure-property relations and organizes them into 30 physicochemical encoders, a reusable intermediate layer on which task-specific models are built. It reports a 7.8% lower task-averaged prediction error than the next-best models on benchmark tasks. In experimental validation it identified a new confined-pocket catalyst for industrial homogeneous polymer synthesis with **9 times the activity of the commercial benchmark**, and guided closed-loop optimization of a copper-based photocatalyst for C-O coupling that surpasses traditional nickel-based systems.

papers.title: Exploiting Feature-invariant Scaling Laws for Efficient A/B Experimentation in Recommendation Systems
papers.abstract: Researchers and engineers improve recommendation systems by performing A/B experiments with new model architectures, optimization methods, and data features. However, running full-scale experiments (e.g., full-model training with online data) for every feature change is prohibitively computationally intensive, while the result from a single small-scale experiment is often misleading. To address this challenge, we show that modern recommendation models exhibit feature-invariant scaling: the change of a model's performance follows a predictable scaling-law even when different feature changes are applied to the baseline model. We introduce an efficient method that exploits scaling-laws and uses statistical inference to predict (with confidence intervals) the full-scale effect of an A/B experiment in recommendation systems. This enables practitioners to efficiently filter out neutral or regressive feature changes with only small-scale experimentation. We validate our method on three distinct recommendation model families---Wukong, HSTU, and LLM-based recommendation models---across more than 40 architectural, optimization, and data changes. Our method accurately distinguishes beneficial feature changes from neutral and regressive ones while using only a fraction of the compute required for full-scale evaluation. It also identifies several changes that improve HSTU's state-of-the-art performance on MovieLens-20M. Our results demonstrate that scaling laws can be practically exploited to make compute-efficient decisions for improving industrial-scale recommendation systems.
papers.summary: Running full-scale A/B experiments for every proposed change to a recommendation model is computationally prohibitive, while a single small-scale experiment is often misleading. The authors show that modern recommendation models exhibit feature-invariant scaling, meaning performance follows a predictable scaling law even when different changes are applied to the baseline, and use it with statistical inference to predict the full-scale effect with confidence intervals. Validated on `Wukong`, `HSTU`, and LLM-based recommenders across more than 40 architectural, optimization, and data changes, the method **separates beneficial changes from neutral and regressive ones using only a fraction of full-scale compute**. It also surfaces several changes that improve `HSTU`'s state-of-the-art result on `MovieLens-20M`.

papers.title: Agent Benchmarks Stop Ranking Before They Run Out of Tasks
papers.abstract: Data-science and ML-engineering agents are evaluated on benchmarks such as MLE-bench, ALE-Bench, SWE-fficiency and AlgoTune, whose tasks yield a quantity (a Kaggle metric, contest score or speedup). When one stops separating the best models, the usual remedy is a harder version. Re-scoring released runs of eight benchmarks, including SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench for breadth, we find much of this saturation lies in the measurement, not the tasks. Most agent benchmarks reduce a run to one pass/fail bit, which fails in two ways. It is too coarse: neighbouring top-ten agents on SWE-bench Verified differ by less than its tests' errors, and correcting them reorders neighbours no more than deleting a random sixth of each agent's passes. It is capped at the reference: ALE-Bench's top ten, separated by contest score, tie when graded against the median human, although nearly half the runs beat that human. On fixed tasks, a higher bar only moves the problem; graded credit fixes it. We derive a clipped log-ratio score with dated anchors and cost as a separate axis. In a Terminal-Bench re-run, pass/fail-tied models differ over tenfold on the quantity the tests discard.
papers.summary: When agent benchmarks stop separating top models, the usual response is a harder version; re-scoring released runs from eight benchmarks, including `MLE-bench`, `ALE-Bench`, `SWE-bench Verified`, and `Terminal-Bench`, suggests much of the saturation comes from pass/fail measurement rather than the tasks. Pass/fail scoring is too coarse, since neighbouring top-ten agents on `SWE-bench Verified` differ by less than the error in its tests, and it is capped at the reference, since `ALE-Bench`'s top ten tie when graded against the median human even though nearly half the runs beat that human. The authors derive a graded clipped log-ratio score with dated anchors and cost reported as a separate axis. In a `Terminal-Bench` re-run, **models tied on pass/fail differ by more than tenfold on the quantity the tests discard**.

papers.title: Sanity Checks for Attention Surgery: Null Models and Matched Interventions for Representation-Motivated Design
papers.abstract: Transformer architectural modifications frequently measure a statistic on internal representations, observe that it is large, remove it architecturally, and report an improvement. Interpreting that sequence requires evaluating whether the statistic exceeds its noise floor, whether it survives a geometric null, and whether the training gain requires the specific direction removed. We formulate these requirements as three reusable checks and apply them to self-attention removal, which deletes the component of an attention head's output aligned with its own value vector. Across nine multi-head pretrained models (5,408 heads, 124M to 6.9B parameters), an earlier-position causal null accounts for 48% to 63% of the head-value cosine alignment, with no monotone scale trend. Under grouped-query attention, this alignment is specific to each head's own key-value group and reverses across groups (+0.24 to +0.27 within-group, -0.11 to -0.19 across-group). Split-half reliability demonstrates that the per-head intervention effect is resolvable in GPT-2 ($r_\Delta = 0.80$) but attenuated in Pythia-160M (0.42) and Pythia-410M (0.53), whereas structural self-cosine reliability is near-perfect in all three ($r_{\text{stat}} > 0.99$); which statistic predicts its own intervention is model-dependent. In a pre-registered 3-arm by 8-seed paired factorial at $4.0 \times 10^8$ tokens per run (399,900,672 tokens), a fixed arbitrary rank-one direction does not differ from baseline (+0.0011 nats, $p = 0.197$), while self-directed removal lowers validation loss (-0.0029 nats, Holm-corrected $p = 0.0023$) and outperforms the fixed arbitrary control directly (-0.0040 nats, $p = 0.0018$). At 50.9M scale the training benefit requires the own-value direction rather than a fixed arbitrary one, but a large cosine alignment alone does not establish redundancy in frozen models.
papers.summary: Architectural changes to transformers are often justified by measuring a large statistic on internal representations, removing it, and reporting a gain, without checking whether the statistic is meaningful. Three reusable checks (noise floor, geometric null, and a matched control intervention) are applied to self-attention removal, which deletes the part of an attention head's output aligned with its own value vector. Across nine pretrained models and 5,408 heads, **an earlier-position causal null accounts for 48% to 63% of the head-value cosine alignment**. In a pre-registered training experiment at 50.9M parameters, removing the own-value direction lowers validation loss by 0.0029 nats while a fixed arbitrary direction does not differ from baseline, so the benefit depends on the specific direction, yet high alignment alone does not establish redundancy in frozen models.

papers.title: Closing the BF16-FP16 Convergence Speed Gap in RL Post-Training with Stochastic Rounding
papers.abstract: BF16 is widely used to pretrain large language models because it has the same dynamic range as FP32 and converges similarly to FP32 training. However, in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where learning rates are typically low, we find that standard mixed-precision BF16 training converges more slowly than FP16 training at the same learning rate. We attribute this gap to weight sticking: when FP32 shadow weights are quantized to BF16 using round-to-nearest, small updates often leave the BF16 weights used for rollout generation and training unchanged. Consequently, several optimizer steps may be needed before updates to the shadow weights are reflected in the BF16 weights. Raising the BF16 learning rate reduces weight sticking and matches FP16's convergence speed, but it also increases the KL divergence from the reference model. We instead apply stochastic rounding when quantizing the FP32 shadow weights to BF16. This approach matches FP16's convergence speed across different models and datasets while reducing the KL divergence relative to BF16 training with a larger learning rate. Unlike FP16, it keeps BF16's wider dynamic range and needs no loss scaling.
papers.summary: In reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where learning rates are low, standard mixed-precision `BF16` training of language models converges more slowly than `FP16` at the same learning rate. The authors trace this to weight sticking: when FP32 shadow weights are rounded to nearest in BF16, small updates often leave the working weights unchanged for several optimizer steps. Raising the learning rate closes the gap but increases KL divergence from the reference model. **Applying stochastic rounding when quantizing the shadow weights matches `FP16`'s convergence speed across models and datasets** with lower KL divergence than the higher-learning-rate fix, while keeping BF16's wider dynamic range and avoiding loss scaling.

papers.title: Massive Activations Confound Sparse Autoencoders
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are commonly evaluated by variance explained and ablation damage. We show how massive activations undermine both evaluations, and propose a correction. Massive activations cause up to 99.9% of activation variance to lie along the first principal component (PC1). Because the PC1 component has no unique sparse decomposition, each SAE run rebuilds it from a different set of features. These features dominate importance rankings: an average of 47 of the 50 most important features are unmatched in a separate run, compared with about 27 of a random 50. A dictionary can also report 99.96% of variance explained while leaving 33% of the variance outside PC1 unexplained. We bypass PC1 by training the SAE on activations with PC1 removed, then adding PC1 to the reconstruction. In affected models, the top-50 feature sharing rate rises from 4-39.5% to 73-99.5%. At the same TopK sparsity, the resulting SAE degrades the model up to 44% less and reduces content reconstruction error by up to 33.9%.
papers.summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are usually judged by variance explained and ablation damage, and both measures are distorted when massive activations push up to 99.9% of activation variance onto the first principal component (PC1). Because PC1 has no unique sparse decomposition, each SAE run rebuilds it from different features, so an average of 47 of the 50 most important features have no match in a separate run, and a dictionary can report 99.96% variance explained while leaving 33% of the non-PC1 variance unexplained. The proposed fix trains the SAE on activations with PC1 removed and adds PC1 back to the reconstruction. In affected models this raises **top-50 feature sharing from 4-39.5% to 73-99.5%**, with up to 44% less model degradation at the same `TopK` sparsity.
papers.highlight_summary:
Standard sparse autoencoder evaluations are distorted by massive activations, which push up to **99.9%** of residual-stream variance onto the first principal component (PC1), so both variance explained and ablation-based feature importance mostly measure how PC1 gets reconstructed. The proposed fix is to train the SAE on activations with PC1 projected out and add the PC1 component back to the reconstruction at inference.

- Because a rank-one signal has no unique sparse decomposition under `TopK`, each seed "tiles" PC1 with a different set of partially aligned features (about 1% of the dictionary) that dominate importance rankings, so in `GPT-2` an average of **47 of the 50** most important features have no match in another run, versus about 27 of a random 50.
- Variance explained is inflated by the same effect, since content error is understated by roughly 1/(1 − w₁), where w₁ is PC1's variance share: the `Qwen-2.5-7B` SAEs report **99.96%** variance explained while leaving **33%** of the variance outside PC1 unexplained, an understatement of about 890×.
- The inversion appears under `TopK`, `BatchTopK` and scheduled-threshold `JumpReLU` but not `ReLU+ℓ1`, and adding an ℓ1 magnitude penalty to `TopK` on `GPT-2` raises top-50 sharing from 6.4% to **94.9%** with under 1% change in sparsity or content error.
- PC1 bypass lifts top-50 cross-seed sharing in affected models from 4–39.5% to **73–99.5%**, degrades the host model up to **44%** less, and cuts content reconstruction error by 33.9% on `Qwen-2.5-7B` (0.8–4.9% on the other models), while a post-hoc variant that simply drops PC1-aligned features from the ranking reaches 77.5–96% sharing without retraining.
- The repair changes which features get ranked rather than fixing seed instability overall: dictionary-wide sharing stays at 44–68%, 12–33% of content variance remains unexplained by standard SAEs, the `Gemma-2` models and low-PC1 layers show no inversion to fix, and downstream gains are mixed, with sparse-probing differences under one point and auto-interpretability scores falling on `Llama-3.1-8B` and `Gemma-2-2B`.

papers.title: Tabular Foundation Models in Financial Predictions
papers.abstract: This technical note introduces tabular foundation models (TFMs) to accounting research and evaluates their performance in one common benchmark task: predicting firms' next-year earnings changes. TFMs produce numeric predictions and learn in context, without post-release training or tuning, making them natural and easy to use for forecasting. The TFMs we study are pretrained on synthetic tabular data, so they avoid look-ahead bias from memorizing firms' outcomes. We compare Google Research's TabFM with a fine-tuned open-weight large language model developed in recent accounting research and with several tree-based models. TabFM is more accurate than all comparison models. It is also faster and less computationally intensive than the large language model. Several tree-based specifications produce predictions more quickly than TabFM, so choosing between them involves a trade-off between accuracy and speed. We conclude that TFMs have promise as a new tool for forecasting in accounting and finance. However, our evaluation is based on a single benchmark task, and no class of models is likely to dominate in all settings.
papers.summary: Tabular foundation models (TFMs), which are pretrained on synthetic tabular data and make numeric predictions in context without further training, are introduced to accounting research and tested on predicting firms' next-year earnings changes. Google Research's `TabFM` is compared with a fine-tuned open-weight large language model from recent accounting work and with several tree-based models. **`TabFM` is more accurate than every comparison model** and cheaper to run than the language model, though some tree-based specifications predict faster. The authors note that the evaluation covers a single benchmark task.

papers.title: How Post-Training Influences Verbalized Algorithmic Computation in Language Models
papers.abstract: Post-training improves language-model reasoning, but how it changes the use of internal information and verbalized chain of thought (CoT) remains unclear. We study successive SFT, DPO, and RLVR checkpoints of Olmo-3-7B-Instruct on multi-digit addition, using carry values as known intermediate state. Probes recover carry information from internal activations with similar accuracy in SFT and RLVR, although manipulating this information does not reliably control model outputs. In contrast, the usefulness of verbalized reasoning differs: CoTs produced by RLVR yield higher accuracy across receiving checkpoints than those produced by SFT or DPO. We also show that carry-related statements receive higher importance scores after RLVR than matched random controls. DPO shows similar sensitivity to carry-related statements but without comparable accuracy gains. These results suggest that post-training changes the usefulness of written reasoning and sensitivity to its content in meaningful ways, although greater sensitivity does not necessarily coincide with better problem performance.
papers.summary: The study asks how successive post-training stages change a language model's use of internal information and of its written chain of thought (CoT), using the SFT, DPO, and RLVR checkpoints of `Olmo-3-7B-Instruct` on multi-digit addition, where carry values serve as known intermediate state. Probes recover carry information from activations about equally well in the SFT and RLVR checkpoints, but manipulating that information does not reliably control outputs. In contrast, **CoTs written by the RLVR checkpoint yield higher accuracy across receiving checkpoints** than those from SFT or DPO. DPO shows similar sensitivity to carry-related statements without the matching accuracy gain, so greater sensitivity to reasoning content does not necessarily track better performance.

papers.title: Darmok: Championship Cryptic Crossword Solving via Constraint Tightening and Resilient Orchestration
papers.abstract:
We present Darmok, the first automated system to reach superhuman performance on British cryptic crosswords. Unlike American-style crosswords, cryptic clues disguise an unmarked definition and compositional wordplay beneath a misleading surface reading, sparse grids leave nearly half of each word's letters unchecked, and tournament rules rank a grid with even a single wrong or blank square behind all error-free solutions regardless of speed. Competing alongside an elite human field at the 55th Times Crossword Championship in London, Darmok solved all seven championship puzzles error-free and finished faster than every human competitor in every round. It solved the Final puzzle in 6m 52s, a full 3m 13s ahead of the human champion.
  Today's frontier AI models can on average solve a whole puzzle in a single try with comparable accuracy and speed. However, cloud API calls still stall, time out, trigger safety refusals, or get stuck in reasoning loops. To simultaneously achieve tournament-grade accuracy, speed, and reliability, Darmok cross-checks clues across three independent models in rounds; uses verified crossing letters to unlock harder clues; and uses a whole-puzzle model and dictionary lookups to fill any remaining gaps without overwriting confirmed words. This design maintained near-zero-error performance across a five-month daily evaluation period. Under normal benchmark conditions, removing backup models, fallback steps, or elaborate prompt instructions barely changes accuracy, making the architecture appear over-engineered. Yet during both the worst days of daily operation and a severe slowdown of our primary model in the live Championship Final, the backup paths carried the solve, showing that as foundation models master the average case, the central challenge in building complex AI systems shifts to resilience in the worst case.
authors: Siddhartha Chatterjee (The University of Texas at Austin)
papers.summary: `Darmok` is an automated solver for British cryptic crosswords, where clues hide a definition and wordplay behind a misleading surface, nearly half of each word's letters are unchecked, and a single wrong square ranks a grid below every error-free one. It cross-checks clues across three independent models in rounds, uses verified crossing letters to unlock harder clues, and fills remaining gaps with a whole-puzzle model and dictionary lookups without overwriting confirmed words. At the 55th Times Crossword Championship it **solved all seven puzzles error-free and faster than every human competitor in every round**, finishing the Final in 6m 52s, 3m 13s ahead of the human champion. Ablations show the backup models and fallback steps barely change accuracy under normal conditions, yet they carried the solve on the worst operating days and during a severe slowdown of the primary model in the live Final.

papers.title: Are Dense Rewards Worth Their Tokens in GRPO?
papers.abstract: RLVR trains language models to reason by rewarding correct final answers. A widely used algorithm, group-relative policy optimization (GRPO), gives every token of a solution the same credit, so dense process rewards have been proposed to credit intermediate steps, for example with a Monte-Carlo reward that scores each step by sampling continuations from it. Comparing such a reward with GRPO per training update, or vetting it with a gradient test on a single batch, leaves out what it costs: in our setting, the continuations alone take 91% of all generated tokens. We introduce a matched-compute protocol that gives every training intervention the same budget, measured in generated tokens and training GPU-hours, and tests it in preregistered studies with controls for side effects. Across 1,668 runs on six models, matching compute reverses the ranking. On Qwen2.5-1.5B, the Monte-Carlo reward leads standard GRPO per update, yet ends 14.3 percentage points lower at equal tokens and 7.8 points lower at equal training time, and none of four dense-reward variants outperforms GRPO even with as much training time. A per-token gradient test orders these rewards as training does but overestimates each by one to two points, as much as the gains it is meant to detect. In contrast, training on the prompts whose predicted success is nearest 1/2 improves accuracy at matched compute, by 1.7 points on Qwen3-0.6B and 0.8 on Qwen2.5-1.5B. These gains replicate on fresh seeds and unseen problems, and a simple rule, that the candidate prompts are predicted to fail more often than not, predicted where they appear in five of six preregistered tests. Both gains come early in training, and standard GRPO with twice the initial learning rate comes within half a point of them. We argue that training interventions should be validated at matched compute, which overturns some apparent gains and confirms others.
papers.summary: Dense process rewards have been proposed to improve on group-relative policy optimization (`GRPO`), which gives every token of a solution the same credit, but comparisons per training update ignore their cost: in this setting the Monte-Carlo continuations alone consume 91% of generated tokens. A matched-compute protocol gives every intervention the same budget in generated tokens and training GPU-hours, tested in preregistered studies across 1,668 runs on six models. On `Qwen2.5-1.5B` the Monte-Carlo reward leads `GRPO` per update but **ends 14.3 percentage points lower at equal tokens** and 7.8 points lower at equal training time, and none of four dense-reward variants beats `GRPO`. Training on prompts whose predicted success is nearest 1/2 does improve accuracy at matched compute, by 1.7 points on `Qwen3-0.6B` and 0.8 on `Qwen2.5-1.5B`, although `GRPO` with twice the initial learning rate comes within half a point of those gains.
papers.highlight_summary:
Dense "process" rewards for `GRPO` are usually judged per training update or with a single-batch gradient test, which ignores their cost: Monte-Carlo continuations alone consume **91%** of all generated tokens. A preregistered matched-compute protocol gives every intervention the same budget in generated tokens and training GPU-hours, across **1,668 runs** on six small Qwen and Llama models, and finds that matching compute reverses the ranking.

- The token budget counts every generated token, including continuations and discarded samples, and controls for side effects (random choice among the same candidate prompts, a retuned learning rate, a strict verifier) accompany pass@1 accuracy on held-out `MATH` problems.
- On `Qwen2.5-1.5B`, the Monte-Carlo reward leads outcome-only `GRPO` by about 1.5 points at equal updates but ends **14.3 points behind at equal tokens** (50 updates versus 584) and **7.8 points behind at equal training time**, and none of four dense-reward variants beats `GRPO` even when given as much training time.
- A per-token gradient efficiency test orders the rewards the same way training does, but overestimates the accuracy each reaches by 0.8 to 1.8 points, which is as large as the gains it is meant to detect.
- Training on the prompts whose predicted success is nearest 1/2 does survive matched compute, gaining **1.7 points** on `Qwen3-0.6B` and **0.8 points** on `Qwen2.5-1.5B` at equal tokens, with both gains replicating on fresh seeds and on 1,543 unseen `MATH` problems.
- That gain appears on only two of six models, is an early head start that fades by twice the budget, and is nearly matched by `GRPO` with twice the initial learning rate (within half a point), while all experiments use models of 4B parameters or smaller on numeric-answer math.

papers.title: Discovering Structurally Plausible and Interpretable Cognitive Models with Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Computational cognitive modeling has traditionally relied on manual model construction, which is a time-intensive process that requires substantial domain expertise. Although recent LLM-based approaches have begun to automate model generation, they often prioritize predictive accuracy at the expense of structural plausibility and parameter identifiability. We introduce DisCo, an LLM-guided framework that discovers interpretable symbolic cognitive models through evolutionary search with two structural components: a Validator that filters structurally invalid models, and a Cleaner that promotes parameter identifiability by removing redundant parameters. Across three behavioral tasks, DisCo consistently discovers models that achieve performance competitive with task-specific baselines. Ablation analyses show that the Validator is important for recovering psychologically meaningful structure. Without this component, models tend to violate behavioral constraints and show less consistent associations with external cognitive measures. These results suggest that LLM-driven model discovery, when coupled with appropriate structural constraints, can yield cognitively plausible models that go beyond predictive fit.
papers.summary: Automated generation of computational cognitive models with large language models tends to favor predictive accuracy over structural plausibility and parameter identifiability. `DisCo` runs an LLM-guided evolutionary search for interpretable symbolic cognitive models, adding a Validator that filters structurally invalid models and a Cleaner that removes redundant parameters. Across three behavioral tasks it finds models competitive with task-specific baselines. Ablations show that **without the Validator, models tend to violate behavioral constraints** and associate less consistently with external cognitive measures.

papers.title: An evidence-traceable benchmark of clinical reasoning in large language models
papers.abstract: Benchmark scores for medical large language models (LLMs) are difficult to interpret when scoring criteria cannot be traced to clinical evidence. Here we developed Med Evidence Bench (MEB; https://www.medevidencebench.org.cn/), comprising 1,536 physician-constructed items across three levels: guideline knowledge, standardized clinical scenarios and real-world laboratory scenarios. Each criterion stating a medical claim is linked to a versioned source-text span. Across ten LLMs, the Evidence Trace Score (ETS) was 0.975-0.997 for guideline knowledge, 0.292-0.658 for standardized scenarios and 0.182-0.447 for real-world scenarios, and rankings varied across levels. For real-world scenarios, scores for identifying clinical information (mean, 0.770) exceeded those for matching evidence (0.165) or formulating recommendations (0.160). On 1,296 criterion-level judgments, automated grading agreed with the majority vote of three physicians (macro-F1, 0.930; 95% confidence interval, 0.915-0.945), although agreement was lower for evidence application. These findings from Chinese-language materials indicate that guideline recall does not ensure patient-specific evidence use and do not establish clinical effectiveness.
