papers.summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) improves a language model by using a copy of itself that is conditioned on reference answers as the teacher for the student's own generated trajectories, but the authors find it degrades under continued training as the evolving student drifts away from the frozen privileged teacher. Bootstrapped On-Policy Distillation (`BOPD`) splits the process in two: OPSD first internalizes the reference-conditioned signal into an intermediate model, and that reference-free intermediate model is then distilled into a fresh copy of the initial model. Across models, **`BOPD` improves mathematical reasoning and code generation beyond both the initial models and the OPSD teachers**.

papers.title: Ego Guidance: Enhancing Robot Policy Learning with Action-Free Human Egocentric Videos
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate how human egocentric videos can benefit robot policy learning without action supervision. Building on a pretrained VLM, we propose Shared Prediction on Action and Representation (SPAR), an MoT architecture in which future visual state prediction can provide independent and complementary learning signals alongside action prediction. We find that representations learned from egocentric videos improve downstream performance on out-of-distribution robot tasks, with further gains as video data scales. We also study the effects of objective choices and data curation, providing insights into how to leverage action-free videos for scalable robot learning.
papers.summary: Human egocentric videos without action labels are studied as a training signal for robot policies. Building on a pretrained vision-language model, Shared Prediction on Action and Representation (`SPAR`) is an architecture in which predicting future visual states provides a learning signal that is independent of and complementary to action prediction. The authors find that **representations learned from egocentric video improve performance on out-of-distribution robot tasks, with further gains as video data scales**, and they also analyze the effects of objective choices and data curation.

papers.title: You Are What You Read: Indian Political News Media Bias Dataset for Hindi Language
papers.abstract: Media bias understanding and detection remains an under-researched problem for Indian context, specifically for Indic languages, such as, Hindi, which is widely spoken in India. In this paper, we introduce a comprehensive, multi-annotator, explainable dataset consisting of 448 unique articles from four leading Indian news agencies publishing in Hindi. We focus on Hindi, the most spoken and an official language of India. The study of media bias is particularly relevant in the Indian context due to the country's linguistic diversity and large population, where the same event is often reported by multiple news agencies in different languages, thereby introducing scope for bias. The dataset comprises Hindi political news articles annotated by 14 experts and classified into four bias categories - selection bias, framing bias, clickbait bias and omission bias - when an article is identified as biased or unbiased. For each biased article, annotators also provide a textual explanation, enabling future semi-automated approaches to incorporate explainability when language models reason over the dataset. Cohen's Kappa scores were 0.81 for simple bias/no-bias classification reflecting strong inter-annotator agreement. For the multi-label task, the Cohen's Kappa values are 0.89, 0.75, 0.81, and 0.79 for clickbait, selection, framing, and omission biases, respectively, resulting in an average Kappa of 0.80, which also reflects strong agreement.
papers.summary: Media bias detection is little studied for Indic languages, and this work contributes a Hindi dataset of **448 political news articles from four leading Indian news agencies, annotated by 14 experts**. Each article is labeled biased or unbiased, and biased ones are further tagged with selection, framing, clickbait, and omission bias plus a written explanation from the annotator. Inter-annotator agreement measured by Cohen's Kappa is 0.81 for the binary task and averages 0.80 across the four bias types.

papers.title: AURA: Auditory Spatial Intelligence via a Unified Representation from a General-Audio Encoder through Complete Alignment
papers.abstract: Answering spatial questions about multi-source scenes requires a model both to identify each sound and to locate it. Existing spatial audio-language models obtain spatial information from a dedicated encoder, which separates spatial and semantic processing into distinct feature spaces. We study whether a general-audio codec trained without spatial supervision can serve both purposes. A controlled layer-wise analysis shows that the frozen codec retains spatial information, with lateral cues carried by the difference between the two ear channels. This information, however, is not readily accessible: in dual-source scenes, a model trained on these features predicts left/right at chance and, on the remaining axes, assigns the detected direction to the queried and the non-queried source equally often. We attribute this failure to an audio--text information asymmetry, in which the audio contains both sources while the answer describes only the queried one. A controlled $2\times2$ experiment shows that either completing the scene description or exposing the inter-channel difference lifts left/right accuracy above chance, whereas binding directions to the queried source requires both. Building on these findings, AURA keeps the codec and the language model frozen and exceeds the strongest dedicated system on SpatialSoundQA by 10.31 points in dual-source direction accuracy, with about 40\% of its trainable parameters.
papers.summary: Spatial audio-language models usually rely on a dedicated spatial encoder, and this study asks whether a frozen general-audio codec trained without spatial supervision can supply both semantic and spatial information. Layer-wise analysis shows the codec retains spatial cues, but a model trained on them predicts left/right at chance in two-source scenes, which the authors attribute to an asymmetry where the audio contains both sources while the text answer describes only one. A 2×2 experiment shows that binding directions to the queried source requires both completing the scene description and exposing the inter-channel difference. The resulting `AURA` system keeps the codec and language model frozen and beats the strongest dedicated system on `SpatialSoundQA` by **10.31 points in dual-source direction accuracy** with about 40% of its trainable parameters.

papers.title: Walrus Technical Report
papers.abstract: We present Walrus, a unified 8B speech-and-audio foundation model handling speech recognition (including code-switching and multi-talker speech), speech-to-text and speech-to-speech translation, text-to-speech, emotion recognition, audio captioning, and general audio understanding. Our main contribution is not a new architecture but a data-centric training recipe; we use a standard decoder-only backbone initialized from Gemma 4, so that gains can be traced to the data. For speech generation, Walrus predicts low-bitrate discrete speech tokens, and a lightweight token-to-waveform decoder converts them into high-fidelity audio. The recipe is a three-stage data curriculum that moves from broad multilingual data to multi-talker, code-switching, and domain-specific data. At each stage, task-aware and dataset-aware weighting balances tasks with very different token budgets and protects core skills from forgetting. Trained on over 600M samples covering more than 20 tasks and 100 languages, Walrus leads on most multilingual, multi-talker, and code-switching ASR, speech translation, and audio understanding benchmarks, outperforming both open speech language models of comparable size and dedicated task-specific models. On most benchmarks, it even matches or surpasses the $4\times$ larger Qwen3-Omni's performance. Results suggest that data engineering is a primary driver of quality in multi-task speech and audio modeling.
papers.summary: `Walrus` is a unified 8B-parameter speech-and-audio model covering speech recognition (including code-switching and multi-talker speech), speech translation, text-to-speech, emotion recognition, audio captioning, and general audio understanding. Rather than a new architecture, it uses a standard decoder-only backbone initialized from `Gemma 4` and a three-stage data curriculum with task-aware and dataset-aware weighting, trained on over 600M samples spanning more than 20 tasks and 100 languages. The authors report that it leads most multilingual, multi-talker, and code-switching recognition, translation, and audio understanding benchmarks among comparable open models, and **matches or surpasses the 4× larger `Qwen3-Omni` on most benchmarks**. They read the results as evidence that data engineering is a primary driver of quality in multi-task speech and audio modeling.

papers.title: Decision-Focused Learning via Neural Optimization Layers for Battery-Assisted Grid-Import Smoothing in AI Data Centers
papers.abstract: Rapid AI data-center power fluctuations challenge grid integration. Sustained grid-import smoothing requires allocating limited battery power and energy under uncertain demand. We formulate risk-aware BESS scheduling that coordinates advance reserve commitments and demand-responsive dispatch, accounting for operating costs, grid-ramp penalties, and their conditional value-at-risk. We develop battery scheduling decision-focused learning (BS-DFL) with a constraint-aware neural optimization layer trained directly from this objective without optimal-solution labels. The trained layer is then frozen to guide demand-predictor learning through scheduling costs and ramping risk, enabling solver-free rolling-horizon scheduling. In a 10,000-minute simulation using loads derived from measured AI workloads, BS-DFL reduces mean absolute minute-to-minute grid-import changes by 71.70% and total scheduling cost by 18.01% relative to an MSE-trained predictor coupled with a mixed-integer linear programming solver, with an average decision time of 18.77 ms.
papers.summary: Rapid power swings from AI data centers complicate grid integration, and smoothing them requires scheduling limited battery power and energy under uncertain demand. The authors formulate a risk-aware battery scheduling problem covering reserve commitments, dispatch, operating costs, and grid-ramp penalties, and propose `BS-DFL`, a decision-focused learning method in which a constraint-aware neural optimization layer is trained directly on the objective without optimal-solution labels and then frozen to guide the demand predictor. In a 10,000-minute simulation with loads derived from measured AI workloads, it **cuts mean minute-to-minute grid-import changes by 71.70% and total scheduling cost by 18.01%** relative to an MSE-trained predictor paired with a mixed-integer linear programming solver, with an average decision time of 18.77 ms.

papers.title: On Private Knowledge Retrieval and Private Inference for secure multi-agent systems
papers.abstract:
Multi-agent systems provide a convenient framework for the massive deployment of agents based on Large Language Models (LLMs). It provides a sound framework where agents can interact with existing software to perform actions in an autonomous way. Agentic AI is the new term to denote these AI-based autonomous systems.
  In real multi-agent systems, agents need to deal with malicious agents some of which can exploit security vulnerabilities to do harm. A memory poisoning attack is an example of exploiting a vulnerability to modify agents knowledge and, thus, affect its behavior. In an agent, there are different types of memory systems (semantic, episodic, and short-term) which have their own characteristics and for which different memory poisoning attacks may be developed.
  In this paper we focus on semantic memory, we discuss its attack, and mitigation strategies. We introduce private knowledge retrieval and private inference. We propose a signature system in the knowledge base to prevent from undesired manipulation. This should avoid memory poisoning attacks by introducing security by design in the construction of the semantic memory. In our architecture, an agent contains a local Prolog-like inference system (i.e., using Horn clauses to represent knowledge) which accesses an external knowledge base to get the required knowledge. This externally signed knowledge base is accessed privately. We provide different implementations in Python using different privacy levels including k-anonymity and information-theoretical privacy (IT-PIR).
papers.summary: Agents in multi-agent systems built on large language models (LLMs) can be targeted by memory poisoning attacks, in which a malicious agent alters another agent's stored knowledge to change its behavior. Focusing on semantic memory, the authors propose an architecture in which each agent runs a local Prolog-like inference engine over Horn clauses and **privately queries an external, cryptographically signed knowledge base so that tampered knowledge can be rejected by design**. They provide Python implementations at several privacy levels, including k-anonymity and information-theoretic private information retrieval (`IT-PIR`).

papers.title: Topological Dynamics Under Non-Stationary Supervision: Persistent Homology of Neural Network Weight Evolution
papers.abstract: We investigate how the persistent topology of neuron- weight point clouds evolves under stable and non-stationary supervision. An identical multilayer perceptron is trained on Fashion-MNIST with correct labels, a fixed random permutation of the training-label vector, or a fresh permutation every epoch. Five paired seeds share initialisation and minibatch order, yielding 15 models trained for 100 epochs. Raw and row-normalised incoming weight clouds are analysed with H0 and H1 Vietoris Rips persistence at 22 checkpoints. Correct-label models reach 89.39% mean true-label test accuracy; fixed-random models fit 67.94% of their assigned training targets without generalising to the original task. Correct-label models have descriptively greater time-averaged normalised fc3 H1 persistence than either random-label condition, but the configured exact comparisons do not reach conventional significance after Holm correction. Early condition classification achieves 60.0% mean balanced accuracy using topology, 66.7% using conventional diagnostics, and 60.0% using both. Thus, no incremental predictive improvement is demonstrated in this setting. The archive contains all 3,300 configured topology cases. Interpretation is limited by five seeds, a single architecture and dataset, 282 capped H1 distance comparisons, and deferred bottleneck analysis.
papers.summary: The study tracks how the persistent homology of neuron-weight point clouds evolves when an identical multilayer perceptron is trained on `Fashion-MNIST` with correct labels, a fixed random label permutation, or a fresh permutation every epoch, using five paired seeds and 22 checkpoints per run. Correct-label models show descriptively higher time-averaged H1 persistence in the third layer, but the differences do not reach significance after Holm correction. Classifying the training condition early gets 60.0% balanced accuracy from topology, 66.7% from conventional diagnostics, and 60.0% from both, so **topological features give no incremental predictive improvement in this setting**. The authors note limits from the small seed count, single architecture and dataset, and capped distance computations.

papers.title: SeqFold: Timestamp-Addressable Compressed States for User Action Sequence Backbones
papers.abstract: Existing sequential user modeling methods mainly focus on improving the backbone encoder or learning task-specific user representations for a single prediction objective. We instead study how to export the multi-layer user states of a frozen long-history backbone as compact, timestamp-addressable representations for downstream training backfill and serving. In this setting, the user state at a given timestamp summarizes the user's actions before that time, so downstream systems need only the state aligned to each target timestamp rather than the full hidden-state timeline. To this end, we present \texttt{SeqFold}, a compressed-state interface that combines learned multi-channel fusion, channel-specific temporal decay, and Lookup-Free Quantization (LFQ) to produce compact discrete codes from frozen backbone states. Task-specific decoders then map these shared codes into flexible embedding spaces for downstream models. To make timestamp-addressable export practical at scale, we further develop a fused streaming implementation that updates the fusion recurrence after every action while materializing states only at target timestamps. On large-scale proprietary datasets, SeqFold reduces per-state representation storage by $3{,}400\times$ while preserving most of the downstream ranking performance of the uncompressed model, showing that SeqFold is an effective interface for reusing long-history sequence backbones in downstream models.
papers.summary: Reusing a frozen long-history user-sequence backbone in downstream recommendation models requires exporting its multi-layer user states in a form that can be stored and looked up by timestamp. `SeqFold` does this by combining learned multi-channel fusion, channel-specific temporal decay, and Lookup-Free Quantization (LFQ) to produce compact discrete codes, which task-specific decoders then map into embeddings for downstream models. A fused streaming implementation updates the recurrence after every action but materializes states only at target timestamps. On large proprietary datasets, it **reduces per-state storage by 3,400×** while preserving most of the uncompressed model's downstream ranking performance.

papers.title: Agentic AI Meets Formal Verification in the Era of Agentic Hardware Development
papers.abstract: As AI agents become increasingly capable of generating and optimizing hardware circuits, ensuring the correctness of AI-generated designs becomes more important. Meanwhile, advances in AI lower the barriers to developing and applying formal methods, creating new opportunities to automate and improve hardware verification. This invited paper presents an overview of the methodologies and applications of hardware formal methods in the AI era. First, we examine how agentic AI advances hardware formal methods across three levels: specification, proof construction, and reasoning engines. Second, we discuss how formal methods support reliable AI-driven hardware development through RTL generation, debugging, and correctness-preserving optimization. We review representative research alongside our recent contributions, highlighting key technical advances and insights from experimental results. Finally, we discuss future research opportunities toward proof-native hardware development, where formal reasoning could become an integral part of autonomous hardware design.
papers.summary: An invited overview of how agentic AI and hardware formal verification intersect, motivated by the need to check the correctness of AI-generated circuit designs. It first covers how agents advance formal methods at three levels: specification, proof construction, and reasoning engines. It then covers how **formal methods in turn support reliable AI-driven hardware development through register-transfer-level code generation, debugging, and correctness-preserving optimization**. The authors review representative work alongside their own results and outline a direction they call proof-native hardware development, where formal reasoning is built into autonomous design.

papers.title: FedVP: Federated Learning across Heterogeneous Models by Pooling Locally Trained Verifiers
papers.abstract: Conventional federated learning relies on the shared model backbone to aggregate client updates, limiting collaboration among institutions that deploy large language models (LLMs) from different families and at different scales. We propose Federated Verifier Pool (FEDVP), a new federated learning paradigm that enables heterogeneous clients to collaborate through shared verification rather than parameter aggregation. Each client trains a verifier using local data and responses generated by its chosen LLM backbone. The server pools these independently trained verifiers and combines their judgments to select answers without merging model parameters. This allows both LLM backbones and verifiers to differ in architecture and size, while keeping the LLM backbones frozen and deriving collaborative gains from improved answer selection. We evaluate FEDVP across five public medical question-answering datasets treated as federated clients, using Qwen and LLaMA backbones ranging from 3B to 14B parameters. FEDVP consistently improves performance across all five clients and outperforms the strongest conventional federated baselines by 1.46-5.79 percentage points in mean accuracy.
papers.summary: Conventional federated learning aggregates updates over a shared model backbone, which blocks collaboration between institutions running large language models (LLMs) of different families and sizes. Federated Verifier Pool (`FedVP`) instead has each client train a verifier on its local data and its own LLM's responses, and the server pools these verifiers to select answers without merging any parameters, leaving the LLM backbones frozen. Across five public medical question-answering datasets treated as clients, with `Qwen` and `LLaMA` backbones from 3B to 14B parameters, it improves all five clients and **beats the strongest conventional federated baselines by 1.46 to 5.79 percentage points in mean accuracy**.

papers.title: AutoManifold: Agentic Design of Data Visualisation Algorithms via Manifold Embedding
papers.abstract: Manifold embedding for data visualisation is dominated by a small set of hand-designed state-of-the-art (SOTA) algorithms. Their design targets are fixed at development time, resulting in inflexible algorithmic behaviour that cannot be readily steered towards user-specified structural priorities. Hand-designing new embedding algorithms to address user priority requires highly specialised expertise and is time consuming. To address autonomous algorithm design tailored to user preference, we introduce an agentic algorithm generation pipeline AutoManifold. It composes new manifold embedding algorithms from a constrained vocabulary of affinity, cost, and optimisation primitives, supported by multi-agent large-language-model (LLM) orchestration. AutoManifold conditions every stage of its design on user-specified structural preservation preferences, and iteratively refines the algorithm configuration through an LLM-guided, metric-grounded iterative loop. We compare the generated algorithms against the three strongest and most frequently used SOTA methods (t-SNE, UMAP, and PaCMAP) on real-world datasets spanning different difficulty regimes under identical evaluation infrastructure. The results demonstrate that LLM-driven, priority-conditioned algorithm synthesis can move beyond hyperparameter tuning, producing genuinely new algorithms that outperform traditional hand-designed methods in their ability to steer towards user-specified properties without compromising the intrinsic structure in the original data. The code of AutoManifold is available at https://github.com/buraksusam/AutoManifold_NeurIPS2026.
papers.summary: Manifold embedding algorithms for data visualisation are hand-designed with fixed targets and cannot easily be steered toward the structural properties a particular user cares about. `AutoManifold` is a multi-agent large-language-model (LLM) pipeline that composes new embedding algorithms from a constrained vocabulary of affinity, cost, and optimisation primitives, conditioning each design stage on user-specified preservation preferences and refining the configuration in a metric-grounded loop. Compared against `t-SNE`, `UMAP`, and `PaCMAP` on real-world datasets under identical evaluation, the authors report that the **generated algorithms outperform the hand-designed methods at steering toward user-specified properties** without compromising the data's intrinsic structure.

papers.title: Broad-Persistent Advising in Interactive Reinforcement Learning via Latent State Encoding
papers.abstract: Deep Interactive Reinforcement Learning (Deep IntRL) accelerates reinforcement learning training by incorporating external advice. However, conventional Deep IntRL uses each piece of advice only in the current step and discards it after a single interaction. Persistent Advising and Broad-Persistent Advising (BPA) extend this process by storing advice in persistent memory and reusing it in similar states through state generalisation based on K-means clustering. This research proposes Encoder BPA, which employs a latent encoder to retrieve and reuse advice. In this framework, a trained encoder is used to map a state sequence into a latent representation at every time step. Advice can be retrieved through latent comparison, together with a top-(k) aggregation and a consistency condition to improve reuse stability. Experimental results show that Encoder BPA improves learning efficiency and advice utilisation at an early stage of training compared with different Deep IntRL approaches, especially in complex and partially observable environments.
papers.summary: Deep Interactive Reinforcement Learning (Deep IntRL) speeds up training with external advice, but typically uses each piece of advice for one step and discards it; Broad-Persistent Advising (BPA) stores advice and reuses it in similar states found by K-means clustering. `Encoder BPA` replaces the clustering with a trained encoder that maps state sequences to latent representations, retrieving advice by latent comparison with top-k aggregation and a consistency condition for stability. Experiments show it **improves early-training learning efficiency and advice utilisation over other Deep IntRL approaches**, especially in complex and partially observable environments.

papers.title: Toward Autonomous RTL and Synthesis Optimization: Benchmarking and Self-Improving Agents
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and autonomous agents are creating new opportunities for hardware design optimization. This paper examines three connected directions toward autonomous RTL and synthesis optimization: (1) Realistic benchmarking. We discuss reference-based and open-ended RTL optimization benchmarks that evaluate optimization opportunities under realistic EDA workflows. (2) Tool-grounded RTL optimization. We present Dr. RTL, a multi-agent framework that automates critical-path analysis, RTL rewriting, and implementation-level evaluation, while continuously improving through reusable optimization skills. Evaluated on 20 real-world RTL designs, Dr.~RTL achieves average WNS/TNS improvements of 21\%/17\% with a 6\% area reduction over commercial synthesis. (3) Design-specific synthesis optimization. We explore agent-driven synthesis script tuning and the discovery of executable synthesis algorithms across intermediate representations, technology-independent optimization, and technology mapping. Finally, we envision AI-native design automation that jointly explores architectural, RTL, and EDA algorithm design spaces, guided by verification constraints and implementation feedback.
papers.summary: Three directions toward autonomous optimization of register-transfer-level (RTL) hardware designs and logic synthesis are examined: realistic benchmarks, tool-grounded RTL rewriting, and design-specific synthesis tuning. The centerpiece is `Dr. RTL`, a multi-agent framework that automates critical-path analysis, RTL rewriting, and implementation-level evaluation while accumulating reusable optimization skills. On 20 real-world designs it achieves **average timing-slack improvements of 21% and 17% (worst and total negative slack) with a 6% area reduction over commercial synthesis**. The authors also explore agent-driven synthesis script tuning and discovery of executable synthesis algorithms.

papers.title: TRUER: Test-Time Reward Correction Using an Error-Aware Rectifier for Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Test-time reinforcement learning enables language models to adapt using rewards derived from their own answers. However, majority voting can reinforce incorrect solutions even when correct alternatives are available. Our training audit shows that false positives (incorrect responses receiving positive rewards) dominate reward errors. We focus on a practical regime where ground-truth rewards are difficult to obtain at scale, while a limited labeled source set is available. We introduce TRUER, a framework that uses limited supervision to train a reward rectifier that distinguishes correctness from consensus. To achieve this goal, we train the rectifier with an emphasis on incorrect majorities and correct minorities, targeting cases where consensus and correctness disagree. After that, we freeze the rectifier and use it to correct rewards during subsequent test-time adaptation. By improving reward accuracy and thereby model performance, TRUER consistently outperforms naive TTRL in both metrics across all evaluated configurations.
papers.summary: Test-time reinforcement learning (`TTRL`) adapts language models using rewards derived from majority voting over their own answers, which can reinforce wrong answers; an audit shows that **false positives, incorrect responses receiving positive reward, dominate the reward errors**. `TRUER` uses a small labeled source set to train a reward rectifier that separates correctness from consensus, with emphasis on incorrect majorities and correct minorities. The rectifier is then frozen and used to correct rewards during test-time adaptation, and the authors report higher reward accuracy and model performance than naive `TTRL` in every evaluated configuration.

papers.title: Weighted-AoI-Driven UAV Trajectory and Reporting for Dynamic CKM Tracking
papers.abstract: Existing channel knowledge map (CKM) construction assumes quasi-static environments, failing when channels rapidly decorrelate. This paper investigates continuous online dynamic CKM tracking over an airborne 2D plane via a UAV fleet. We formulate a long-term error minimization problem under UAV mobility and reporting constraints. This problem, however, is intractable with unobservable errors for unmeasured cells. To tackle this, we propose a metric-driven scheduling approach featuring the Weighted-Age of Information (W-AoI). W-AoI evaluates cells by combining exact temporal staleness with spatial uncertainty predicted by a 2D U-Net. We prove that top-$K$ W-AoI selection maximizes the one-slot error reduction bound. Guided by this guarantee, we develop a lightweight greedy trajectory policy incorporating continuous along-path sensing. Simulations demonstrate our method reduces steady-state error by 3.8 dB$^2$ and 4.8 dB$^2$ over AoI-only and FIFO baselines, closely approaching an idealized oracle.
papers.summary: Channel knowledge maps (CKMs), which record wireless channel conditions by location, are usually built assuming a near-static environment and break down when channels change quickly. The authors study continuous online tracking of a dynamic CKM by a fleet of drones and propose scheduling measurements by Weighted Age of Information (`W-AoI`), which combines how stale each cell's measurement is with spatial uncertainty predicted by a 2D `U-Net`. They prove that selecting the top-K cells by this metric maximizes a one-slot error reduction bound and build a lightweight greedy trajectory policy on it. Simulations show **steady-state error reductions of 3.8 dB² and 4.8 dB² over age-only and first-in-first-out baselines**, close to an idealized oracle.

papers.title: Deterministic, Reproducible Inference in Exact Integer Arithmetic, and Verifiable Distributed Inference as Its Consequence
papers.abstract: Optimized floating-point inference is not reproducible across environments: the same model on different hardware, compilers or thread counts can produce different bits. We present tritify, an open-source runtime that executes the forward pass of real models -- decoder-only language models, Mixture-of-Experts decoders, and the Segment Anything 2.1 image/video stack -- with the entire run-time path in exact integer arithmetic; floating point is confined to offline quantization and the float reference used for verification. We make three separate claims and verify each. (1) Cross-hardware reproducibility: the integer path produces bit-identical output run to run, across CPU instruction-set architectures, and across CPU/GPU, carried by a reproducing SHA-256 of the output. (2) Decision fidelity: the integer path reproduces the float reference's decision on the models and inputs tested, with the numeric exceptions measured; per-layer fidelity through sixteen layers of OLMoE-1B-7B and of a 106-billion-parameter MoE shows no fidelity cliff. (3) Location independence: a model's computation can be split across instruction sets, CPU and GPU, and networked machines with zero effect on the output bits. GLM-4.5-Air (106,852,251,264 parameters, 427 GB of integer codes) generated its answer across three machines, none of which can hold its integer codes in RAM, bit-identically to a single-host reference. The consequence is verifiable distributed inference: an untrusted server or a fleet of devices runs the model while an open scalar oracle re-derives the exact bytes; a guarantee against a dishonest server is future work. We do not claim a per-device speed-up, bit-equality of floating-valued intermediates, or confidentiality. Code: https://github.com/pelloran-inc/tritify
papers.summary: Floating-point inference can produce different bits for the same model across hardware, compilers, and thread counts. `tritify` is an open-source runtime that runs the forward pass of decoder-only language models, Mixture-of-Experts decoders, and the `Segment Anything 2.1` stack entirely in exact integer arithmetic, yielding output that is bit-identical across runs, CPU architectures, and CPU/GPU while reproducing the float reference's decisions on the tested inputs. Because the computation can be split across devices with no effect on the output, **the 106-billion-parameter `GLM-4.5-Air` generated its answer across three machines, none able to hold the model in RAM, bit-identically to a single-host reference**. The authors frame this as enabling verifiable distributed inference, and explicitly do not claim a speed-up, confidentiality, or a guarantee against a dishonest server.

papers.title: Plug-and-Play ADMM for Inverse Problems with Flow Matching Denoiser
papers.abstract: Plug-and-Play (PnP) methods with generative priors have achieved strong performance in inverse problems, with recent flow matching models enabling fast and scalable reconstruction. However, a key challenge in PnP methods is maintaining consistency between data fidelity updates and the learned generative prior, as data-consistency steps can move iterates away from the flow trajectory. We propose an ADMM-based PnP framework for flow matching priors that enforces stronger consistency between the measurement model and the prior through auxiliary variables and dual updates. In addition, we introduce a trajectory correction mechanism that restores consistency with the flow via a combination of deterministic and stochastic projections. Our method provides a more principled integration of flow priors within PnP frameworks, achieving high-quality reconstructions with reduced computational cost.
papers.summary: Plug-and-Play (PnP) methods solve inverse problems by pairing a data-fidelity step with a learned generative prior, but with flow matching priors the data-consistency step can push iterates off the flow trajectory. The proposed framework uses the alternating direction method of multipliers (`ADMM`), with auxiliary variables and dual updates, to tie the measurement model and prior together more tightly, and adds a trajectory correction step that combines deterministic and stochastic projections. The authors claim **high-quality reconstructions at reduced computational cost**, without reporting specific figures in the abstract.

papers.title: Do Language Models Feel the Sentiment? Investigating Emotion Vectors
papers.abstract: Emotion vectors are directions in a language model's internal representations that are associated with emotional concepts. Prior work shows that these vectors can influence model behavior, but their role in sentiment classification remains unclear. This study investigates emotion directions in Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct. Eight directions extracted from GoEmotions are evaluated through sentiment probing, activation interventions, and supervised correction. Emotion-only probes achieve 88.66% and 90.70% accuracy on binary TweetEval. In exploratory matched-ablation experiments, raw emotion-space removal causes 2.39 and 1.10 percentage points more accuracy loss than matched isotropic random-subspace removal for 0.5B and 3B, respectively. All four TweetEval raw and denoised effects are significant after Holm adjustment across eight comparisons. An exploratory SST-2 extension shows smaller raw excess losses of 0.66 and 0.57 points, with no effects surviving Holm adjustment. Frozen sentiment-correction classifiers are also tested on 20,000 Amazon Polarity reviews. Emotion-based correction improves accuracy over uncorrected Qwen, but does not consistently outperform margin-only baselines. These results distinguish sentiment information available in model representations, the effects of changing those representations, and their practical value for classification. They do not establish a uniquely emotional mechanism.
papers.summary: Emotion vectors, directions in a language model's internal representations tied to emotional concepts, are tested for their role in sentiment classification in `Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct` and `Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct`. Probes using only eight directions extracted from `GoEmotions` reach 88.66% and 90.70% accuracy on binary `TweetEval`, and removing the emotion subspace costs **2.39 and 1.10 percentage points more accuracy than removing a matched random subspace**; the effect is smaller and not significant on `SST-2`. Emotion-based correction classifiers improve accuracy on `Amazon Polarity` reviews but do not consistently beat margin-only baselines. The authors conclude that the results separate available information, intervention effects, and practical value, and do not establish a uniquely emotional mechanism.

papers.title: When Covariance Is Not Enough: Kernel-Based Regularization for Single-Cell Counterfactuals
papers.abstract: Counterfactual editing of single cells, predicting how an observed cell would look had one factor been different, enables in-silico screening where experiments are infeasible, but is useful only if the edit is faithful to the individual and not merely to the condition. Concept bottleneck generative models make the effects of interventions interpretable by decomposing a cell's representation into known and unknown factors. Previous work uses a linear cross-covariance penalty to disentangle known and unknown dimensions. We demonstrate that this first-order criterion does not fully separate information when non-linear interactions are present. We first demonstrate the inadequacy of linear cross-factor penalization with simulation experiments with controlled edits and known non-linear covariate effects. We then demonstrate that adding a nonlinear kernel criterion, the normalized Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion, is able to recover the true intervention effects on simulation data. Finally, we apply the non-linear concept bottleneck model to a complex single-cell RNA-seq dataset and find that it improves the ability to generate counterfactual expression profiles of cells under different tissue environments.
papers.summary: Counterfactual editing of single cells predicts how an observed cell would look had one factor differed, and concept bottleneck generative models support this by splitting a cell's representation into known and unknown factors. Prior work disentangles the two with a linear cross-covariance penalty, which the authors show in controlled simulations fails to separate information when covariate effects are non-linear. Adding a kernel-based penalty, the normalized Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion, **recovers the true intervention effects on simulated data**, and on a single-cell RNA-seq dataset it improves generated counterfactual expression profiles across tissue environments.

papers.title: Word-Level Alignment of OCR and Ground Truth under Zoning and Reading-Order Errors
papers.abstract: OCR post-processing needs OCR text aligned word by word with its ground truth. Data sets rarely provide that mapping, and a monotone aligner can lose its place when zoning errors permute the reading order. We revisit this problem, the Zoning Problem of our 2019 paper, with a protocol that tests correctness under such permutations. We apply OCR-side reading-order permutations with construction-time word-level gold and score correct-match F1, cascade length and recovery. We compare the 2019 location-aware aligner, a re-anchoring extension of it, a RETAS-style baseline (RETAS-lite), a multi-region aligner that combines unique-word and unique n-gram anchors with chunk-to-window assignment, genalog's RETAS and the original Java RETAS. Experiments use synthetic character noise with block moves, paragraph swaps and column interleaving, historical newspaper reading-order permutations, geometry-derived gold for Tesseract OCR, and a small word-box set. Synthetic tests show where local tracking fails after large displacements and where unique-anchor methods collapse when unique anchors are scarce. On our synthetic boilerplate page the 2019 method had the highest F1 among those tested. Historical newspaper and geometry-derived evaluations carry the limitations of approximate gold and the article-order convention. The first multi-region version has a quadratic scaling cost. Local tracking remains fragile under large reading-order changes; the tested anchor-based methods handle many of those cases but fail when unique anchors are scarce. Approximate gold, the article-order convention, missing residual annotation, and the lack of modern multi-column word-level ground truth remain limitations.
papers.summary: Post-processing optical character recognition (OCR) output needs it aligned word by word with ground truth, and monotone aligners lose their place when zoning errors scramble reading order. The authors introduce an evaluation protocol that applies reading-order permutations with known word-level gold and compare six aligners, including their 2019 location-aware method, a re-anchoring extension, `RETAS` variants, and a multi-region aligner based on unique-word and n-gram anchors. Results are mixed: **local tracking stays fragile under large reading-order changes, while anchor-based methods handle many such cases but collapse when unique anchors are scarce**. They also note approximate gold data, a quadratic cost in the multi-region aligner, and the absence of modern multi-column word-level ground truth as limitations.

papers.title: A Hardware-Trained Generative Quantum Eigensolver for Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization of Organotin Hydroxides up to 70 Qubits
papers.abstract: Quantum hardware can provide feedback for training circuit generators beyond the reach of exact classical simulation. We train generative quantum eigensolver (GQE) policies, transformers conditioned on molecular descriptors, to generate the state-preparation circuits for sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD). Training runs first on a noiseless simulator and then with the IBM Heron processor ibm_kobe inside the loop, at 46 and 70 qubits ($1.2 \times 10^8$ shots for the four main training runs). A classical CCSD(T) reference energy of the training molecules enters only an admission gate and two auxiliary reward terms. During hardware training, a reward penalty prevents collapse to circuits that sample only the Hartree-Fock determinant. Policies trained on transition-metal complexes are applied without retraining to Sn(OH)$_3$-Me and its hydrates, minimal models of organotin photoresists for extreme-ultraviolet lithography, from 32 to 70 qubits. After one round of hardware sampling, followed by classical ranking and recovery of the cached counts with the molecular Hamiltonian and no further QPU calls, 27 of 28 runs at 46-70 qubits are within 15 mHa of the density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) reference (median 4.5 mHa), and in all eight runs with an untrained control the trained policy is more accurate. At 56-70 qubits the selected circuits use 34-72 times fewer two-qubit gates than the local unitary cluster Jastrow (LUCJ) circuit transpiled for the same device. These results demonstrate that circuit generators can be trained with quantum hardware at 70 qubits.
papers.summary: Generative quantum eigensolver (GQE) policies, transformers conditioned on molecular descriptors, are trained to generate state-preparation circuits for sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), first on a noiseless simulator and then with an `IBM Heron` processor in the training loop at 46 and 70 qubits. Policies trained on transition-metal complexes are applied without retraining to organotin hydroxide molecules that model extreme-ultraviolet photoresists, from 32 to 70 qubits. After one round of hardware sampling and classical post-processing, **27 of 28 runs at 46-70 qubits land within 15 mHa of the density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) reference**, with a median of 4.5 mHa, and the trained policy beats an untrained control in all eight comparisons. At 56-70 qubits the selected circuits use 34-72 times fewer two-qubit gates than the local unitary cluster Jastrow (LUCJ) circuit.

papers.title: Mixed Signals: Weight-Space Programming for EEG and ECG
papers.abstract: Weight-space programming allows language models to read a trained neural network's weights and edit them. This opens the door to ``training'' by reasoning rather than through gradient descent. Prior work has demonstrated its functionality and promise for game-playing networks and fixing specific failures in language models, even extending to diffusion models. In this work, we present its applicability to models trained on biosignal data, specifically EEG and ECG data. We show that frontier models are not only able to debug specific faults planted in biosignal-based models without being told what these faults are, but are even capable of writing all the weights of a network from scratch, given only the architecture, the task, and a minimal set of training subjects. In particular, in one set of experiments, a language model was able to match standard gradient-descent training using $6\times$ fewer training subjects, through reasoning alone and without any gradient descent step. Networks written by Claude Opus 5.5 also scored higher than classic hand-crafted EEG pipelines (alpha band power, and common spatial patterns with linear discriminant analysis) when built from the same 5 subjects. We also highlight some of the limitations, which include the inability of language models to improve already well-trained classification models, and their incapacity to reliably recognize, from the weights alone, the task a network was trained on. Overall, our results indicate that weight-space programming can be useful for small networks, such as those deployed on edge devices and wearables, but the concept still requires further investigation before it can be used in practice.
papers.summary: Weight-space programming, in which a language model reads and edits a trained network's weights directly, is extended to small networks trained on EEG and ECG biosignal data. Frontier models located and fixed planted faults without being told what they were, and could write every weight of a network from scratch given only the architecture, the task, and a few training subjects. In one set of experiments a language model **matched standard gradient-descent training using 6x fewer training subjects**, and networks written by `Claude Opus 5.5` beat hand-crafted EEG pipelines built from the same 5 subjects. The reported limits are that language models could not improve already well-trained classifiers and could not reliably identify a network's task from its weights alone.

papers.title: Beyond Interaction Scores: Selecting Feature Interactions via Independent Replication
papers.abstract: Learning feature interactions is essential for accurate prediction and interpretable modeling, yet a high interaction score may reflect fitting noise rather than a reproducible pattern. Ranking methods score feature pairs but leave the cutoff to the user; testing methods set the cutoff but rely on repeated model refits or a model of the joint feature distribution. We present LENS, a model-agnostic framework for selecting feature interactions through independent replication. LENS trains two models with the same learning algorithm on disjoint data and accesses them only through predictions. For each feature pair, it removes main effects from the joint-effect surface to isolate an interaction pattern, ranks pairs by its strength, and tests whether the second model reproduces it at a meaningful strength. A single multiple-testing correction determines which pairs to retain, using only two model fits regardless of the number of features. We prove that a replication ratio alone can retain arbitrarily weak patterns shared by both fits, whereas a strength floor restores selection consistency, and we characterize when normalization in Friedman's $H^2$ reverses interaction rankings. On 16 synthetic designs, LENS matches leading model-specific ranking methods (e.g., TreeSHAP) and recovers 91% of material interactions, against 45% for the knockoff-based DIAMOND, without selecting false pairs; with 1,225 candidate pairs and no interactions, it makes substantially fewer false discoveries. On large-scale French motor insurance data, it identifies interactions documented in the actuarial literature and recovers 90% of the deviance gain obtained using all pairs. On two credit datasets, LENS selects few pairs while maintaining or slightly improving predictive performance over the additive baseline.
papers.summary: High feature-interaction scores can reflect fitted noise, and existing methods either leave the cutoff to the user or require many model refits or a model of the joint feature distribution. `LENS` trains two models on disjoint data, accesses them only through predictions, isolates each pair's interaction pattern by removing main effects, and tests whether the second model reproduces it at a meaningful strength under a single multiple-testing correction. The authors prove that a replication ratio alone can retain arbitrarily weak shared patterns while a strength floor restores selection consistency. On 16 synthetic designs it matches ranking methods such as `TreeSHAP` and **recovers 91% of material interactions versus 45% for the knockoff-based `DIAMOND`** without selecting false pairs, and it recovers 90% of the deviance gain on French motor insurance data.

papers.title: DisasterAgent: An Evidence-Driven Agent for Verifiable Disaster Report Generation From Remote Sensing Imagery
papers.abstract: Remote sensing disaster assessment is moving from simple damage classification toward comprehensive report-level analysis. In this setting, responders need not only damage descriptions but also verifiable evidence to guide response and recovery. Recent vision-language models (VLMs) and tool-augmented agents offer strong multimodal reasoning and perception, but they struggle to provide the evidence required for high-stakes verification. To address these limitations, we propose DisasterAgent, an evidence-driven agent that uses a Perception-Augmentation-Generation workflow to generate verifiable disaster reports from bitemporal optical imagery. DisasterAgent first invokes a specialized vision expert toolkit in the perception phase to build a Spatiotemporal Perception Graph (STPG), serving as a structured memory to store and organize disaster-induced changes across space and time. Evidence-based Augmentation (EA) then extracts evidence from the STPG, attaching inline citations that form a closed evidence loop from each statement to the supporting visual evidence. Extensive experiments on the DisasterM3 and RSCC benchmarks demonstrate that DisasterAgent consistently outperforms general-domain VLMs, remote sensing-specialized models, and existing remote sensing agents. Notably, compared with the original model, it improves the average score for disaster report generation on DisasterM3 by 13.5\% and ST5-SCS on RSCC by 15.34\%, providing a more accurate and verifiable solution for disaster emergency response. The code will be available at https://github.com/ZhijianLi2003/DisasterAgent.
papers.summary: Disaster assessment from remote sensing imagery increasingly calls for full reports whose statements responders can verify, which vision-language models (VLMs) and tool-augmented agents struggle to back with evidence. `DisasterAgent` follows a Perception-Augmentation-Generation workflow: a vision expert toolkit builds a Spatiotemporal Perception Graph (`STPG`) of changes between before and after images, and an Evidence-based Augmentation step attaches inline citations linking each statement to its supporting visual evidence. On the `DisasterM3` and `RSCC` benchmarks it outperforms general-domain VLMs, remote-sensing-specialized models, and existing remote sensing agents, **raising the average report-generation score on `DisasterM3` by 13.5%** and `ST5-SCS` on `RSCC` by 15.34% over the original model.

papers.title: Omni-JEV: Text and Dual-Stream Speech Decisions
papers.abstract: A user utterance does not uniquely determine the next action in full-duplex dialogue: its consequences depend on the assistant's response state and interaction history. Speech activity, utterance completion, and interruption intent provide related evidence, whose implications for a response require an explicit action policy. We formulate this task at collected-segment endpoints and introduce Omni-JEV, which maps text or role-indexed user and assistant-reference speech to probabilities over five interaction actions. An aligned speech-to-speech understanding backbone encodes the acoustic roles separately and shares its candidate readout with text inputs. Bilingual weak supervision supports cross-entropy fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning for probability-sensitive decisions (RLCD). We compare Gaussian-logit and categorical Choice RLCD from the same supervised initialization under matched training exposure, observing different trade-offs between classification and probability quality. Gaussian Omni-JEV achieves test accuracies of 84.08% for audio and 96.55% for text. This common action interface supports decisions about when a full-duplex voice assistant should respond, preserve ongoing speech, interrupt, or resume an interrupted response.
papers.summary: In full-duplex spoken dialogue the right next action after a user utterance depends on what the assistant is currently saying and on the interaction history, not on the utterance alone. `Omni-JEV` maps either text or separately encoded user and assistant speech streams to probabilities over five interaction actions, such as responding, preserving ongoing speech, interrupting, or resuming an interrupted response. It is trained with bilingual weak supervision, first by cross-entropy fine-tuning and then by reinforcement learning for probability-sensitive decisions (`RLCD`), with Gaussian-logit and categorical variants showing different trade-offs between classification and probability quality. The Gaussian variant reaches **test accuracies of 84.08% for audio and 96.55% for text**.

papers.title: Softness is something you also need! Why compliance helps control: information metrics of a passive walker with compliant ankle
papers.abstract:
A great gap in adaptivity, flexibility, and dexterity still exists between intelligent robots, whether they are made of rigid or (partially) compliant components, and their naturally evolved animal and vegetal counterparts. One reason could be of `paradigm' nature. On the one hand, most robots (both rigid and soft) are still designed by following a `Cartesian' approach, with top-down control and a clear mind-body separation. Designing artificial agents on the basis of the principles that we observe in biology is not an easy task. The principles of organization of animals and plants rely on morphological computation and emergence of fit behaviors from loosely coupled networks of embodied agents.
  Modeling and control require radically new approaches. In this paper we briefly recall and explain some seminal mathematical results linking information metrics and dynamics of the agents, already published years ago; we integrate them with some recent methods developed by us and by the community, we highlight some brief remarks about their relevance and we hint to our current and near future work towards finding concrete and efficient ways for the modeling and control of completely or partially compliant artificial agents and for a better understanding of physical intelligence in nature. We present a technical note summarizing phase-space volume calculations for inverted-pendulum and passive-dynamic walking models, following our proposed framework. Starting from the McGeer compass gait, we introduce knee-ankle compliance, foot-rocker effects, and a Ruina-style compass gait with distributed leg inertia. Standard heel-strike maps are derived and used in the estimation of viable phase-space volumes $W(\gamma)$, based on a state-dependent Monte-Carlo and Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces methods. We show how the methods based on RKHS allow deeper and more subtle analysis.
papers.summary: The gap in adaptivity between robots and animals is attributed here partly to top-down control designs that separate mind from body, in contrast to the morphological computation seen in biology. This technical note recalls earlier mathematical results linking information metrics to agent dynamics and applies them to phase-space volume calculations for inverted-pendulum and passive-dynamic walking models. Starting from the `McGeer` compass gait, it adds knee-ankle compliance, foot-rocker effects, and a Ruina-style gait with distributed leg inertia, then estimates viable phase-space volumes using state-dependent Monte Carlo and Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) methods. The authors report that **the RKHS-based methods allow a deeper and more subtle analysis** of these walkers.

papers.title: Integrating Action Prefix Prediction and Alignment Across Modalities for Multimodal Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Learning representations from multimodal observations is difficult in reinforcement learning with limited interaction data. Multimodal Joint Predictive Representation combines multimodal latent prediction with contrastive learning across modalities, but its recursive rollout depends on earlier predictions and its pairwise alignment focuses on correspondence between modalities. We propose Improved Predictive Representation, which combines prediction from action prefixes with alignment at the observed anchor based on Contrastive Multimodal learning. At each horizon, it predicts future representations directly from the observed anchor and the corresponding sequence of actions. We evaluate two crop configurations: IPR-S with a minimum retained crop area of 10%, and IPR-H with 50%. Across five DeepMind Control Suite tasks, IPR-H achieves an average return across tasks that is 10.0% higher than the baseline with visual and depth images and 3.4% higher with visual images and position vectors. The relative performance of the two configurations varies across tasks. In Webots, both IPR configurations achieve higher mean final returns than the baseline without LiDAR, but not when LiDAR is available.
papers.summary: Representation learning from multimodal observations is hard in reinforcement learning when interaction data is limited, and the existing `Multimodal Joint Predictive Representation` method relies on recursive rollouts that compound earlier prediction errors. `Improved Predictive Representation` (`IPR`) instead predicts each future representation directly from the observed anchor and the corresponding action prefix, and aligns modalities at that anchor with contrastive multimodal learning. Across five `DeepMind Control Suite` tasks the `IPR-H` configuration achieves an **average return 10.0% higher than the baseline with visual and depth images** and 3.4% higher with visual images and position vectors. In `Webots` both configurations beat the baseline without LiDAR but not when LiDAR is available.

papers.title: LLM Validation Makes Minimal-Pair Benchmarks Easier for Language Models
papers.abstract: Minimal-pair benchmarks are only as good as their labels, and LLMs are an obvious substitute for costly human validation. We test it on BLiMP (English) and QFrBLiMP (Quebec French), the two public minimal-pair datasets releasing every forced-choice human judgment. Three LLMs validate by forced choice, by rating, and as a panel, scored against human panels of one, three and five judges in two pre-registered phases. On BLiMP, forced-choice validators agree with held-out human majorities more often than five-judge panels, yet catch far fewer pairs whose label humans reject than one judge does. By point estimate, no validator is worth more than one judge. The errors are not random. On both datasets, across 10 open LMs, human-supported pairs that the pre-registered LLM filter flags are 18.9 points harder than those it accepts, in all 70 LM-validator combinations, and harder than pairs a single human judge flags. Filtering thus removes items on which LMs fail but humans do not, raising accuracy more than random removal. A protocol frozen before any output replicates the gap and the lift on Dutch BLiMP-NL. LLM validation makes minimal-pair benchmarks easier for the models they are meant to test; we release code, validator outputs and item-level scores.
papers.summary: Using LLMs in place of human judges to validate minimal-pair linguistic benchmarks is tested on `BLiMP` (English) and `QFrBLiMP` (Quebec French), the two public datasets that release every human forced-choice judgment. Three LLM validators agree with held-out human majorities more often than five-judge panels on `BLiMP`, yet catch far fewer pairs whose labels humans reject than a single judge does. Their errors are systematic: across 10 open language models, human-supported pairs that the LLM filter flags are **18.9 points harder than the pairs it accepts, in all 70 model-validator combinations**. Filtering therefore removes items that models fail but humans do not, inflating accuracy more than random removal, a result that replicates on Dutch `BLiMP-NL` under a pre-frozen protocol.

papers.title: AnchorMTS: Multi-View Signal Representation and Forecast-Anchored Fusion for Long-Term Time-Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Long-term time-series forecasters typically optimize a single numerical representation, even though the same history exposes complementary geometry, recurrence, and semantic structure. We propose AnchorMTS, which derives self-aligned visual and textual views from each observed window and uses them only to refine a complete numerical forecast. A trainable evidence path produces a candidate forecast, while a parameter-free output projection enforces an exact per-variable bound on its displacement from the numerical anchor. Across six benchmarks and four horizons, AnchorMTS achieves the best macro MSE/MAE (0.336/0.367) among seven supervised baselines and wins 18 of 24 MSE settings against the cellwise baseline envelope; removing the auxiliary path raises macro MSE to 0.340. The projection leaves 95.8% of candidate refinements unchanged while yielding zero bound violations, showing that complementary multi-view evidence can improve forecasting while its final influence remains explicitly controlled.
papers.summary: Long-term time-series forecasters usually optimize a single numerical representation even though the same history also exposes geometric, recurrence, and semantic structure. `AnchorMTS` derives visual and textual views from each observed window and uses them only to refine a complete numerical forecast, with a parameter-free output projection that enforces an exact per-variable bound on how far the refinement can move from that numerical anchor. Across six benchmarks and four horizons it achieves the **best macro MSE/MAE of 0.336/0.367 among seven supervised baselines** and wins 18 of 24 MSE settings, while removing the auxiliary path raises macro MSE to 0.340. The projection leaves 95.8% of candidate refinements unchanged and yields zero bound violations.

papers.title: Bridging Graph and Pairwise Learning for Gene Regulatory Network Inference from scRNA-seq Data
papers.abstract: Motivation: Gene regulatory networks (GRNs) capture the underlying interactions through which transcription factors (TFs) regulate genes. Based on gene expression data, existing GRN inference approaches generally fall into two categories: graph-based methods, which model the GRN as a whole graph, and pairwise-based methods, which decompose the GRN into individual TF-target gene pairs for modeling. However, each approach exhibits limitations that are precisely the strengths of its counterpart. Graph-based methods tend to overfit due to their reliance on a single training graph, whereas pairwise-based methods benefit from abundant TF-target training pairs. In contrast, pairwise-based methods overlook the global topological structure, which is essential for comprehensively capturing regulatory mechanisms. Results: To address these limitations, we propose scGPL, an end-to-end unified framework that jointly models global regulatory topology and local interactions. scGPL extracts macro-level features from the global regulatory graph and introduces a dynamic, importance-guided subgraph sampling mechanism to capture fine-grained local dependencies. By fusing global representations with subgraph-enhanced local features, our framework bridges the gap between the two paradigms, incorporating essential whole-graph topological dependencies while retaining the data abundance advantage of pairwise methods. Extensive experiments on seven benchmark datasets demonstrate that scGPL consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance, with up to 13.7% improvement over the strongest baseline, validating the effectiveness of our integrative design. Availability and implementation: The source code is maintained on GitHub (https://github.com/talent-hang/scGPL), and the datasets and versioned releases are archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21608485 for reproducibility.
papers.summary: Inferring gene regulatory networks (GRNs), the interactions by which transcription factors (TFs) regulate genes, from single-cell expression data is usually done either with graph-based methods that overfit to a single training graph or with pairwise methods that ignore global topology. `scGPL` is an end-to-end framework that extracts macro-level features from the global regulatory graph and combines them with local features from a dynamic, importance-guided subgraph sampling mechanism. This keeps whole-graph topological dependencies while retaining the abundant TF-target training pairs of pairwise methods. On seven benchmark datasets it reports state-of-the-art performance with **up to 13.7% improvement over the strongest baseline**.

papers.title: Relaxing Cross-Modal Correspondence for Multimodal Remote Sensing Pretraining
papers.abstract: Multimodal remote sensing pretraining commonly relies on exact instance-level correspondence across modalities, implicitly treating strictly paired observations as a prerequisite for learning transferable representations. In this work, we revisit this assumption by relaxing cross-modal correspondence from the instance level to the semantic level. We introduce Semantic Pairing (SemPair), a pairing-relaxed pretraining strategy that replaces exact instance pairs with class-consistent cross-instance pairs. To characterize the effect of correspondence relaxation, we formulate a latent-factor model that separates cross-modal dependence into shared semantic structure and instance-specific correlation, showing that SemPair preserves the former while marginalizing instance-specific cross-modal correlations in expectation. We further introduce Mixed Pairing (MixPair) as a controlled interpolation between semantic and exact pairing to study correspondence granularity along a continuous spectrum. Extensive experiments consistently show that SemPair achieves transfer performance comparable to exact pairing (ExaPair), while MixPair reveals a non-monotonic relationship between downstream transfer and the instance-pairing ratio. These results demonstrate that exact instance correspondence is not a prerequisite for effective multimodal remote sensing pretraining and establish cross-modal correspondence granularity as an important design dimension for transferable multimodal representation learning. More broadly, this finding suggests a practical route toward scaling multimodal pretraining with reduced dependence on costly instance-aligned data.
papers.summary: Multimodal remote sensing pretraining normally assumes strictly paired observations of the same instance across modalities. `SemPair` replaces exact instance pairs with class-consistent pairs drawn from different instances, and a latent-factor model shows this preserves shared semantic structure while averaging out instance-specific cross-modal correlations. A `MixPair` variant interpolates between semantic and exact pairing to study the full spectrum. Experiments show that **semantic pairing achieves transfer performance comparable to exact pairing**, and that downstream transfer varies non-monotonically with the instance-pairing ratio.

papers.title: Antalia-2 Mini: A 7.6-million-parameter Turkish text-to-speech model trained entirely on synthetic speech
papers.abstract: Antalia-2 Mini is a single-voice Turkish text-to-speech model with 7,620,931 parameters. It reads characters and produces 48 kHz audio at 41 times real time on an Apple M5 laptop CPU (2 threads). Its training audio came only from VoxCPM2 (the teacher), about 300 times larger, cloning one synthetic clip; automatic checks kept about 1,790 h. Fine-tuning the vocoder on the acoustic model's own mel spectrograms cut the word error rate (WER) of Whisper's transcripts from a mean of 3.89% to 1.75% at adjacent pre-release checkpoints. The teacher corrupts the start of a clip when the first word begins with \"o, the student learned this, and a spoken prefix we cut from the output hides it. On the 495-sentence Freya-TR-Eval benchmark, where we tuned settings, version 1.0.1 has WER 1.09% and character error rate 0.22% on our public harness. A paired bootstrap cannot distinguish these from EMA Lightning, an 8.6M Turkish model, which scores higher on full-band UTMOS, an English-trained quality proxy. No human listening test exists. Weights, inference code and the benchmark harness are public under Apache-2.0; training code and data are not.
papers.summary: `Antalia-2 Mini` is a single-voice Turkish text-to-speech model with 7.6 million parameters that reads characters and produces 48 kHz audio at **41 times real time on two threads of an Apple M5 laptop CPU**. Its roughly 1,790 hours of training audio were generated entirely by `VoxCPM2`, a teacher about 300 times larger, and filtered automatically; fine-tuning the vocoder on the acoustic model's own mel spectrograms cut the word error rate (WER) of `Whisper` transcripts from 3.89% to 1.75%. On the 495-sentence `Freya-TR-Eval` benchmark it scores 1.09% WER and 0.22% character error rate, statistically indistinguishable from the 8.6M-parameter `EMA Lightning`, which scores higher on the `UTMOS` quality proxy. No human listening test was run, and weights and inference code are released under Apache-2.0 while training code and data are not.

papers.title: Swanada: Split-Encoder Capability-Routed Conformer CTC and Sub-30 MB On-Device Speech Recognition Across Twelve Scripts
papers.abstract:
Client-side automatic speech recognition (ASR) across Indic and Classical scripts eliminates cloud transcription costs, network tail latency, and server-side audio retention, yet neural exports face four systems bottlenecks in browsers and mobile runtimes: (1) monolithic per-language Conformer checkpoints require ~177 MiB per script (> 2.1 GiB across 12 scripts), exhausting CacheStorage quotas; (2) static relative positional encoding tables embed 10.2-20.5 MB of FP32 constants while 1x1 Conv1d layers trigger slow or unsupported ConvInteger kernels in WebAssembly SIMD; (3) sliding-window CTC flickers on boundary tokens; and (4) mobile WebAudio pipelines suffer 44.1/48 kHz sample-rate mismatches and silent AudioWorklet stalls under iOS WKWebView.
  We present Swanada, an open-source 16 kHz streaming ASR system spanning Classical Sanskrit, Indian English, and ten Indian languages (sa, en, hi, kn, mr, bn, ta, te, ml, gu, pa, or) across browser WebAssembly, Node.js, and Python. Swanada pairs capability-routed shared INT8 Conformer encoders (a 17-layer 177.38 MiB Studio tier at $d = 512$ for desktop/servers and a distilled 14-layer 25.35 MiB Mobile tier at $d = 256$ for phones) with twelve hot-swappable 515.0 KiB native-script linear CTC heads ($257 \times 512$), cutting 12-language storage by $11.6\times$ (183.4 MiB) and $67.8\times$ (31.39 MiB; 25.85 MiB first load). Runtime protobuf tail surgery exposes the shared representation in $< 2$ ms, while dynamic positional synthesis, MatMul pointwise convolutions, and post-quantization QInt8 head calibration preserve sub-30 MB accuracy. Across $N = 480$ held-out and $N = 1,280$ open public test clips (FLEURS, LibriSpeech, GLOBE, AMI, wild Sanskrit), Swanada achieves 5.43% held-out and 8.87% 12-language open CER on Studio (18.56% and 19.23% on Mobile) at $0.0097\times$-$0.0264\times$ RTF, with 30.6 ms median TTFT and 0.00% committed-prefix churn.
papers.summary: Running automatic speech recognition (ASR) in browsers and on phones across many Indic scripts is blocked by per-language model size, slow or unsupported WebAssembly kernels, flickering streaming output, and mobile audio pipeline quirks. `Swanada` is an open-source streaming system for Sanskrit, Indian English, and ten Indian languages that shares one quantized INT8 Conformer encoder, in a 177 MiB desktop tier or a distilled 25 MiB mobile tier, across twelve hot-swappable 515 KiB per-script CTC output heads. This **cuts twelve-language storage by 11.6x on the desktop tier and 67.8x on the mobile tier, to 31.39 MiB**. On open public test clips including `FLEURS` and `LibriSpeech`, the desktop tier reaches 8.87% character error rate and the mobile tier 19.23%, with 30.6 ms median time to first token.

papers.title: Adaptive Policy-Guided Error Mitigation (APGEM): A Unified Learning-Based Framework for Noise Resilience in Quantum Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Error mitigation stands between variational quantum algorithms and useful results on today's noisy hardware, yet in practice a mitigation method is usually chosen once, by hand, and applied unchanged for the life of an experiment. This is a poor fit for quantum machine learning (QML), where the circuit and the noise drift as training proceeds, so the best strategy in one regime is often wrong in another. We present a generalized form of Adaptive Policy-Guided Error Mitigation (APGEM), which treats the choice of mitigation technique as an online decision made from an algorithm's own feedback. A single contextual-bandit controller observes signals any variational algorithm already produces, such as fidelity, entropy, reward or loss, and gradient behavior, and selects among Zero-Noise Extrapolation, Probabilistic Error Cancellation, Measurement Error Mitigation, Dynamical Decoupling, and circuit optimization per step. Because it depends only on this shared feedback interface, the framework applies unchanged across supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, and hybrid quantum-classical learning. Evaluated on five paradigms across 80 algorithm-and-noise conditions, adaptive selection reaches 95.5% of an oracle that always picks the best technique and significantly outperforms all six fixed strategies (Friedman $\chi^{2}=92.18$, $p\approx1.1\times10^{-17}$; pairwise Wilcoxon $p<4\times10^{-6}$). The learned policy is noise-aware: its favored technique shifts as depolarizing and readout error rise. On noise models from eight real IBM devices, APGEM tracks the oracle almost exactly (99.9% of oracle utility) at a flat cost of roughly $1.3\times10^{4}$ shots from three to eight qubits.
papers.summary: Error mitigation for quantum machine learning (QML) is usually chosen once by hand, even though the circuit and noise drift during training. Adaptive Policy-Guided Error Mitigation (`APGEM`) uses a contextual-bandit controller that observes signals any variational algorithm already produces, such as fidelity, entropy, loss, and gradient behavior, and selects per step among five techniques including Zero-Noise Extrapolation and Probabilistic Error Cancellation. Across five learning paradigms and 80 algorithm-and-noise conditions, adaptive selection **reaches 95.5% of an oracle that always picks the best technique** and significantly outperforms all six fixed strategies. On noise models from eight real IBM devices it achieves 99.9% of oracle utility at a flat cost of roughly 13,000 shots from three to eight qubits.

papers.title: CASCADE: Constraint-Aware SCAffolded DEcomposition for Logical Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Logical Anomaly Detection (LAD) requires verifying whether all category-specific constraints, such as object counts, pairing relations, and measurement ranges, are satisfied by a query image given only a few normal references. Recent LAD methods based on Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) formulate this as checklist verification, decomposing the decision into independent textual checks. This decomposition, however, is text-only. Every item still reads the same unmodified query image, so the LVLM must extract different forms of visual evidence from one raw image. We identify this text-image mismatch as a constraint-specific perception gap, the source of two failure modes: instance conflation for binding constraints and scale drift for calibration constraints. To diagnose whether these failures stem from insufficient reasoning or insufficient perception, we compare textual reasoning guides and visual perception guides in a training-free setting. Our analysis shows that reasoning over the same image provides little benefit, whereas adapting the visual input to each constraint substantially improves verification accuracy.
