Based on this finding, we propose CASCADE, a training-free framework that extends checklist decomposition using constraint-specific visual scaffolds. We further introduce CASCADE++, which adapts these scaffolds at the object level by deriving their configurations from the constraint structure and reference distribution. Across MVTec-LOCO and VID-AD, CASCADE++ surpasses the full-shot state of the art by 3.9 AUROC points with only three references, and improves over the strongest VID-AD baseline by 11.4, transferring across multiple LVLM backbones without any training.
papers.summary: Logical Anomaly Detection (LAD) checks whether an image satisfies constraints such as object counts, pairings, and measurement ranges, and recent methods have Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) verify a textual checklist against the same unmodified image. The authors identify a constraint-specific perception gap in this setup and find that extra textual reasoning over the same image helps little, whereas adapting the visual input to each constraint substantially improves accuracy. `CASCADE` is a training-free framework that adds constraint-specific visual scaffolds to checklist decomposition, and `CASCADE++` configures those scaffolds per object from the constraint structure and reference distribution. Across `MVTec-LOCO` and `VID-AD`, `CASCADE++` **surpasses the full-shot state of the art by 3.9 AUROC points using only three reference images**.

papers.title: JAX-WAVE: A Differentiable Physics-Supervised Framework for Inverse Wave Design in Heterogeneous Media
papers.abstract: Designing a prescribed wave field in a heterogeneous medium requires an initial pressure distribution that compensates for the medium's propagation response. Repeated numerical inversion solves this task afresh for each target and environment. We introduce JAX-WAVE for amortized inverse wave design: a shared neural network maps desired terminal fields and known wave-speed maps directly to bounded initial pressures. Training through a differentiable finite-difference time-domain solver uses the physical design objective without requiring optimized control labels. Linear propagation and symmetric pressure bounds imply an exact sign-reversal relation for the regularized optimum. A shared-weight projection enforces this relation, preserves feasibility, and satisfies an exact identity for the paired-sign objective. We characterize the discrete propagator and its weighted adjoint to connect learning, numerical inversion, and optimality assessment. On an independent confirmation set, three trained models achieve unseen-material errors of 25.24% for geometric targets and 4.77% for reachable targets. Matched-capacity comparisons show improved reconstruction with the sign parameterization. Within a 5 ms median online budget, the learned map reduces mean error by 45% relative to accelerated numerical inversion on the heterogeneous benchmark; longer numerical solves recover greater accuracy. The results establish a reusable inverse-design procedure and show how its accuracy and computational value depend on target structure and query workload.
papers.summary: Producing a prescribed wave field in a heterogeneous medium requires finding an initial pressure distribution that compensates for how the medium propagates waves, which numerical inversion solves from scratch for every target. `JAX-WAVE` trains a shared neural network to map desired terminal fields and known wave-speed maps directly to bounded initial pressures, supervised by a differentiable finite-difference time-domain solver rather than by optimized control labels, and with an exact sign-reversal symmetry built into the network. On unseen materials the trained models reach errors of 25.24% for geometric targets and 4.77% for reachable targets. Within a 5 ms online budget the learned map **reduces mean error by 45% relative to accelerated numerical inversion**, though longer numerical solves recover greater accuracy.

papers.title: Ceci n'est pas une pipe -- Toward a Symbolic Solver for the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus Using Evolutionary Computation
papers.abstract: The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) is a benchmark designed to assess the capability of Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems to generalize starting from a few samples, a task humans excel at. The ARC-AGI contests held since 2020 have been the focus of intense competition, with participants proposing approaches ranging from traditional symbolic AI to Transformer architectures. Despite a long history of successes, evolutionary algorithms (EAs) were notably absent from the approaches appearing in the main contest. As score-and-search program synthesis approaches, EAs suffer from issues related to choosing the proper representation in the Domain-Specific Language applied to the problem (for example, pixel-level or object-level), and distinguishing between two candidate solutions producing the same outputs. In this work, we present the first fully symbolic, evolutionary-based program synthesis approach submitted to the ARC-AGI-2 main contest. The main contributions are: evolving the grid parser and the output projector together with the program that transforms the grid, so that a task-specific language emerges during program synthesis; grounding the symbols the parser can extract in core knowledge theory from cognitive psychology; and an object-aware fitness that grades partially correct outputs beyond pixel-level discrepancies.
papers.summary: Evolutionary algorithms (EAs) have been largely absent from the main contests on the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (`ARC`), a benchmark of generalizing from a few examples, partly because program search depends heavily on choosing the right grid representation. The authors describe **the first fully symbolic, evolutionary program synthesis approach submitted to the `ARC-AGI-2` main contest**. It evolves the grid parser and output projector together with the transformation program so that a task-specific language emerges during search, grounds the parser's symbols in core knowledge theory from cognitive psychology, and uses an object-aware fitness function that grades partially correct outputs beyond pixel-level differences.

papers.title: MusicFlux: Flexible Conditioning for Text-Guided Music Generation and Editing
papers.abstract: Music editing transforms existing recordings while preserving their original attributes. Recent approaches adapt pretrained text-to-music models for tasks like inpainting, event insertion, or restoration by conditioning them with context audio. It was recently proposed for image editing to unify generation and editing by treating the source image as in-context information. However, applying this directly to music is computationally expensive due to long audio sequences. In this work, we develop MusicFlux, a text-guided music editor built on an efficient pretrained flow-matching text-to-audio model. We introduce two conditioning approaches that trade off editing performance and computational efficiency. Experiments show that both are competitive with strong baselines, with one achieving better editing quality and the other preserving the original sequence length and substantially improving computational efficiency.
authors: Leonardo Boulitreau de Menezes Martins Marques (IP Paris
papers.summary: Text-guided music editing must transform a recording while preserving its original attributes, and treating the source audio as in-context input, as done in image editing, is computationally expensive for long audio sequences. `MusicFlux` builds a music editor on an efficient pretrained flow-matching text-to-audio model and introduces two ways of conditioning on the source that trade editing performance against compute. Both are **competitive with strong baselines**: one achieves better editing quality, while the other preserves the original sequence length and substantially improves computational efficiency.

papers.title: PolyRoute: A Twelve-Language and Code-Mixed Benchmark for Typed-Decision Routing, with Baselines and a Leaderboard
papers.abstract: Typed-decision encoders answer a question about a text in one forward pass, but their behaviour outside English is rarely measured on a fixed yardstick. We release PolyRoute: 322 native-language support messages in 12 languages and 9 writing systems, 156 code-mixed or romanised messages (Hinglish, Spanglish, Arabizi), 967 optional native training rows, and a protocol for a three-way department-routing decision. Labels come from Qwen3.8-27B with a blind second pass (91% of candidates kept); an independent model, gemma4-31b, agrees on 97.2% of test items, and the largest character 5-gram similarity between any test text and any training text is 0.33. A leaderboard of 13 systems gives 61.2% for the English-root checkpoint, 77.3% for the shipped multilingual one and 96.6% for the best fine-tune; TF-IDF with logistic regression reaches 91.9%. On four withheld languages the three multilingual systems score 77%, 90% and 93%. On code-mixed text the English root (85%) is nominally ahead of the shipped multilingual checkpoint (79%; p=0.134). The split resolves differences only above about 4 points. All texts and labels are LLM-generated.
papers.summary: `PolyRoute` is a benchmark for how well single-pass text classifiers route customer support messages to one of three departments outside English, comprising 322 messages in 12 languages and 9 writing systems, 156 code-mixed or romanised messages such as Hinglish and Arabizi, and 967 optional training rows. Labels come from `Qwen3.8-27B` with a blind second pass, and an independent model, `gemma4-31b`, agrees on 97.2% of test items. A leaderboard of 13 systems gives 61.2% for an English-root checkpoint, 77.3% for the shipped multilingual one, and **96.6% for the best fine-tune, while TF-IDF with logistic regression reaches 91.9%**. All texts and labels are LLM-generated, and the test split only resolves differences above about 4 points.

papers.title: Alania-2: Turkish text-to-speech with instant and fine-tuned voice cloning
papers.abstract: We present Alania-2, a Turkish text-to-speech (TTS) system with two built-in voices, voice design from text descriptions, and two kinds of voice cloning. Alania-2 is a 488M-parameter model with the VoxCPM architecture, which generates continuous audio latents with a diffusion head on top of a language-model backbone. We train it from scratch on 18,195 hours of Turkish speech, 90% of which is synthetic speech produced by a larger teacher model and filtered automatically. A text normalizer rewrites numbers, abbreviations and foreign names into the words a Turkish speaker would say; without it, none of 96 test sentences with digits kept all its critical parts, such as an amount or a date, through synthesis and speech recognition, against 86 with it. On Freya-TR-Eval, a public benchmark of 495 Turkish sentences scored with automatic speech recognition, Alania-2 reaches a word error rate of 1.44%, compared with 5.99% for our previous system. On its built-in voices, it comes within half a point of character error rate of a 2.3B-parameter model at under a quarter of the size, and a 7.6M-parameter single-voice model trained with the same recipe matches the most intelligible systems we measured, which suggests that training data matters more for intelligibility than model size. We also report practical findings on voice cloning: conditioning on the reference audio alone, rather than continuing it, cuts skipped words from 21.9% to 1.7%; 20-30 seconds of reference audio works best; and a low-rank adapter trained in about two minutes raises speaker similarity well above instant cloning. Finally, we describe inference-engine changes that bring first audio down to 32 ms for a single stream. We release our evaluation harness and three Turkish speech and text datasets.
papers.summary: `Alania-2` is a 488M-parameter Turkish text-to-speech (TTS) system built on the `VoxCPM` architecture, offering two built-in voices, voice design from text descriptions, and both instant and fine-tuned voice cloning. It is trained from scratch on 18,195 hours of Turkish speech, 90% of it synthetic output from a larger teacher model, and paired with a text normalizer that rewrites numbers, abbreviations, and foreign names into spoken Turkish. On the `Freya-TR-Eval` benchmark it reaches a **word error rate of 1.44%, compared with 5.99% for the authors' previous system**, and comes within half a point of character error rate of a 2.3B-parameter model. For cloning, conditioning on the reference audio alone instead of continuing it cuts skipped words from 21.9% to 1.7%, and a low-rank adapter trained in about two minutes raises speaker similarity well above instant cloning.

papers.title: Optimal Last-Iterate Bounds for Nonexpansive Stochastic Approximation
papers.abstract: We establish last-iterate mean-square residual bounds for nonexpansive stochastic approximation (SA), or stochastic Krasnoselskii-Mann (KM) iterations. In particular, we consider fixed-point mappings that are nonexpansive with respect to the Euclidean norm, and focus on polynomially decaying stepsizes. We study three conditions on the conditional second moment of the noise, and obtain bounds that are optimal up to logarithmic factors in each case. When it scales linearly with the squared residual, the best rate is $O(1/k^{1-\epsilon})$ for any $\epsilon>0$. In this case, for all considered stepsizes, our bounds match those of the noiseless KM iteration. When it is bounded by a constant, the best rate is $O(\log^2 k/\sqrt{k})$. When it scales affinely with the squared norm of the iterate, the best rate is $O(1/k^{1/2-\epsilon})$, and the mean-square residual can diverge if the stepsizes are not square-summable. Thus, unlike for contractive SA, square-summable stepsizes are necessary for nonexpansive SA. We demonstrate how various algorithms with cocoercive maps, such as stochastic gradient descent, linear SA, and learning in cocoercive games, fit into our framework, and how the different noise conditions arise in each of them.
papers.summary: Last-iterate mean-square residual bounds are established for stochastic Krasnoselskii-Mann (KM) iterations, that is, stochastic approximation (SA) with a fixed-point mapping that is nonexpansive in the Euclidean norm, under polynomially decaying stepsizes. Three conditions on the noise's conditional second moment are analyzed, each with bounds optimal up to logarithmic factors: nearly O(1/k) when noise scales with the squared residual, O(log^2 k / sqrt(k)) when it is bounded by a constant, and nearly O(1/sqrt(k)) when it scales affinely with the squared iterate norm. In the last case the residual can diverge without square-summable stepsizes, so **square-summable stepsizes are necessary for nonexpansive SA, unlike for contractive SA**. The framework covers stochastic gradient descent, linear SA, and learning in cocoercive games.

papers.title: Satellite Pretraining Is Not One Thing: A Matched-Pair Study of Generic and Earth-Observation Foundation Models for Scene Classification
papers.abstract: Geospatial foundation models are pretrained on satellite and aerial imagery, but whether such an encoder beats a strong generic one for few-label land-use/land-cover mapping remains unclear, as prior comparisons rarely isolate the pretraining data. We study five matched pairs of Earth-observation (EO) and generic encoders sharing objective and architecture (DINO/SatDINO, DINOv3/DINOv3-SAT, MAE/SatMAE, MAE/Scale-MAE, CLIP/RemoteCLIP) within a benchmark of 14 frozen encoders on five RGB scene-classification datasets (0.06-30 m GSD). With native preprocessing, we evaluate k-NN, linear and attentive probes and image retrieval over six low-label splits, using paired per-image significance tests. EO pretraining is not uniformly helpful: on most datasets and metrics, it significantly improves three pairs (SatDINO, Scale-MAE, RemoteCLIP, the latter evaluated only on unseen datasets) and significantly hurts two (linear probe: DINOv3-SAT by up to 22.5 points, SatMAE by up to 8.8), with opposite outcomes even for two MAEs pretrained on the same fMoW-RGB imagery. These effects are robust to patch-token pooling and attentive probing, concentrate on small man-made objects, and are largest with 1-5% labels. Across encoders, the silhouette score of frozen embeddings predicts k-NN accuracy and retrieval mAP almost perfectly (Spearman $\rho \geq 0.96$ on four of five datasets). Pretraining on satellite imagery is thus not a reliable selection criterion; candidate checkpoints must be validated on target data.
papers.summary: Whether encoders pretrained on satellite imagery actually beat strong generic encoders for few-label land-use and land-cover classification is tested by comparing five matched pairs of Earth-observation (EO) and generic models that share objective and architecture, within a benchmark of 14 frozen encoders on five RGB scene-classification datasets. Using k-NN, linear and attentive probes plus image retrieval, the study finds that **EO pretraining significantly helps three pairs (`SatDINO`, `Scale-MAE`, `RemoteCLIP`) and significantly hurts two (`DINOv3-SAT` by up to 22.5 linear-probe points, `SatMAE` by up to 8.8)**, with opposite outcomes even for two masked autoencoders pretrained on the same `fMoW-RGB` imagery. The effects concentrate on small man-made objects and are largest with 1-5% of labels, and the silhouette score of frozen embeddings predicts k-NN accuracy and retrieval quality almost perfectly (Spearman correlation of at least 0.96 on four of five datasets). The authors conclude that satellite pretraining is not a reliable selection criterion and that candidate checkpoints must be validated on target data.

papers.title: Taxonomy-Agnostic Neurosymbolic Grounding of Robot Kinematics
papers.abstract: While symbolic reasoning for task allocation requires grounding a robot's physical capabilities, standard Unified Robot Description Format (URDF) files provide only low-level kinematics without the formal semantic context needed for reasoning. We present URDF2Ontology, an automated, taxonomy-agnostic neurosymbolic framework that transforms raw URDF files into populated, grounded OWL ontologies. It leverages a Large Language Model (LLM) for targeted semantic reasoning, coupled with an iterative sequential graph-purging mechanism to prevent context window saturation. To process complex kinematic structures, it employs a morphology-aware dual-track architecture featuring a bottom-up Tree Track for branching assemblies and a top-down Chain Track for serial limbs. Guided by neurosymbolic guardrails, the framework extracts functional sub-graphs and asserts populated ontologies aligned with arbitrary user-provided taxonomies. Empirical evaluation across a diverse fleet of heterogeneous robots demonstrates strong schema alignment, valid structural extraction, and a significant reduction in manual domain authoring overhead.
papers.summary: Unified Robot Description Format (URDF) files describe a robot's low-level kinematics but lack the semantic context that symbolic task-allocation reasoning needs. `URDF2Ontology` converts raw URDF files into populated OWL ontologies aligned with any user-provided taxonomy, using a large language model for targeted semantic reasoning, an iterative graph-purging step to avoid saturating the context window, and a dual-track design with a bottom-up Tree Track for branching assemblies and a top-down Chain Track for serial limbs. Evaluation on a fleet of heterogeneous robots is reported to show **strong schema alignment, valid structural extraction, and a significant reduction in manual domain authoring effort**, though the abstract gives no figures.

papers.title: Beyond Passive Imitation: On-Policy Mid-Training Distillation for Language Models
papers.abstract: Continual pre-training (CPT) adapts large language models (LLMs) to specialized domains, yet its standard next-token prediction (NTP) objective treats every corpus token as a fixed target, regardless of its utility to the current model. In a controlled study on the same 1B-token mathematical corpus, we observe sharply different outcomes across base models: NTP improves Llama-3.2-3B's performance on mathematical benchmarks but substantially degrades Qwen3-1.7B-Base's performance, indicating that, under a fixed training recipe, the same training sequences can have model-dependent effects. To address this problem, we introduce On-Policy Mid-Training Distillation (OPMD), which reformulates mid-training from offline text imitation into active, query-driven knowledge acquisition. At selected anchor positions, OPMD samples trajectories from the evolving student policy and applies dense token-level reverse-KL rewards from a frozen teacher, training the model on states it actually visits rather than only on ground-truth prefixes. This on-policy objective reduces the training-generation mismatch of teacher-forced NTP. On MATH-500 and Minerva, OPMD improves the Qwen student over its base performance and outperforms the evaluated NTP baseline, which degrades on both benchmarks. OPMD integrates into CPT pipelines without added inference-time overhead and offers a model-aware alternative to passive domain adaptation.
papers.summary: Continual pre-training (CPT) with standard next-token prediction (NTP) treats every corpus token as a fixed target, and a controlled study on a 1B-token mathematical corpus shows the same recipe improves `Llama-3.2-3B` on math benchmarks while substantially degrading `Qwen3-1.7B-Base`. On-Policy Mid-Training Distillation (`OPMD`) instead samples trajectories from the evolving student at selected anchor positions and applies dense token-level reverse-KL rewards from a frozen teacher, so the model trains on states it actually visits rather than only on ground-truth prefixes. On `MATH-500` and `Minerva`, **`OPMD` improves the Qwen student over its base performance while the NTP baseline degrades on both benchmarks**, with no added inference-time overhead.

papers.title: Where to Approximate in Neurosymbolic Inference?
papers.abstract: Probabilistic neurosymbolic methods rely on weighted model counting (WMC) to combine neural predictors with symbolic constraints. Exact WMC is #P-hard and typically scales poorly, so many methods resort to approximations. By unifying existing approaches under a three-step bottom-up approximate compilation pipeline, we study where approximation budget is best allocated. Inspired by tensor networks, we instantiate two steps with tensor train decompositions and derive new pipelines that exactly multiply approximated factors and recompress their products via SVD- or interpolation-based schemes. Across six tasks in Sudoku, arithmetic reasoning, and scene understanding, and across increasing problem sizes, our pipelines produce WMC estimates orders-of-magnitude more accurate than prior methods. This translates into stronger downstream learning on tasks where reasoning relies on tight interactions between symbolic factors, where cruder approximations ignore these dependencies. Our pipelines open novel design space for effective approximate compilation of challenging probabilistic reasoning tasks.
papers.summary: Probabilistic neurosymbolic methods combine neural predictors with symbolic constraints through weighted model counting (WMC), which is #P-hard to compute exactly and so is usually approximated. The authors unify existing approaches under a three-step bottom-up approximate compilation pipeline and ask where the approximation budget is best spent, instantiating two steps with tensor train decompositions that exactly multiply approximated factors and then recompress the products using SVD- or interpolation-based schemes. Across six tasks in Sudoku, arithmetic reasoning, and scene understanding, the new pipelines give **WMC estimates orders of magnitude more accurate than prior methods**, which translates into stronger downstream learning on tasks where symbolic factors interact tightly.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Deep Neural Networks: Methods, Frameworks, and Perspectives
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks underpin fundamental tasks in a wide range of signal domains, such as image, audio, and language processing. However, their internal mechanisms are notably difficult to interpret. Internal activations are structured signals transformed across layers that may encode a multitude of interdependent relationships, as individual neurons frequently represent multiple underlying concepts. Mechanistic interpretability aims to uncover the internal mechanisms of neural networks by identifying components whose activations are causally responsible for specific behaviors. In such a context, this article provides an overview of advances in mechanistic interpretability for the analysis of causal inference in deep neural networks.
papers.summary: Internal activations of deep neural networks are hard to interpret, in part because individual neurons frequently represent several underlying concepts at once. This overview article surveys advances in mechanistic interpretability, a field that **aims to identify the components whose activations are causally responsible for specific model behaviors**, covering methods, frameworks, and perspectives across image, audio, and language domains.

papers.title: Outliers and the Hard-Margin Linear SVM in High-Dimension, Low-Sample-Size Settings
papers.abstract: We study how outliers affect the hard-margin linear support vector machine when the dimension grows while the sample sizes remain fixed. For one-sided contamination, the centered Gram matrix converges to a constant inlier block plus an outlier-diagonal component, and the limiting dual problem has a closed-form solution. All outliers act through one effective distance. This representation yields explicit thresholds for loss of inlier support, margin shrinkage. intercept displacement, and asymptotic misclassification. We then treat contamination in both classes. The limiting intercept is the multiplier of the class-balance constraint, and the two classes pull it in opposite directions. Consequently, at most one class can collapse or be asymptotically misclassified, whereas symmetric contamination leaves the limiting discriminant function unchanged even though the margin shrinks. Seven numerical experiments verify the dual allocation, phase transitions, and discriminant limits.
papers.summary: The effect of outliers on the hard-margin linear support vector machine is analyzed in the regime where dimension grows while sample sizes stay fixed. For contamination in one class, the centered Gram matrix converges to a constant inlier block plus an outlier-diagonal component, the limiting dual problem has a closed-form solution, and all outliers act through a single effective distance, giving explicit thresholds for loss of inlier support, margin shrinkage, intercept displacement, and asymptotic misclassification. With contamination in both classes, **at most one class can collapse or be asymptotically misclassified, and symmetric contamination leaves the limiting discriminant function unchanged even though the margin shrinks**. Seven numerical experiments check the dual allocation, phase transitions, and discriminant limits.

papers.title: Transparency Disclosures for Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is one of the most valuable tools for monitoring advanced AI systems, but it is under threat. We argue that frontier AI developers should report specific indicators to make these threats trackable and to better facilitate coordination to preserve CoT monitorability. We identify five indicators that are both highly relevant and reasonably feasible to disclose, one for each link in a five-step chain on which CoT monitoring depends. The first, third-party CoT access and base architecture specifications, also underpins external verification of the rest. The others span CoT quality (naturalness and faithfulness) and monitoring effectiveness (detection and uplift). An audit of current disclosures by Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google DeepMind shows that no developer covers the full set, but that every indicator has been reported by at least one frontier developer. Because current disclosures rely largely on developers' own evaluations, we also recommend that a cross-developer audit be repeated with deeper access than public disclosures allow, either by embedded evaluators working within developers or by an Independent Verification Organization.
papers.summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is used to oversee advanced AI systems, and the authors argue that frontier developers should publicly report specific indicators so that threats to it can be tracked. They propose five indicators, one for each link in a five-step chain that CoT monitoring depends on: third-party CoT access and base architecture specifications, CoT naturalness and faithfulness, and monitor detection and uplift. An audit of current disclosures from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google DeepMind finds that **no developer covers the full set, but every indicator has been reported by at least one of them**. Because disclosures rest largely on developers' own evaluations, the authors also recommend repeating the audit with deeper access through embedded evaluators or an Independent Verification Organization.

papers.title: Region-Wise Logit Fusion and Utility-Gated Refinement for Brain Metastasis Segmentation
papers.abstract: BraTS-METS 2026 Task 1 evaluates segmentation of brain metastases and postoperative resection cavities on heterogeneous multiparametric MRI, requiring detection of small enhancing foci while preserving the geometry and hierarchy of enhancing tumor (ET), tumor core (TC), whole tumor (WT), and resection cavity (RC). We present COMPASS-METS (Component-Aware Multi-Trainer Probability Assembly with Structured Segmentation), which combines three five-fold nnU-Net configurations into aligned regional probability ensembles. A structured-probability anchor applies region-specific component decisions, TC boundary completion, RC filtering, and hierarchy-preserving conversion. Omitted ET candidates are recovered additively using learned component confidence and deterministic multi-trainer support for ET and its TC/WT parents; a final utility gate admits only disconnected candidates with sufficient lesion-existence and geometry-safety probabilities. On the reused 179-case challenge development cohort, COMPASS-METS (Team: MicroBT) achieved Small F1 0.354, lesion-wise DSC 0.712, NSD 0.714, All F1 0.779, and HD95 56.6 mm. Relative to ResEncXL, it improved DSC, NSD, and All F1 and reduced HD95, while Small F1 changed from 0.367 to 0.354. Stagewise analysis attributes the principal geometric gains to structured probability construction and shows that guarded ET refinement recovers most of the associated small-lesion detection loss. These 179-case results remain selection-aware development estimates. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/leonlou921/COMPASS-METS.
papers.summary: Segmenting brain metastases and postoperative resection cavities on heterogeneous multiparametric MRI, as posed by `BraTS-METS 2026` Task 1, requires detecting small enhancing foci while keeping the hierarchy of tumor regions consistent. `COMPASS-METS` ensembles three five-fold `nnU-Net` configurations into aligned regional probability maps, applies region-specific component decisions and hierarchy-preserving conversion, and then additively recovers omitted enhancing-tumor candidates through a utility gate that checks lesion-existence and geometry-safety probabilities. On the 179-case development cohort it reaches **lesion-wise Dice of 0.712 and All F1 of 0.779, improving on `ResEncXL` in Dice, surface distance, and All F1 while Small F1 slips from 0.367 to 0.354**. The authors note these figures are selection-aware development estimates rather than held-out results.

papers.title: Are Causal Neuron Circuits Unique and Transferable?
papers.abstract: Interpretability demonstrations often show that intervening on a group of neurons changes a model's answer. A recent example removes an 18-neuron group in Qwen3-32B and the model answers "Simba" instead of "Scar" to a two-hop Lion King riddle. Such a demonstration establishes that the group matters, but not how much of it is necessary, whether other groups could do the same, or whether the effect carries over to other inputs. We ask: when intervening on a group of neurons changes a model's answer, how much of that group is actually necessary? For every selected group we measure all 4,096 subsets of 12 MLP neurons. On a two-alternative capital task (Qwen3-0.6B), zero-ablating 12 selected neurons lowers the answer margin by 27% while random neurons barely change it, yet replacing the same neurons with their values from other questions also barely changes it: their activations are nearly constant across questions, and we find no evidence that they carry question-specific content. On two-hop relation chains, patching 12 neurons with activations from the first-hop question shifts the answer to the bridge entity (from Scar to Simba): the greedy answer starts with the bridge in 9/11 chains for Qwen3-1.7B, 9/11 for Llama-3.2-1B and 8/10 for Gemma-3-1B; random neurons never do. The full group is rarely necessary: a few neurons often suffice, and in many chains disjoint subsets each flip the answer on their own, in an exploratory analysis most often when the model is less confident. Group effects transfer to rephrasings of the same chain but are much weaker on other tested chains. We study neuron-level causal interventions and alternative subsets; we do not recover the full connectivity of circuits.
papers.summary: Interpretability demonstrations often show that intervening on a group of neurons changes a model's answer, without establishing how much of the group is needed, whether other groups would work, or whether the effect generalizes. This study exhaustively measures all 4,096 subsets of 12 selected MLP neurons in small `Qwen3`, `Llama-3.2-1B`, and `Gemma-3-1B` models on a capital-city task and on two-hop relation chains. Patching 12 neurons with first-hop activations shifts the answer to the bridge entity in roughly 8 or 9 of every 10 or 11 chains while random neurons never do, yet **the full group is rarely necessary: a few neurons often suffice, and disjoint subsets can each flip the answer on their own**. Group effects transfer to rephrasings of the same chain but are much weaker on other chains, and on the capital task the ablated neurons turn out to have nearly constant activations with no evidence of question-specific content.

papers.title: Conformal Risk Control for QoT-Aware Lightpath Feasibility Under Technology-Driven Domain Shift
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML)-based regression models support operational decision-making in optical networks but typically expose only point predictions, which carry no statistically controlled information about their reliability. This paper proposes a post-hoc conformal risk control (CRC) framework that keeps a pretrained AI/ML regressor fixed, provides a finite-sample guarantee on uncertainty band miscoverage, and maps the band to operational decisions through policy rules. The guarantee applies to interval miscoverage, while decision-error rates are evaluated empirically. We instantiate the framework for quality of transmission (QoT)-aware lightpath (LP) feasibility assessment, in which a regressor predicts optical signal-to-noise ratio (OSNR) under domain shifts caused by fiber, amplifier, and switching upgrades. Feature shift contribution scores identify the LP features whose relation to QoT changes the most across a technology transition, and two policies translate the bands into feasibility decisions, allowing operators to tune the trade-off between conservatively rejecting or aggressively accepting LP realizations. Experiments on open space-division multiplexing (SDM) QoT datasets over the CONUS topology show that, for a target coverage of 90%, the uncertainty bands meet the target in all 170 trials spanning 17 domain shifts and ten calibration-test partitions, whereas a source-only quantile regression (QR) baseline meets it in none. Under severe shifts, the efficiency-oriented (EO) policy empirically improves zero-shot (ZS) feasibility-decision accuracy from about 85% to above 99%, approaching a transfer learning (TL) policy while avoiding retraining. The framework provides finite-sample control of uncertainty band miscoverage for regression-based optical network decision support, with potential applications beyond QoT-aware LP feasibility assessment.
papers.summary: Machine-learning regressors used for optical network decisions typically give point predictions with no statistically controlled reliability information. A post-hoc conformal risk control (CRC) framework keeps a pretrained regressor fixed, provides a finite-sample guarantee on uncertainty-band miscoverage, and maps the bands to decisions through policy rules, instantiated here for quality of transmission (QoT)-aware lightpath feasibility where optical signal-to-noise ratio is predicted under shifts caused by fiber, amplifier, and switching upgrades. On open space-division multiplexing QoT datasets over the `CONUS` topology with a 90% coverage target, **the bands meet the target in all 170 trials spanning 17 domain shifts, whereas a source-only quantile regression baseline meets it in none**. Under severe shifts, the efficiency-oriented policy raises zero-shot feasibility-decision accuracy from about 85% to above 99% without retraining.

papers.title: Beyond Fluent Responses: Finding User Dissatisfaction in Human-AI Interactions
papers.abstract: As large language models generate increasingly high-quality responses, recent work on response evaluation has moved beyond response-centered criteria, such as correctness and coherence, toward user-centered criteria, including user preferences and perceived usefulness. This shift is fundamentally important for developing technologies that are truly useful to real-world users. While conventional response evaluation quantifies the quality of the response itself, users' satisfaction in real conversations also depends on their subjective preferences and perceptions of usefulness, which do not necessarily align with response quality. This study investigates whether such user-centered signals can be detected from conversational text. Specifically, we analyze user utterances with self-reported dissatisfaction labels to examine whether user dissatisfaction in text can be detected. In English interaction, models using user utterances exceeded the 17.8% dissatisfaction label prevalence in AUPRC by up to 15 percentage points. These results suggest that user utterances reveal cues to implicit dissatisfaction. Furthermore, changes from the immediately preceding user utterance may improve dissatisfaction detection, with anomaly detection methods appearing particularly effective.
papers.summary: User satisfaction with large language model responses depends on subjective preferences and perceived usefulness, which do not necessarily track response quality. The study tests whether dissatisfaction can be detected from the text of user utterances, using conversations with self-reported dissatisfaction labels. In English interactions, **models using user utterances exceeded the 17.8% label-prevalence baseline in AUPRC by up to 15 percentage points**, suggesting that utterances carry cues to implicit dissatisfaction. Changes relative to the immediately preceding user utterance may help further, with anomaly detection methods appearing particularly effective.

papers.title: Target Selection with a Disappearing-Stimulus Mixed-Reality P300 Interface: Feasibility and Object-Distinguishable Versus Uniform Cues
papers.abstract: Mixed-reality (MR) P300 interfaces can register selectable destinations, such as wheelchair goals, directly in the user's surroundings. When the cues disappear between flashes, however, the user must retain an intended target that is no longer visible. We tested whether such an interface supports target selection and whether giving each cue a stable colour-shape identity improves it compared with visually uniform spheres. Six healthy adults completed four trials in each cue condition of a 5x5 row/column task on a head-mounted MR display, with EEG from Fz, Cz, and Pz. Shrinkage linear discriminant analysis was evaluated with nested validation in which complete trials were held out from class balancing, hyperparameter selection, and fitting. Both conditions evoked a parietal target-related positivity. The decoded cell was correct in 18 of 48 held-out trials, against 1.9 expected by chance (binomial p < 1e-12), and in three participants individually. Cue format made no detectable difference: complete-target accuracy was 9/24 in both conditions (paired difference 0.0 percentage points, 95% CI [-37, 37]), and held-out AUC was 0.609 for spheres and 0.585 for object cues. Disappearing-stimulus MR P300 selection is therefore feasible under strict trial-level evaluation, but the benefit of object identity, if any, is too small to resolve in a pilot of this size.
papers.summary: Mixed-reality (MR) brain-computer interfaces based on the P300 brain response can place selectable targets such as wheelchair destinations in the user's surroundings, but when cues disappear between flashes the user must remember a target that is no longer visible. A pilot with six healthy adults tested a 5x5 row/column selection task on a head-mounted display with three EEG channels, comparing cues with stable colour-shape identities against uniform spheres and decoding with shrinkage linear discriminant analysis under nested trial-level validation. **The decoded cell was correct in 18 of 48 held-out trials against 1.9 expected by chance**, while cue format made no detectable difference (9 of 24 correct in both conditions). The authors conclude that selection is feasible but any benefit of object identity is too small to resolve at this sample size.

papers.title: MicroBT: Centroid-Guided Synergistic Learning for Multi-Modal Micro Brain Tumor Segmentation and Counting
papers.abstract: Multi-modal brain tumor segmentation is essential for clinical diagnosis, radiotherapy planning, and longitudinal monitoring. While recent studies have achieved remarkable overall segmentation performance, they rely on overlap-based objectives that inherently favor large regions, causing sub-3 mm micro-lesions to be systematically suppressed during training. Moreover, existing pixel-level segmentation frameworks lack explicit instance-level modeling, leading to unreliable lesion counting that directly impacts clinical staging and therapeutic decisions. To address these challenges, we propose MicroBT, a unified multi-modal framework for micro brain tumor segmentation and counting. Our core insight is that a fundamental geometric property is inherently scale-invariant: regardless of size, each lesion possesses a well-defined centroid. Leveraging this, we first devise a centroid-anchored synergistic paradigm that utilizes predicted centroids as shared anchors to simultaneously condition dense segmentation and instance-level localization. To counteract the tumor size imbalance, we further devise a Volume-Calibrated Loss (VC-Loss) that adaptively amplifies the gradient contribution of micro-lesions, alongside a Size-Aware Curriculum Optimization (SACO) that stabilizes multi-task training by establishing global representations before progressively unlocking fine-grained localization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MicroBT outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly on metastases, where micro-lesion ($\leq 3$ mm) localization precision improves by approximately 7% and counting estimation errors decrease by approximately 26%. The code is available at https://github.com/leonlou921/MicroBT.
papers.summary: Overlap-based training objectives for brain tumor segmentation favor large regions, so lesions under 3 mm tend to be suppressed, and pixel-level frameworks lack the instance-level modeling needed for reliable lesion counting. `MicroBT` uses predicted lesion centroids as shared anchors that condition both dense segmentation and instance localization, paired with a Volume-Calibrated Loss (`VC-Loss`) that amplifies gradients from tiny lesions and a Size-Aware Curriculum Optimization (`SACO`) schedule that learns global representations before fine-grained localization. The authors report gains over prior methods, particularly on metastases, where **localization precision for lesions of 3 mm or smaller improves by about 7% and counting error falls by about 26%**.

papers.title: Learning from First Discrepancies with Joint Reset and Pilot Guarantees
papers.abstract: A run that stops at its first wrong decision shows the queries and their correct labels up to and including that decision, and nothing after it. We study how many such runs are needed for learning. Each run tests a hypothesis, the pilot, chosen beforehand from a fixed binary class of VC dimension at most $d$, on a fresh record of at most $D$ queries drawn from one unknown distribution that does not depend on the pilot. The terminal information of a record is shown only if the pilot makes no discrepancy, and a bounded loss, fixed in advance, is attached to the position where a hypothesis stops. If the discrepancy probabilities of members of the class have infimum at most $f$ and their risks have infimum at most $r$, one learner uses $\widetilde O((d+1)[D(f+\varepsilon)+r]/\varepsilon^2)$ runs and $\widetilde O(D(1+f/\varepsilon))$ distinct pilots on every history. It returns a member of the class and an interval of width at most $\varepsilon$ containing, with probability at least $1-\delta$, both the output's risk and the optimal risk. We also treat unknown ceilings and expected costs. Lower bounds for finite classes show that each order is necessary in the worst case, possibly on different instances, at positive dimension, small accuracy and fixed confidence. The learner enumerates label patterns of the class on displayed queries, possibly in exponential time; the results, under standard measurability conditions, concern statistical resources only. The proof combines a gain computable from stopped displays, exponential weights, a sparse depth-robust graph and a harmonic-mean bound.
papers.summary: The sample complexity of learning is studied in a setting where each run tests a pre-chosen hypothesis (the pilot) on a fresh sequence of at most D queries and stops at the first wrong decision, revealing queries and correct labels only up to that point. For a binary class of VC dimension at most d, with best discrepancy probability f and best risk r, the authors give a learner that **needs on the order of (d+1)[D(f+epsilon)+r]/epsilon^2 runs, up to logarithmic factors**, and returns a hypothesis together with an interval of width at most epsilon that contains both its risk and the optimal risk with high probability. Lower bounds for finite classes show each term is necessary in the worst case. The learner may take exponential time, so the results concern statistical resources only.

papers.title: From Counterfactual Edits to Human Narratives: LLM-Driven Interpretations for Recommender System Explanations
papers.abstract: Recommender systems increasingly influence what users discover and consume online, yet the decision logic behind their outputs often remains opaque. Counterfactual explanation (CFX) methods provide an effective way to show which changes to a user's interaction history would alter a recommendation. In recommendation settings, however, CFXs often require many edits, producing long, low-level lists that are hard for users to interpret. Moreover, most evaluations emphasize edit counts while largely overlooking whether the resulting CFXs are coherent and actionable for users. We argue that this gap between generating valid CFXs and communicating model behavior stems from the lack of user-centered abstraction and limited qualitative evaluation. To bridge this gap, we investigate large language models as mediators that summarize raw CFX interaction edit lists into concise natural language explanations describing higher-level preference patterns. We optimize these mediators for correctness, informativeness, and linguistic quality through preference optimization, and evaluate the resulting explanations with human-calibrated metrics derived from separate human-labeled datasets. On the MovieLens-1M dataset, across multiple counterfactual generators and language models, the resulting summaries achieve high overall linguistic quality, while the strongest semantic results are obtained with high-success CFX methods such as ACCENT and SPINRec. Direct Preference Optimization improves the semantic metrics in almost all evaluated settings.
papers.summary: Counterfactual explanation (CFX) methods for recommender systems show which changes to a user's interaction history would alter a recommendation, but they often produce long, low-level edit lists that are hard to interpret. The authors use large language models as mediators that summarize these edit lists into concise natural-language explanations of higher-level preference patterns, tune them with preference optimization for correctness, informativeness, and linguistic quality, and evaluate with human-calibrated metrics. On `MovieLens-1M`, summaries achieve high linguistic quality across counterfactual generators and language models, the strongest semantic results come from high-success CFX methods such as `ACCENT` and `SPINRec`, and **Direct Preference Optimization improves the semantic metrics in almost all evaluated settings**.

papers.title: Dual-Space Preconditioning for Variational Inequalities and Root-Finding Problems
papers.abstract: This paper develops a dual-space preconditioning framework for variational inequalities and root-finding problems beyond classical cocoercivity and Lipschitz continuity assumptions. To this end, we introduce both a novel cocoercivity-type condition and a relaxed Lipschitz continuity condition, and derive convergence of deterministic and stochastic methods under these generalized conditions. For isotropic preconditioners, the resulting algorithms can be interpreted as variable-stepsize variants of classical methods, extending recent analyses based on $(L_0, L_1)$-type growth conditions while allowing simpler proofs and larger stepsize ranges. We also show that the framework naturally handles variational inequalities through weak Minty-type arguments. Finally, we study the associated continuous-time dynamics and derive a variational and optimal control interpretation of the preconditioned flow. Overall, the results show that dual-space preconditioning provides a flexible mechanism for designing and analyzing operator methods beyond the standard Euclidean Lipschitz setting.
papers.summary: A dual-space preconditioning framework is developed for variational inequalities and root-finding problems that fall outside the classical cocoercivity and Lipschitz continuity assumptions. The authors introduce a new cocoercivity-type condition and a relaxed Lipschitz condition, and prove convergence of deterministic and stochastic methods under them. With isotropic preconditioners the algorithms become variable-stepsize variants of classical methods, **extending recent (L0, L1)-type growth analyses while allowing simpler proofs and larger stepsize ranges**. The work also handles variational inequalities through weak Minty-type arguments and gives a variational and optimal control interpretation of the associated continuous-time flow.

papers.title: CAppleNet: A Coordinate Attention-Based YOLO11 for Real-Time Apple Stem Cavity and Calyx Detection
papers.abstract: Automated fruit grading, sorting, and orientation systems require real-time, accurate detection of fruit-level morphological landmarks rather than the fruit boundary alone. This paper presents a custom, fully self-collected and self-annotated dataset of 1506 apple images (1054 training, 301 validation, 151 test) captured under controlled, fixed-camera conditions and annotated for three target classes: fruit body, stem cavity, and calyx. A YOLO11s detector trained with default hyperparameters is adopted as the baseline, and a systematic, one-factor-at-a-time ablation study is conducted across input resolution, data augmentation policy, optimizer configuration, and lightweight architectural enhancement to identify the factors that most improve detection of these fine-grained landmarks under high inter-cultivar color and texture variability. Neither increased input resolution, nor any of six tested augmentation variants, nor manual optimizer tuning improved on the untuned baseline (F1 = 0.9047); only a same-slot architectural substitution of the backbone's C2PSA block with Coordinate Attention (CA) matched the baseline's overall F1 (0.9038) while reducing parameter count by 10.2% and achieving the study's best mAP@0.5 (0.935) and best stem-cavity F1 (0.8217). A confidence-threshold sweep identified 0.15 as the deployment operating point for this model, and a confirmatory experiment combining the CA-swap architecture with the best-performing augmentation variant showed the two effects do not combine additively, reversing the architectural gain rather than compounding it. The resulting design recommendations --- the CA-swap architecture alone, at a 0.15 confidence threshold --- target real-time apple landmark detection for orientation-aware industrial sorting and alignment systems.
papers.summary: Automated apple grading and orientation systems need real-time detection of the stem cavity and calyx, not just the fruit outline. Using a self-collected dataset of 1,506 annotated apple images, the authors run a one-factor-at-a-time ablation over input resolution, augmentation, optimizer settings, and architecture on a `YOLO11s` baseline. **None of the resolution, augmentation, or optimizer changes beat the untuned baseline (F1 of 0.9047)**; only swapping the backbone's `C2PSA` block for Coordinate Attention matched it (F1 of 0.9038) while cutting parameters by 10.2% and giving the best mAP@0.5 of 0.935. Combining that swap with the best augmentation variant reversed the gain rather than compounding it.

papers.title: Domain-Invariant and Language-Model-Assisted Acoustic Side-Channel Attacks on Keyboards
papers.abstract: Acoustic side-channel attacks (ASCA) recover typed text from the sound of keystrokes, using only a commodity microphone and no access to the victim's device. Prior work establishes that such attacks succeed under idealized laboratory conditions - a single keyboard, a fixed microphone, a quiet room, and training and testing on the same device but leaves open the question that matters for security: whether keystroke inference survives the open world of unseen keyboards, diverse users, noisy environments, and compressed transmission channels. The answer developed here is that it does, provided the acoustic model is made explicitly domain-invariant and its noisy predictions are corrected by a language model.
papers.summary: Acoustic side-channel attacks (ASCA) recover typed text from keystroke sounds using only a commodity microphone, but prior demonstrations relied on idealized conditions with a single keyboard, a fixed microphone, a quiet room, and the same device for training and testing. This work asks whether keystroke inference holds up with unseen keyboards, diverse users, noisy environments, and compressed transmission channels. The authors claim that **the attack does survive these open-world conditions, provided the acoustic model is made explicitly domain-invariant and its noisy predictions are corrected by a language model**; the abstract reports no quantitative results.

papers.title: Beyond Proxy Metrics: MLLMs as Human Surrogates for Explainable AI Evaluation
papers.abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) has expanded into a broad and impactful research area, but the fundamental question of how best to evaluate explanation techniques has proven frustratingly elusive. Methodologies typically revolve around either proxy metrics which tell us little about the utility of an explanation, or human evaluation which---while generally considered the gold standard---is expensive, difficult to scale, and challenging to reproduce. In this paper, we investigate if Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can act as surrogate human participants to automate the evaluation of XAI. To do this, we first propose a ``purpose-grounded'' evaluation framework with metrics applicable to both MLLMs and human users alike. Then, we offer some conceptual insights as to why and when we can trust these models to automate this process. Lastly, we conduct extensive empirical testing across five purpose-grounded areas such as model improvement and fourteen popular MLLMs. Results indicate that all models trend positively, but OpenAI and Qwen models generally show higher alignment compared to other variants, which would be the recommended choices in practice. We expect our insights not to replace user testing, but rather to help XAI researchers complement their current evaluation methodologies and move the field away from heavy reliance on proxy metrics for measuring explanation utility.
papers.summary: Evaluating explainable AI (XAI) techniques usually relies either on proxy metrics that say little about an explanation's usefulness or on human studies that are expensive and hard to reproduce. The authors test whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can stand in for human participants, proposing a purpose-grounded evaluation framework with metrics applicable to both models and people and discussing when such surrogates can be trusted. Across five purpose-grounded areas and fourteen MLLMs, **all models trend positively in alignment with humans, with OpenAI and `Qwen` models generally aligning best**. The authors position the approach as a complement to user testing rather than a replacement.

papers.title: TAPCO-G: LLM-Guided Design-Adaptive Timing and Power Co-Optimization with Graph-Based Physical Priors
papers.abstract: Post-placement timing and power co-optimization is critical to meeting setup timing targets and reducing power within placement constraints. A cell replacement can improve timing along one path while increasing power or reducing slack on others. Conventional optimizers follow fixed rules for scheduling and accepting repairs, limiting their ability to address design-specific bottlenecks. A large language model (LLM) can propose changes to these rules, but on its own it cannot reliably estimate how a cell replacement affects endpoint slack and power. TAPCO-G combines LLM-guided optimizer adaptation with graph-based physical priors to evaluate candidate cell replacements. The outer loop tunes tool settings using physical-design feedback and revises executable repair policies when tuning stalls. The inner loop anchors delay estimates to static timing analysis snapshots, accounts for upstream driver-load changes, and propagates delay shifts to timing endpoints. It combines these estimates with coarse-to-fine power screening to prioritize candidates for physical trials. TAPCO-G produced placement-legal, logic-equivalent implementations and outscored CERBERUS on all eight ASAP7 benchmarks from the MLCAD 2026 Contest, with a mean quality score gain of 5.516 points, and scored 21.648 points higher than TAPCO on average. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed co-optimization framework.
papers.summary: Post-placement chip optimization must trade off timing and power, since replacing a cell can speed up one path while raising power or hurting slack on others, and conventional optimizers follow fixed repair rules. `TAPCO-G` pairs a large language model (LLM) outer loop, which tunes tool settings from physical-design feedback and rewrites executable repair policies when tuning stalls, with a graph-based inner loop that anchors delay estimates to static timing analysis snapshots, propagates delay shifts to timing endpoints, and screens candidates for power. It produced placement-legal, logic-equivalent implementations and **outscored `CERBERUS` on all eight `ASAP7` benchmarks from the `MLCAD 2026 Contest`, with a mean quality score gain of 5.516 points**, and scored 21.648 points higher than `TAPCO` on average.

papers.title: The Case for AI-Enabled Gate Monitoring as Farm Security in the UK: A PRISMA-Guided Review of the Evidence on Rural Crime, Livestock Predation and Farm Access
papers.abstract: Farm security in the UK rests on thinner evidence than its cost suggests. We ran a PRISMA guided review: twelve searches of Web of Science and Scopus on 2nd -4th November 2026 returned 1,183 records (761 unique), and grey-literature and hand-searches added 35 assessed sources. We synthesised 96 database records and 24 grey sources narratively. UK peer-reviewed evidence is small (16 records), and the main UK survey of crime and farmer mental health has 80 responses. Cost estimates rest on insurer claims: NFU Mutual put UK rural crime at {\pounds}41.5 million in 2025, with livestock theft up almost 30% to about {\pounds}4.5 million and dog attacks on livestock costing {\pounds}1.95 million. The Home Office states that agricultural crime cannot be separately identified in its central data. We found no independent evaluation of cameras, sensors, trackers or marking; light and sound deterrents lost effect within one to five months in a systematic review of anti-predator interventions; and no study examined how often farm gates are left open or what follows. Camera-trap AI papers report accuracy on ecological datasets, none at a farm gate in the records we found, and in one comparison machine learning detected 41% of wildlife against 81% for analysts. We argue, as an inference from these gaps and not as a demonstrated effect, that continuous gate-level AI-mediated monitoring, as implemented in Fieldmark AI, would be highly beneficial for UK farm security. It would create the farm-level, time-stamped record that no official source holds, verify events that periodic human checks miss, resolve whether foxes, dogs or people were responsible, and give every other security measure something to be tested against. No study has yet shown that it reduces loss, and we set out the evaluation needed to show it.
papers.summary: A PRISMA-guided literature review of UK rural crime, livestock predation and farm access screened 1,183 database records plus grey literature to assess the evidence behind farm security measures. The UK peer-reviewed base is small (16 records), cost figures rest on insurer claims, and **no independent evaluation of cameras, sensors, trackers or marking was found**, nor any study of how often farm gates are left open. From these gaps the authors argue, explicitly as an inference and not a demonstrated effect, that continuous gate-level AI monitoring as implemented in `Fieldmark AI` would be beneficial, and they outline the evaluation needed to test that.

papers.title: Dual-Core Tensor Wheel Decomposition with Structure-Cached Acceleration for Tensor Recovery
papers.abstract: Tensor wheel decomposition captures complex correlations in high-dimensional data through interactions between outer-ring factors and a high-order central core. However, updating these components requires the explicit construction and manipulation of large-scale matrices, which limits computational efficiency and incurs particularly high computational and memory costs for the central-core update. To address these limitations, we propose dual-core tensor wheel decomposition (DCTW), which factorizes the central core into two lower-order cores linked by a shared latent bond. Each core is coupled to a different group of outer-ring factors. We further propose a structure-cached acceleration strategy that avoids explicit large-scale matrix multi- plications and caches intermediate tensors generated during tensor network contractions for reuse across block updates. This reuse reduces redundant computation and avoids the explicit construction of large matrices. Complexity analysis and experiments show that the strategy based on structural caching accelerates optimization compared with explicit and implicit up- date schemes while limiting the increase in peak memory as the ranks grow. Experiments on color video completion and robust denoising show that DCTW matches or outperforms representative tensor network methods in reconstruction quality, computational efficiency, and scalability.
papers.summary: Tensor wheel decomposition models high-dimensional data with a ring of factors around a high-order central core, but updating that core requires building large matrices at high compute and memory cost. Dual-core tensor wheel decomposition (`DCTW`) splits the central core into two lower-order cores joined by a shared latent bond, and a structure-cached acceleration strategy reuses intermediate tensors from network contractions across block updates. On color video completion and robust denoising, `DCTW` **matches or outperforms representative tensor network methods** in reconstruction quality, efficiency and scalability, while caching limits peak memory growth as ranks increase.

papers.title: Tailoring Optimization Approaches with Domain Knowledge in Industry Process for Meta-heuristic Development
papers.abstract: The paper presents an Industry Process for Meta-heuristic Development (IPMD) schema, a systematic methodology for applying meta- and hyper-heuristic applications to optimization problems. In this context, we present a case study of Balancing Non-dominated Tournament Genetic Programming (BNTGP) applied to solve two NP-hard multi-objective optimization problems: routing (Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows) and scheduling (Multi-Skill Resource Constrained Project Scheduling Problem). The BNTGP method is based on a metaheuristic design. Its genetic programming-based representation makes BNTGP a hyper-heuristic, as it enables the exploration of a search space of heuristics for solving problems in general. The resulting heuristic can then be applied across a set of problem instances.
papers.summary: Applying meta-heuristics and hyper-heuristics to industrial optimization problems is often ad hoc, so the authors propose the Industry Process for Meta-heuristic Development (`IPMD`), a systematic methodology for doing so. A case study applies Balancing Non-dominated Tournament Genetic Programming (`BNTGP`) to two NP-hard multi-objective problems: the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows and the Multi-Skill Resource Constrained Project Scheduling Problem. Because its genetic programming representation searches a space of heuristics, the authors claim that **the evolved heuristic can be reused across a set of problem instances**.

papers.title: PARDIG: Global Precipitation Estimates Learned from Sparse Satellite Observations
papers.abstract: Estimating precipitation at the global scale is vital for Earth system science and disaster response, yet observational coverage and measurement precision remain constrained. Existing solutions provide options that trade off desirable traits such as skill, latency, geographical coverage, temporal coverage, and spatial and temporal resolution. We present PARDIG, an artificial intelligence framework based on a spherical graph-mesh transformer architecture that produces near-real-time global precipitation estimates. PARDIG is trained on dense multi-modal inputs, including atmospheric state analyses and multi-spectral geostationary satellite imagery, to predict sparse, high-precision precipitation measurements from spaceborne radar. At inference, the trained model is applied densely across the globe at $0.1^\circ$ spatial and 15-minute temporal resolution, producing complete near-real-time precipitation fields from 2016 to the present, alongside a historical variant extending the record back to 1999. Evaluation against three independent radar networks (over the US, Europe, and Japan) and against over 36,000 surface stations worldwide shows that PARDIG consistently outperforms IMERG V07 (Final and Early), MSWEP V3, ERA5, and HRES across precipitation thresholds and regions, with the largest improvements at extreme intensities. Case studies of extreme precipitation events demonstrate that PARDIG successfully captures their spatial structure and timing. The improvements also extend to forecasting: WeatherNext 3, a global weather model, produces more skillful precipitation forecasts when trained to predict PARDIG. Both the historical and near-real-time PARDIG datasets are openly available under a CC BY 4.0 license.
papers.summary: Global precipitation products trade off skill, latency, coverage and resolution. `PARDIG` uses a spherical graph-mesh transformer trained on atmospheric state analyses and multi-spectral geostationary satellite imagery to predict sparse, high-precision spaceborne radar measurements, and is then applied densely to produce global fields at 0.1 degree and 15-minute resolution from 2016 onward, with a historical variant back to 1999. Evaluated against three independent radar networks and more than 36,000 surface stations, it **consistently outperforms `IMERG V07`, `MSWEP V3`, `ERA5` and `HRES` across thresholds and regions**, with the largest gains at extreme intensities. The `WeatherNext 3` forecasting model also produces more skillful precipitation forecasts when trained to predict `PARDIG`, and both datasets are openly released.

papers.title: Chem World: A Large-Scale Benchmark and Physics-Aware Framework for Trustworthy Molecular Property Prediction
papers.abstract: Molecular property prediction is fundamental to computational chemistry and drug formulation research, yet existing benchmarks remain fragmented across datasets, properties, and evaluation protocols, limiting systematic evaluation of model generalization. We introduce Chem World, a large-scale benchmark integrating 17 public datasets with over 800,000 molecular and chemical-system instances across 10 property tracks, covering single-molecule and multi-component systems, including drug solubility. Chem World provides a unified testbed for evaluating molecular representations and compositional modeling across diverse chemical properties. Building on the benchmark, we propose PACM (Physics-Aware Compositional Modeling), which combines molecular representations with composition-aware modeling and domain-specific physical constraints. Extensive experiments show that molecular language models provide strong and transferable representations, while PACM consistently improves prediction across diverse chemical systems. Chem World and our PACM-powered drug-property prediction Agent support generalizable chemical modeling and offer a foundation for AI-assisted biomedical research and drug formulation development.
papers.summary: Benchmarks for molecular property prediction are fragmented across datasets, properties and evaluation protocols, which makes it hard to assess how well models generalize. `Chem World` integrates **17 public datasets with over 800,000 molecular and chemical-system instances across 10 property tracks**, covering both single molecules and multi-component systems such as drug solubility. On top of it the authors propose Physics-Aware Compositional Modeling (`PACM`), which combines molecular representations with composition-aware modeling and domain-specific physical constraints. Experiments indicate that molecular language models give strong, transferable representations and that `PACM` consistently improves predictions across chemical systems.

papers.title: TreeAgent: Structure-Aware Memory Agent for Processing Long Hierarchical Data
papers.abstract: Practical Web applications increasingly require agents to interpret long conversations or documents. For inputs exceeding the context windows of large language models (LLMs), memory agents process segments sequentially and retain past information in bounded memory. However, they typically divide inputs into flat token segments without preserving structure or hierarchy, causing three limitations for structured data such as API responses or HTML documents. First, fixed-length segmentation can split fields of the same record, breaking their relationships. Second, segments lack hierarchical information, obscuring their structural context and positions. Third, successive memory updates may discard details of earlier sibling records needed for reasoning on later segments. To address these limitations, we propose TreeAgent, a structure-aware agent that uses the input hierarchy to guide both segment-wise context processing and access to past information. Specifically, TreeAgent constructs segments from complete subtrees and groups of adjacent sibling subtrees to preserve local structural relationships. We provide theoretical guarantees on segment counts to guide token budget selection toward matching the segment count of fixed-length segmentation. We further attach structural paths to the segments for the agent to identify their ancestors and hierarchical positions. We also introduce residual memory links from the segments of low-level children to the segments of high-level parents, enabling direct information flows beyond successive memory updates. We evaluate TreeAgent with four representative memory agents on eight retrieval and aggregation tasks. The inputs are derived from real-world application data in JSON, HTML, YAML, and JavaScript and range from 8K to 1M tokens. TreeAgent improves the average score across the four datasets for all four agents, with 3.61% performance gain on average.
papers.summary: Memory agents that process inputs longer than a model's context window usually cut them into flat fixed-length segments, which splits records, hides hierarchy, and loses details of earlier sibling records in structured data such as API responses or HTML. `TreeAgent` instead builds segments from complete subtrees and groups of adjacent siblings, attaches structural paths so the agent knows each segment's position, and adds residual memory links from child segments to parent segments. It comes with theoretical guarantees on segment counts for choosing token budgets. Across eight retrieval and aggregation tasks on JSON, HTML, YAML and JavaScript inputs of 8K to 1M tokens, it improves all four tested memory agents, with a **3.61% average performance gain**.

papers.title: Geometry-Dependent Approximation and Stability Properties of Shallow ReLU$^k$ Networks on Bounded Euclidean Domains
papers.abstract:
On bounded Euclidean domains, we study how hidden-parameter geometry affects shallow ReLU$^k$ networks through results on approximation rates, saturation-type lower bounds, Gram and stiffness matrix spectra, Bernstein and Marcinkiewicz--Zygmund inequalities, discrete least-squares recovery, and inverse approximation.
  Our analysis uses smooth localization and dyadic Fourier estimates. We quantify parameter geometry by the fill distance $h$ and antipodal separation distance $\underline h$. For the prescribed network space $L_n^k$, representative approximation estimates take the form \begin{equation*} \begin{aligned} \inf_{g_n\in L_n^k}\|f-g_n\|_{\mathcal L^2(\Omega')}&\lesssim h^r\|f\|_{\mathcal H^r(\Omega)},\\ \inf_{g_n\in L_n^k}\|f-g_n\|_{\mathcal L^2(\Omega)}&\gtrsim \underline h^{\frac{d+2k+1}{2}}\|f\|_{\mathcal L^2(\Omega')}. \end{aligned} \end{equation*} The upper bound exploits target regularity up to the critical order $\frac{d+2k+1}{2}$, while the lower bound applies asymptotically to fixed targets smoother than this order. The upper estimate holds on an interior subdomain $\Omega'$, whereas the lower estimate concerns the larger domain $\Omega$.
  We also obtain geometry-dependent spectral estimates that quantify conditioning and coefficient stability. Further results establish norm discretization and regularized recovery from function values, and infer target regularity from approximation rates under coefficient or separation conditions. Altogether, these results describe how parameter geometry governs approximation accuracy, the stability of coefficient representations, discrete recovery, and the regularity information contained in convergence rates.
papers.summary: The arrangement of hidden parameters in shallow ReLU-k networks on bounded Euclidean domains is analyzed for its effect on approximation and stability, using smooth localization and dyadic Fourier estimates. Parameter geometry is quantified by the fill distance and the antipodal separation distance, yielding **approximation upper bounds that scale with the fill distance raised to the target's smoothness order, alongside saturation-type lower bounds in the separation distance**. Further results cover Gram and stiffness matrix spectra, Bernstein and Marcinkiewicz-Zygmund inequalities, discrete least-squares recovery from function values, and inverse theorems that infer target regularity from convergence rates.

papers.title: RB-LDC: Redundancy-Balanced Latent Coding for Noise-Robust Diffusion Latents
papers.abstract: Latent diffusion models decode approximately correct latents, making decoder sensitivity to perturbations relevant to image quality. After whitening, forward diffusion corrupts every direction at the same signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), despite unequal decoder sensitivities. We study an invertible linear layer between the encoder and diffusion process that shifts each direction's log-SNR. Its linear minimum mean-square-error (LMMSE) recovery risk has an exact spectral expression for any whitened latent distribution. Under an energy budget and a floor ensuring invertibility, minimizing decoder-sensitivity-weighted LMMSE risk integrated over the diffusion schedule yields a unique optimal allocation. The layer aligns with the decoder's expected pullback metric and equalizes marginal risk reduction across directions, computed by a deterministic spectral solver. At large budgets, the allocation follows a power law in sensitivity whose exponent is determined by the low-SNR tail of the loss weighting: one half for noise prediction and two thirds for data prediction under the cosine schedule, with a crossover on truncated schedules. We instantiate this principle as RB-LDC using Jacobian-based sensitivity estimates. On ImageNet at 256 x 256 resolution with SD-VAE and VA-VAE, trained RB-LDC improves reconstruction from noisy latents over budget-matched isotropic coding in all four metrics and five coding configurations, averaged over 15 SNRs and three pipeline seeds. It reduces average perturbed FID by 17.1 for VA-VAE block-local coding while preserving clean reconstruction. We also report intermediate SNRs where perturbed FID worsens. With a frozen diffusion model, RB-LDC yields lower FID point estimates in all 12 tested combinations of sampling progress and channel SNR under corruption during sampling.
papers.summary: Forward diffusion corrupts every whitened latent direction at the same signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) even though the decoder is far more sensitive to errors in some directions than others.
