The authors analyze an invertible linear layer between encoder and diffusion process that shifts each direction's log-SNR, and derive a unique optimal allocation by minimizing decoder-sensitivity-weighted linear minimum mean-square-error (LMMSE) recovery risk under an energy budget; at large budgets it follows a power law in sensitivity. Instantiated as `RB-LDC` with Jacobian-based sensitivity estimates on `ImageNet` 256 x 256 with `SD-VAE` and `VA-VAE`, it beats budget-matched isotropic coding on all four metrics and **reduces average perturbed FID by 17.1 for `VA-VAE` block-local coding** while preserving clean reconstruction. The authors also report intermediate SNRs where perturbed FID worsens.

papers.title: AVCC: Audio-Visual Conversation Corpus for Turn-Taking Prediction with a Human Benchmark
papers.abstract: } Predicting who will speak next, and when, is a prerequisite for conversational agents and social robots that take turns without waiting for silence. Multiparty next-speaker prediction (NSP) has been studied on corpora with per-speaker sensors, each with its own event definitions. No public benchmark covers the single camera and microphone a robot has, and no model has been compared against how well people perform the same prediction. We turn AVCC, a 31-hour audio-visual corpus of two- and three-speaker online conversation recorded with a single static camera and microphone, into a public NSP benchmark. We add a speaker-disjoint seven-video test partition with 865 hold and 865 shift events at mutual-silence gaps, word-level forced-aligned transcripts for the whole corpus, and a human reference benchmark collected at the same events. We score an audio-only Role-Relative VAP model (RoleVAP) and the multimodal MuVAP model. Labels, transcripts, per-response human data, and the scripts that reproduce every number are released.
papers.summary: Next-speaker prediction (NSP), deciding who will speak next and when, has mostly been studied on corpora with per-speaker sensors, with no public benchmark matching the single camera and microphone a robot has and no comparison against human performance. The authors turn `AVCC`, a 31-hour audio-visual corpus of two- and three-speaker online conversations, into such a benchmark by adding **a speaker-disjoint test partition with 865 hold and 865 shift events plus a human reference benchmark collected at the same events**, along with word-level forced-aligned transcripts. They score the audio-only `RoleVAP` model and the multimodal `MuVAP` model, and release labels, transcripts, per-response human data and reproduction scripts.

papers.title: From Attack Surface to Defense Architecture: Compositional Security for Agentic Coding Harnesses
papers.abstract:
AI coding harnesses couple language models to shells, filesystems, and network sockets, turning the harness into an automated Living-off-the-Land (LotL) platform: once an adversary injects instructions into retrieved content, dual-use binaries such as bash, curl, and find become the payload. We argue that security in agentic systems is a structural property of the cognitive architecture and permission composition rather than an emergent property of individual models. Static regex blacklists miss structural evasions, whereas LLM-as-a-Judge guardrails incur high latency while over-blocking benign work.
  We present ActiveSecHarness, a neurosymbolic reference-monitor architecture built around Separation of Intelligence and Authority. It combines (1) Macaroon-inspired HMAC capability tokens across four Trust and Authority Rings, (2) a 2D product taint lattice $\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{trust}} \times \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sens}}$ and a workspace provenance ledger that prevents secret laundering across disk, (3) deterministic Ring-0 OS/tool guards, and (4) bytecode certificates, split-horizon audit logs, self-healing security test synthesis, and an adaptive UserWikiManager.
  Across $N=252$ fixtures ($120$ attack, $120$ benign, $12$ kill chains), a live local LLM judge (qwen3:4b) refuses $98.3\%$ of benign work at $142.3\,\mathrm{ms}$ latency, whereas Ring 0 achieves $\mathrm{ABR}=1.000$ and $\mathrm{FPR}=0.000$ in $12.7\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ ($11{,}200\times$ faster). In a multi-step trajectory ablation, an oracle Conseca-style stateless policy misses $4/12$ kill chains ($\mathrm{ABR}=0.667$) and coarse Boolean taint blocks $83.3\%$ of benign workflows, while our 2D product lattice achieves $\mathrm{ABR}=1.000$ and $\mathrm{FPR}=0.000$ at $\approx 20\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ per step.
papers.summary: AI coding harnesses connect language models to shells, filesystems and networks, so injected instructions can turn ordinary binaries such as bash and curl into a Living-off-the-Land (LotL) attack payload. `ActiveSecHarness` is a reference-monitor architecture that separates the model's intelligence from its authority, combining HMAC capability tokens across four trust rings, a two-dimensional taint lattice over trust and sensitivity with a workspace provenance ledger, and deterministic operating-system and tool guards. On 252 fixtures, the deterministic Ring 0 guard **blocks every attack with zero false positives in 12.7 microseconds**, whereas a local LLM judge (`qwen3:4b`) refuses 98.3% of benign work at 142.3 ms. In multi-step tests, a stateless policy baseline misses 4 of 12 kill chains and Boolean taint blocks 83.3% of benign workflows, while the two-dimensional lattice blocks all attacks without false positives.

papers.title: Controlled Knowledge Engineering for Taxonomy Induction with Tool-Grounded LLM Agents and Runtime-Adaptive Policies
papers.abstract: Taxonomies are structured knowledge representations that support semantic search, recommendation, product catalog organization, and retrieval-augmented generation. Their automated construction from a fixed set of candidate entities requires more than plausible text generation: the resulting hierarchy must be complete, structurally valid, and semantically coherent. Large Language Models (LLMs) are promising for this task, but iterative free-form generation remains vulnerable to omitted or hallucinated entities, invalid hierarchical relations, and inconsistent organizational principles. We introduce TIGA (Taxonomy Induction with Tool-Grounded Agents), a knowledge-engineering architecture that formulates taxonomy induction as an iterative decision process over an explicit state and constrained action space. TIGA combines executable taxonomy-editing tools, an memory that records tool calls, rationales, and outcomes, and a runtime-adaptive organizational policy that the agent revises during inference. An optional global reviewer evaluates the constructed taxonomy against the candidate set and the active policy. We evaluate TIGA on four benchmark taxonomies using two LLM backbones and compare it with single-shot and iterative prompting-based baselines. TIGA achieves the strongest structural-quality results in most evaluated configurations, but does not dominate on every precision measure. The gains are accompanied by substantially higher token consumption, API-call volume, and inference time. Ablation results show consistent benefits from the policy and interaction-memory components, whereas the effect of global review depends on the dataset and the available revision budget. These findings characterize tool grounding and runtime policy adaptation as promising but costly mechanisms for improving the controlled construction of structured knowledge representations.
papers.summary: Building a taxonomy from a fixed set of candidate entities with large language models is prone to omitted or hallucinated entities, invalid parent-child relations and inconsistent organizing principles. `TIGA` (Taxonomy Induction with Tool-Grounded Agents) treats the task as an iterative decision process over an explicit state, using executable taxonomy-editing tools, a memory of tool calls and outcomes, an organizational policy the agent revises at runtime, and an optional global reviewer. On four benchmark taxonomies with two model backbones, it **achieves the strongest structural quality in most configurations but does not dominate on every precision measure**, and it costs substantially more tokens, API calls and inference time. Ablations show consistent benefit from the policy and memory components, while the reviewer's effect depends on dataset and revision budget.

papers.title: Counterfactual Analysis of Extent Leakage from Annotation-Derived Prompts in Vision-Language Medical Image Segmentation
papers.abstract: Text-guided segmentation models receive an image and a short caption about the lesion, and on public benchmarks the caption improves accuracy considerably. On colonoscopy and breast ultrasound, however, the size, count and location words of each caption were computed from the mask that later scores the prediction, and the chest X-ray captions were written by benchmark annotators. We tested what two published models take from them. On colonoscopy and chest X-ray, it is mostly the lesion's extent. Keeping only the size word or the lung-zone phrase recovers 84 to 98 percent of the improvement over an empty caption, and removing it loses 52 to 77 percent. The rest matters little, and a polyp called a rock is segmented just as well. We call this extent leakage. On breast ultrasound, nearly half the captions also name the diagnosis, which carries part of the benefit. Retraining on three datasets shows that models pick up this habit from their training captions, though only partly on breast ultrasound, and that it weakens their segmentation from the image alone. The leak can be measured without training a model, since caption words alone predict lesion area (coefficient of determination 0.54 to 0.77 on six of seven test sets). Without the test mask, the best method we tested, which estimates extent from the image, reaches 74.59 Dice on colonoscopy against the published 77.23. We propose an evaluation protocol that keeps what a caption says about the image apart from what it copies from the label.
papers.summary: Text-guided medical segmentation benchmarks often pair images with captions whose size, count and location words were computed from the very mask used for scoring. Counterfactual caption edits on two published models show that on colonoscopy and chest X-ray the benefit comes mostly from lesion extent: **keeping only the size word or lung-zone phrase recovers 84 to 98 percent of the improvement over an empty caption**, and calling a polyp a rock changes nothing. The authors call this extent leakage, show that models learn the habit from training captions at the expense of image-only segmentation, and find that caption words alone predict lesion area. Without the test mask, the best tested method reaches 74.59 Dice on colonoscopy against the published 77.23, and an evaluation protocol separating image description from label-derived content is proposed.

papers.title: TransGHOST: Real-Time, Synthesis-Free Reconstruction of Instrument-Occluded Regions in Ophthalmic Microsurgery
papers.abstract: Intraoperative scene perception in ophthalmic microsurgery is limited by instrument occlusion: when a tool enters the high-magnification field, it conceals tissue from both the surgeon and the perception components of robot-assisted systems that process the video. Generative inpainting can remove the occluder but replaces the missing image content with synthesis, which is unsuitable when visual provenance matters. Many video inpainters also depend on future frames and cannot operate online. We present TransGHOST, a causal reference-guided reconstruction pipeline whose non-generative safe mode operates in real time. Every restored value is obtained by resampling a recorded frame using geometric transforms fitted only to visible regions. The system provides per-pixel confidence and provenance and marks unsupported pixels as abstentions. We evaluate TransGHOST on a new veterinary clinical corpus of canine cataract surgery with pixel-level instrument and anatomy labels. Only the occluded region is scored, and each scoring target is verified to differ from the reference supplied to the system. Safe mode reaches 31.89 dB masked PSNR and 0.915 masked SSIM at 51.7 ms median and 85.5 ms 95th-percentile latency. On a pre-declared held-out cohort using instrument cutouts excluded from segmentation training, it reaches 29.83 dB masked PSNR, while matched-mask evaluation on validation shows a 3.45 dB advantage over LaMa. Region-aware reference selection improves masked PSNR by 3.60 dB over recency when candidate references can themselves be occluded. Reference-age analysis further defines the operating interval for the brief, repeated occlusions targeted by TransGHOST.
papers.summary: Instruments entering the field of view in ophthalmic microsurgery hide tissue, and generative inpainting fills the gap with synthesized content whose provenance cannot be trusted. `TransGHOST` is a causal, reference-guided pipeline whose safe mode restores occluded pixels only by resampling previously recorded frames with geometric transforms fitted to visible regions, reporting per-pixel confidence and abstaining where unsupported. On a new canine cataract surgery corpus, safe mode reaches **31.89 dB masked PSNR and 0.915 masked SSIM at 51.7 ms median latency**, with a 3.45 dB advantage over `LaMa` in matched-mask evaluation. Region-aware reference selection adds 3.60 dB over choosing the most recent frame.

papers.title: Data Quality Challenges in Multimodal Tourism Recommender Systems
papers.abstract: Modern recommender systems increasingly consider diverse data modalities to enhance model performance. However, the quality of the underlying multimodal data (e.g. data from social media platforms) has received limited attention so far. Focusing on tourism recommendation, we examine real-world challenges encountered when using datasets from Yelp and Instagram. Issues include noise from fake reviews, hallucinated content from LLMs, modality contradictions, and demographic bias. We outline future directions such as quality-aware fusion, structured and controlled LLM-based content generation to reduce hallucinations, and user group differentiation to improve the robustness and reliability of multimodal recommendation systems.
papers.summary: Multimodal recommender systems rely on data whose quality has received little scrutiny. Focusing on tourism recommendation with `Yelp` and `Instagram` datasets, the authors describe problems encountered in practice, arguing that **fake reviews, hallucinated LLM content, contradictions between modalities and demographic bias undermine such systems**. They outline future directions including quality-aware fusion, structured and controlled LLM-based content generation, and differentiating user groups.

papers.title: On the Spectral Estimation of VARMA Processes
papers.abstract: We consider the problem of estimating the power spectral density of a Vector-valued Autoregressive Moving-Average (VARMA) process. A well-established approach to accomplishing this task consists of formulating a moment problem that selects the spectral density maximizing an entropy-like index while matching certain moments of the underlying process. However, existing methods assume that the moving-average (MA) component is either fixed or scalar, thereby reducing the class of ARMA models over which the optimal spectral density is sought. In this paper, we propose a new moment problem, based on the notion of transportation entropy, for learning the spectral density of a VARMA process without fixing the MA component or restricting it to be scalar.
papers.summary: Estimating the power spectral density of a Vector-valued Autoregressive Moving-Average (VARMA) process is commonly posed as a moment problem that picks the density maximizing an entropy-like index while matching certain moments. Existing formulations assume the moving-average component is either fixed or scalar, which shrinks the class of models searched. The authors propose **a new moment problem based on transportation entropy that estimates the spectral density without fixing the moving-average component or restricting it to be scalar**.

papers.title: Understanding Mixture-of-Experts Language Models Beyond Expert Boundaries
papers.abstract: In Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, the nature of expert specialization remains controversial. Reports of domain-associated expert preferences contrast with analyses attributing routing primarily to token identity or syntactic patterns. To clarify these differing accounts, we look beyond expert-level routing to investigate the neuron-level organization of domain-specialized computation using Routing-Aware Magnitude Profiling (RAMP), a measure developed for this analysis. Using mixed-domain calibration data, we identify domain-specialized neuron sets with 58-74% overlap across multi-source samples of the same domain, compared with 15-24% across domains. To understand how this organization evolves during training, we trace neuron importance throughout pre-training and post-training across three fully open MoE families. Neuron importance continues to reorganize between pre-training checkpoints despite comparatively stable expert-level importance rankings, while post-training largely preserves neuron rankings. Building on these neuron-level perspectives, we further introduce RAMP-based Pruning (RAMPr) to select neurons across experts for balanced multi-domain capability preservation. At 75% neuron retention, RAMPr preserves average 91-98% of original full performance across six models. At 50% retention, our pruning method can reduce resident GPU memory by 36-43% and improves batched prefill throughput by 17-39% effectively. Our code is available at https://github.com/ydyjya/Neuron-Level-Specialization-in-MoE
papers.summary: Whether experts in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models specialize by domain or merely by token and syntax is disputed, so the authors look at the neuron level using Routing-Aware Magnitude Profiling (`RAMP`). They find domain-specialized neuron sets with 58-74% overlap across samples of the same domain versus 15-24% across domains, and observe that neuron importance keeps reorganizing during pre-training while post-training largely preserves it. A derived pruning method, `RAMPr`, selects neurons across experts and **preserves 91-98% of full performance at 75% neuron retention across six models**. At 50% retention it cuts resident GPU memory by 36-43% and raises batched prefill throughput by 17-39%.

papers.title: Gradient Inversion through Linear and Affine Subspace Constraints
papers.abstract: Federated learning enables multiple clients to collaboratively train a machine-learning model without directly sharing their local datasets. However, as prior works have shown, the gradients exchanged during training may reveal sensitive information about client data. Most existing attacks usually optimize dummy inputs to match the true client gradients (Gradient Inversion Attacks), while some attempt to reconstruct them based on the observation that aggregate gradients from a fully connected (FC) layer are a linear combination of its inputs. In this work, we extend this observation by showing that aggregate gradients from an FC layer with the correct scaling are actually an affine combination of its inputs. We evaluate a gradient inversion attack that leverages either known linear-subspace information or its affine-subspace counterpart at each FC layer to improve reconstruction accuracy. Our results show that subspace-based methods can substantially improve reconstruction quality over the chosen baselines in certain settings. We further demonstrate that moderate overestimation of the batch size can generally improve or preserve reconstruction quality, even when the true batch size is unknown. We additionally examine reconstruction under gradient perturbations introduced by a differential privacy (DP) mechanism, providing insight into the effectiveness of the considered formulations under noisy conditions.
papers.summary: Gradients shared in federated learning can leak client data, and some attacks exploit the fact that aggregate gradients of a fully connected layer are a linear combination of its inputs. The authors show that **with the correct scaling these aggregate gradients are an affine combination of the inputs**, and build a gradient inversion attack that constrains reconstruction to the resulting linear or affine subspace at each fully connected layer. The subspace constraints substantially improve reconstruction quality over the chosen baselines in certain settings, and moderately overestimating an unknown batch size generally preserves or improves results. Behavior under differential privacy noise is also examined.

papers.title: On the information rate of phones, syllables and words
papers.abstract: Which linguistic units minimise the bitrate required to encode speech content: phones, syllables, words, maybe larger units, or something in between? This question has implications for the development of speech and language systems and theories of human language processing. Using a transcribed corpus of 960 hours of English audiobooks, I compare the information rates of phones, syllables, words, multi-word combinations and intermediate tokenisations. While all units are equivalent under a perfect language model, it makes sense to compare these under limited modelling budgets; I use $n$-gram and transformer language models. The lowest bitrates are achieved using words, with slightly longer units sometimes performing best. The results show that, when modelling capacity is limited, units larger than syllables but smaller than long multi-word phrases provide the most efficient representation in terms of information rate.
papers.summary: Which linguistic unit encodes speech content at the lowest bitrate is tested on a transcribed corpus of 960 hours of English audiobooks, comparing phones, syllables, words, multi-word combinations and intermediate tokenisations. All units are equivalent under a perfect language model, so the comparison is made under limited modelling budgets using n-gram and transformer language models. **Words achieve the lowest bitrates, with slightly longer units sometimes performing best**, indicating that units larger than syllables but shorter than long multi-word phrases are the most efficient when modelling capacity is constrained.

papers.title: Universal Approximation Theorem for Metaplectic Neural Operators
papers.abstract: We prove universal approximation for metaplectic neural operators on nonempty bounded Lipschitz domains. The nonlocal branches are whole-space metaplectic multipliers with zero extension and restriction, associated with any fixed free symplectic matrix. Assuming a smooth, globally Lipschitz, nonpolynomial activation, we obtain compact-uniform approximation of continuous operators from $C^s$ to $C^r$ and from $H^s$ to $H^r$ in the respective output norms, for arbitrary nonnegative integers $s,r$ and finite input and output channel dimensions. In the Sobolev setting, compact input sets must additionally be uniformly bounded in $L^\infty$. One hidden operator layer with one nonlocal branch suffices. A single scalar symbol atom and finitely many positional features are prescribed by the transform and domain independently of the target operator, compact set and accuracy. The proof combines averaging neural operator theory with an exact chirp-conjugated averaging identity and derivative estimates. The result includes Fourier and fixed nondegenerate fractional Fourier multiplier constructions.
papers.summary: A universal approximation theorem is proved for metaplectic neural operators on bounded Lipschitz domains, where the nonlocal branches are whole-space metaplectic multipliers associated with any fixed free symplectic matrix. With a smooth, globally Lipschitz, nonpolynomial activation, such networks approximate continuous operators between spaces of continuously differentiable functions and between Sobolev spaces uniformly on compact sets, and **one hidden operator layer with a single nonlocal branch suffices**. The proof combines averaging neural operator theory with an exact chirp-conjugated averaging identity, and the result covers Fourier and fixed nondegenerate fractional Fourier multiplier constructions.

papers.title: Pulse or Provenance? What rPPG-Based Deepfake Detectors Learn
papers.abstract: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) has been proposed as a physiological cue for deepfake detection, based on the premise that synthesized faces lack a genuine cardiac signal. We examine what rPPG-style detectors learn on Celeb-DF++ (22 forgery methods) and FaceForensics++ (FF++), using one identically sampled window per real and fake video. On talking-face forgeries, simple chrominance traces reach an AUC of 0.998, exceeding a dedicated rPPG extractor (0.87). Controlled experiments indicate that this signal is not physiological in origin. On fully synthesized forgeries, it is equally discriminative when extracted from background regions or from full frames without face detection, and it is concentrated above the 0.7 to 4 Hz heart-rate band. It is largely removed by shuffling frame order but persists after normalizing resolution, frame rate and encoding, and an independent reimplementation reproduces these findings. Removing high-frequency content makes most synthesized videos appear real, adding it makes real videos appear fake, and injecting a synthetic pulse has little effect. In controlled self-reenactment experiments with two generators, animating a face from a single frame introduces the same high-frequency signal, whereas reconstructing each frame from its own source does not. Face-based chrominance detectors trained on Celeb-DF++ classify over 99% of real FF++ videos as fake, indicating that they largely encode video source rather than manipulation, and a CLIP-based detector exhibits the same behavior. A frozen CLIP backbone matches or exceeds fusions of CLIP with rPPG and frequency features. Finally, we show that the official Celeb-DF and Celeb-DF++ splits share identities and source-video content between training and test, and that custom protocols reusing test videos and identities in training inflate weaker detectors by up to 0.30 AUC.
papers.summary: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) is used for deepfake detection on the premise that synthesized faces lack a real cardiac signal, and the authors test what such detectors actually learn on `Celeb-DF++` and `FaceForensics++`. Simple chrominance traces reach an AUC of 0.998 on talking-face forgeries, but the signal is not physiological: it is equally discriminative from background regions, sits above the heart-rate frequency band, and is unaffected by injecting a synthetic pulse. Detectors trained on `Celeb-DF++` **classify over 99% of real `FaceForensics++` videos as fake**, indicating that they encode video source instead of manipulation, and a `CLIP`-based detector behaves the same way. The official `Celeb-DF` and `Celeb-DF++` splits are also shown to share identities and source videos between training and test, inflating weaker detectors by up to 0.30 AUC.

papers.title: Temporal Behavior Trees for Reinforcement Learning: Specifications as Rewards, Curricula, and Diagnostics
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning from formal specifications often separates task definition, reward shaping, curriculum design, and policy diagnostics into different mathematical objects. This fragmentation requires additional conversion steps and discards structure already present in the specification, such as subtask boundaries, ordering constraints, and quantitative measures. We introduce TBTCL (Temporal Behavior Tree Centric Learning), a framework that uses Temporal Behavior Trees (TBTs) as a unified interface for specification-guided reinforcement learning. A single TBT specifies the task, induces dense robustness-based rewards, defines a curriculum, and supports better understanding of learned policies. By adapting TBT syntax and semantics for specification-guided reinforcement learning, we provide a formalism that is more expressive than popular specification languages such as LTL and inherently hierarchical. We present algorithms to automatically extract a curriculum DAG and derive dense, robustness-based rewards directly from TBT semantics. Furthermore, we utilize TBT trace segmentation to build understandable competence profiles and automatically adapt the reward toward bottlenecks. We evaluate TBTCL on six specifications across discrete and continuous domains and show that Temporal Behavior Trees can serve as a specification, a reward, a curriculum, and a diagnostic.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning from formal specifications usually splits task definition, reward shaping, curriculum design, and policy diagnostics across separate mathematical objects, losing structure such as subtask boundaries and ordering constraints. `TBTCL` (Temporal Behavior Tree Centric Learning) uses a single Temporal Behavior Tree (TBT) for all four roles, with algorithms that extract a curriculum graph and dense robustness-based rewards directly from the tree's semantics, and trace segmentation that builds competence profiles and shifts reward toward bottlenecks. The authors argue the formalism is inherently hierarchical and more expressive than `LTL`, and across six specifications in discrete and continuous domains they report that **one tree can serve as specification, reward, curriculum, and diagnostic at once**.

papers.title: BioXArena-Pro: a research-grade benchmark for autonomous biomedical machine learning agents
papers.abstract: Coding agents are increasingly proposed as autonomous builders of biomedical models, but existing benchmarks are small, near saturation or open to leaked information. We present BioXArena-Pro, 64 research-level modelling tasks from eight biomedical domains, each rebuilt from a published study; most hold out whole biological units such as species or cohorts. Across 22 agent configurations, the best scores 55.1 of 100, and the scaffold matters almost as much as the model. We re-ran a published method for every task: where the published recipe applies unchanged, the best agent and the methods tie; on rebuilt tasks the methods trail by 8.2 points, suggesting that agents gain by adapting to new data. Pretrained models (including biological foundation models) matter where the strongest agent uses them: forbidding them decreases its score on those tasks by 9 points. Every task was audited in several AI-assisted rounds and a final human review.
papers.summary: Existing benchmarks for coding agents that build biomedical models are small, near saturation, or open to leaked information. `BioXArena-Pro` offers 64 research-level modelling tasks from eight biomedical domains, each rebuilt from a published study and mostly holding out whole biological units such as species or cohorts. Across 22 agent configurations **the best scores 55.1 out of 100**, and the scaffold matters almost as much as the model. Agents tie re-run published methods where the original recipe applies unchanged and lead by 8.2 points on rebuilt tasks, while forbidding pretrained models costs the strongest agent 9 points on the tasks where it uses them.

papers.title: Specify Privacy Yourself: Assessing Inference-Time Personalized Privacy Preservation Ability of Large Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities but raise significant privacy concerns due to their abilities to infer sensitive personal information from images with high precision. While current LVLMs are relatively well aligned to protect universal privacy, e.g., credit card data, we argue that privacy is inherently personalized and context-dependent. This work pivots towards a novel task: can LVLMs achieve Inference-Time Personalized Privacy Protection (ITP$^3$), allowing users to dynamically specify privacy boundaries through language specifications? To this end, we present SPY-Bench, the first systematic assessment of ITP$^3$ ability, which comprises (1) 32,700 unique samples with image-question pairs and personalized privacy instructions across 67 categories and 24 real-world scenarios, and (2) novel metrics grounded in user specifications and context awareness. Benchmarking the ITP$^3$ ability of 21 SOTA LVLMs, we reveal that: (i) most models, even the top-performing o4-mini, perform poorly, with only $\sim$24% compliance accuracy; (ii) they show quite limited contextual privacy understanding capability. Therefore, we implemented initial ITP$^3$ alignment methods, including a novel Noise Contrastive Alignment variant which achieves 96.88% accuracy while maintaining reasonable general performance. These results mark an initial step towards the ethical deployment of more controllable LVLMs. Code and data are available at https://github.com/achernarwang/specify-privacy-yourself
papers.summary: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) are reasonably well aligned to protect universally sensitive data such as credit card details, but privacy boundaries vary by person and context. `SPY-Bench` tests whether models can follow privacy limits a user specifies in language at inference time, using 32,700 samples of image-question pairs with personalized privacy instructions across 67 categories and 24 real-world scenarios. Among 21 models, **even the top-performing `o4-mini` reaches only about 24% compliance accuracy**, and contextual privacy understanding is limited. An initial alignment method, a variant of `Noise Contrastive Alignment`, reaches 96.88% accuracy while keeping reasonable general performance.

papers.title: LUMIR: Decoupled Multimodal Representation Learning from Heterogeneous Data for Next-POI Recommendation
papers.abstract: As multimodal tourism-related information collected from heterogeneous data sources has become increasingly available, learning effective representations has attracted attention for improving recommendation performance. Existing approaches often tightly couple multimodal fusion with the architecture and optimization objective of a specific downstream model, which limits the generality and reusability of the learned representations. To address these limitations, we propose LUMIR, a decoupled multimodal representation learning framework based on contrastive learning. Multimodal information collected from heterogeneous data sources is first semantically unified into a shared textual representation space using large language models (LLMs). An interaction-aware fusion mechanism is then designed to model cross-modal interactions, while sequential signals are incorporated as a structural constraint to guide representation learning. To evaluate the learned representations, experiments are conducted on a multimodal point-of-interest (POI) dataset under the next-POI recommendation setting across multiple sequential recommendation backbones. The results show that LUMIR consistently outperforms existing multimodal fusion baselines in both accuracy-oriented and beyond-accuracy metrics, demonstrating that decoupling representation learning from downstream optimization provides an effective paradigm for learning reusable multimodal representations. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/wzehui/LUMIR.
papers.summary: Multimodal fusion for recommendation is usually tied to the architecture and objective of one downstream model, which limits reuse of the learned representations. `LUMIR` decouples the two with contrastive learning: large language models first convert heterogeneous multimodal tourism data into a shared textual space, an interaction-aware fusion mechanism models cross-modal interactions, and sequential signals act as a structural constraint. On a multimodal point-of-interest (POI) dataset evaluated across several sequential recommendation backbones, it **consistently outperforms existing multimodal fusion baselines on both accuracy and beyond-accuracy metrics**.

papers.title: Normalizing Flows for Classical Simulation of Quantum Circuits in Phase Space
papers.abstract: We present a novel framework to learn a representation of quantum circuits based on the phase space formulation of many-body systems. Given that $N$-qubit states can be represented as probability distributions on a smooth $2N$-dimensional manifold, we show how unitary gates can be parameterized as normalizing flows between these distributions, opening a new avenue for quantum circuit simulation using generative models. We evaluate our method on three common families of quantum circuits, and show that its accuracy exceeds that of current state-of-the-art neural network methods for large system sizes.
papers.summary: Classical simulation of quantum circuits is approached here through the phase space formulation of many-body systems, in which an N-qubit state is a probability distribution on a smooth 2N-dimensional manifold. Unitary gates are parameterized as normalizing flows between these distributions, which lets generative models perform the simulation. On three common families of quantum circuits, the authors report that **accuracy exceeds current state-of-the-art neural network methods at large system sizes**.

papers.title: Coding Agent Memory Post-Training II: Unlocking the Memory Potential of Pre-trained File Operations for Long-Horizon Tasks via On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: Language-model agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks whose interaction histories exceed the model's active context. They must therefore decide what to write down and what to read back, and when to do either. Recent work has begun to use on-policy distillation (OPD) to make memory control part of the policy, relying on memory tools and compaction protocols that lie outside either model's pre-training. However, this weakens the distillation on both sides: the teacher cannot give useful guidance on an interface it has never used, and the student samples too few meaningful memory actions for that guidance to take effect. To study this problem, we introduce Coding Agent Memory Gym II (CAMG-II), a suite of long-horizon agentic-RL environments spanning Shop, Coding, AutoResearch, General, and Visual. Alongside each environment's native task interface, CAMG-II provides ordinary Bash access and an episode-persistent workspace, enabling the policy to create, revise, search, and reuse files as memory across context replacements. We also introduce Coding Agent Memory Post-Training II (CAMP-II), which trains a single policy jointly across all five environments with fully asynchronous OPD to learn this file-based memory behavior directly from a frozen teacher with a prior for file operations. On CAMG-II, CAMP-II obtains 2.97 times the gain of the strongest OPD baseline. The memory behavior CAMP-II learns generalizes to two external benchmarks, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2, with improved success rates.
papers.summary: Agents on long-horizon tasks must decide what to write down and read back once the interaction history exceeds their context, and prior on-policy distillation (OPD) approaches rely on memory tools that neither teacher nor student saw in pre-training. `CAMG-II` is a suite of long-horizon agentic environments spanning Shop, Coding, AutoResearch, General, and Visual that adds ordinary Bash access and an episode-persistent workspace, so files serve as memory across context replacements. `CAMP-II` trains one policy across all five environments with fully asynchronous OPD from a frozen teacher that already has a prior for file operations. It obtains **2.97 times the gain of the strongest OPD baseline** on `CAMG-II`, and the learned memory behavior improves success rates on `Terminal-Bench 2.1` and `SWE-Bench Pro V2`.

papers.title: One Sequence Is Enough: Fingerprinting Language Models from Fixed-Length Integer Sequences
papers.abstract: Users of model APIs and third-party platforms often rely on the declared model name to identify the model responding to their requests. However, the actual model may differ from the declared one, motivating identity verification based on observable outputs. Previous studies have shown that preferences in simple numerical-choice tasks can serve as model fingerprints. We investigate whether a single fixed-length integer sequence can combine multiple numerical observations to identify its source model. For this task, we introduce NumPrint, a benchmark of 5,036 answers from 51 models, collected using Chinese, Japanese, and English prompts that request 294 integers between 1 and 355 in one response. We propose the Shallow MLP and Causal Transformer (SMCT) to capture aggregate numerical preferences and behavioral patterns in generated sequences. In 51-class closed-set evaluation, SMCT achieves 92.72% accuracy from a single sequence, outperforming all methods compared in this study. Using two and four answers increases accuracy to 96.06% and 97.12%, respectively. These results show that a single integer sequence contains useful model fingerprints and that additional answers further improve identification.
papers.summary: Users of model APIs and third-party platforms cannot easily confirm that the model answering is the one declared, which motivates identification from outputs alone. `NumPrint` collects 5,036 answers from 51 models to Chinese, Japanese, and English prompts that request 294 integers between 1 and 355 in one response. A classifier called `SMCT` (Shallow MLP and Causal Transformer) captures aggregate numerical preferences and sequence patterns, reaching **92.72% accuracy from a single sequence** in 51-class closed-set evaluation. Using two and four answers raises accuracy to 96.06% and 97.12%.

papers.title: A Stage-Wise Explainable Pipeline for Arteriolar-to-Venular Ratio Estimation and Retinopathy Screening
papers.abstract: The arteriolar-to-venular diameter ratio (AVR) is a clinically motivated marker of retinal vascular health. We present a five-stage pipeline for AVR estimation and exploratory retinopathy screening from fundus images, with inspectable intermediate outputs at each stage. The pipeline combines vessel and artery-vein masks, optic-disc localization, vessel-calibre estimation using a minimal-chord boundary walk, and AVR computation from dominant arterial and venular branches. An explicit threshold-based rule produces the screening decision, enabling errors to be traced to individual processing stages. On an exploratory cohort of 30 HRF images, we report 96.7% accuracy, an F1-score of 0.968 and ROC-AUC of 0.978. Ablation studies and an exploratory comparison with VascX examine the effects of vessel pairing, calibre measurement and aggregation. Interpretation is limited by the small cohort, proxy disease labels and absence of independent reference calibre measurements. The pipeline provides a transparent framework for investigating retinal vascular biomarkers, with further validation needed on larger, clinically graded cohorts.
papers.summary: The arteriolar-to-venular diameter ratio (AVR) is a marker of retinal vascular health, and this five-stage pipeline estimates it from fundus images with inspectable outputs at every stage. It combines vessel and artery-vein masks, optic-disc localization, vessel-calibre estimation via a minimal-chord boundary walk, and an explicit threshold rule for the screening decision, so errors can be traced to a specific stage. On an exploratory cohort of **only 30 `HRF` images it reports 96.7% accuracy** with a ROC-AUC of 0.978, alongside ablations and a comparison with `VascX`. The authors note that interpretation is limited by the small cohort, proxy disease labels, and the absence of independent reference calibre measurements.

papers.title: Margin-Guided Token Credit for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
papers.abstract: In reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, a language model is rewarded for a correct final answer, and GRPO passes that reward to every token of the solution in equal measure. We instead place the credit where the model hesitated, in a method we call MCPO (Margin-Credit Policy Optimization). We measure hesitation by the top-2 margin $M=p_1-p_2$ of the policy's next-token distribution, map it to a score with two fixed thresholds, and spread each solution's advantage over its tokens so that the mean stays unchanged. The margin is read from a forward pass the trainer already performs, so the method needs no extra model evaluation and no batch statistics. We train MiniCPM5-2B-Base with LoRA for 200 steps on 2,048 DAPO-Math problems and evaluate on six competition-math benchmarks. MCPO beats an unmodified GRPO baseline for all five data seeds, by 6.55 points of macro avg@32 on average (95\% CI $[4.1, 9.0]$), and a Qwen3-4B-Base replication improves for all three seeds ($+4.75$). The gain is largest on problems that GRPO solves only some of the time and grows with $k$ in pass@$k$, reaching 13.8 points at pass@32. MCPO models also write two to three times longer answers, and runs that write longer score higher; our experiments do not separate the two effects.
papers.summary: In reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, `GRPO` spreads the reward for a correct final answer equally over every token of the solution. `MCPO` (Margin-Credit Policy Optimization) instead concentrates credit where the model hesitated, measured by the gap between the top two next-token probabilities, which is read from a forward pass the trainer already performs. Training `MiniCPM5-2B-Base` with LoRA for 200 steps on 2,048 `DAPO-Math` problems, it beats the `GRPO` baseline on all five seeds by **6.55 points of macro avg@32 on average** across six competition-math benchmarks, and a `Qwen3-4B-Base` replication gains 4.75 points. The resulting models also write two to three times longer answers, and the experiments do not separate that effect from the credit scheme.

papers.title: Personalized Memory Rubrics: Learning What to Remember per User via Rubric-Guided Credit Assignment
papers.abstract: Long-horizon personalized agents maintain an evolving memory by continuously deciding what to add, modify, or discard. However, learning an optimal update policy remains challenging. Conventional training relies solely on terminal question-answering accuracy, yielding a coarse feedback signal that treats all intermediate updates identically. Furthermore, update utility is inherently user-specific, as identical memory actions may yield opposite effects across different user personas. Existing methods fail to address this heterogeneity, relying on globally shared evaluation standards with at most a single scalar intermediate reward. To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{Personalized Memory Rubrics} (\textbf{PMR}), a framework that translates terminal feedback into fine-grained, per-step, and per-user credit assignment. PMR decomposes evaluation into a universal layer capturing cross-persona failure patterns and a per-user adaptive layer modeling individual traits as a specialized delta over the universal baseline. Through \textbf{Rubric-Guided Credit Assignment}, PMR redistributes credit at the token level, selectively amplifying validated decisions on successful trajectories while falling back to standard policy optimization on failed ones to avoid unreliable attribution. The rubric and memory policy \textbf{co-evolve} in a closed loop with anti-circularity guarantees. Crucially, PMR incurs zero inference overhead, operating without any rubric or external judge during deployment. Extensive experiments across four benchmarks demonstrate consistent gains over strong memory-augmented baselines.
papers.summary: Personalized agents with evolving memory are typically trained only on final question-answering accuracy, a coarse signal that treats every intermediate memory update alike and ignores that the same update can help one user and hurt another. `PMR` (Personalized Memory Rubrics) splits evaluation into a universal layer of cross-persona failure patterns and a per-user layer modeled as a delta over that baseline, then uses the rubric to redistribute credit at the token level on successful trajectories while falling back to standard policy optimization on failed ones. The rubric and memory policy co-evolve during training, and **no rubric or external judge is needed at deployment**. Experiments on four benchmarks show consistent gains over memory-augmented baselines.

papers.title: Interleaving anatomical inspection and diagnostic reasoning for explainable radiology report generation
papers.abstract: Automated radiology report generation can draft clinically plausible reports, yet the pathway from visual evidence to reported findings remains opaque, leaving the diagnostic basis of these reports unexplained and the generated reports difficult to review or revise. We introduce ARIVE (Anatomy-guided Reasoning with Interleaved Visual Evidence), an explainable report generation framework that interleaves anatomical inspection with diagnostic reasoning prior to final report composition. To support this process, we constructed 159,416 multimodal chain-of-thought (MCoT) trajectories from MIMIC-CXR, wherein visual evidence from inspected anatomical regions informs subsequent clinical interpretation. Trained on these trajectories and further optimized using anatomical and clinical-content rewards, ARIVE achieved superior clinical-efficacy performance compared with strong baselines on MIMIC-CXR and the abnormality-centered MIMIC-ABN. ARIVE's reports were competitive with those of leading models in blinded expert grading, and its MCoT trajectories earned high ratings for diagnostic traceability. Furthermore, a paired review evaluation suggests that access to MCoT can aid in identifying errors within generated reports.
papers.summary: Automated radiology report generators produce plausible reports without showing how visual evidence led to each finding, which makes the output hard to review or revise. `ARIVE` (Anatomy-guided Reasoning with Interleaved Visual Evidence) alternates inspection of anatomical regions with diagnostic reasoning before composing the report, trained on **159,416 multimodal chain-of-thought (MCoT) trajectories built from `MIMIC-CXR`** and further optimized with anatomical and clinical-content rewards. It outperforms strong baselines on clinical-efficacy metrics on `MIMIC-CXR` and `MIMIC-ABN`, and is competitive with leading models in blinded expert grading. A paired review evaluation suggests that access to the reasoning trajectories can help reviewers identify errors in generated reports.

papers.title: Program-Aided Patchable Skill Evolution
papers.abstract: Agent skills have emerged as an effective means of enabling LLM agents to solve complex, interactive tasks by encoding reusable knowledge without modifying model parameters. Recent approaches further improve skill adaptation by distilling reusable experience from agent execution trajectories and evolving skills based on downstream task feedback. However, existing methods primarily represent skills as natural language documents, intertwining procedural logic with descriptive knowledge and making skills difficult to maintain and evolve. To address this limitation, we propose PASE (Program-Aided Patchable Skill Evolution), a program-aided framework that iteratively evolves skills by associating them with executable programs. Unlike prior approaches that encode trajectory-derived experience primarily in natural language, PASE separates reusable procedural logic into editable programs, enabling targeted updates to executable components while reducing the need to repeatedly revise natural language skills. Extensive experiments across diverse models and benchmarks demonstrate that PASE consistently outperforms all baselines, by achieving over 2.8% improvements. Further analyses show that PASE exhibits greater evolutionary stability and generalisation capability, highlighting the critical role of programmatic knowledge in skill evolution. We will release all data and code via GitHub.
papers.summary: Agent skills are usually stored as natural language documents that mix procedural logic with descriptive knowledge, which makes them hard to maintain and evolve from execution feedback. `PASE` (Program-Aided Patchable Skill Evolution) attaches executable programs to skills and moves reusable procedural logic into them, so that updates can patch specific code rather than repeatedly rewrite prose. Across multiple models and benchmarks it outperforms all baselines, with **improvements of over 2.8%**, and further analyses indicate greater stability during evolution and better generalization.

papers.title: Few-Step Streaming Video Generation via Condition Shifting
papers.abstract: Few-step sampling reduces the cost of streaming video generation. Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) supervises few-step generators with a separate fake-score network, which adds training memory and computation and must track the evolving generator. We extend APEX to streaming video by using condition shifting to estimate the velocity field of the generated distribution within the generator. The original text condition selects generation, while a shifted condition selects fake estimation using the same parameters. This removes the independent fake network while retaining S2-Avatar's frozen reference teacher, Self-Replay Forcing, and perceptual regularization. We evaluate APEX on 180-second videos using three backbone evaluations per block and a one-step spatial Refiner, with a 70-case human study and a 320-case StreamAV-Bench comparison. Compared with S2-Avatar, APEX achieves higher video instruction fulfillment on the Progressive track (3.856 versus 3.831) and higher visual aesthetics across both tracks (0.641898 versus 0.632606). Human raters favor APEX most strongly on instruction following, with +30.0% net preference, followed by consistency and video quality at +4.3% each. Motion quality favors S2-Avatar, audiovisual synchronization is predominantly tied, and usability is unchanged. Separate measurements under matched training settings show 4.4% lower peak allocated GPU memory per GPU and 9.2% shorter mean iteration time than DMD.
papers.summary: Distribution Matching Distillation (`DMD`) trains few-step video generators using a separate fake-score network, which adds memory and computation. This work extends `APEX` to streaming video with condition shifting: the original text condition selects generation while a shifted condition makes the same parameters estimate the velocity field of the generated distribution, removing the separate network. On 180-second videos, human raters prefer it over `S2-Avatar` most clearly on instruction following (**+30.0% net preference**), while automated metric differences are small, motion quality favors `S2-Avatar`, and audiovisual synchronization is mostly tied. Under matched training settings it uses 4.4% less peak GPU memory and 9.2% less time per iteration than `DMD`.
papers.highlight_summary:
Distribution Matching Distillation (`DMD`) makes streaming video generators few-step, but it needs a separate fake-score network that adds training memory and compute and must keep tracking the evolving generator. `APEX` folds that estimator into the generator itself through condition shifting, so one set of parameters both generates video and estimates the velocity field of its own output distribution.

- The original projected text condition selects generation while its negation (`c_shift = -c`) selects fake-velocity estimation on the same parameters, slotted into `S2-Avatar`'s `Self-Replay Forcing` with its frozen teacher and perceptual regularization kept unchanged.
- On all 320 `StreamAV-Bench` scenarios with 180-second videos at 3 backbone NFE per block, `APEX` edges out `S2-Avatar` on pooled video instruction fulfillment (**3.891 vs 3.834**) and visual aesthetics (**0.642 vs 0.633**), ranking first on VA, VIF, and AIF among 12 models.
- In a 70-pair expert study against `S2-Avatar`, instruction following shows **+30.0%** net preference (22 wins, 47 ties, 1 loss), consistency and video quality each gain +4.3%, and the instruction advantage persists at 2 NFE (+27.1%), though every other dimension turns negative there.
- Under matched training settings, dropping the independent fake network cuts peak GPU memory by **4.4%** (102.7 to 98.2 GiB per GPU) and mean iteration time by **9.2%** (35.9 to 32.6 s) relative to `DMD`, a modest saving since the frozen teacher remains.
- The gains are narrow and come with trade-offs: motion quality favors `S2-Avatar` (-8.6%), audio quality, audiovisual alignment, and subject consistency dip on both tracks, pooled sync error rises from 1.319 to 1.341 s, and usability is identical at 62 of 70 sequences.

papers.title: ScaleBrain: A Scale-Consistent Framework for EEG Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Foundation models pre-trained on large unlabeled electroencephalography (EEG) corpora have emerged as a transformative paradigm for Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) applications. Recent EEG foundation models have shown that multi-scale representations derived from fixed-length patches can improve EEG representation learning. Existing frameworks commonly construct temporal scales through feature-level operations. However, these operations leave the correspondence between learned features and scale-specific characteristics of the original EEG signals implicit. Moreover, when the self-supervised objective is not aligned with the multi-scale input representations, information at some temporal scales may receive insufficient supervision during pre-training. In light of this, we propose ScaleBrain, a scale-consistent pre-training framework that explicitly coordinates multi-scale representations of EEG from both the model input and optimization objective sides. Specifically, ScaleBrain introduces multi-scale EEG tokenization to represent the same EEG segment through analysis windows with different temporal spans and shared temporal anchors, and pairs these representations with scale-specific reconstruction to align with the multi-scale input structure and provide supervision across temporal resolutions during self-supervised learning. We further develop an axial spatio-temporal attention mechanism to contextualize the fused multi-scale representation along spatial and temporal dimensions. Extensive evaluations on six public BCI benchmarks against 12 representative baselines show that ScaleBrain achieves the highest mean Balanced Accuracy on five datasets and ranks third on the remaining one, with only 5.0M parameters, demonstrating strong performance and favorable parameter efficiency.
papers.summary: Foundation models for electroencephalography (EEG) often build multiple temporal scales through feature-level operations, leaving the link to scale-specific signal characteristics implicit and some scales under-supervised during pre-training. `ScaleBrain` tokenizes the same EEG segment with analysis windows of different temporal spans that share temporal anchors, pairs this with scale-specific reconstruction objectives, and adds axial spatio-temporal attention over the fused representation. Against 12 baselines on six public Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) benchmarks, it achieves **the highest mean balanced accuracy on five datasets with only 5.0M parameters** and ranks third on the remaining one.

papers.title: MISO-BR: An Open Corpus for Misogyny Detection in Brazilian Portuguese
papers.abstract: Misogyny is among the most prevalent forms of online hate speech directed at Brazilian users, yet open and auditable resources dedicated to it in Brazilian Portuguese remain scarce. We introduce MISO-BR, an open, documented and versioned corpus of 896 balanced social media texts annotated for binary misogyny, released with its construction protocol and reproducible baselines. The corpus combines lexicon- and target-guided scraping from X with items imported from OLID-BR, a large language model triage stage whose prompt and decoding parameters are released, and manual annotation by three annotators following a written guide. Inter-annotator reliability reaches a Fleiss' kappa of 0.788 over 816 items. Under a single fixed protocol we compare four classical classifiers (Multinomial and Bernoulli Naive Bayes, a linear SVM and a random forest) with fine-tuned BERTimbau Base and Large. The classical models cluster between 0.651 and 0.676 macro-F1 and are precision-oriented but recall-poor. The transformers reach 0.833 macro-F1 and accuracy (Wilson 95% CI for accuracy [0.77, 0.88]), a gap of roughly 16 points, while Base and Large are indistinguishable on the test set despite a 2.6x difference in training cost. We argue that the value of the resource lies less in its headline scores than in the auditability of its pipeline, and we state three limits that users must reckon with: the artificial class balance, whose effect on precision under realistic prevalence we quantify; the association between provenance and label, which the released source field makes measurable; and the selection bias induced by lexicon-guided sampling and automatic triage. The corpus, annotation guide, models and experimental scripts are publicly available.
papers.summary: Open, auditable resources for detecting misogyny in Brazilian Portuguese are scarce. `MISO-BR` is a versioned corpus of 896 balanced social media texts with binary labels, built from lexicon- and target-guided scraping of X plus items from `OLID-BR`, a documented large language model triage stage, and manual annotation by three annotators (Fleiss' kappa 0.788). Fine-tuned `BERTimbau` Base and Large reach **0.833 macro-F1 versus 0.651 to 0.676 for four classical classifiers**, with the two transformer sizes indistinguishable despite a 2.6x difference in training cost. The authors spell out three limits: the artificial class balance, an association between data source and label, and selection bias from lexicon-guided sampling and automatic triage.

papers.title: Thermodynamics of words
papers.abstract: We introduce the word thermalization hypothesis according to which in a literary work there are effective interactions between words that drive them to thermalization where their word frequency distribution is the same as for the phenomenon of Rayleigh-Jeans (RJ) thermalization and condensation. In this concept, the different words play a role of classical oscillators (particles) and their word frequencies, or related tokens, are analogous to certain filling factors over energy state levels. The thermalization process is characterized by the conservation of total system energy, or total number of words/tokens, and total probability norm, or total number of different words. We apply this approach to analyze 16 literary works, including Bible, complete works of Shakespeare, and data from American National Corpus. We show that for these cases the effective system energy is very low and thus there is the RJ condensation phenomenon with a big fraction of total probability concentrated at the lowest energy states corresponding to a big fraction of rare words appearing only once or twice in the whole text. Such a RJ condensation is observed for light propagation in multimode optical fibers and other physical systems. We relate the thermalization of words to the recently proposed wealth thermalization for households in world countries. The economy concepts of Lorenz and Pareto curves, and also Zipf curves, are applied to the word frequency distributions of the selected 16 cases and it is shown that the thermalization theory gives a strikingly good description of real data.
papers.summary: A word thermalization hypothesis is proposed, under which effective interactions between the words of a literary work drive their frequency distribution toward that of Rayleigh-Jeans (RJ) thermalization and condensation, treating words as classical oscillators with the total token count and the number of distinct words as conserved quantities. Applied to 16 corpora including the Bible, the complete works of Shakespeare, and data from the `American National Corpus`, the effective system energy is found to be very low, giving **an RJ condensate in which a large share of probability sits on rare words that appear only once or twice**. The authors connect this to a recently proposed thermalization model of household wealth and report that the theory describes the Lorenz, Pareto, and Zipf curves of the real data well.

papers.title: Structured Confidence Perturbation via Fisher Geometry for Adversarial Training
papers.abstract: Adversarial training is often plagued by "pseudo-attacks", perturbations that significantly increase the loss value but fail to truly alter the model's confidence structure. To address this, we propose two complementary approaches to directly attack and defend against confidence structure deformation. First, building upon the traditional loss maximization perspective, we introduce a hybrid objective that integrates cross-entropy and KL divergence, encouraging adversarial examples to simultaneously disrupt prediction accuracy and distribution consistency. Second, we geometrically reconstruct adversarial training by generating perturbations that maximize the distribution distance on the confidence manifold. Theoretical analysis shows that the optimal perturbation direction aligns with the principal eigenvectors of the Fisher information matrix. We also propose an efficient algorithm to avoid high-dimensional matrix computations. Experiments on multiple datasets and model architectures demonstrate that our method outperforms existing methods in adversarial robustness and robust transferability, particularly excelling in structural perturbations within high-confidence regions.
papers.summary: Adversarial training can be dominated by perturbations that raise the loss sharply without actually changing the structure of the model's confidence distribution. Two complementary remedies are proposed: a hybrid attack objective combining cross-entropy with KL divergence, and a geometric reformulation that generates perturbations maximizing distribution distance on the confidence manifold. The theoretical analysis shows that **the optimal perturbation direction aligns with the principal eigenvectors of the Fisher information matrix**, and an efficient algorithm avoids high-dimensional matrix computations. Experiments across multiple datasets and architectures report better adversarial robustness and robust transferability than existing methods.

papers.title: Can KV Cache Be Reused Across Model Updates? A DeepSeek-V4-Flash Case Study
papers.abstract: Reusing key--value (KV) caches across language model updates could avoid repeated computation of shared context, but changes in model weights raise a fundamental question about what these caches preserve. We investigate direct cache reuse across four model updates, with a detailed study of DeepSeek-V4-Flash to Flash-0731. Our central finding is that caches can retain useful task information without faithfully reproducing the updated model's behavior. Retrieval accuracy varies substantially across updates, ranging from near-native performance to large losses. With source caches already available, reuse achieves median time-to-first-token speedups of $2.10$--$5.08\times$ on three longer-prefix QA benchmarks. To characterize the behavioral differences behind these outcomes, we introduce Functional Cache Divergence, which compares next-token distributions under reused and native caches. Direct KV cache reuse better preserves native model behavior in natural-text continuation, whereas compatibility degrades with increasing prefix length in single-token retrieval tasks. Answer-margin analyses help explain how correct retrieval decisions survive substantial internal state changes. Yet even agreement on the first generated token does not ensure agreement in answer content or stopping behavior. These findings establish task utility and fidelity to native inference as distinct criteria for evaluating cross-version KV cache reuse.
papers.summary: Reusing key-value (KV) caches after a language model's weights are updated could avoid recomputing shared context, but it is unclear what those caches still preserve. A study of direct reuse across four model updates, centered on `DeepSeek-V4-Flash` to `Flash-0731`, finds that caches can retain useful task information without faithfully reproducing the updated model's behavior, with retrieval accuracy ranging from near-native to large losses depending on the update. When source caches are already available, reuse yields **median time-to-first-token speedups of 2.10 to 5.08x** on three longer-prefix question-answering benchmarks. A new metric, `Functional Cache Divergence`, shows behavior is better preserved in natural-text continuation than in single-token retrieval with long prefixes, and agreement on the first generated token does not ensure agreement in answer content or stopping behavior.

papers.title: HandsOnAid: Building and Evaluating an Offline First-Aid Assistant for Emergency Response Scenarios
papers.abstract: Emergencies can occur where there is no phone signal and no ambulance nearby. A small language model on a phone can be helpful in such situations, but its advice needs to be safe and accurate. We built HandsOnAid, a 4-bit Gemma 2B model fine-tuned with QLoRA on FirstAidQA dataset, a corpus of 5,550 first-aid question-answer pairs. We compared seven configurations, including the base, 4-bit and 8-bit fine-tuned models, and versions with a length floor, safety gate, or retrieval. We used a 41-pair question-answer bank with medically reviewed references that followed ANZCOR guidelines, and a strict 0-5 score rubric, with twelve safety overrides. Four frontier LLM judges (GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Opus 5, DeepSeek V4 Pro, GLM-5.3) blindly scored every answer, with 45 hidden controls used to check judge reliability. Fine-tuning improved the mean score by +1.08 over the base model to 2.34. The best configuration scored 2.51 out of 5 which was the fine-tuned 4-bit model with retrieval. A medical professional also conducted a blind evaluation of 40 answers across the base, the 4-bit fine-tuned, and the retrieval configurations, and the scores were similar to the LLM judges' average scores. A keyword audit found limited coverage of several details of ANZCOR guidelines in the training corpus, that are required by the rubric, which suggests that missing information in the training data could be a cause of the low scores. On a smartphone device (Pixel 7 Pro) with six CPU threads and no network connection, the 4-bit fine-tuned model produced its first displayable text in 6.86 seconds and a complete answer in 14.88 seconds on average over ten questions.
papers.summary: `HandsOnAid` is an offline first-aid assistant for places with no phone signal, built by fine-tuning a 4-bit `Gemma 2B` model with QLoRA on the 5,550 question-answer pairs of `FirstAidQA`. Seven configurations were scored by four frontier LLM judges against 41 medically reviewed reference answers on a strict 0-5 rubric with safety overrides, and a medical professional's blind review of 40 answers gave similar scores. Fine-tuning raised the mean score by 1.08 to 2.34, and **the best configuration, the fine-tuned 4-bit model with retrieval, scored only 2.51 out of 5**, which a keyword audit links to guideline details missing from the training data. On a Pixel 7 Pro with no network, the model shows its first text in 6.86 seconds and a complete answer in 14.88 seconds on average.

papers.title: Where Do Vision-Language Models Get Left and Right? Position-Code Counterfactuals in Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-VL and InternVL3
papers.abstract: A vision-language model may take left-right direction from the orientation of image content within patches, its vision transformer's (ViT) position code, or token positions and order in its language model (LLM). Ablations show the ViT code is necessary; we test sufficiency by mirroring only a position code. In Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Qwen3-VL-4B and InternVL3-2B, mirroring ViT width positions reproduces the flipped-image answer on 84.3-93.2% of CV-Bench left-right questions (Qwen2.5-VL-3B: 87.5%, partly a left fallback). With two options, this also counts disruption; a half-grid shift flips most answers too. With the ViT code intact, LLM-side id and token-order mirrors change few left-right answers in all three series (a weak id test in Qwen2.5-VL). In Qwen2.5-VL-7B the effect sits in the global-attention ViT blocks, mostly the last. On What'sUp, flipping content and token order, not the position code, keeps more on/under than left-right answers at the flipped-image answer. Post hoc analyses qualify these results. On CV-Bench items with located objects, random permutations flip 18.9-31.0 points more answers when reversing the objects' order than when keeping it. On What'sUp, in Qwen2.5-VL and Qwen3-VL, the share of the left-right changes made by random permutations that land on the mirror relation is mostly below chance. Counted as returns to the original answer, the What'sUp contrast of support with left-right relations is clear only in InternVL3-2B. Most remaining errors give the same relation whichever object is asked about, suggesting that repair may target relation binding, object localization or use of the reference object.
papers.summary: Vision-language models could derive left versus right from image content within patches, from the position code of the vision transformer (ViT), or from token positions and order in the language model. Mirroring only the ViT width positions in `Qwen2.5-VL-7B`, `Qwen3-VL-4B`, and `InternVL3-2B` reproduces the flipped-image answer on **84.3 to 93.2% of `CV-Bench` left-right questions**, whereas mirroring language-model-side ids or token order changes few answers; in `Qwen2.5-VL-7B` the effect sits in the global-attention ViT blocks, mostly the last. Post hoc analyses qualify the result: a half-grid shift and random permutations also flip many answers, and on `What'sUp` the changes caused by random permutations land on the mirror relation mostly below chance in the two Qwen series. Most remaining errors give the same relation whichever object is asked about, pointing to relation binding, object localization, or use of the reference object as targets for repair.

papers.title: Generalizing Causal Decision-Making: Markov Equivalence, Transportability and Counterfactuals
papers.abstract: Structural causal bandits use causal knowledge to guide exploration when reward mechanisms are unknown. This paper extends the approach to partially known causal structure, information from other environments, and realizable counterfactual actions. First, we develop graphical criteria for minimal intervention sets under Markov equivalence and characterize possibly-optimal minimal intervention sets for maximal ancestral graphs. A search algorithm finds sets that are possibly optimal in at least one graph represented by a partial ancestral graph. Second, we derive target reward bounds from source distributions through partial transportability, accounting for non-manipulable variables. Dominance relations provide further bounds for action pruning and restricted exploration, with a regret guarantee under valid prior bounds. Third, we formulate counterfactual structural causal bandits over actions supported by specified experimental capabilities. Graphical characterizations of minimality and possible optimality yield algorithms that remove equivalent or dominated choices while preserving an optimal action. Experiments with specified structural causal models examine how these reductions and transferred bounds affect learning. Together, these results clarify how causal knowledge and experimental capabilities determine which actions merit exploration and guide learning within the retained action space.
papers.summary: Structural causal bandits, which use causal knowledge to guide exploration when reward mechanisms are unknown, are extended to three settings: partially known causal structure, information transferred from other environments, and realizable counterfactual actions. The work gives graphical criteria for minimal intervention sets under Markov equivalence, derives target reward bounds from source distributions through partial transportability, and formulates counterfactual bandits over actions supported by specified experimental capabilities. The resulting algorithms **remove equivalent or dominated actions while preserving an optimal one**, with a regret guarantee under valid prior bounds, and experiments on specified structural causal models examine how these reductions affect learning.

papers.title: What a CAGE 4 Score Measures: An Audit of a Learned Cyber-Defense Benchmark, Its Reference Defenders, and the Tables Built on Them
papers.abstract: CAGE Challenge 4 is the benchmark on which learned multi-agent cyber defenders are compared. We reproduce its two reference defenders, KEEP and H-MARL Expert, in a pinned container and show that three things read from it measure less than they are taken to measure. First, the simulator silently discards any action asserted for an agent whose previous action is still running, and charges one point for a discarded Restore as for one that runs. The documented observation does not expose the busy flag. Both reference defenders read it in their own wrappers, and switching that check off at evaluation costs KEEP's released policy 99.58 points per episode and H-MARL's 145.98, in both cases the charge for Restores sent to busy agents, with H-MARL's executed actions unchanged step for step. On a supervisory harness, holding interventions until the agent is idle is worth 25.3 and 27.6 points per episode at the published setting. In training, the check decides how a busy step enters the trajectory. Trained without it, KEEP leads at a hundred updates in all four paired seeds and trails from two hundred on in all four. Continued to two thousand updates on three seeds, the repaired recipe ends inside the released interval on one seed and short on two, by 27 and 125 points, a spread across training seeds far wider than the released reproduction interval. Second, the evaluation seeds the environment but not the policy, so a reported mean is one draw, and 88.9% of per-episode outcome variance is the policy's own sampling draw. Third, recovery precision depends on the truth it is scored against. Across five published comparison tables, none states the artifact, sampling, criterion and adversary that would make its numbers comparable. We release the instrument, our patches to both defenders, the traces and checkpoints behind every number, and a five-item disclosure checklist.
papers.summary: An audit of `CAGE Challenge 4`, the benchmark used to compare learned multi-agent cyber defenders, reproduces its two reference defenders, `KEEP` and `H-MARL Expert`, in a pinned container. The simulator silently discards actions sent to an agent that is still busy while still charging for a discarded Restore, and the documented observation does not expose the busy flag that both defenders read in their own wrappers; switching that check off at evaluation costs `KEEP` 99.58 points per episode and `H-MARL Expert` 145.98.
