Evaluation seeds the environment but not the policy, so **88.9% of per-episode outcome variance comes from the policy's own sampling draw**, and none of five published comparison tables states enough to make its numbers comparable. The authors release their instrument, patches, traces, checkpoints, and a five-item disclosure checklist.

papers.title: Obscured Wildfire Flame Detection by Spatio-temporal Analysis of Smoke Patterns Using Frame-wise Transformers
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose a new paradigm in wildfire management for detecting both visible and obscured fire using Deep Learning (DL). The essence of our method is the joint spatial and temporal analysis of RGB videos, embracing the fact that temporal patterns of smoke motions in consecutive video frames can indicate obscured fire flames. This perspective contrasts the traditional approach of independently analyzing images and individual video frames. To this end, we propose a frame-wise transformer architecture that applies an attention mechanism between the consecutive frames while preserving spatial information within frames as opposed to regular attention mechanisms like the non-local block, which combines spatial and temporal information into a single vector. We also optimize the temporal pattern lengths under different spatial resolutions to achieve the highest performance while reducing the computational cost. To investigate the applicability of our method in aerial image processing, we applied it to a curated version of the FLAME2 dataset that includes dual-mode RGB/IR videos. The IR video feed is used to extract ground truth, while the model is trained only on RGB videos to maintain applicability to lowcost commercial drones (which are equipped only with regular cameras) and facilitate processing existing RGB-only datasets. Our proposed method achieves a Segmentation Foreground Dice score of 92.61%, an Object Detection Precision and Recall rate of 93.21% and 91.73%, and clip-level classification accuracy of 98.02%, respectively. We also investigated the efficacy and generalizability of our method through ablation study
papers.summary: Wildfire flames hidden behind smoke are detected from ordinary RGB video by analyzing how smoke moves across consecutive frames rather than treating each frame independently. A frame-wise transformer applies attention between frames while preserving spatial information within each frame, and the temporal window length is tuned per spatial resolution to balance accuracy and compute. Trained only on RGB video from a curated version of the `FLAME2` dataset, with infrared footage used solely to derive ground truth, the method reports a **segmentation foreground Dice score of 92.61%**, detection precision and recall of 93.21% and 91.73%, and clip-level classification accuracy of 98.02%.

papers.title: ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision
papers.abstract: Fine-grained visual perception requires Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to locate and interpret subtle evidence within complex scenes. Constructing supervision for this ability is challenging: questions must have correct, unambiguous answers that depend on actual fine-grained visual details rather than coarse cues or language priors. Verifying these properties makes manual annotation labor-intensive and automatic generation difficult for models that themselves struggle with fine-grained perception. Yet the same models can often recognize such details once the region is zoomed in. We exploit this global-to-zoom perception gap and introduce ZoomGain, a data construction pipeline that constructs questions about the full image from visual information gained only by zooming in. It verifies each answer on the zoomed view with multiple models, ensures that each question remains unambiguous in the full image and cannot be answered from language priors, and specifically generates high-quality distractors for multiple-choice questions. With this pipeline and human-only screening (no manual QA editing), we build ZoomGainBench, a 1,000-question bilingual benchmark on which the best of 28 VLMs achieves only 61.08. Failure analysis reveals that models favor a particular type of distractor when answering multiple-choice questions incorrectly. Beyond evaluation, training on just 9K ZoomGain samples substantially improves the visual perception capabilities of our 4B/9B models, enabling them to outperform several hundred-billion-parameter models across various perception benchmarks. The trained 9B model achieves SoTA performance on several benchmarks, such as 90.25 on HR-Bench 4K. These results establish global-to-zoom perception gaps as a practical basis for scaling fine-grained visual supervision for both evaluation and training. Our code is available at https://github.com/inclusionAI/ZoomGain.
papers.summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) often miss fine-grained details in a full image yet recognize them once the region is zoomed in, and `ZoomGain` exploits this gap to build supervision automatically. The pipeline writes questions about the full image using information gained only from the zoomed view, verifies answers with multiple models, filters out questions that are ambiguous or answerable from language priors, and generates distractors for multiple-choice items. The resulting `ZoomGainBench`, a 1,000-question bilingual benchmark, is hard for current models, with **the best of 28 VLMs scoring only 61.08**. Training on just 9K `ZoomGain` samples lets the authors' 4B and 9B models outperform several much larger models on perception benchmarks, including 90.25 on `HR-Bench 4K` for the 9B model.

papers.title: From Bias to Positionality: A critical grammar for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Bias has become a default lens for understanding what machine learning systems do and how we should relate to them. Bias is at root a deviation from a standard; in decision making systems we can supply a standard from outside: a law, a protected attribute, a benchmark, a statistical property. However, even there, biased is often used as a shorthand, without stating what the position taken is - a silent ``relative to''. In a general use of language models, nothing supplies the standard: there is no decision to audit and no counterfactual output, so the shorthand fails. We argue that positionality -- the located, articulated, owned and contestable position from which anything is said -- is the better grammar for the question these models now force: who is speaking, from where? Against the vendors' answer of nowhere and the seductive possibility of everywhere, we argue that when a model is taken as-if speaking, it speaks from somewhere, and this means positionality can describe models, and the way they are believed beyond their warrant, even though they are not accountable speakers. A model's positionality is laminar -- laid down across corpus, tuning, system prompt, application and the live conversation. We separate three sets of factors: the positionality of a model's creators, the behaviour they intend for it, and the behaviour it enacts, and situate current work within this matrix. This lets us highlight what each stratum inherits from the one below, with ruptures and collapses where that inheritance is disavowed. We then return to where models speak from, and discuss the implications for how models are made, read and held accountable.
papers.summary: Bias is defined as deviation from a standard, and the authors argue that in general-purpose use of large language models no such standard exists, since there is no decision to audit and no counterfactual output. They propose positionality, the located and contestable position from which something is said, as the better framing, arguing that **a model taken as speaking always speaks from somewhere, rather than from nowhere or everywhere**. A model's positionality is described as layered across corpus, tuning, system prompt, application, and live conversation, and the analysis separates the positionality of a model's creators, the behaviour they intend, and the behaviour the model enacts. Existing work is situated within this matrix, followed by a discussion of implications for how models are made, read, and held accountable.

papers.title: Sable: A Small-Field Sumcheck Argument for Bit-Exact Inference of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: We present Sable, an argument system and single-GPU prover for the statement that a committed, integer-quantized transformer produced a given token sequence from a given prompt, bit for bit. Sable fixes an integer function F_O with no floating-point step, in which every rounding, normalization, softmax and sampling decision is determined by its inputs, and proves it with a constraint system whose relations provably never wrap modulo the 31-bit KoalaBear prime. The proof batches zerochecks and LogUp-GKR lookups into one sumcheck per domain, and commits to every witness tensor and weight in one multilinear commitment built from Reed-Solomon codes, BLAKE3 Merkle trees and a mixed-length BaseFold opening. The prover streams the model layer by layer on one GPU. On one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU, Sable proves all 64 layers of Qwen2.5-32B in 92.5 s for 4,096 tokens and 398 s for 16,384 tokens, and covers Qwen3-32B and the mixture-of-experts Qwen3-30B-A3B (4,096 tokens in 121.8 and 84.7 s). A proof costs 41 to 50 times the serving time, or 6.4 cents per 4,096-token request at public GPU prices, and 40 to 64 times less time per parameter and token than zkLLM. On WikiText-2, F_O's greedy token matches the BF16 model's at 86.3% of positions; on Qwen3, F_O is within 1.6 points of BF16 on MMLU and 1.7 points on GSM8K. A verifier with a compiled core checks a proof on one CPU core in 19 to 56 s. In the random-oracle model, the interactive proof has round-by-round soundness error 2^-103. The proof is not zero-knowledge, so the system targets open-weight models. Code: https://github.com/moonmath-ai/Sable
papers.summary: `Sable` is an argument system and single-GPU prover for the claim that a committed, integer-quantized transformer produced a given token sequence from a given prompt, bit for bit. It defines an integer-only inference function with no floating-point steps and proves it using batched sumchecks, `LogUp-GKR` lookups, and a multilinear commitment over the 31-bit `KoalaBear` prime field, streaming the model layer by layer. On one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU, it **proves all 64 layers of `Qwen2.5-32B` in 92.5 seconds for 4,096 tokens**, which is 41 to 50 times the serving time, about 6.4 cents per request, and 40 to 64 times less time per parameter and token than `zkLLM`. The integer function stays within 1.6 points of the BF16 model on `MMLU` and 1.7 on `GSM8K` for `Qwen3`, and the proof is not zero-knowledge, so the system targets open-weight models.

papers.title: BODYinTRANSIT-Lab: A Multimodal Dataset for Investigating Sensory-Driven Transformations in Body Perception and Affective Experiences
papers.abstract: Multimodal datasets that combine synchronised behavioural and physiological signals with subjective affective and body perception measures are still rare. This limits both the understanding of embodied experience and the development of computational models that infer subjective states from sensor data. We introduce BODYinTRANSIT-Lab, a multimodal dataset that addresses this gap by capturing affective, perceptual, and behavioural responses to the Footsteps Illusion. In this closed-loop paradigm, participants perform walking tasks while receiving real-time manipulated auditory feedback of their own footsteps intended to alter perceived body weight. The dataset comprises synchronised recordings from 101 participants recruited through systematic stratification by eating-disorder symptomatology and physical activity level. BODYinTRANSIT-Lab combines full-body kinematics with electromyography, electrocardiography, respiration, and electrodermal activity. Its annotations capture both immediate and post-trial experience, including within-trial perceived-weight ratings, post-trial assessments of body feelings and affective experience, 3D avatar body visualisations, and quantitative body maps. Psychological, behavioural, demographic, and social measures provide further information about factors that may influence individual responses. We provide a deep learning benchmark that uses walking kinematics to classify relative affective valence and perceived weight within subjects. On within-session, segment-level splits, the baseline model achieved mean balanced accuracies of 45.9% for affective valence and 44.5% for perceived weight. The BODYinTRANSIT-Lab dataset provides an experimentally controlled resource for cognitive neuroscience and affective computing research, with potential applications in affect-aware interactive systems, health and well-being technologies, and creative embodied experiences.
papers.summary: `BODYinTRANSIT-Lab` is a multimodal dataset pairing synchronised behavioural and physiological recordings with subjective reports of affect and body perception, collected during the Footsteps Illusion, in which altered real-time audio of a walker's own footsteps is intended to change perceived body weight. It covers 101 participants stratified by eating-disorder symptomatology and physical activity level, with full-body kinematics, electromyography, electrocardiography, respiration, and electrodermal activity alongside perceived-weight ratings, body maps, and 3D avatar visualisations. A deep learning baseline that classifies within-subject states from walking kinematics reaches **mean balanced accuracies of 45.9% for affective valence and 44.5% for perceived weight**.

papers.title: Stylization as Geodesic Navigation on Diffusion Manifolds
papers.abstract: Facial stylization asks for a delicate transformation: the image should look unmistakably artistic, yet the person should remain unmistakably the same. Existing training-free and instruction-driven methods often fail to expose such control, either drifting away from identity or producing only weak stylization. We introduce Stylus, a training-free framework that treats facial style transfer as navigation on the curved latent manifold of a pretrained diffusion model. Rather than interpolating in flat Euclidean space, \method refines the interpolated content--style point by lowering a ratio-weighted discrete geodesic energy under the pullback metric, made tractable by a rank-one power-iteration approximation of the Jacobian. This principle drives two complementary controls: content--style latent interpolation for smooth semantic fusion, and self-attention query optimization for spatially adaptive style injection. The resulting dual-control mechanism provides continuous, fine-grained control over stylization strength while preserving identity-critical facial structure, all without additional training. Experiments show that Stylus achieves the strongest identity and content preservation at competitive stylization strength.
papers.summary: Facial stylization must make an image look clearly artistic while keeping the person recognizable, and existing training-free and instruction-driven methods tend either to lose identity or to stylize only weakly. `Stylus` is a training-free framework that treats style transfer as navigation on the curved latent manifold of a pretrained diffusion model, refining an interpolated content-style point by lowering a discrete geodesic energy under the pullback metric, made tractable by a rank-one power-iteration approximation of the Jacobian. This drives two controls, latent interpolation and self-attention query optimization, giving continuous control over stylization strength. Experiments report that `Stylus` achieves **the strongest identity and content preservation at competitive stylization strength**.

papers.title: CUVE: Making Supervised Classification more Accessible through Visualization
papers.abstract: We present CUVE, an interface that enables people to build classifiers by generating visualizations that are interpretable by both humans and learning algorithms (the Visualization as Intermediate Representation approach). This UI enables users to create supervised classifiers and to visually investigate how to improve them and how they carry out their function. A preliminary study investigates the usability of our prototype and compares it with a traditional text-based programming interface.
papers.summary: `CUVE` is an interface for building supervised classifiers by generating visualizations meant to be interpretable by both humans and learning algorithms, an approach the authors call Visualization as Intermediate Representation. Users can create classifiers and visually inspect how they work and how to improve them, and **a preliminary study examines the prototype's usability against a traditional text-based programming interface**.

papers.title: Opportunity-Cost Option-Critic: Adaptive Switching Costs for Robust Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Deliberation costs are commonly used in hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) to prevent options from collapsing to primitive actions. Existing approaches rely on fixed penalties or duration-based adaptations, both of which are indirect proxies for an option's utility. This paper argues that option persistence should instead depend on the opportunity cost of abandoning the current behavior. We propose the Opportunity-Cost Option-Critic ($OC^2$) framework, which defines a state-dependent deliberation cost using the positive value gap between the active option and its best alternative. This encourages persistence when the current option is clearly preferable and allows rapid switching when a better option emerges. We show that directly learning such costs leads to a degenerate zero-cost solution and introduces an auxiliary objective that aligns the learned cost with the value-gap target. The approach is evaluated in Four Rooms and Pinball domains under stationary, goal-shift, and geometry-shift conditions. In the Pinball goal-shift task, the $OC^2$ framework achieves a 52\% first-ten-episode success rate compared with 18\% for a fixed-cost baseline. The results suggest that opportunity-cost-based persistence improves adaptation in non-stationary environments.
papers.summary: Deliberation costs in hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) keep options from collapsing into primitive actions, but fixed or duration-based penalties are only indirect proxies for an option's usefulness. The Opportunity-Cost Option-Critic (`OC2`) framework instead sets a state-dependent cost equal to the positive value gap between the active option and its best alternative, so the agent persists when its current option is clearly better and switches quickly otherwise. Because learning such costs directly collapses to a zero-cost solution, an auxiliary objective aligns the learned cost with the value-gap target. In the `Pinball` goal-shift task, `OC2` reaches a **52% first-ten-episode success rate versus 18% for a fixed-cost baseline**, with further evaluation on `Four Rooms` under stationary and shifted conditions.

papers.title: Sckwoky at SHROOM-Visions: Character-Level Hallucination-Span Detection in Image-Conditioned VLMs via Dual-Prompted LoRA Decoders
papers.abstract: We present our system for the SHROOM-visions 2026 shared task on character-level hallucination span detection in image-conditioned vision-language model (VLM) responses, evaluated across English, French, Italian, and Chinese. The detector is built on a frozen Gemma-4-12B-it backbone with trainable LoRA adapters (approximately 10.7M parameters). Because the backbone is a causal decoder, hidden states read from a single copy of an answer cannot attend to subsequent tokens; we therefore repeat the candidate answer within one prompt and extract features from its second occurrence, giving every position approximate bidirectional context in a single non-autoregressive pass. A character-level locator combines intermediate hidden states to predict hallucination probabilities, BIO boundaries, and a response-level abstention score, while separate language-specific classifiers assign one of five hallucination types to each predicted span. On the closed test set, our system reaches a macro-averaged character IoU of 0.4404, more than doubling the official baseline (0.1854), and ranks 5th-6th on IoU across the four languages. On the English tuning split, controlled ablations attribute a gain to the repeated answer that is comparable to that of LoRA adaptation (its held-out gain is smaller and concentrated on hallucinated answers), and they show that the detector relies on the image-answer pairing: shuffling images across examples drives IoU down to the level of the predict-nothing floor or below it in every language. In deployments where the same Gemma-4-12B-it model also generates answers, its base weights can be reused, making the approach practical for local question-answering systems that cannot run a separate verifier.
papers.summary: A system for the `SHROOM-visions 2026` shared task detects hallucinated character spans in vision-language model (VLM) answers about images across English, French, Italian, and Chinese. It uses a frozen `Gemma-4-12B-it` backbone with LoRA adapters of about 10.7M parameters, and repeats the candidate answer within the prompt so that features read from the second copy have approximate bidirectional context in a single pass. On the closed test set it reaches a **macro-averaged character IoU of 0.4404, more than double the official baseline of 0.1854**, ranking 5th to 6th across the four languages. Ablations attribute a gain to the repeated answer comparable to that of LoRA adaptation on the tuning split, and shuffling images across examples drops IoU to the predict-nothing floor or below.

papers.title: ProofCoder: Continuous Reasoning for Automated Software Verification
papers.abstract: Formal verification using proof assistants provides strong correctness guarantees for software, but constructing proofs remains labor-intensive and requires significant expertise. Recent approaches based on large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in automating proof synthesis. However, these approaches typically constrain the model to a rigid tactic-generation loop, in which the surrounding system controls premise retrieval, proof-state management, and backtracking. We introduce ProofCoder, an agentic proof-synthesis system for Rocq that approaches theorem proving from a coding-agent perspective. Rather than generating tactics within a fixed loop, ProofCoder reasons continuously throughout proof search and uses proof-assistant feedback to decide when to gather additional information, inspect proof states, revise previously generated proof fragments, or backtrack to an earlier point in the proof. This allows it to iteratively construct, repair, and refine proofs, at either tactic-level or whole-proof granularity. We evaluate ProofCoder on 280 challenging verification tasks from the AutoRocq Benchmark. On the best-performing configurations, ProofCoder increases proof success from 47% to 60% over the state-of-theart AutoRocq system, corresponding to a 27.7% relative improvement at approximately half the cost. Our ablations identify continuous reasoning as a key design choice: without it, the agent solves fewer lemmas at substantially higher cost, backtracks four to six times more often, and more frequently discards its own revisions. Whole-proof and tactic-level generation achieve similar success rates but follow distinct search and repair strategies. These results suggest that effective automated software verification requires more than improved tactic selection: continuous reasoning and feedback-guided proof revision are critical ingredients for robust proof synthesis.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) approaches to proof synthesis usually confine the model to a rigid tactic-generation loop in which the surrounding system controls premise retrieval, proof-state management, and backtracking. `ProofCoder` is an agentic system for the `Rocq` proof assistant that works like a coding agent, reasoning continuously and using proof-assistant feedback to decide when to gather information, inspect proof states, revise earlier fragments, or backtrack. On 280 verification tasks from the `AutoRocq Benchmark`, its best configurations **raise proof success from 47% to 60% over `AutoRocq` at roughly half the cost**. Ablations show that without continuous reasoning the agent solves fewer lemmas at higher cost and backtracks four to six times more often, while whole-proof and tactic-level generation reach similar success rates.

papers.title: Model-Free Runtime Measurement of Task-Relevant Information
papers.abstract: Autonomous systems increasingly monitor physical kinematics, environmental states and task completion outcomes. While existing work provides methods to plan information seeking actions and interpret acquired observations, current approaches do not monitor whether the live process of information gathering is functioning properly. Consequently, such systems can remain operationally active without resolving outstanding mission requirements. To address this limitation, we introduce Acquisition-State Telemetry (AST), a model free architecture that evaluates ongoing information acquisition from observable evidence relative to declared task requirements. Specifically, a domain interface maps raw observations into task resolution coordinates and normalized comparative representations, which are processed by a fixed causal monitor. This monitor emits two continuous real time signals that quantify (i) prospective progress across unresolved requirements and (ii) informational friction generated when recurrent evidence yields negligible informational gain. We evaluated a single, unadjusted monitor configuration across eight diverse domains including search and rescue dialogue, spatial grid exploration, hierarchical capability acquisition, continuous robotic manipulation, and probabilistic intent estimation. We show that across these domains the friction channel distinguished unproductive stagnation from purposeful exploration prior to task completion, while remaining muted during post completion activity. Furthermore, in closed loop reinforcement learning experiments under early termination constraints, we demonstrate that penalizing informational friction allowed agents to sustain high mission success, whereas unpenalized policies and baselines with matched operational costs failed to complete required tasks.
papers.summary: Autonomous systems can stay operationally active without actually resolving their mission requirements, because existing methods do not monitor whether live information gathering is working. Acquisition-State Telemetry (`AST`) is a model-free architecture in which a domain interface maps observations into task-resolution coordinates and a fixed causal monitor emits two real-time signals: prospective progress across unresolved requirements, and informational friction when repeated evidence yields negligible gain. With a single unadjusted configuration across eight domains, including search-and-rescue dialogue, grid exploration, and robotic manipulation, the **friction signal distinguished unproductive stagnation from purposeful exploration before task completion**. In closed-loop reinforcement learning experiments with early termination, penalizing friction let agents sustain high mission success where unpenalized policies and cost-matched baselines failed.

papers.title: Looking One Step Ahead: An Anticipation-guided Agent for Object State Readout in Videos
papers.abstract: Understanding the progress of an activity requires tracking how the objects involved change over time. Object state readout provides this information by describing a target object's states and transitions across video frames. Although multimodal large language models (MLLMs) generate detailed visual descriptions, these descriptions may leave the attributes needed to distinguish successive states insufficiently specified. In this paper, we propose look-ahead state readout (LASER), an anticipation-guided agent for object state readout that uses possible next-step changes to determine which attributes to inspect in the present. Given temporally ordered frames and a target object, LASER converts anticipated changes into targeted visual questions and inspects the current frame to establish attribute values. It then checks state readouts and forecasts against independent observations of subsequent frames, refining a state record used to generate the final description. Reusable textual observation skills guide this process and are refined by tracing discrepancies with reference captions to the responsible instructions. Candidate revisions are selected on separate videos based on improved caption quality without increased contradictions with reference facts. Model parameters remain frozen throughout adaptation and inference, and the revised skills remain fixed during evaluation. Experiment results and further analysis on OSCaR and PLM RCap show consistent improvements of LASER over strong baselines and existing approaches, which demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach.
papers.summary: Describing how a target object's state changes across video frames is hard for multimodal large language models (MLLMs), whose descriptions can leave out the attributes that distinguish successive states. Look-ahead state readout (`LASER`) is an agent that anticipates possible next-step changes, turns them into targeted visual questions about the current frame, and then checks its readouts and forecasts against later frames to refine a state record. Reusable textual observation skills guide the process and are revised by tracing discrepancies with reference captions, while model parameters stay frozen. On `OSCaR` and `PLM RCap`, the authors report **consistent improvements over strong baselines and existing approaches**.

papers.title: Visual Similarity in Adult Word Extension and Artificial Word Learning
papers.abstract: When two objects share a name, how much does their visual similarity explain, and what do the teaching examples add? First, we reanalyzed trial-level data from a large adult word-extension study (Lewis & Frank, 2018), computing each test image's distance to the examples shown in the space of a frozen self-supervised visual encoder (DINOv2). Distance was associated with extension (log odds -3.23 per standard deviation; 520 people), and an exploratory post hoc analysis suggested that this association persisted within the taught domain after controlling for taxonomic level and teaching condition. Example composition also mattered: after three examples, adults extended a word to 1.1% of superordinate items when the examples were subordinate and to 77.5% when they were superordinate. Second, in an artificial learner using the same encoder, words joining two categories were learned less accurately the farther apart the categories were (84.7%, 65.4%, and 53.0% naming accuracy for near, mid, and far pairs). The encoder's distances correlated with human similarity and confusability measures from three datasets (rho = .501-.795), but this representational alignment did not translate into conclusive evidence that human-derived distances predict learner difficulty, and a second encoder trained on one child's experience reproduced the tier ordering but not the pair-level effect. The secondary human data were analyzed under an internal plan fixed before the confirmatory analyses (not externally preregistered). Visual similarity accounts for part of how generalization is organized in both systems, while the composition of examples contributes what the distance we used does not capture.

papers.title: Hx2Dx: From Anamnesis to Diagnosis - A Multimodal Arena for Conversational Clinical Reasoning in LLMs
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve expert-level diagnostic accuracy in static evaluations, where the model receives a curated vignette or case report that already condenses the diagnostically relevant findings. Such evaluations measure inference over already selected evidence; the evaluations do not account for the inquiry used to obtain it. In clinical practice, however, diagnosis is an iterative process of inquiry. Clinicians take the patient's history, or anamnesis (Hx), through targeted questioning, examine the patient, and request and interpret tests, progressively narrowing the differential until they reach a final diagnosis (Dx). We introduce Hx2Dx ARENA, an interactive benchmark of 1'000 clinical cases from the New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM). Each case is a simulated encounter that proceeds from initial presentation through history taking and physical examination to diagnostic workup. We evaluate open- and closed-source LLMs under multiple configurations. Performance varies considerably across models in the interactive setting, and every model loses diagnostic accuracy relative to the static setting, where the full case is presented upfront. The ability to ask the right questions accounts for much of both the gap between models and the loss of accuracy: diagnosis improves as questions become more targeted and build a more complete clinical picture. LLMs thus reason well once the relevant data are available but remain limited in hypothesis-driven information gathering, in knowing what to ask in order to know. Closing this gap is a prerequisite for their safe integration into real-world diagnostic workflows.
papers.summary: Static diagnostic evaluations hand a large language model (LLM) a curated case that already contains the relevant findings, which measures inference but not the inquiry needed to obtain that evidence. `Hx2Dx ARENA` is an interactive benchmark of 1,000 clinical cases from the New England Journal of Medicine, each simulated as an encounter that moves from initial presentation through history taking and physical examination to diagnostic workup. Across open- and closed-source models, **every model loses diagnostic accuracy in the interactive setting relative to the static one**, and performance varies considerably between models. The ability to ask targeted questions accounts for much of both the gap between models and the accuracy loss.

papers.title: CroCoMAE: Cross-modal self-supervised collaborative representation learning for SAR-optical remote sensing data
papers.abstract: Remote sensing increasingly captures the Earth's surface through complementary sensors such as SAR and optical, yet ground-truth annotations remain scarce, limiting supervised approaches. Self-supervised learning (SSL) addresses the label scarcity, and cross-modal SSL further exploits the complementarity between co-located sensors, but existing cross-modal frameworks align modalities mostly through global image-level representations or treat them as largely redundant, leaving their fine-grained complementary structure underexploited. We propose CroCoMAE, a cross-modal SSL framework for SAR-optical remote sensing that unifies contrastive learning and masked image modeling within a ViT-based architecture, operating at two complementary levels. At the image level, an intra-modality contrastive loss on the class token yields globally discriminative, augmentation-invariant representations. At the patch level, masked image modeling drives fine-grained per-modality representations, while a cross-modal contrastive objective aligns a shared subspace across SAR and optical patch tokens, leaving the complementary subspace unconstrained to retain modality-specific information. On two SAR-optical benchmarks covering scene classification and semantic segmentation, CroCoMAE improves over uni-modal SSL baselines and outperforms state-of-the-art cross-modal frameworks in most configurations, with gains in both single-modality and multi-modal evaluation across varying label regimes and the largest improvements on semantic segmentation.
papers.summary: `CroCoMAE` is a cross-modal self-supervised learning (SSL) framework for paired SAR and optical remote sensing imagery, aimed at the scarcity of labels and at the tendency of existing methods to align modalities only at the global image level. Built on a ViT, it combines an intra-modality contrastive loss on the class token with patch-level masked image modeling, plus a cross-modal contrastive objective that aligns a shared subspace of patch tokens while leaving a complementary subspace unconstrained for modality-specific information. On two SAR-optical benchmarks covering scene classification and semantic segmentation, it improves over uni-modal baselines and **outperforms state-of-the-art cross-modal frameworks in most configurations**, with the largest gains on segmentation.

papers.title: Hierarchical Graph Representation Learning with Pooling-Induced Substructures
papers.abstract: Hierarchical graph-level tasks that require reasoning over substructures that extend beyond local neighborhoods are posing challenges for standard Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). While graph pooling aims to address this by coarsening graphs into hierarchical representations, existing methods often fail to explicitly preserve the substructures they induce, leading to inconsistent empirical performance. Moreover, evaluating such approaches remains challenging due to the lack of benchmarks with explicit hierarchical structure. We propose Pooled-Substructure-Aware GNNs, an approach to graph pooling that explicitly preserves and processes substructures uncovered by structure-based pooling schemes. We show that this design enhances the expressive power of pooling-based GNNs in the sense of the Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) test. To enable principled evaluation, we introduce two new synthetic datasets with controllable hierarchical structure and propose a metric to characterize the prevalence of hierarchical patterns in real-world graph-level benchmarks. On tasks with relevant hierarchical structure, our approach outperforms matched pooling baselines, while remaining competitive on structurally simpler benchmarks. Code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/lsbicego/PSA-GNN/.
papers.summary: Standard Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) struggle with graph-level tasks that require reasoning over substructures beyond local neighborhoods, and existing graph pooling methods often fail to preserve the substructures they induce. `Pooled-Substructure-Aware GNNs` explicitly keep and process the substructures uncovered by structure-based pooling, which the authors show increases expressive power in the sense of the Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) test. Two new synthetic datasets with controllable hierarchical structure and a metric for how prevalent hierarchical patterns are in real benchmarks support the evaluation. The approach **outperforms matched pooling baselines on tasks with relevant hierarchical structure** while remaining competitive on structurally simpler benchmarks.

papers.title: Continuous 3D Spatial Transcriptomics Reconstruction via Histology-Informed Implicit Neural Representations
papers.abstract: Three-dimensional spatial transcriptomics (3D ST) enables the analysis of gene-expression patterns across tissue depths. However, 3D ST measurements are acquired from discrete 2D tissue sections, which are often sparsely sampled due to high acquisition costs. To address this limitation, we propose a histology-informed multi-task implicit neural representation (HIM-INR) for continuous 3D gene-expression reconstruction from sparse ST observations. HIM-INR jointly reconstructs gene-expression profiles and histological representations using an INR with a shared backbone, leveraging densely sampled histological images as auxiliary spatial supervision. Once trained, HIM-INR predicts gene expression at arbitrary 3D coordinates without requiring histological images. Experiments on two 3D ST datasets demonstrate improved reconstruction over existing methods, particularly as the number of missing ST sections increases.
papers.summary: Three-dimensional spatial transcriptomics (3D ST) measures gene expression across tissue depth, but the data come from discrete 2D sections that are sparsely sampled because acquisition is costly. A histology-informed multi-task implicit neural representation (`HIM-INR`) jointly reconstructs gene-expression profiles and histological representations with a shared backbone, using densely sampled histology images as auxiliary spatial supervision. Once trained, it predicts gene expression at arbitrary 3D coordinates without needing histology images. Experiments on two 3D ST datasets show **improved reconstruction over existing methods, particularly as more sections are missing**.

papers.title: Right for the Wrong Reasons? Evaluating Plausibility and Behavioral Change in Explanation-Guided Learning
papers.abstract: Explanation-Guided Learning (EGL) promises models that are not only accurate but also rely on task-relevant evidence. However, whether improved agreement between model explanations and human-provided rationales also implies a changed decision strategy remains unclear. We study this tension under controlled synthetic shortcut introduction using a constructed shortcut dataset. Inspired by real-world applications, our benchmark covers shortcuts of different kinds, including localized, background-based, and global cues. This allows us to evaluate whether different EGL objectives produce behavioral changesand explanatory changes. Across these axes, we find that the effects of EGL are strongly objective-specific. Rationale-based data augmentation provides the clearest robustness gains when shortcut evidence can be separated from task-relevant foreground information, reaching average accuracy improvements of up to +4.8 percentage points (pp) together with increased foreground reliance. Attribution-constraining objectives primarily improve explanation plausibility, increasing Importance Mass by up to +14 pp on average, but provide weaker and less consistent behavioral correction, with average accuracy gains of at most +1.6 pp. Moreover, neither improved robustness nor improved plausibility reliably implies higher perturbation-based fidelity. Overall, our results show that EGL can be useful, but its success cannot be inferred from rationale agreement alone and should instead be evaluated along complementary behavioral and explanation-level axes. We publicly release all experimental results to enable further analysis (https://right-for-wrong-reasons.dfki.de/).
papers.summary: Explanation-Guided Learning (EGL) trains models to agree with human-provided rationales, and this study asks whether better agreement actually means the model changed how it decides. Using a constructed dataset with controlled synthetic shortcuts of localized, background-based, and global kinds, it compares EGL objectives on both behavior and explanations. Rationale-based data augmentation gives the clearest robustness gains, up to +4.8 percentage points in average accuracy, while **attribution-constraining objectives raise explanation plausibility by up to +14 points but improve accuracy by at most +1.6 points**. Neither improved robustness nor improved plausibility reliably implies higher perturbation-based fidelity.

papers.title: HaiRuo: Forecasting Ocean Eddies as Fields and Objects with a Satellite-Altimetry Foundation Model
papers.abstract: Mesoscale eddies carry most of the ocean's kinetic energy and move heat, salt and nutrients across basins, yet where an eddy will be two weeks ahead is still read off ocean models with post-hoc tracking heuristics. We introduce HaiRuo, which forecasts eddies as fields and as objects at once: from 30 days of satellite sea-level maps, one forward pass returns 15 days of sea level and geostrophic velocity, daily eddy masks and the trajectory of every eddy alive today. HaiRuo pairs two components with a clear division of labour: (1) HaiRuo-1B, an open-weight 1.05-billion-parameter foundation model pretrained without labels on 24 years of global satellite-altimetry observations, which supplies the 15-day physical fields and masks (+0.14 field skill and +1.1 mIoU points under the same decoder) and further lowers 15-day centre error by 1.2 km frozen (1.35 km over training from scratch); and (2) XuanJi, a Lagrangian object decoder that samples the evolving forecast in each eddy's co-moving polar frame and refines the 15-day path across three look-ahead rounds, removing 2.5 km on HaiRuo-1B (2.9 km with joint fine-tuning) and 2.5-3.3 km via its object attention across six published backbones. Under one pre-registered global evaluation over the whole ocean, HaiRuo improves on fourteen methods on every endpoint (25.2 vs. 30.6 km 15-day centre error, -18%), holding its margin outside the labelled regions and through both phases of the El Nino-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), while reproducing westward drift, 50-60 deg S eastward reversal and poleward cyclone-anticyclone deflection. Over ten days through one fixed tracker, HaiRuo's forecast field cuts the eddy-centre error of WenHai and XiHe by 37-43% (-2.8 km vs. day 0 while they degrade +4.3-8.7 km), and its object trajectories cut pipeline error by 77-78% globally. Open-weight checkpoints, code and project page: https://github.com/xkqin/HaiRuo
papers.summary: Forecasting where mesoscale ocean eddies will be two weeks ahead usually relies on ocean models plus post-hoc tracking heuristics. `HaiRuo` instead takes 30 days of satellite sea-level maps and returns, in one forward pass, 15 days of sea level and geostrophic velocity fields, daily eddy masks, and a trajectory for every eddy, by pairing `HaiRuo-1B`, an open-weight 1.05-billion-parameter foundation model pretrained without labels on 24 years of satellite altimetry, with `XuanJi`, an object decoder that refines each eddy's path in its co-moving frame. In a pre-registered global evaluation it beats fourteen methods on every endpoint, with a **15-day eddy-centre error of 25.2 km versus 30.6 km (18% lower)**, and the margin holds outside labelled regions and through both phases of the El Nino-Southern Oscillation (ENSO).

papers.title: Deviation-Aware Pretraining for Cardiovascular Disease Detection from Electrocardiograms
papers.abstract: Electrocardiogram (ECG) signals are critical for cardiovascular disease (CVD) detection. Most current deep learning models rely on supervised, task-specific training, which limits their ability to generalize across diseases, patient populations, and acquisition settings. This paper presents a self-supervised ECG feature extraction framework that learns from nearly one million unlabeled 12-lead ECG recordings. The framework includes two modules: Deviation Localization Embedding (DLE), which detects waveform-level deviations from normal patterns, and Association Reconstruction Embedding (ARE), which models cross-lead associations through deviation-guided reconstruction to capture abnormal patterns expressed across multiple leads. These modules enable the framework to capture subtle deviation-related patterns and their cross-lead context. The framework achieves up to 6.5% AUROC and 12.8% F1 improvements over prior methods on multiple public datasets, even without additional fine-tuning the pretrained feature extractor. Embedding visualizations show that the learned features support meaningful disease grouping and anomaly identification. The approach reduces the need for labeled data and can support clinicians in diverse healthcare settings. The framework has potential to improve early detection and monitoring of cardiovascular diseases, contributing to more accessible and equitable heart care.
papers.summary: Supervised, task-specific models for detecting cardiovascular disease (CVD) from electrocardiograms (ECG) generalize poorly across diseases, patient populations, and acquisition settings. The authors pretrain a self-supervised feature extractor on nearly one million unlabeled 12-lead recordings using two modules: Deviation Localization Embedding (`DLE`), which detects waveform-level deviations from normal patterns, and Association Reconstruction Embedding (`ARE`), which models cross-lead associations through deviation-guided reconstruction. They report **up to 6.5% AUROC and 12.8% F1 improvements over prior methods** on multiple public datasets without fine-tuning the pretrained extractor.

papers.title: Unipolar Neuron Networks Trained by Recirculation for Reward-Based Continual Learning
papers.abstract: Unipolar neurons are the predominant type of nerve cell in the octopus and in most other invertebrates. A single neurite (a fiber extending from the cell body) branches into a tree that carries both input and output synapses. The branches send graded local outputs to nearby cells, and one site on the main neurite sends a global output to distant targets. This paper proposes a network of such neurons and a learning rule for it. Each neuron is modeled as a tree of passive segments, whose activations are computed exactly as the steady state of a linear system. The network learns from reward alone, with a rule called recirculation. After each forward pass, a second pass sends requested changes of the outputs back through the same connections. Each synapse then adjusts its weight using only quantities available at its own location. Because the system of each neuron is symmetric, this update closely follows the gradient of the error in the predicted reward. Two mechanisms limit forgetting when tasks are learned in sequence: a task code inhibits a different subset of branches in each task, while consolidation lowers the learning rate of synapses that changed strongly in the recent past. The model is evaluated on a sequence of MNIST and Iris tasks. The network maintains high accuracy with low forgetting, whereas gradient-based training of the same network forgets earlier tasks almost completely.
papers.summary: Unipolar neurons, the dominant nerve cell type in octopuses and most invertebrates, carry both input and output synapses on a single branching neurite, and the authors build a network model of them along with a learning rule. Each neuron is a tree of passive segments whose activations are the exact steady state of a linear system, and a rule called recirculation learns from reward alone by sending requested output changes back through the same connections so that each synapse updates using only local quantities. Forgetting is limited by a task code that inhibits different branches per task and by consolidation that lowers the learning rate of recently changed synapses. On a sequence of `MNIST` and `Iris` tasks the network **keeps high accuracy with low forgetting, whereas gradient-based training of the same network forgets earlier tasks almost completely**.

papers.title: Nonadaptive One-Sided Testing of Binary Rank
papers.abstract: The binary rank of a binary matrix is the minimum number of disjoint all-one rectangles that partition its one-entries. We study entry-query testing of binary rank at most $d$, with one-sided error and nonadaptive queries. We give a tester using $\tilde O(d^4/\epsilon^2)$ queries, independent of the matrix dimensions and a general lower bound of $\tilde \Omega(d^{3/2}/\epsilon)$.
papers.summary: The binary rank of a binary matrix is the minimum number of disjoint all-one rectangles needed to partition its one-entries. The authors study testing whether a matrix has binary rank at most d by querying individual entries, restricted to one-sided error and nonadaptive queries. They give a tester using **about d^4/eps^2 queries (up to logarithmic factors), independent of the matrix dimensions**, together with a general lower bound of about d^(3/2)/eps.

papers.title: Representational Atoms in Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Understanding the internal representations of neural networks and characterizing their relationship with human conceptual structure are two critical questions for elucidating model mechanisms. The former reveals how learned knowledge is organized in internal representations, whereas the latter provides a basis for interpreting these representations through human conceptual structure. Here, we formally define fundamental representational units (FRUs) and establish two evaluation criteria: fidelity and stability. We further prove that threshold-activated sparse autoencoders (TSAEs) can identify FRUs with high fidelity and stability under appropriate conditions, and validate this result through large-scale experiments. Further analyses reveal that FRUs with higher stability exhibit greater monosemanticity and can be composed across layers to recover semantic organization corresponding to human conceptual structure. These results provide a unified framework for defining, evaluating and identifying FRUs in neural networks, and establish a foundation for characterizing the relationship between neural network representations and human conceptual structure.
papers.summary: To pin down how neural networks organize learned knowledge and how that relates to human concepts, the authors formally define fundamental representational units (FRUs) and propose two criteria for evaluating them, fidelity and stability. They prove that threshold-activated sparse autoencoders (`TSAEs`) can identify FRUs with high fidelity and stability under appropriate conditions, and back this with large-scale experiments. Further analysis finds that **FRUs with higher stability are more monosemantic and can be composed across layers to recover semantic organization matching human conceptual structure**.

papers.title: BARS: Budget-Aware Sequential Sampling with Refusal for Majority Identification under Unknown Distributions
papers.abstract: Repeated sampling with majority selection is an effective means of enforcing self-consistency in large language models. Recently, a variant has also been introduced that terminates early to save costs when the output distribution is favorable. But it still cannot yield a correct confidence estimate from the answer distribution. For this issue, we formalize this as majority identification under an unknown distribution with a budget and a target error rate, and propose BARS, a sequential rule certifying the top-two gap and returning an early stop, a budgeted majority vote, or a refusal when feasibility cannot be established. A refusal is a statement about the rule and its budget, not a claim that a question is unanswerable, and it tells practitioners when to widen the budget or switch models. A certified mode carries proven bounds on the joint answering error and on refusing an instance the budget could handle, while a practical mode, used in our experiments, replaces them with empirical calibration. On synthetic instances drawn from known distributions over thousands of seeds, the difficulty-driven behavior is recovered and the price of the certified mode is measured.On GSM8K the practical mode draws 22.3\% fewer samples than fixed-8 sampling over the same pool, refused questions included, at the cost of declining 18.8\% of the questions. On MATH, it greatly improves the accuracy of its output answers into 82.5\% at the cost of honestly refusing to answer half of the difficult questions that the model itself is unable to solve.
papers.summary: Sampling a language model repeatedly and taking the majority answer enforces self-consistency, but existing early-stopping variants do not produce a correct confidence estimate from the answer distribution. `BARS` frames this as majority identification under an unknown distribution with a sampling budget and target error rate, using a sequential rule that certifies the gap between the top two answers and then either stops early, returns a budgeted majority vote, or refuses when the budget cannot establish the answer. A certified mode carries proven error bounds, while the practical mode used in experiments substitutes empirical calibration. On `GSM8K` the practical mode draws **22.3% fewer samples than fixed-8 sampling while declining 18.8% of questions**, and on `MATH` it reaches 82.5% accuracy on answered questions by refusing about half of the difficult ones.

papers.title: Cross-Border Fulfillment Center Selection via Doubly Robust Estimation and Linear Programming
papers.abstract: We introduce the cross-border (XB) fulfillment center (FC) Selection Model: a multi-stage optimization framework combining forecasting, doubly robust estimation, and linear programming to select optimal source FCs. For each source-destination shipping arc, the objective is to choose a subset of source-country FCs that minimize delivery time and cost while maximizing profit and shipped units under a fixed domestic network. We evaluate the model on three production-scale international shipping corridors for a large e-commerce company using 12 months of shipment data, employing both aggregate offline replay and shipment-level counterfactual nearest-neighbor matching. Across all shipping corridors, the XB FC Selection Model achieves 8.5-51.1% reductions in delivery time and 4.4-48.3% reductions in logistics cost relative to human expert-defined FC selection policies, with up to 6.5 percentage-point improvements in 5/5 target compliance (5 days, $5 USD). Pareto analysis shows the model consistently dominates single-objective ranking strategies and unconstrained LP on the efficiency-reallocation frontier, with all results statistically significant.
papers.summary: Choosing which source-country fulfillment centers (FCs) should serve each cross-border (XB) shipping arc is typically done by human experts. The proposed XB FC Selection Model is a multi-stage pipeline combining forecasting, doubly robust estimation, and linear programming to pick FC subsets that minimize delivery time and cost while maximizing profit and shipped units under a fixed domestic network. Evaluated on three production-scale corridors of a large e-commerce company with 12 months of shipment data, it achieves **8.5-51.1% reductions in delivery time and 4.4-48.3% reductions in logistics cost** relative to expert-defined policies, using offline replay and counterfactual nearest-neighbor matching.

papers.title: SpecValley: Aggregation as Spectral Valley in Dense Heterophilic Graphs
papers.abstract: Node classification in heterophilic graphs remains an open problem: aggregating over neighbourhoods can damp precisely the part of the signal that carries the labels. The field has answered with ever more expressive propagation operators, leaving the aggregation step that precedes them fixed by degree normalisation. However, degree normalisation acts as a spectral valley in its own right, attenuating a fixed middle band whose position at lambda equal 1 is set by the normalisation rather than by the data, exactly where the eigenvalues of dense graphs accumulate. We therefore begin with the representations rather than the propagation, in two stages: a learnable aggregation followed by an ordinary spectral filter. The first, SpecValley learns the position, sharpness and flank gains of the valley for every graph. We show formally how the aggregation operator and downstream filter interact. We establish that the response 1 minus lambda of degree normalisation vanishes exactly at that accumulation point. A spectral energy budget shows that what aggregation removes from a band, no linear spectral filter can recover. Crowding alone says nothing about the benefit. That is decided by how much label energy the valley removes, which we measure for every graph. SpecValley achieves strong results across heterophilic benchmarks, and a controlled ablation over aggregation operators and downstream filters attributes the gain to aggregation rather than the filter.
papers.summary: Node classification on heterophilic graphs suffers because neighbourhood aggregation can damp the part of the signal that carries the labels, and most work responds with more expressive propagation operators while leaving degree-normalised aggregation fixed. The authors show that degree normalisation itself attenuates a fixed middle spectral band at eigenvalue 1, exactly where the eigenvalues of dense graphs accumulate, and that no downstream linear spectral filter can recover what aggregation removes. `SpecValley` instead learns the position, sharpness, and flank gains of this spectral valley per graph, followed by an ordinary spectral filter. It achieves strong results on heterophilic benchmarks, and **a controlled ablation attributes the gain to the learned aggregation rather than the downstream filter**.

papers.title: An Augmented Lagrangian Approach to Lifted Bellman Linear Programming
papers.abstract: Temporal-difference critics regress onto a bootstrapped target and usually need a target network. Lifted Bellman Linear Programming (LBLP) instead expresses the in-sample optimal values of offline RL as the solution to a linear program over the dataset. Its neural solver ALBUM relaxes the constraints into hinge penalties with fixed coefficients, and its guarantees are conditions on coefficients chosen in advance. We solve the same program with the method of multipliers: the coefficients become multipliers learned by dual ascent, with one penalty parameter $\rho$. In the convex case the fixed points are the KKT pairs of LBLP, and at every stationary point the applied constraint weights balance the objective exactly. The critic can serve a Gaussian actor, a flow actor, and best-of-N sampling, and for the Gaussian actor we propose an advantage-normalized DDPG+BC objective. With a single $Q$ and $V$ and no target network, our AL-LBLP with best-of-N reaches 60.1\% average success on the 50 state-based OGBench tasks. On long-horizon tasks, it reaches 81.5% on humanoidmaze-giant and 79.8% on antmaze-giant. It does not collapse up to batch size 8192.
papers.summary: Lifted Bellman Linear Programming (`LBLP`) expresses the in-sample optimal values of offline reinforcement learning as a linear program over the dataset, avoiding bootstrapped targets, but its neural solver `ALBUM` uses hinge penalties with coefficients fixed in advance. The authors solve the same program with the method of multipliers, so the coefficients become multipliers learned by dual ascent with a single penalty parameter, and show that in the convex case the fixed points are the program's KKT pairs. The resulting critic works with Gaussian actors, flow actors, and best-of-N sampling. Using a single Q and V and no target network, `AL-LBLP` with best-of-N reaches **60.1% average success on the 50 state-based `OGBench` tasks**, including 81.5% on humanoidmaze-giant, and does not collapse up to batch size 8192.

papers.title: Joint Quantization and Dynamic Partitioning for Context-Aware Edge Vision Transformers
papers.abstract: Deploying vision transformer models across connected and automated vehicles (CAVs) requires joint management of computation and Vehicle-to-Vehicle (V2V) communication. Static split-inference methods use fixed partition points and cannot adapt to time-varying link bandwidth, processing load, and concurrent multi-stream traffic. This paper proposes an edge orchestration framework that jointly selects model partition points, per-layer quantization bitwidths, and execution placement across heterogeneous vehicular compute nodes. The joint partitioning and mixed-precision allocation problem is formulated as a Mixed-Integer Linear Program (MILP) that minimizes compute and communication energy subject to end-to-end latency and task-quality constraints. The framework is evaluated on Jetson Orin Nano (8~GB), Jetson Orin NX (16~GB), and Jetson AGX Orin (32~GB) nodes using OPV2V-driven multi-stream workloads with $K \in \{2,4,6,8\}$. Across the evaluated configurations, the proposed formulation reduces V2V communication energy by $33.3$--$36.0\%$ relative to a Uniform INT8 split. At $K=8$, end-to-end task completion latency is reduced by $34.0\%$ on the Orin Nano and $33.1\%$ on the Orin NX relative to the same baseline, while limiting the reduction in 3D detection accuracy to $3.1$--$4.1$ percentage points in $\mathrm{mAP}_{50}$ relative to FP16 execution.
papers.summary: Running vision transformers across connected and automated vehicles (CAVs) requires balancing on-board computation against Vehicle-to-Vehicle (V2V) communication, and static split-inference schemes cannot adapt to changing bandwidth, load, and concurrent streams. The proposed orchestration framework jointly picks model partition points, per-layer quantization bitwidths, and execution placement, formulated as a Mixed-Integer Linear Program (MILP) that minimizes energy under latency and task-quality constraints. Tested on three Jetson Orin devices with `OPV2V`-driven workloads of 2 to 8 streams, it **cuts V2V communication energy by 33.3-36.0% relative to a uniform INT8 split**, and at 8 streams reduces end-to-end latency by about a third on the smaller devices, with a 3.1-4.1 percentage-point loss in mAP50 relative to FP16 execution.

papers.title: Breakdown of Autoregressive Multi-Step Reasoning Under Concentrated vs. Diffuse Attention Head Dropout
papers.abstract: During extended wakefulness, mammalian neocortical networks experience localized periods of transient neuronal silence termed off-states. Here, we examine how analogous spatiotemporally concentrated disruptions affect sequential reasoning in autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs). Evaluating 250 paired derivations on the GSM8K benchmark across two 8B models (Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct), we contrast clustered bursts of attention head masking against budget-matched diffuse i.i.d. dropout. Concentrated bursts induce substantial reasoning degradation: at onset parameter $\mathcal{B}=0.10$ (scheduling $\sim 5.7\%$ of vulnerable head-token volume), Qwen3-8B accuracy drops from $91.2\%$ under diffuse noise to $78.8\%$ under burst dropout ($\Delta = -12.4$ percentage points [pp], exact McNemar $p = 5.5 \times 10^{-6}$), while LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct drops from $84.0\%$ to $76.8\%$ ($\Delta = -7.2$ pp, $p = 0.0198$). Conversely, dispersing the identical cumulative budget uniformly across generation steps via stratified quintile matching yields substantially milder degradation (retaining $91.2\%$ in Qwen and $84.0\%$ in LLaMA). In an exploratory factorial dissociation ($N=100$), single-step dropout density is associated with an acute drop in a single schedule draw ($-10.0$ pp on Qwen, $p_{\text{holm}} = 0.0425$), while multi-token continuity exhibits an inconclusive compounding trend ($-7.0$ pp, $p_{\text{holm}} = 0.1892$). Error analysis reveals that Qwen failures reflect derivation errors within formatted responses (conditional accuracy drop of $-11.4$ pp), whereas in LLaMA $22.2\%$ of discordant losses lack a final answer format line (conditional gap narrows to $-5.0$ pp). These findings demonstrate that autoregressive reasoning chains are particularly vulnerable to concentrated structural disruptions, providing empirical benchmarks for fault tolerance in transformer architectures.
papers.summary: Inspired by the localized periods of neuronal silence seen in sleep-deprived mammalian cortex, the authors test whether clustered bursts of attention-head masking harm step-by-step reasoning more than the same masking budget spread out as diffuse random dropout. On 250 paired `GSM8K` derivations with `Qwen3-8B` and `LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct`, concentrated bursts are clearly worse: **`Qwen3-8B` accuracy falls from 91.2% under diffuse dropout to 78.8% under burst dropout**, and `LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct` falls from 84.0% to 76.8%. An exploratory follow-up on 100 items links single-step dropout density to an acute accuracy drop, while the effect of multi-token continuity is inconclusive.

papers.title: Tree-Ising: Repairing Language Models with Bit-Level Ising Edits
papers.abstract: Weight-space programming, introduced in recent MIT work by Takehi et al., enables a frontier LLM agent to read a network's weights and write a repair. Their GPT-6 Astra agent corrected the reasoning loops of Qwen3.5-0.8B without gradients, using 158 agent turns, 89.7 million tokens, and 50 forward-pass requests. Our method, Tree-Ising, casts this repair as a sparse discrete optimization problem over the model's own BF16 weights. Forward statistics define an objective that weakens a loop direction, strengthens a concluding direction, and preserves the layer's output on productive tokens. Within a state-tree representation, where lossless BF16 storage acts as a special case, the admissible edits are sign flips and exponent shifts that preserve all shared group exponents and mantissas. We decompose this objective exactly into independent QUBO (Ising) problems, one per output row, which we solve on a GPU using simulated annealing or quantum-inspired simulated bifurcation. On the agent's two layers, Tree-Ising achieves 54.6% on MATH-500, outperforming the agent's edit (51.7%) under the same evaluation protocol, while the base model scores 7.9% as reported. The simulated bifurcation solver yields a statistically indistinguishable repair at 55.1%. Both solvers outperform the agent edit across all five math benchmarks, with statistically significant improvements on MATH-500 and GSM8K after correcting for multiple comparisons. Our approach modifies 13% to 17% fewer weights and reduces BF16 bit flips by a factor of 2.2 to 2.3. It requires only four forward-pass requests and zero LLM tokens, with the annealing recipe costing about $0.90 in GPU time. On Qwen3.5-2B, with layers and dose selected using only the base model, the same recipe increases greedy GSM8K accuracy from 21.6% to 69.4%. As a proof of concept, we execute an eight-variable repair subproblem using QAOA on an IBM Heron processor.
papers.summary: Prior work on weight-space programming had a frontier LLM agent read a small model's weights and write a gradient-free repair for its reasoning loops, at a cost of 158 agent turns and 89.7 million tokens. `Tree-Ising` recasts the repair as sparse discrete optimization over the model's BF16 weights, where the allowed edits are sign flips and exponent shifts, and decomposes the objective exactly into independent QUBO (Ising) problems per output row that are solved on a GPU with simulated annealing or simulated bifurcation. On the same two layers of `Qwen3.5-0.8B` it reaches **54.6% on `MATH-500` versus 51.7% for the agent's edit (base model 7.9%), using four forward-pass requests, zero LLM tokens, and about $0.90 of GPU time**, while changing fewer weights and bits. On `Qwen3.5-2B` the same recipe raises greedy `GSM8K` accuracy from 21.6% to 69.4%.
papers.highlight_summary:
Small reasoning models such as `Qwen3.5-0.8B` get stuck repeating text in thinking mode until the token cap (93% of `MATH-500` completions, **7.9%** accuracy), and the prior fix relied on a frontier LLM agent reading and rewriting weights at a cost of 89.7M tokens and $312. `Tree-Ising` instead casts the repair as a sparse discrete optimization over the stored BF16 bits, solved as a batch of Ising problems using forward passes only.

- Forward statistics from the base model's own looping and successful traces define a loop direction and a concluding direction, and the objective reduces the layer's write along their combination on loop tokens, penalizes output change on productive tokens, and limits the number of changed weights.
- Edits are restricted to sign flips and power-of-two exponent shifts that leave every shared group exponent and mantissa untouched, which lets the objective split exactly into **2,048 independent 512-spin QUBOs** (one per output row), solved on a GPU by simulated annealing or simulated bifurcation.
- On the same two layers the agent edited, it reaches **54.6%** on `MATH-500` versus **51.7%** for the agent edit (p ≈ 0.003), leads on all five math benchmarks (significant on `MATH-500` and `GSM8K` after Bonferroni correction), and cuts answers hitting the cap from 31.6% to 23.9%, while changing 13% fewer weights and **2.2× fewer** BF16 bits in **31 minutes for about $0.90**.
- On `Qwen3.5-2B`, with layers picked by a forward scan and the dose set from the base model alone, greedy `GSM8K` accuracy rises from **21.6% to 69.4%**, though the edit breaks 38 of the 285 problems the base model originally solved and was tested only under greedy decoding on that one benchmark.
- The cost comparison pits the agent's discovery run against a fixed recipe designed after reading the agent's logs, reusing its layers and a dose set to 1.6× its edit (so not dose-matched); a closed-form rank-one edit of the same objective matches accuracy on the practice screen while rewriting 96% of the weights, and the eight-variable `QAOA` run on IBM Heron hardware is a proof of concept with no claim of quantum advantage.

papers.title: Verifiable Agentic Traffic Class: A Policed Quality-of-Service Mechanism for Agentic AI Traffic, Evaluated from Simulation to Real-Kernel Adversarial Testing
papers.abstract: Software agents built on large language models generate traffic unlike human web traffic, yet routers have no class for it and cannot verify a sender's claim to be an agent. This paper proposes the Verifiable Agentic Traffic Class (VATC), which combines a reserved Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) value declaring agent traffic, a router-side classifier that demotes flows contradicting the declaration to a class served after best-effort traffic, and a rate-limited priority queue. VATC was compared with static Differentiated Services (DiffServ), a dedicated class that trusts the marking, and fq_codel, a per-flow fair-queuing scheduler, in two simulators and on a real Linux kernel. VATC matched DiffServ under steady load. In a constructed burst it cut mean agent queuing delay by 98% relative to DiffServ in simulation (assuming an immediate verdict), at a 12% increase in human delay; most of the gain came from the separate class. Under a spoofed flood in the kernel, the rate limit held human latency 11 times below DiffServ's. Without verification, DiffServ and a tightly configured fq_codel gave legitimate agents lower latency than VATC; a live four-feature classifier then demoted all 20 bulk-shaped spoofers and gave agents 0.30 ms, but missed six spoofers that copied the agent pattern. With emulated network delay, a timing feature of the classifier stopped separating agent from human flows. In real agent harnesses on a congested link, router queueing took 13% to 63% of task time, depending on harness and assumed model latency. The traffic was synthetic or sandbox-scale.
papers.summary: Traffic from LLM-based software agents differs from human web traffic, but routers have no class for it and cannot verify a sender's claim to be an agent. The Verifiable Agentic Traffic Class (`VATC`) combines a reserved Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) value declaring agent traffic, a router-side classifier that demotes flows contradicting the declaration, and a rate-limited priority queue, and is compared against static DiffServ, a trusting dedicated class, and `fq_codel` in two simulators and a real Linux kernel. Results are mixed: `VATC` matched DiffServ under steady load and **under a spoofed flood in the kernel its rate limit held human latency 11 times below DiffServ's**, but the live classifier missed six spoofers that copied the agent pattern and a timing feature failed under emulated network delay. The authors note that all traffic was synthetic or sandbox-scale.

papers.title: Stagewise and interpretable emergence of inside-outside computation in Transformer-based language models
papers.abstract: Variability in syntactic structure and parsing ambiguity are fundamental aspects of natural language which modern LLMs have to learn to deal with proficiently. Previous "post-mortem" studies have shown that fully trained Transformers indeed approximate canonical parsing algorithms such as inside-outside, but little is established theoretically about how this is actually learned. Here, we make a first step towards addressing this by studying the learning dynamics in synthetic context-free grammars with variable parse tree topology. The stagewise learning curves are fully interpretable, in the sense that all of the loss stages a) can be computed analytically, and b) can be clearly associated to the representation of a hidden latent tree variable, which allows to lift ambiguity and utilize information from wider contexts. By probing representations, we visualize the emergence of inside-outside computation across depth and during training: while during early stages local (bigram/trigram) information is used and involves only a few initial layers, gradually the Transformer develops an encoder-decoder structure where the most abstract latent information is encoded in the middle, and the latter half of the network is used to progressively refine the final token prediction. This organization of computation is reminiscent of findings in real-world LLMs, and importantly applies here to a synthetic model which allows full analytical control of the data statistics, thus opening the door to theoretical progress.
papers.summary: Fully trained Transformers are known to approximate parsing algorithms such as inside-outside, but how this computation is learned is poorly understood theoretically. The authors study training dynamics on synthetic context-free grammars with variable parse tree topology, where the data statistics are under full analytical control. They find that **every stage of the stagewise loss curve can be computed analytically and tied to the representation of a hidden latent tree variable**. Probing shows the model first uses local bigram and trigram information in a few early layers, then gradually develops an encoder-decoder organization with the most abstract latent information in the middle layers and later layers refining the token prediction.

papers.title: StaRSE: Compact Russian Sentence Embeddings with a Sign-Coded Static Encoder
papers.abstract: Transformer sentence encoders provide strong retrieval quality, but their inference cost becomes a bottleneck when embeddings must be produced on CPUs or refreshed frequently. We introduce StaRSE, a compact Russian static sentence encoder that removes Transformer inference at deployment time: token directions are stored as sign bits, token norms are stored separately, and sentences are encoded by mean pooling over norm-scaled sign directions. StaRSE is initialized from ruBERT-base, fine-tuned on Russian adjacent-sentence and task-shaped pairs, and post-trained with a contrastive stage that directly optimizes the sign-projected token table. On RuMTEB, StaRSE reaches a task mean of $51.16$, $7.98$ points above the strongest included static baseline. The packaged model occupies $11.3$ MiB and has a mean CPU latency of $0.08$ ms per sentence, compared with an estimated $55.7$ MiB 16-bit parameter footprint and $1.43$ ms mean CPU latency for the closest-quality contextual encoder. Ablations examine adjacent-sentence supervision, token norms, and direct sign-projected post-training.
