papers.summary: Transformer sentence encoders are costly when embeddings must be computed on CPUs or refreshed often. `StaRSE` is a static Russian sentence encoder with no Transformer inference at deployment: token directions are stored as sign bits, token norms separately, and sentences are encoded by mean pooling over norm-scaled sign directions, with the table initialized from `ruBERT-base` and trained contrastively. On `RuMTEB` it reaches a task mean of 51.16, which is 7.98 points above the strongest included static baseline. The packaged model takes **11.3 MiB and 0.08 ms mean CPU latency per sentence**, compared with an estimated 55.7 MiB and 1.43 ms for the closest-quality contextual encoder.

papers.title: On Federated Averaging with Partial Participation under a General Variance Condition
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study the convergence of Federated Averaging (FedAvg) with partial participation under a general variance condition. In each communication round, the server samples $S$ of the $n$ clients uniformly at random without replacement. The stochastic gradients are assumed to satisfy the so-called ABC condition, which allows their variance to grow with the local objective gaps. For smooth nonconvex objectives, we establish a finite-time stationarity bound in terms of the heterogeneity measure $\sigma_f^\star:=f^\star-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i^\star$ and the client sampling factor $I_S:=(n-S)/(n-1)$. Here, $f^\star$ and $f_i^\star$ denote the infima of the global average objective and client $i$'s local objective, respectively. The bound exhibits a linear speedup in the number of sampled clients $S$ and recovers the full-participation result when $S=n$. Under diminishing stepsizes, we further prove that the gradient norm converges to zero both in expectation and almost surely. Notably, compared with existing analyses of FedAvg with partial participation, our results require no additional data heterogeneity assumption such as bounded gradient dissimilarity (BGD), and the sampling-induced term in our bound is not amplified by the number of local updates at the leading order. The importance of removing the BGD assumption is illustrated by an example that is smooth and lower bounded but violates BGD, yet is covered by our analysis.
papers.summary: The convergence of Federated Averaging (`FedAvg`) is analyzed when the server samples S of n clients uniformly without replacement each round and stochastic gradients satisfy the ABC condition, which lets their variance grow with local objective gaps. For smooth nonconvex objectives the authors derive a finite-time stationarity bound with linear speedup in the number of sampled clients that recovers the full-participation result when all clients participate, and under diminishing stepsizes they prove the gradient norm converges to zero in expectation and almost surely. Unlike existing partial-participation analyses, **the results need no extra data heterogeneity assumption such as bounded gradient dissimilarity (BGD)**, and the sampling-induced term is not amplified by the number of local updates at leading order.

papers.title: Dyship: Leveraging Acoustic Features For Speaker Relationship Classification From Dyadic Conversations
papers.abstract: We introduce DyShip, a framework for classifying speaker familiarity and kinship from dyadic conversations in the Seamless Interaction corpus. We compare five speech representations: spectrograms, MFCCs, self-supervised WavLM representations, x-vectors, and estimated articulatory movements. Spectral features perform best for familiarity classification, reaching an accuracy of 87.81%, while WavLM achieves the highest kinship accuracy of 85.17%. X-vectors and articulatory features yield weaker results on familiarity classifiaction, but shine for kinship classification, with an AUC of 0.909 for x-vectors. Most classifiers exceed previously reported human and audio language model scores on the same dataset. These findings highlight the potential of conventional acoustic features for relationship inference and motivate further investigation of the conversational cues captured by different representations.
papers.summary: `DyShip` classifies how familiar two speakers are and whether they are kin, using two-person conversations from the `Seamless Interaction` corpus. Five speech representations are compared: spectrograms, MFCCs, self-supervised `WavLM` features, x-vectors, and estimated articulatory movements. **Spectral features do best on familiarity at 87.81% accuracy, while `WavLM` gives the highest kinship accuracy at 85.17%**, and x-vectors reach an AUC of 0.909 on kinship despite weaker familiarity results. Most classifiers exceed previously reported human and audio language model scores on the same dataset.

papers.title: An AI Assistant for Automating Anti-Corruption Expertise of Draft Legislation Based on the TRACE Framework
papers.abstract: We present an AI assistant for automating anti-corruption expertise of draft legislation based on the TRACE architecture, designed to screen bills for corruption risks: pinpoint provisions an expert would criticise and name the regulatory defect in each. The pipeline combines a deterministic parsing core, model-guided single-provision qualification, rule-based factor assignment, and external human oversight. To evaluate the assistant, we constructed an open benchmark from the published conclusions of Ukraine's National Agency on Corruption Prevention (NAZK), comprising 132 draft laws with 474 model-extracted findings. A system flag agrees with a finding when it targets a compatible provision and an LLM judge rates the risk as the same (strict) or partly the same (lenient). On 100 draft laws, the pipeline matches 0.28 of the findings within its top ten flags using the local Gemma 4 31B model, 0.30 with Sonnet 5.5, and 0.43-0.46 across all flags (non-blind; the frozen blind baseline achieves 0.21, 95% CI 0.16-0.26). Across all runs, most misses occur on provisions that the system located but qualified as a different risk, and none of the 32 legal-collision findings was matched. On 21 acts held out from tuning, the pipeline outperforms a monolithic prompt containing the full methodology under the strict measure, though not under the lenient one, and Opus 5.5 adds nothing over Sonnet. The reported scores reflect agreement with model-extracted findings rated by an LLM judge whose two access routes agree on 73 of 74 labels, without human expert validation.
authors: State Scientific Research Institute of Armament
papers.summary: An assistant built on the `TRACE` architecture screens draft legislation for corruption risks by flagging provisions an expert would criticise and naming the regulatory defect, combining deterministic parsing, model-guided qualification of single provisions, rule-based factor assignment, and human oversight. It is evaluated on an open benchmark built from published conclusions of Ukraine's National Agency on Corruption Prevention (NAZK), covering 132 draft laws and 474 model-extracted findings. On 100 draft laws the pipeline **matches 0.28 of findings within its top ten flags using the local `Gemma 4 31B` model and 0.30 with `Sonnet 5.5`**, rising to 0.43-0.46 across all flags in a non-blind setting, with most misses on provisions it located but labelled as a different risk and none of the 32 legal-collision findings matched. The scores measure agreement with model-extracted findings as rated by an LLM judge, without human expert validation.

papers.title: SinkState: On-the-Fly SVD of Recurrent States for Efficient Hybrid LLM Serving
papers.abstract: Hybrid models combine softmax attention with linear attention, which compresses history into fixed-size recurrent states to balance model quality and inference efficiency. However, linear attention has not pushed this compression to its limit: we find that the queries, keys, and values of linear layers concentrate in a stable, low-dimensional subspace, a phenomenon we call the linear attention sink, so each state is effectively low-rank, with a rank that varies across states. Yet existing serving systems keep these redundant states dense, reading and rewriting them in full at every decoding step, so their memory traffic grows with the batch size and dominates the decoding cost. Thus SinkState stores each recurrent state in an adaptive low-rank form throughout inference with buffered updates and a local SVD restricted to the top subspace. SinkState further consolidates the remaining components asynchronously on the CPU. On four hybrid models with Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet (GDN) layers, from 4B to 120B parameters, SinkState reduces the peak memory of recurrent states by up to 2.6x (1.9x on average) and speeds up decoding by up to 1.58x (1.25x on average) over Mamba-SSM and FLA, while maintaining accuracy.
papers.summary: Hybrid language models mix softmax attention with linear attention layers that compress history into fixed-size recurrent states, yet serving systems keep these states dense and rewrite them in full at every decoding step, so memory traffic dominates decoding cost at larger batch sizes. The authors observe that queries, keys, and values in linear layers concentrate in a stable low-dimensional subspace, which they call the linear attention sink, making each state effectively low-rank. `SinkState` stores each state in an adaptive low-rank form during inference using buffered updates and a local SVD on the top subspace, consolidating the remainder asynchronously on the CPU. Across four hybrid models with `Mamba-2` and Gated DeltaNet (`GDN`) layers from 4B to 120B parameters, it **reduces peak recurrent-state memory by up to 2.6x and speeds up decoding by up to 1.58x** over `Mamba-SSM` and `FLA` while maintaining accuracy.

papers.title: Personalized Affective Perception via Continual Learning in Human-Agent Negotiation
papers.abstract: Self-interested intelligent agents that negotiate with humans should interpret nonverbal expressions and adapt their behavior accordingly. However, generic facial-affect models degrade across individuals and contexts, creating a generalization gap. We introduce an affect-adaptive negotiation strategy that incorporates Continual Learning with Imagination for Facial Expression Recognition (CLIFER) to personalize valence-arousal perception in real time. Differential feedback converts changes in valence-arousal direction and intensity into adjustments of the agent's target utility. An asynchronous architecture updates CLIFER in the background during live interaction. In a counterbalanced within-subject study in which 66 participants negotiated with a humanoid robot, the CL-enabled agent achieved significantly higher individual utility and elicited higher participant concession rates than the FaceChannel baseline. The CL condition yielded significantly higher mean arousal estimates, alongside a broader output range. Participant utility and Nash distance did not change significantly between conditions. These outcomes support the practical value of coupling continual affective personalization with differential feedback for real-time negotiation.
papers.summary: Generic facial-affect models degrade across individuals and contexts, which hampers agents that negotiate with humans and need to read nonverbal expressions. The authors build a negotiation strategy around Continual Learning with Imagination for Facial Expression Recognition (`CLIFER`), which personalizes valence-arousal perception in the background during live interaction, and convert changes in perceived affect into adjustments of the agent's target utility. In a counterbalanced within-subject study where 66 participants negotiated with a humanoid robot, **the continual-learning agent achieved significantly higher individual utility and elicited higher participant concession rates than the `FaceChannel` baseline**. Participant utility and Nash distance did not differ significantly between conditions.

papers.title: Semantic Chains: From Reachable Facts to Justified Answers
papers.abstract: How can the facts that justify an answer be found from a question and presented as a sequence of connected statements? This paper models a context as a graph of logical facts and takes as given which expressions represent each fact. A parent fact can express a relation among its subfacts, and a preserving edge allows the content of a subfact to be recovered within a full representation of its parent. Suppose a root fact justifies the full answer and a path of preserving edges leads from that root to a fact that designates an object shared by the question and the answer. Under the conditions of the model, a search starting from the objects in the question reaches the root and covers every fact in the selected expansion. The root then admits a text that forms a single link connecting the question to the full answer and justifying it. For chains with several links, the paper gives a complete enumeration of candidate orders within the stated class and specifies when the link texts jointly preserve the justification and support every transition.
papers.summary: The question addressed is how to find the facts that justify an answer and present them as a sequence of connected statements. A context is modeled as a graph of logical facts, in which parent facts express relations among subfacts and preserving edges let a subfact's content be recovered from its parent's representation. Under the model's conditions, **a search starting from the objects in the question provably reaches the root fact that justifies the full answer** and covers every fact in the selected expansion, yielding a single-link text connecting question to answer. For multi-link chains, the work enumerates all candidate orders within a stated class and specifies when the link texts jointly preserve the justification.

papers.title: A Cross-Scenario Survey and Analysis of Self-Evolving Multimodal Agents
papers.abstract: Recent work shows that multimodal agents increasingly self-improve without recurring human annotation. However, each self-improvement mechanism is designed and evaluated within a single scenario, leaving its preconditions unverified under cross-scenario transfer. This survey investigates the structural source of asymmetric mechanism transfer across four scenarios: multimodal reasoning, multimodal generation, GUI and Web navigation, and embodied manipulation. We first formalize the self-evolving multimodal agent by four criteria and a differentia of self-reference, and adopt the three-stage self-evolving loop of experience generation, feedback acquisition, and update consolidation as our analytical framework to position the scenarios along ceilings on rollout count and feedback fidelity. Comparing self-evolving with fixed loops within each scenario separates the limitations that the scenario imposes from those inherent in the self-evolving design. We then recast each mechanism as a trade-off that raises a scarce factor by presupposing a task-structural resource, such as output equivalence or checkable outcomes, and judge it portable, conditional, blocked, or redundant across scenarios. We attribute the asymmetry to divergent combinations of scarce factors and resources across opposite transfer directions, and identify the matched-budget measurements that could overturn these still untested verdicts.
papers.summary: Self-improvement mechanisms for multimodal agents are typically designed and tested within a single scenario, so it is unclear whether they transfer. This survey compares four scenarios (multimodal reasoning, multimodal generation, GUI and Web navigation, and embodied manipulation) using a three-stage loop of experience generation, feedback acquisition, and update consolidation, positioning each scenario by its ceilings on rollout count and feedback fidelity. Each mechanism is recast as a trade-off that raises a scarce factor by relying on a task-structural resource such as output equivalence or checkable outcomes, and is judged **portable, conditional, blocked, or redundant** across scenarios. The authors attribute asymmetric transfer to differing combinations of scarce factors and resources, and note that these verdicts are untested and name the matched-budget measurements that could overturn them.

papers.title: Lilo: A Multi-Agent Conversational Sandbox for Children's Digital Communication
papers.abstract: Children's peer conflicts increasingly play out in group chats, where tone and timing are stripped away, and a hurtful message is easier to send than to say aloud. We present Lilo, a multi-agent conversational system that lets children practice such conversations, so they are better prepared when they encounter them in real digital communication. In Lilo, the child joins two AI-driven peers mid-argument, coached by a mentor character, also named Lilo, through a Stop-Think-Act traffic light. Through an exploratory study with 28 children (aged 9-11), we examine how children engage with Lilo's simulated peer conflict and the mentor's traffic-light interventions. The study included an intervention with Lilo, surveys before and after the intervention, and exit interviews. Participants reported significantly higher self-efficacy for coping with unpleasant messages after their interaction with Lilo. They felt safe experimenting, knowing nothing they wrote would be held against them.
papers.summary: Children's peer conflicts increasingly happen in group chats, where tone and timing are lost. `Lilo` is a multi-agent conversational system in which a child joins two AI-driven peers mid-argument and is coached by a mentor character through a Stop-Think-Act traffic light. In an exploratory study with 28 children aged 9-11, using pre- and post-intervention surveys and exit interviews, participants reported **significantly higher self-efficacy for coping with unpleasant messages** after using the system. They also said they felt safe experimenting because nothing they wrote would be held against them.

papers.title: Recurrent Modular Structure in Spiking Neural Network Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Biological neural circuits are both modular and recurrent, with dense communities sparsely linked to one another. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) for reinforcement learning are usually feed-forward, and it is unclear how to obtain functional modules in a recurrent SNN or what they buy. In this work, we introduce a class of spiking networks, called Community Recurrent SNNs (CoRe SNNs): recurrent networks partitioned into communities with fixed roles. A controller community receives the stimulus, each action has its own community, and latent communities carry internal state. Spiking activity is then a walk between communities, and the action is the community the walk reaches. All learning is local and three-factor, and the recurrent communities are closer to cortical microcircuits than a feed-forward actor. We compare three regimes for obtaining the communities: dynamic modularity, in which a new learning rule we introduce, Map-STDP, encourages modular structure during learning; partial modularity, in which a stochastic block model (SBM) initialization enforces it partly; and full modularity, in which sealing enforces it fully. On CartPole, across three spiking neuron models, Map-STDP improves learning over the same network without it matches full modularity (sealed communities) on two of the three models, and makes the observed spike walk more compressible. Replacing the feed-forward actor of a TD-STDP actor-critic with recurrent action communities improves on the feed-forward network on CartPole and LunarLander, and matches it on Acrobot. How strongly to enforce modularity depends on the task: full modularity helps most on Acrobot, while on LunarLander the dynamic, partial and full regimes perform alike. Overall, these recurrent modular networks can match or even improve upon feed-forward approaches, with improvements in bio-plausibility and energy efficiency.
papers.summary: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) for reinforcement learning are usually feed-forward, unlike biological circuits, which are modular and recurrent. Community Recurrent SNNs (`CoRe SNNs`) partition a recurrent network into communities with fixed roles (a controller, one community per action, and latent state communities), so that the chosen action is the community that spiking activity reaches, with all learning local and three-factor. Three ways of obtaining modularity are compared: a new learning rule called `Map-STDP`, a stochastic block model initialization, and fully sealed communities. On `CartPole`, `Map-STDP` improves learning and matches full modularity on two of three neuron models, and **replacing the feed-forward actor of a `TD-STDP` actor-critic with recurrent action communities improves results on `CartPole` and `LunarLander` and matches them on `Acrobot`**.

papers.title: Chain of Physics: Supporting Fault Diagnosis with Engineering-Inspired Large Language Model Reasoning
papers.abstract: Fault diagnosis in complex systems requires linking observed changes in physical quantities to the failure mechanisms that produce them. Experienced engineers perform this task by combining sensor information with knowledge of system behavior and fault propagation. Large Language Models (LLMs) can support this process, but their diagnostic reasoning depends on the availability of asset-specific engineering knowledge and on how this knowledge is represented and used during inference. This work introduces Chain of Physics (CoP), an LLM-based fault-diagnosis framework built around a Constrained Knowledge Graph (CKG) generated automatically from asset-specific reference documentation. CoP addresses failure-sensor association from textual engineering knowledge. The CKG stores diagnostic chains connecting failure modes, changes in physical quantities, and monitoring sensors. During inference, semantically similar graph paths are retrieved for each question and used as both information and in-context examples for the reasoning process. Candidate failure modes are extracted from the question and analysed independently through dedicated LLM calls, which generate plausible failure-to-observation chains. A final decision module compares these chains with the available answer choices. CoP is evaluated on the FailureSensorIQ benchmark across four industrial asset classes and three LLMs. Compared with direct prompting and conventional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), CoP improves diagnostic accuracy across all evaluated models, with gains ranging from 7.8 to 19.6 percentage points and from 11.7 to 18.2 percentage points, respectively. The results show that structured engineering knowledge can improve LLM-based diagnostic reasoning when graph retrieval is combined with in-context examples of fault propagation.
papers.summary: Diagnosing faults in industrial systems requires linking sensor-observed changes in physical quantities to the failure mechanisms behind them, which large language models (LLMs) handle poorly without asset-specific engineering knowledge. `Chain of Physics` (`CoP`) automatically builds a Constrained Knowledge Graph from reference documentation, storing chains that connect failure modes, physical-quantity changes, and monitoring sensors. At inference it retrieves similar graph paths as both information and in-context examples, analyses each candidate failure mode in a separate LLM call, and compares the resulting chains with the answer choices. On the `FailureSensorIQ` benchmark across four asset classes and three LLMs, accuracy improves by **7.8 to 19.6 percentage points over direct prompting** and 11.7 to 18.2 points over conventional retrieval-augmented generation.

papers.title: Physics-Constrained Autoencoder for Interpretable Health Representation Learning in Turbofan Engines
papers.abstract: Health Indices (HIs) summarize degradation from operational data and support diagnostic and prognostic tasks in Prognostics and Health Management (PHM). Their usefulness depends on capturing degradation and interpreting system condition. Autoencoders learn such representations from unlabelled monitoring data; however, when training is driven only by reconstruction, the physical meaning of latent variables remains undefined, limiting their interpretation and diagnostic value. This work proposes a physics-constrained autoencoder that embeds system knowledge as an inductive bias in the decoder architecture and as a learning bias in the loss function. The decoder contains differentiable physical equations that receive latent variables and operating conditions as inputs, structurally guiding each latent variable to represent a predefined physical quantity and enabling component-level analysis before aggregation into a system-level HI.The methodology is benchmarked on the N-CMAPSS dataset against alternative representations. Reconstruction reaches an $R^2$ of 0.9993 and an MAE of 0.0036, comparable to fully data-driven models. After operating-condition correction, the inferred physical quantities track degradation, and their aggregation produces an HI with a Spearman correlation of 0.9791 with the ground truth, an RMSE of 0.0286, and an MAE of 0.0233. The methodology is further evaluated using a single model trained across four datasets representing distinct degradation scenarios. This model preserves component-level signatures that distinguish compression-side from expansion-side degradation without diagnostic labels.Finally, the proposed framework enables degradation trends to be visualized on component maps, providing a health representation in a form familiar to engine operators and domain experts.
papers.summary: Autoencoders can learn health indices that summarize machine degradation from unlabelled monitoring data, but their latent variables have no defined physical meaning when training is driven by reconstruction alone. The proposed physics-constrained autoencoder places differentiable physical equations in the decoder and adds a physics term to the loss, so each latent variable represents a predefined physical quantity and components can be analysed before aggregation into a system-level index. On the `N-CMAPSS` turbofan dataset, reconstruction reaches an R² of 0.9993, and the aggregated health index achieves a **Spearman correlation of 0.9791 with the ground truth**. A single model trained across four degradation scenarios distinguishes compression-side from expansion-side degradation without diagnostic labels.

papers.title: Achieving Robust Channel Estimation Neural Networks on Doppler effects by Designed Training Data
papers.abstract: Channel estimation is crucial in wireless communication systems. Many existing works train and test their models using the same or similar channel. However, practical channels are infinitely diverse and time-variant while data-driven algorithms often degrade on new and previously unseen channels. This prohibits the practical implementation of neural networks for channel estimation, particularly in high speed scenarios characterized by rapidly channel profile changes and very high Doppler shifts. Online training can fine-tune models to adapt to new channels, but requires high computation resource and incurs significant latency for physical-layer devices. Moreover, online training cannot exhaustively cover all possible channels because there are infinitely many possible channels. Therefore, we investigate the ability of neural networks to generalize to wireless channels. This paper proposes design criteria to generate synthetic training data, which guaranty that the resulting networks perform robustly across wireless channels, especially for very high Doppler shifts and different Doppler spectra. It ensures that offline-trained neural networks require no prior information or online training to precisely estimate the new channels. To demonstrate general applicability, we use neural networks with different levels of complexity to show that the generalization achieved appears to be independent of architecture. From simulation results, neural networks achieve a certain performance across wireless channels with different unseen power delay profiles (PDP) and Doppler shifts.
papers.summary: Neural networks for wireless channel estimation often degrade on channels unlike those seen in training, especially in high-speed scenarios with very high Doppler shifts, and online fine-tuning is too costly and slow for physical-layer devices. The authors propose design criteria for generating synthetic training data intended to make offline-trained networks robust across channels without prior information or online training. In simulations, networks of differing complexity **maintain performance on unseen power delay profiles and Doppler shifts**, and the generalization appears to be independent of architecture.

papers.title: Federated Learning for Cross-Regional Epidemic Forecasting with Asynchronous Outbreaks
papers.abstract:
Objective: Epidemic outbreaks are often asynchronous across regions, yet collaborative forecasting is hampered by privacy laws and heterogeneous public health interventions. We developed and evaluated, as a proof of concept, a federated learning (FL) framework for cross-regional COVID-19 forecasting under asynchronous outbreaks among Guangdong, Macau, and Portugal, while maintaining data sovereignty.
  Methods: Using daily case data from WHO and China CDC for the three regions, whose outbreaks were asynchronous and interventions heterogeneous, we trained Long Short-Term Memory networks via FL for short-term forecasting, benchmarked against localized and centralized training using Root Mean Square Error, Mean Absolute Error, and Symmetric Mean Absolute Percentage Error. All experiments used the Flower FL framework with consistent hyperparameters across sites. Publicly available, aggregated case-count data were used so that the centralized benchmark could be computed as a reference.
  Results: The dataset comprised 1,233 daily observations (411 days) of new confirmed COVID-19 cases from November 24, 2021, to January 8, 2023. The earlier Omicron wave in Portugal supplied transmission dynamics that improved forecasts in the later-onset regions of Macau and Guangdong. The FL model achieved a normalized Root Mean Square Error of 0.028, an 88.3% improvement over the local model (0.240) and comparable to the centralized model, with network overhead mainly determined by model size and aggregation rounds.
  Conclusion: FL achieved short-term forecasting accuracy close to centralized training while maintaining data residency, with acceptable overhead. Leveraging asynchronous outbreaks across regions may offer a practical path to privacy-preserving collaborative forecasting, though prospective validation is required.
papers.summary: Collaborative epidemic forecasting across regions is hampered by privacy laws and differing public health interventions, even though outbreaks arriving at different times could inform each other. This proof of concept trains Long Short-Term Memory networks with federated learning, using the `Flower` framework, on daily COVID-19 case counts from Guangdong, Macau, and Portugal, and compares against local and centralized training. The federated model reaches a normalized root mean square error of 0.028, an **88.3% improvement over the local model (0.240)** and comparable to centralized training, with Portugal's earlier Omicron wave improving forecasts for the later-onset regions. The authors note that prospective validation is still required.

papers.title: Compositional random forest
papers.abstract: Compositional data have been analysed in the literature from three main points of view: directly on the simplex, in log-ratio coordinates, and as directional data on the unit sphere. In this paper, we construct a random forest framework for compositional responses that accommodates all three. Random forests are ensembles of decision trees, and the split criterion determines how each tree grows. We use the log-likelihood gain as the split criterion and consider distributions defined on the different spaces in which compositions can be represented. The Dirichlet likelihood has been studied in the literature, but its covariance is fixed by its mean up to a single scalar, and its maximum likelihood estimator has no closed form. To obtain more flexible criteria, we use two well-known transformations. First, the square-root transformation maps compositions onto the unit sphere, where existing directional distributions require numerical estimation. We introduce a tangent-normal (TN) distribution, which shares its parameters with the Kent distribution, and construct a split criterion whose gain is computed from additive sufficient statistics: the shape parameters are maximised out in closed form, up to an exponentially small truncation constant, so that no parameter is estimated iteratively. Second, the log-ratio transformation maps compositions to Euclidean space, where the multivariate logistic-normal distribution has a flexible covariance and a closed-form maximum log-likelihood, also based on additive sufficient statistics. Both criteria respond to a shift of the mean, measured relative to the covariance, and to a change in the covariance itself. In simulations, the most accurate forest depended on the covariance structure of the composition. The TN forest was the most accurate in two of the three designs.
papers.summary: Compositional data (vectors of proportions) can be analysed on the simplex, in log-ratio coordinates, or as directions on the unit sphere, and this work builds a random forest framework for compositional responses that covers all three. Trees split on log-likelihood gain, and two criteria more flexible than the Dirichlet are introduced: a new tangent-normal (`TN`) distribution on the sphere and the multivariate logistic-normal in log-ratio space, both computed in closed form from additive sufficient statistics without iterative estimation. In simulations the most accurate forest depended on the composition's covariance structure, with the **`TN` forest most accurate in two of three designs**.

papers.title: Ninety-Six Ways to Measure a Scribe: Fragmented Evaluation of Ambient Scribes in Healthcare
papers.abstract: Ambient artificial intelligence (AI) scribes have moved rapidly from experimental pilots to enterprise-wide deployment across health systems, promising reduced documentation burden and improved clinician experience. While research evaluating these tools has expanded quickly, there are no agreed-upon protocols or standardized metrics for assessing their performance, making it difficult to compare findings or cumulatively synthesize evidence across studies. Across 54 recent evaluation studies, we identify ten evaluation dimensions and 40 distinct metrics, operationalized in 96 different ways-35 of them (36%) used by only a single study. Assessment is dominated by documentation efficiency and time, measured in 44 of 54 studies. The other dimensions appear at broadly similar rates (16-24 studies each), and safety and clinical outcome least consistently of all. Ripple effects on the broader care system, such as impact on patients' care outcomes, redistribution of work, changes in billing and coding intensity, and downstream use of notes by other clinicians are rarely assessed. Moreover, the metrics used rely heavily on self-report and are fragmented and inconsistently operationalized, which limits comparability and hinders synthesis across studies. As an effort to support more rigorous and cumulative evaluation, in this paper we review the study designs, data sources, and metrics commonly used to evaluate ambient AI scribes in healthcare settings, discuss the limitations of current evaluation practice, and argue for a more holistic approach grounded in a standardized, multi-dimensional set of metrics.
papers.summary: Ambient AI scribes that draft clinical notes are being deployed across health systems, yet there are no agreed protocols or standard metrics for evaluating them. A review of 54 recent evaluation studies identifies ten evaluation dimensions and 40 distinct metrics that are **operationalized in 96 different ways, 35 of them used by only a single study**. Documentation efficiency and time dominate, appearing in 44 of 54 studies, while safety, clinical outcomes, and wider effects such as billing intensity or redistribution of work are rarely or inconsistently assessed, and many metrics rely on self-report. The authors argue for a standardized, multi-dimensional metric set.

papers.title: LM-SimBench: A Unified Framework, Dataset, and Benchmark for Large Language Model Training Simulation
papers.abstract: Evaluating candidate parallelization strategies through distributed training runs makes strategy selection prohibitively expensive at scale. Performance simulation offers a lower cost alternative, yet controlled comparisons among existing simulators remain difficult because they differ in the training stages they model and the workloads on which they are evaluated. We introduce LM-SimBench, a unified framework, profiling dataset, and benchmark for evaluating LLM training simulators. The framework decomposes simulation into functional stages from model compilation to schedule level aggregation, connecting execution representations and cost estimators to measurable evaluation targets. Following this framework, we profile 23 model settings from 10 dense and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLM families on an Ascend Neural Processing Unit (NPU) cluster. The resulting dataset contains 348 feasible configurations that jointly vary five parallelism dimensions and activation recomputation, with six views spanning configuration, rank, operator, event, and kernel granularity. Evaluations of representative training simulators demonstrate how LM-SimBench supports comparisons of prediction accuracy, assessment of configuration selection, and diagnosis of prediction errors. Matched GPU-NPU experiments validate the cross-platform applicability of the collection and evaluation protocol and demonstrate NPU-guided GPU configuration selection.
papers.summary: Choosing a parallelization strategy for large language model training by running real distributed jobs is expensive, and existing performance simulators are hard to compare because they model different training stages and workloads. `LM-SimBench` provides a framework that decomposes simulation into stages from model compilation to schedule-level aggregation, together with a profiling dataset and benchmark. The dataset covers 23 model settings from 10 dense and Mixture-of-Experts model families profiled on an Ascend Neural Processing Unit (NPU) cluster, giving **348 feasible configurations** that vary five parallelism dimensions and activation recomputation. Evaluations of representative simulators show how it supports comparing prediction accuracy and configuration selection, and matched GPU-NPU experiments demonstrate NPU-guided GPU configuration selection.

papers.title: MMDM: Measuring Massive Multitask Decision Making
papers.abstract: System-1 Decision Models directly make structured probabilistic decisions over query-specified options given a state in a single forward pass, without autoregressively generating reasoning trajectories or textual responses. Recent evaluations cover diverse tasks but often rely on existing benchmarks, where prior exposure to test material can obscure generalization. Moreover, real-world decision making often involves long contexts, large option spaces, and complex logical dependencies, challenges that existing benchmarks do not adequately capture together. Thus, we introduce MMDM (Massive Multitask Decision Making), a benchmark of 5,448 high-quality questions across 16 task categories, combining newly constructed tasks with source-grounded recompositions and rewrites for single-select, multi-select, and soft-label decision making in fresh contexts. It covers realistic scenarios such as agent state tracking, tool and skill selection, preference judgments, and rubric scoring, with option spaces ranging from 2 to 1,024 and inputs extending to 64,817 tokens. With MMDM, we conduct a comprehensive quantitative evaluation of 28 decision models, showing that many perform well on common knowledge yet struggle with interdependent options, constrained decisions, and multi-select tasks. For example, Perplexity Decider-V1.2 reaches 78.75% Hard Single-select Accuracy on world knowledge, but only 53.95% on option logic and 47.95% on constraint planning, while the best Hard Multi-select Accuracy across all models is 36.81%. These results highlight joint reasoning, constraint-aware selection, and complete multi-select recovery as key priorities for decision model development, with MMDM providing a testbed for measuring this progress.
papers.summary: System-1 decision models output structured probabilistic choices over given options in a single forward pass, without generating reasoning text, and existing benchmarks for them risk test-set exposure and do not combine long contexts, large option spaces, and logical dependencies. `MMDM` is a benchmark of 5,448 questions across 16 task categories covering single-select, multi-select, and soft-label decisions, including agent state tracking and tool selection, with up to 1,024 options and inputs up to 64,817 tokens. An evaluation of 28 decision models finds that many do well on common knowledge but struggle with interdependent options and constraints. For example, `Perplexity Decider-V1.2` scores 78.75% hard single-select accuracy on world knowledge but 47.95% on constraint planning, and **the best hard multi-select accuracy of any model is 36.81%**.
papers.highlight_summary:
System-1 decision models emit a probability distribution over query-specified options in a single forward pass, but existing benchmarks for them reuse public test sets and rarely combine long contexts, large option spaces and interdependent options. `MMDM` is a **5,448-question** benchmark across **16 task categories** that tests single-select, multi-select and soft-label decisions on freshly constructed or rewritten instances.

- The benchmark has 4,112 single-select, 633 multi-select and 703 soft-label questions with **2 to 1,024 options** and inputs up to **64,817 tokens**, built from new tasks plus source-grounded rewrites and recompositions of sets such as `QuALITY`, `BIRD` and `ToolTalk`, then filtered by five-model majority screening, human review of borderline cases and an option-only shortcut probe.
- Across **28 decision models**, `WeMM-JEV 27B` leads with **76.00%** single-select accuracy and also the best multi-select accuracy at only **36.81%**, while every model's Separation–Balance F-score stays below **0.20**, showing that recovering the complete valid set remains largely unsolved.
- Joint-consistency tasks are the weak spot: `Perplexity Decider-V1.2` scores **78.75%** on world knowledge but **53.95%** on option logic and **47.95%** on constraint planning, and `KnowLine 31B Gen1` drops from 86.0% on deductive reasoning to 54.6% and 48.5% on the same two categories.
- Accuracy does not predict probability quality or scaling behaviour, since `KnowLine 31B Gen1` trails `WeMM-JEV 27B` by under one point in accuracy yet has roughly half the Soft Brier error (**0.1233 vs 0.2327**) and under a third of the score error (**0.0624 vs 0.2203**), and `OpenJev 4B` beats `Intern-Decision 4B` in every option-count bin but falls to 15.5% against 34.5% on 8K–16K-token inputs.
- The benchmark is text-only with a fixed state, query and option set, its multi-select and soft-label questions are concentrated in a few categories (mostly rubric scoring for soft targets), and rewritten instances may still benefit from prior exposure to the underlying public sources.

papers.title: Multimodal Abstention That Preserves Acquired Correct Answers
papers.abstract: Adding abstention to a task-adapted multimodal model can discard correct answers, including capabilities acquired during adaptation. We formulate abstention repair as maximizing correct abstention on unanswerable questions under a budget on newly lost correct answers. We propose ReFrain (Regression-Free Abstention), which combines a linear probe on first-token logits, threshold calibration on held-out image clusters, and a deterministic veto that replaces rejected outputs with the displayed "none of the above" option while preserving all other responses. "Regression-free" denotes zero loss on the calibration set at the zero-budget target. All abstention methods in our main comparison start from the same answering-SFT checkpoint; we separately track lost correct answers, repaired errors, and retained SFT gains. On Qwen2.5-VL-3B, ReFrain at zero budget retains all 57 SFT-gained answers with no losses and improves correct abstention by 7.30 percentage points. At a 0.5% calibration budget, it reaches 74.05% correct abstention with 8 losses and retains 55 gains; CLIP-UP EmbLoRA reaches 64.65% with 62 losses, 41 repairs, and 40 retained gains. The same probe at its default threshold loses 298 correct answers. With models and thresholds frozen, confirmation on 228 independent question clusters yields 66.05% correct abstention and no losses at the 0.5% point, exceeding EmbLoRA by 32.72 percentage points. Ordinary refusal SFT achieves higher correct abstention at greater regression cost. Code and reproduction materials: https://github.com/ModeLiberaL/ReFrain.
papers.summary: Teaching a fine-tuned multimodal model to abstain on unanswerable questions can make it discard correct answers, including ones gained during fine-tuning. `ReFrain` (Regression-Free Abstention) treats this as maximizing correct abstention under a budget on newly lost correct answers, combining a linear probe on first-token logits, threshold calibration on held-out image clusters, and a deterministic veto that swaps rejected outputs for the displayed none-of-the-above option. On `Qwen2.5-VL-3B` at zero budget it retains all 57 fine-tuning gains with no losses while improving correct abstention by 7.30 percentage points. At a 0.5% budget it reaches **74.05% correct abstention with 8 lost answers, versus 64.65% with 62 losses for `CLIP-UP EmbLoRA`**.

papers.title: PSL-RGHA: Parallel Split Learning with Reference Gradient Half-Space Alignment for Mitigating Gradient Divergence
papers.abstract: The escalating complexity of deep neural networks hinders the deployment of federated learning (FL) on resource-constrained devices, especially for multimedia applications such as on-device image classification and speech recognition. Parallel split learning (PSL) has emerged as a promising solution by offloading a substantial portion of the computational workload to the server through layer-wise model partitioning, making it particularly suitable for resource-limited visual and speech intelligence scenarios. However, the absence of client-side aggregation renders PSL sus ceptible to severe training divergence and potential convergence failure under heterogeneous data distributions. To address this challenge, we propose PSL-RGHA, a gradient-aligned PSL framework that employs reference gradient half-space alignment mechanism to mitigate training divergence among client devices. PSL-RGHA comprises two novel components: reference gradient progressive construction (RGPC) and gradient half-space alignment (GHA). Specifically, RGPC evaluates the directional consistency of client gradients and progressively synthesizes a robust reference gradient via Weiszfeld updates, effectively approximating the global descent direction. Then, GHA constrains client gradients within the reference half-space defined by RGPC to mitigate gradient conflicts and rectify local updates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our PSL-RGHA framework outperforms existing baselines in various settings.
papers.summary: Parallel split learning (PSL) offloads most of a model's computation from resource-limited devices to a server, but without client-side aggregation it can diverge when clients hold heterogeneous data. `PSL-RGHA` adds two components: reference gradient progressive construction, which checks the directional consistency of client gradients and builds a robust reference gradient via Weiszfeld updates, and gradient half-space alignment, which constrains client gradients to the half-space defined by that reference to reduce conflicts. The authors report that the framework **outperforms existing baselines across various settings**, without giving specific figures in the abstract.

papers.title: MammothDP: Private Boosted Decision Trees Ready for Trusted Hardware and Leakage-free Hyperparameters
papers.abstract: Data spaces like the European Health Data Space (EHDS) require the protection of sensitive data in studies during the data's processing and the study's release alike. In this work, we investigate how to implement this mandate using established trusted execution environments (TEEs) and timing side-channel hardening to protect the processing even under a compromised server, and the state-of-the-art differential privacy (DP) notion to protect the release of studies on tabular data. This combined setup could seem to complete the picture, but in fact raises unexpected security challenges that we mitigate by introducing MammothDP: a significant milestone towards a holistic machine learning system based on the recent gradient boosted decision tree learner S-BDT that is provably DP if used within a privacy filter, timing side-channel hardened, and deployed on a TEE. To achieve a strong privacy-utility tradeoff, we introduce two novel components: an early stopping criterion that adaptively selects the number of trees without any privacy overhead, and an improved rollback protection that is no longer vulnerable under timing side-channel attacks.
papers.summary: Data spaces such as the European Health Data Space require sensitive data to be protected both while it is processed and when study results are released. `MammothDP` combines trusted execution environments, timing side-channel hardening, and differential privacy in a system built on the gradient boosted decision tree learner `S-BDT`, addressing security problems that arise when these protections are combined. It adds an **early stopping criterion that adaptively selects the number of trees with no extra privacy cost**, and a rollback protection that is no longer vulnerable to timing side-channel attacks.

papers.title: Don't Just Trust Your Memory: Evidence-Linked Memory Reduces Memory-Induced Degradation in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: External memory enables LLM agents to improve from experience by distilling trajectories of past tasks into concise lessons for new tasks. However, memory can also lead to memory-induced degradation, where an agent fails on tasks it would solve without memory, often because it follows a lesson that is incorrect, or misapplies or misreads a valid one. This is because lessons are inferred from trajectories labeled only with task success or failure, yet are typically provided without the trajectories they came from, leaving the agent no way to check them. To address this, we introduce WikiTrace, an evidence-linked memory system designed to let agents check each lesson against its original trajectory. Specifically, motivated by the finding that a trajectory often still holds the evidence needed to catch an erroneous lesson, WikiTrace stores each lesson as a concise insight linked to a summary of why its trajectory succeeded or failed and to the raw trajectory itself. Then, on a new task, the agent starts from all insights and, whenever one lacks details needed to act, conflicts with another, or comes from a failed task, descends through its links with terminal tools to fill in missing details or correct the insight before acting. We validate WikiTrace on five agentic benchmarks, showing that it consistently outperforms existing memory approaches and a baseline given the same insights alone, while also reducing memory-induced degradation. Our code is available at https://github.com/yukyeongleee/wikitrace
papers.summary: External memory lets LLM agents distill past trajectories into lessons, but it can also make an agent fail tasks it would solve without memory, because lessons may be wrong or misapplied and arrive without the trajectories needed to check them. `WikiTrace` stores each lesson as a concise insight linked to a summary of why its trajectory succeeded or failed and to the raw trajectory itself. On a new task the agent starts from all insights and uses terminal tools to follow those links whenever an insight lacks detail, conflicts with another, or comes from a failed task. Across five agentic benchmarks it **consistently outperforms existing memory approaches and a baseline given the same insights alone**, while reducing memory-induced degradation.

papers.title: Auditing the Judge: Internal Signals for LLM Reasoning Assurance
papers.abstract: Language-model systems use self-judgment to decide which answers to release, review, or recompute. Because intervention is costly, an assurance score must rank errors well at the available budget, not merely over the full ranking. We compare the judge's continuous verdict-token score with a supervised correctness probe trained on attention-head activations from the same prompt. Exact identities link fixed-budget error recall to residual risk and show that AUROC averages recall over all budgets. Across three open 7-12B models on GSM8K and MATH, the probe finds 1.3-22.5 additional percentage points of errors at 5% review in all six model-dataset settings (median 7.4 points). At 10% routing, probe-guided allocation improves accuracy over equal-cost random allocation in both GSM8K experiments, but beats judge-guided routing only for the weaker judge. Cross-dataset transfer lowers probe AUROC for every model in both directions relative to target-domain training. Because dataset, weight precision, and generation budget change together, this measures a joint protocol shift rather than a dataset-only effect. Internal signals can improve supervised, in-domain budget allocation, but are not domain-general confidence estimators.
papers.summary: Systems that use an LLM to judge its own answers need a score that ranks errors well at a limited review budget, not just on average. The study compares the judge's continuous verdict-token score with a supervised correctness probe trained on attention-head activations from the same prompt, and derives identities linking fixed-budget error recall to residual risk. Across three open 7-12B models on `GSM8K` and `MATH`, the probe catches **1.3 to 22.5 more percentage points of errors at a 5% review budget** in all six settings (median 7.4), though for routing it beats the judge's own score only for the weaker judge. Probe quality drops under cross-dataset transfer, so the authors conclude that internal signals help in-domain budget allocation but are not domain-general confidence estimators.

papers.title: Point-in-Time Encoders for Earnings Calls
papers.abstract: Text encoders turn earnings calls into vectors for search, for language models that answer from retrieved passages, and for forecasting models. A live retriever can use an encoder trained once on all available text, as finance retrievers are, but a backtest needs an encoder that read no text written after the date of each vector. To address this look-ahead bias, from 412,248 calls we train vintages under four pretraining recipes, with yearly cutoffs from 2010 to 2024, and each vintage reads only text dated on or before its cutoff. We then fine-tune each vintage on the question-answer pairs of the calls themselves. The vintages we train on calls alone, with 33.8M parameters, retrieve answers on held-out calls better than the general retrievers we tested in every test quarter. Their vectors also raise by about half the rank correlation between next-day returns and forecasts built from past returns and firm size. When each vintage continues the previous one, a later vintage retrieves better on earlier quarters than the vintage available at the time, and a point-in-time language model that answers from the passages the later vintage retrieves inherits the gain. The 2024 vintage of our families also forecasts earnings surprises better, although the interval of this gain includes zero on calls that no vintage read. It forecasts returns no better, so point-in-time vintages matter most for retrieval and little for forecasts of returns.
papers.summary: Backtests that use text embeddings of earnings calls suffer look-ahead bias if the encoder was trained on text written after the date being simulated. To avoid this, the authors train yearly encoder vintages from 2010 to 2024 on 412,248 calls under four pretraining recipes, each reading only text up to its cutoff, then fine-tune on the calls' own question-answer pairs. The **33.8M-parameter vintages trained on calls alone retrieve answers on held-out calls better than the general retrievers tested in every test quarter**, and their vectors raise by about half the rank correlation between next-day returns and baseline forecasts. The 2024 vintage forecasts returns no better than earlier ones, so point-in-time training matters mostly for retrieval rather than return forecasting.

papers.title: When Should Agents Remember? Falsification-Gated Self-Evolution for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly operate in long-horizon, verifier-rich environments, but current self-improvement mechanisms often write episode-derived lessons directly into memory, making local success an unreliable signal for reusable and safe knowledge. This paper addresses the core question of when an experience-derived behavioral update should be admitted into persistent agent state. We propose Falsification-Gated Self-Evolution (FGSE), a verifier-grounded framework that represents each candidate lesson as a structured hypothesis with an explicit precondition, behavior change, expected effect, and verifier. FGSE applies the hypothesis only in a temporary state, tests it on target-transfer, falsification, and archived-regression probes, and then commits, refines, or rejects it according to measured gain and risk. Across web, app, tool-use, and long-term memory benchmarks, FGSE achieves strong task performance, including 39.8 WebArena success rate, 78.8 AppWorld average completion, and 0.724/0.487 Pass$^1$ on $\tau$-Retail/$\tau$-Airline, while reducing falsification failures to 5.0%, regression damage to 1.3%, and harmful committed updates to 3.6%. These results suggest that testing memory updates as hypotheses supports more reliable long-term adaptation.
papers.summary: LLM agents that write lessons from individual episodes straight into memory can store knowledge that is neither reusable nor safe. Falsification-Gated Self-Evolution (`FGSE`) represents each candidate lesson as a structured hypothesis with a precondition, behavior change, expected effect, and verifier, applies it only in a temporary state, and tests it on transfer, falsification, and archived-regression probes before committing, refining, or rejecting it. It reports a 39.8 success rate on `WebArena`, 78.8 average completion on `AppWorld`, and 0.724/0.487 Pass^1 on `τ-Retail`/`τ-Airline`. It also **reduces harmful committed updates to 3.6%**, with regression damage at 1.3% and falsification failures at 5.0%.

papers.title: Forward-Value Discretization: Faster Stochastic Diffusion Sampling Without High-Order Approximation
papers.abstract: Stochastic diffusion samplers often require substantially more neural function evaluations (NFEs) than deterministic samplers to achieve comparable sample quality. Although higher-order discretization accelerates deterministic sampling, its benefits for stochastic sampling remains unclear. We establish matching upper and worst-case lower bounds showing that stochastic samplers with higher-order approximations remain first-order convergent, even with exact score functions. Thus, increasing the approximation order does not generally improve the convergence order. Motivated by this limitation, we introduce forward-value discretization, a training-free framework that evaluates the data/noise prediction model at a lookahead estimate constructed from previous predictions. For deterministic sampling, the resulting Forward DPMSolver (F-DPMSolver), improves sample quality at low NFE budgets through its DDIM-based variant, despite remaining first-order convergent. For stochastic sampling, we develop Forward DDPM (F-DDPM), which evaluates the model at a cleaner lookahead point adjusted for subsequent noise injection. This estimate reuses both the previous model prediction and the previously injected noise. Both variants admit first-order convergence guarantees with one model evaluation per iteration. Across CIFAR-10, ImageNet, FFHQ, and LSUN, F-DDPM consistently achieves lower FID than the evaluated stochastic baselines at matched NFE budgets. With 1.5 times as many NFEs as deterministic baselines, it achieves competitive sample quality, narrowing the practical efficiency gap between stochastic and deterministic sampling. Code is available at https://github.com/Na-Li66/F-DDPM.
papers.summary: Stochastic diffusion samplers usually need many more neural function evaluations (NFEs) than deterministic ones for comparable quality. The authors prove matching upper and worst-case lower bounds showing that **stochastic samplers with higher-order approximations remain first-order convergent even with exact score functions**. They instead propose forward-value discretization, a training-free approach that evaluates the prediction model at a lookahead estimate built from previous predictions, yielding `F-DPMSolver` for deterministic sampling and `F-DDPM` for stochastic sampling at one model evaluation per step. On `CIFAR-10`, `ImageNet`, `FFHQ`, and `LSUN`, `F-DDPM` achieves lower FID than the stochastic baselines at matched NFEs and is competitive with deterministic baselines when given 1.5 times as many NFEs.

papers.title: AI Isn't Getting Dumber, We're Getting Pickier: Rising Standards in Human Evaluation of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Users often complain that AI assistants such as ChatGPT are getting worse. Some versions do change, but human evaluation leaves a second possibility untested: the people judging may change. We separate the two on Chatbot Arena, a public platform where people compare answers from two anonymous large language models (LLMs) and pick the better one or say both are bad. We study 1,260,967 blind votes cast from May 2023 to August 2024 on pairs of models whose versions are fixed: dated vendor snapshots and models with fixed open weights. For the same pair of unchanged models, the share of votes saying "both are bad" rises by 1.71 percentage points a month on a mean of 17.1%, and by 1.91 points a month in 2024. In fourteen pairs observed often in both 2023 and 2024, it rose in every one, from 15.5% to 23.3%. The ranking does not trend: in 2024, the stronger model's share of decisive votes is flat. The rise holds within the same voter and on the same pair, and across arrival cohorts from their first recorded vote. It holds with prompt controls, in every major language, for dated vendor snapshots, open-weight models and models with stable answer length, and between interface changes. The drift is shared across models: month effects estimated from other models' pairs remove it from each model's own pairs. Platform-wide, the average model would be expected to score 78% against the 2023 average, yet the share of "both are bad" votes ended near where it began. The pattern fits a standard that follows the category's progress, so a product that stands still is judged as declining. Absolute verdicts on AI drifted while relative comparisons held steady, an evaluation drift that matters for LLM leaderboards and for the human feedback used to train models.
papers.summary: Complaints that AI assistants are getting worse could reflect changing judges and not changing models, and this study separates the two using 1,260,967 blind votes on `Chatbot Arena` between May 2023 and August 2024, restricted to pairs of large language models (LLMs) whose versions are fixed. For the same unchanged pair, **the share of votes saying 'both are bad' rises by 1.71 percentage points a month on a mean of 17.1%**, while the stronger model's share of decisive votes stays flat. The rise holds within the same voter, across arrival cohorts, languages, prompt controls and interface changes, and is shared across models. The authors read this as a standard that tracks the field's progress, so absolute verdicts drift while relative comparisons hold steady, which affects leaderboards and human feedback used for training.

papers.title: CLADE: Category-Level Answering from Deficient Evidence in Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented systems often retrieve passages that are accurate and relevant but state the answer at a coarser level of granularity than the question requires. For example, a question may ask which specific disease a drug treats (familial hyperlipidemia), while the retrieved passage mentions the broader disease family (hyperlipidemia). Prior work on context sufficiency treats such coarse passages simply as insufficient. We argue that they form a distinct case, which we call resolvable insufficiency: text alone cannot settle the fine-grained answer, but the broader category it mentions maps to a short list of candidate answers in a domain ontology. When language models read these coarse, family-only passages, they exhibit a phenomenon we call Clade (Category-Level Answering from Deficient Evidence): they answer instead of abstaining or searching further. On biomedical questions from PrimeKG, family-only passages reduce abstention by 13.8 points compared to uninformative passages, and the resulting guesses are wrong about half the time. A counterfactual test confirms the cause: replacing an exact disease name with its broader family name lowers abstention by 17.4 points compared to deleting the sentence. Simple fixes like confidence filtering, scaling to a larger model, and explicitly instructing the model to abstain cannot resolve Clade, and this replicates on ecological species interactions in GloBI. Finally, we test whether an ontology can turn coarse passages into exact answers. Given the correct family, an ontology list includes the true answer in 98.5% of cases, but string matching finds that family on the page for only 19.8%. Letting the model choose the family raises this to 30.0% and end-to-end recovery from 10.0% to 26.8%. Overall, our results show when language models should stop guessing and consult an ontology, and highlight which steps of that process remain unsolved.
papers.summary: Retrieval-augmented systems often retrieve passages that are accurate but name only a broader category than the question asks for, such as a disease family instead of the specific disease. The authors call the resulting behaviour `Clade` (Category-Level Answering from Deficient Evidence): models answer from these coarse passages instead of abstaining or searching further. On biomedical questions from `PrimeKG`, **family-only passages cut abstention by 13.8 points compared to uninformative passages, and the resulting guesses are wrong about half the time**; confidence filtering, a larger model and explicit abstention instructions do not fix it, and the effect replicates on species interactions in `GloBI`. An ontology lookup contains the true answer in 98.5% of cases when given the correct family, but identifying that family is the bottleneck, and end-to-end recovery reaches only 26.8%.

papers.title: EngineAgent: Agentizing On-Device LLM Inference Engines with Inference Stack Hierarchy Awareness and Hardware Abilities
papers.abstract: Rapidly evolving LLM architectures and heterogeneous mobile hardware make supporting new models in on-device inference engines a recurring and costly system challenge. Each model may require coordinated changes across conversion, graph construction, operators, and hardware backends. Existing coding agents often miss these cross-layer dependencies and struggle to diagnose failures across host--device execution paths. We present EngineAgent, an agentic system for automating on-device LLM model enablement. Its key insight is to separate reusable engine and hardware knowledge from model-specific implementation. Before enablement, EngineAgent constructs a hierarchy-aware engine index that captures engine abstraction layers and cross-layer dependencies, and pre-validates backend-specific build, execution, and debugging workflows using already supported models. For each new model, a builder uses this knowledge to coordinate cross-layer changes, while an auditor checks implementation completeness and drives iterative debugging through device-side validation. Across 12 tasks spanning three mobile LLMs and four engine--backend pairs on CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs, EngineAgent achieves 75% end-to-end success with either of two underlying LLMs, versus 33.3% for the strongest coding-agent baseline. Success requires compilation, on-device execution, and output-logit agreement with reference implementations. EngineAgent also reduces average per-task time and model-API cost relative to baselines using the same underlying LLMs.
papers.summary: Adding support for a new model to an on-device LLM inference engine requires coordinated changes across conversion, graph construction, operators and hardware backends, which general coding agents tend to miss. `EngineAgent` first builds a hierarchy-aware index of the engine's abstraction layers and cross-layer dependencies and pre-validates build, execution and debugging workflows on already supported models; a builder then makes the changes for a new model while an auditor checks completeness and drives debugging through on-device validation. Across 12 tasks covering three mobile LLMs and four engine-backend pairs on CPUs, GPUs and NPUs, it reaches **75% end-to-end success versus 33.3% for the strongest coding-agent baseline**, where success requires compilation, on-device execution and logit agreement with a reference implementation. It also lowers average per-task time and API cost relative to baselines using the same underlying LLMs.

papers.title: The Unused Input: The Initial State as a Conditioning Interface for Recurrent TSFMs
papers.abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) forecast unseen series without task-specific training. Increasingly they are built on recurrent backbones, whose constant per-step cost makes long-context inference cheap, and which, unlike transformers, carry a state. A recurrent backbone computes its prediction from two inputs: the observed context window and the initial recurrent state. In practice only the first is utilised and the initial state is unused by convention. We ask whether the initial state can be utilised in recurrent TSFMs. Using the xLSTM-based zero-shot forecaster TiRex as a case study, we freeze the backbone and train only a small head that writes a context vector into the initial state, so that any change in accuracy is attributable to the injected state rather than to adapted weights. A spectral summary of the input window, learned once and applied unchanged to every series, lowers mean GiftEval MASE by 0.175%, with every seed improving, which neither a parameter-matched LoRA adapter nor a learnable static state reproduces. An embedding of text attached to each series, evaluated on six MoTime datasets, reveals two roles for the state. As a per-dataset adaptation surface, a static state lowers MASE by 0.04-6.96% of the zero-shot baseline (8-70% of the gain of full fine-tuning). As a channel for exogenous information, the text-conditioned state lowers it by a further 0.15-0.41% of the zero-shot baseline on four of six datasets and, combined with a LoRA adapter, exceeds full fine-tuning, which has no access to the text, on one of them. In TiRex, the effect concentrates in the mLSTM blocks and is strongest at short context. The results are preliminary and the improvements small, but they point to the initial state as a direction for further research.
papers.summary: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) built on recurrent backbones take both a context window and an initial recurrent state, but the state is left unused by convention. Using the `xLSTM`-based zero-shot forecaster `TiRex` with the backbone frozen, the authors train only a small head that writes a context vector into the initial state. A spectral summary of the input window **lowers mean `GiftEval` MASE by 0.175% with every seed improving**, which neither a parameter-matched `LoRA` adapter nor a learnable static state reproduces, and on six `MoTime` datasets a text-conditioned state gives a further 0.15-0.41% reduction on four of them. The authors describe the results as preliminary and the improvements as small.

papers.title: ARE-bench: Benchmarking Agents' Research Ability in Real-World Researcher Sessions and Workspaces
papers.abstract: Research agents achieve increasingly strong benchmark scores, yet these scores do not necessarily translate into reliable delivery in ongoing research projects. Many research-agent benchmarks emphasize standalone tasks and relatively self-contained workflows in clean or curated workspaces. However, researchers ask agents to complete one step within an ongoing project, where requests depend on earlier session decisions and workspaces contain unfinished files, outdated versions, and failed attempts. We introduce ARE-bench to evaluate whether research agents advance ongoing projects while respecting prior decisions and existing workspace state, grounded in real session context and in-progress workspaces. ARE-bench includes 75 tasks built on agent sessions and full workspaces from recruited researchers' own projects, spanning seven research stages, 33 requirements, and 150 sub-requirements, with 1,173 binary checklist items in total. Each task is anchored at a real user request, preserves its requirements, and summarizes the earlier requests still in effect as background. The complete workspace is replayed to that boundary without cleanup, preserving artifacts from earlier turns. Each checklist is compiled from an intent-aligned rubric and credits any valid solution. Across seven frontier models, the strongest passes every checklist item on only 66.2% of tasks, and Design and Execution rank among the hardest stages for every model. Three models pass about 69% of tasks when only delivery contracts and general norms are checked, but just 28.4% to 40.0% once historical and material or workspace requirements are also checked. Evaluating delivery without these contextual requirements can therefore overestimate research agents and mask differences between them.
papers.summary: Research-agent benchmarks mostly test standalone tasks in clean workspaces, whereas real requests arrive mid-project and depend on earlier decisions and messy files. `ARE-bench` contains 75 tasks built from recruited researchers' real agent sessions and full workspaces, replayed without cleanup to the point of a real user request and scored with 1,173 binary checklist items across seven research stages. Among seven frontier models the strongest passes every checklist item on only 66.2% of tasks, with Design and Execution among the hardest stages. Three models pass about 69% of tasks when only delivery contracts and general norms are checked, but **just 28.4% to 40.0% once historical and workspace requirements are also checked**.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware Hybrid Offline Reinforcement Learning with Online Action Selection Enabled by Sparse Gaussian-Process Critics
papers.abstract: Start-ups and grade changes remain largely operator-driven, while developing and maintaining dynamic models for model-based control requires substantial engineering effort. Hybrid Offline Learning and Online Optimisation (HOFLON) uses one-step offline reinforcement learning to select actions from historical transition data. In its original implementation, the online objective combines the predicted return from a tree-ensemble critic with an adversarial-autoencoder (AAE) penalty for unfamiliar state-action pairs. We examine the effect of this penalty and replace the critic and AAE with a sparse variational Gaussian-process (sGP) critic. Actions maximise $\mu - \kappa\sigma$, an uncertainty-adjusted estimate of the return from one action followed by the historical operating practice. On the HOFLON polymerisation-reactor benchmark, removing the AAE from HOFLON led to 4 failed start-ups in 15 runs over five critics. At its published weight, the variation in the AAE penalty is four orders of magnitude smaller than the variation in the tree-ensemble critic. Nevertheless, it changes actions when the predicted returns of competing candidates are nearly equal, and paired runs with and without the penalty diverged from the first move. With a Mat\'ern-5/2 sGP critic, $\kappa = 0$ led to failure in 13 of 15 runs, whereas with $\kappa = 3$ none of 15 runs (five critics, three noise realisations) failed. The median and lowest returns were 13,464 and 13,398 (HOFLON: 13,393 and 12,411). A squared-exponential sGP critic with learned inducing inputs needed $\kappa \geq 3$ to remain within the empirical data support in steady state, and then settled with a temperature offset of 2.0 K.
authors: Marco Chan (Sargent Centre for Process Systems Engineering
Christos Evripidou (Sargent Centre for Process Systems Engineering
Liqiu Dong (Sargent Centre for Process Systems Engineering
Benoit Chachuat (Sargent Centre for Process Systems Engineering
Mehmet Mercang\"oz (Sargent Centre for Process Systems Engineering
papers.summary: Hybrid Offline Learning and Online Optimisation (`HOFLON`) selects process-control actions from historical data using one-step offline reinforcement learning, originally combining a tree-ensemble critic with an adversarial-autoencoder (AAE) penalty for unfamiliar state-action pairs. This work examines that penalty and replaces both components with a sparse variational Gaussian-process (sGP) critic, choosing actions that maximise the predicted return minus kappa times its predictive uncertainty. On the `HOFLON` polymerisation-reactor start-up benchmark, removing the AAE caused 4 failed start-ups in 15 runs. With a Matérn-5/2 sGP critic, **ignoring uncertainty (kappa = 0) failed in 13 of 15 runs while kappa = 3 failed in none**, with a median return of 13,464 against 13,393 for the original method.

papers.title: Cognitive Mapping of Learning by Thinking Mechanisms in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly exhibit capabilities that resemble human Learning by Thinking (LbT), the acquisition of new insight through internal processes such as explanation and reasoning, without new external input. A systematic account of the cognitive mechanisms behind these capabilities, and of their limits, remains underdeveloped.
