This paper proposes a Cognitive LbT Framework that maps four mechanisms (Reflective Reasoning, Synthetic Memory Formation, Internal Simulation, and Conceptual Self-Organization) onto computational processes in LLMs. Drawing on representative methods, including chain-of-thought prompting, self-consistency, self-reflection, Tree-of-Thoughts search, Self-Instruct, and self-taught reasoning, the analysis argues that selected methods can functionally approximate aspects of these mechanisms and can improve performance on some tasks without additional labeled examples, although this does not always constitute durable learning in model parameters. For example, Self-Instruct generated approximately 52,000 instructions from 175 seed tasks and reported a 33% absolute improvement on Super-NaturalInstructions (Y. Wang et al., 2023). The same mechanisms also produce characteristic failures, including hallucination diffusion, model collapse, concept drift, and high computational cost. These failures are not isolated technical defects but follow from four structural asymmetries between LLMs and human cognition: the identity of generator and monitor, closed learning loops without external grounding, symbolic rather than sensorimotor simulation, and the cost of inference-time computation. The framework yields testable propositions about when LbT in LLMs should succeed or fail and offers a structured basis for designing more reliable autonomous learning systems.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) show behaviours resembling human Learning by Thinking (LbT), meaning gaining insight through internal processes such as explanation and reasoning without new external input. This conceptual analysis proposes a framework mapping four mechanisms (reflective reasoning, synthetic memory formation, internal simulation and conceptual self-organization) onto existing methods such as chain-of-thought prompting, self-consistency, `Tree-of-Thoughts` and `Self-Instruct`, drawing on results reported in prior work. It argues that these methods can improve performance without new labeled examples, though not always as durable learning in model parameters. Characteristic failures such as hallucination diffusion, model collapse and concept drift are attributed to **four structural asymmetries between LLMs and human cognition**, including the generator and monitor being the same system and learning loops that lack external grounding.

papers.title: An Energy-Based Perspective on Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Energy-based models (EBMs) define a distribution through a scalar energy, $p_\theta(x)\propto\exp(-E_\theta(x))$, and are usually presented as one model family among many. This tutorial has a broader goal: beyond introducing EBMs, it uses them as a single lens that connects the different aspects of machine learning. Any EBM is specified by three choices, the energy, which determines what the model represents; the inference procedure, which samples from or optimizes the energy; and the learning method, which fits the energy to data. We first develop these components, including sampling, variational inference, and learning by maximum likelihood, noise contrastive estimation, pseudolikelihood, score matching, and adversarial training, and show that the learning methods share one contrastive structure. We then show that discriminative models, generative models such as GANs, normalizing flows, diffusion and autoregressive models, representation learning methods such as contrastive learning, word2vec, BERT, denoising auto-encoders, and diffusion representations, reinforcement learning with EBM policies and world models, inverse reinforcement learning, and planning, as well as inference-time computation with verifiers, are all EBMs that differ in these three choices, mostly in how they handle the partition function and sampling. This view explains existing methods, organizes them into a common framework, and suggests new algorithms by replacing one component while keeping the others, with composition of energies as a principled way to combine learned models at inference time.
papers.summary: Energy-based models (EBMs), which define a distribution through a scalar energy function, are used in this tutorial as a single lens on machine learning. It develops three defining choices (the energy, the inference procedure and the learning method), covering sampling, variational inference, maximum likelihood, noise contrastive estimation, score matching and adversarial training, and shows these learning methods share one contrastive structure. It then argues that **discriminative models, GANs, normalizing flows, diffusion and autoregressive models, contrastive and masked representation learning, reinforcement learning, planning and verifier-based inference-time computation are all EBMs differing in those three choices**, mostly in how they handle the partition function and sampling. The framing is also used to suggest new algorithms by swapping one component and to compose energies for combining learned models at inference time.

papers.title: Blurring the Block Boundaries: Overlapping Block Denoising for Efficient Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have emerged as effective alternatives to autoregressive models for latency-critical tasks, enabling faster token generation. Recent advances employ block diffusion with self-editing capabilities, where each block refines tokens iteratively before advancing to the next one. Yet each block is only as fast as its slowest token, and the next block cannot start before it. We suggest Blurring the Block Boundaries (B3), a novel method with which two blocks are refined in parallel within a shared forward pass. B3 calibrates itself on the fly, opening the next block only once the model is ready to start generating it. It is a training-free and hyperparameter-free acceleration method which seamlessly integrates within any self-editing block diffusion model. Evaluated on state-of-the-art DLMs across 10 diverse datasets spanning varied tasks and difficulty levels, B3 results in on par generation quality and 11.5-14.5% speedup compared to the base model, pushing the Pareto frontier for latency-quality trade-offs in DLM inference.
papers.summary: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) that use block diffusion with self-editing refine one block of tokens at a time, so each block is as slow as its slowest token and the next cannot start until it finishes. Blurring the Block Boundaries (`B3`) refines two blocks in parallel within a shared forward pass and calibrates on the fly when to open the next block. It requires no training or hyperparameters and applies to any self-editing block diffusion model. Across 10 datasets on current DLMs it gives **an 11.5-14.5% speedup with on-par generation quality** relative to the base model.

papers.title: A Margin Perspective on LoRA: Robustness to Catastrophic Forgetting and Adapter Merging (MaLoRA)
papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the de facto method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large neural networks, achieving strong task adaptation with minimal trainable parameters and low optimization cost. Beyond this efficiency, practitioners have observed two striking properties: \textit{robustness to catastrophic forgetting} and the ability to \textit{merge independently trained adapters} into a single model that performs competitively across multiple tasks. These properties are central to continual and multi-task learning, yet remain poorly understood. In this work, we provide a theoretical explanation through a unified \textit{margin-based perspective}. We analyze LoRA in multiclass linear classification under a near-orthogonal task regime with $\ell_2$-regularization, and characterize the optimal LoRA adapter across regularization regimes. Our analysis shows that, in an intermediate regime of regularization parameters, the optimal adapter aligns with the \emph{max-margin solution} on the fine-tuning data. Building on this characterization, we derive two key consequences. First, we obtain closed-form expressions for the margins on pre-training and fine-tuning data, revealing a precise margin trade-off: the regularization parameter controls the balance between retention and adaptation. Second, we analyze adapter merging, proving that merged models achieve positive margin on each task and deriving optimal mixing coefficients that balance margins across tasks and maximize the margin over their union. These results lead to a simple, training-free merging rule, which we term \textit{margin-based LoRA merging} (MaLoRA). Experiments on modern architectures and real datasets validate our theoretical predictions, showing that MaLoRA matches or outperforms several adapter-merging baselines across a range of vision and language classification tasks.
papers.summary: Low-rank adaptation (`LoRA`) is observed to resist catastrophic forgetting and to allow independently trained adapters to be merged, but neither property is well understood. The authors analyze `LoRA` in multiclass linear classification with near-orthogonal tasks and L2 regularization, showing that **in an intermediate regularization regime the optimal adapter aligns with the max-margin solution on the fine-tuning data**. This yields closed-form margins on pre-training and fine-tuning data, with the regularization parameter controlling the balance between retention and adaptation, and a proof that merged adapters keep a positive margin on each task with derivable optimal mixing coefficients. The resulting training-free merging rule, `MaLoRA`, matches or outperforms several merging baselines on vision and language classification tasks.

papers.title: REAL Loss: Optimizing Real Expected Acceptance Length for Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference by having a draft model propose multiple tokens for the target model to verify in one pass. The speedup is governed by the expected acceptance length (EAL), yet standard training objectives such as cross-entropy, KL divergence, and total variation focus only on distribution matching or single-step overlap. Recent studies instead propose block-level training objectives, aiming to optimize EAL directly. However, these objectives remain surrogates rather than exact formulations of EAL. For example, some average later acceptance over target-distributed continuations rather than the verification branches selected by accepted tokens, introducing a covariance gap that can reverse the gradient direction. We analyze this gap and derive REAL, a real EAL training loss that uses path weights for unbiased estimation and Rao-Blackwellization for variance reduction. In a controlled loss-level comparison with a Qwen3.6-35B-A3B target and a Domino drafter, REAL outperforms WTV, VSD, DBLast, and the static LK baseline on probabilistic serving acceptance length across 9 task subsets and 5 evaluation seeds. These gains require only a change to the training loss, with no modification to the drafter architecture or inference procedure, demonstrating the practicality of real EAL training. A reference implementation of the REAL loss is available at https://github.com/King-ty/speculators/tree/real-loss.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding speeds up LLM inference by letting a draft model propose several tokens that the target model verifies in one pass, with speedup governed by the expected acceptance length (EAL). Existing training objectives, including recent block-level ones, are surrogates for EAL; some average later acceptance over target-distributed continuations instead of the branches actually selected by accepted tokens, creating a covariance gap that can reverse the gradient direction. The `REAL` loss targets EAL directly, using path weights for unbiased estimation and Rao-Blackwellization to reduce variance. With a `Qwen3.6-35B-A3B` target and a `Domino` drafter, **`REAL` outperforms `WTV`, `VSD`, `DBLast` and a static `LK` baseline on acceptance length across 9 task subsets and 5 seeds**, changing only the training loss.

papers.title: Discovering Equations for the Thermodynamics of South Asian Monsoon Precipitation
papers.abstract: South Asian monsoon precipitation depends on the thermodynamic structure of the lower troposphere, but how its ingredients combine to shape precipitation remains unclear, partly because this dependence is nonlocal in the vertical. We use symbolic distillation, which combines neural networks and symbolic regression, to discover interpretable precipitation equations from 21 years of June-August reanalysis data. Neural networks first learn the vertical thermodynamic structure most relevant to precipitation, condensing each variable into a single interpretable feature not tied to a particular vertical grid. Then, symbolic regression derives closed-form equations from these features and the surface state. Our best equation explains 1.5 times as much precipitation variance as a widely used buoyancy-based diagnostic and recovers about 85% of neural network skill while using about a thousand times fewer parameters. Unlike the buoyancy diagnostic, which adds moisture and instability, the equations treat them as competing controls, with the heaviest precipitation occurring when the lower free troposphere is humid. Over ocean, sensible heating is associated with additional precipitation mainly when near-surface air is warm and moist, improving predicted precipitation and its diurnal cycle. Although the learned features were optimized only for precipitation prediction, the equations largely respond to each feature as expected from convective physics, consistent with the reanalysis. These responses reduce the dependence of monsoon precipitation on the entire vertical column to a few simple, testable constraints that could guide data-driven precipitation models to make them more physically consistent.
papers.summary: How lower-troposphere thermodynamics combine to shape South Asian monsoon precipitation is unclear, partly because the dependence spans the vertical column. The authors apply symbolic distillation to 21 years of June-August reanalysis data: neural networks condense each variable's vertical structure into a single feature, then symbolic regression derives closed-form equations from those features and the surface state. The best equation **explains 1.5 times as much precipitation variance as a widely used buoyancy-based diagnostic and recovers about 85% of neural network skill with roughly a thousand times fewer parameters**. Unlike the buoyancy diagnostic, the equations treat moisture and instability as competing controls, with the heaviest precipitation when the lower free troposphere is humid.

papers.title: Causal Concept Explanations for Deep Neural Models
papers.abstract: Concept-based explanations in neural models are important for the development, certification, and adoption of autonomous systems. Yet, interpretability remains correlational. Without methods to guide and quantify causal relationships between explanations, a concept explanation can be provided without being necessary or sufficient for the observed output thereby appearing correct while misleading. We introduce Causal Concept Wrapper Network (CCW-Net), the first use of interventional mediation analysis from fields such as economics, medicine, and epidemiology as a training objective to align causal effects of concept-based explanations with a model's output. We further apply mediation analysis as an evaluation tool to quantify, per concept label combination, how much of any model's output is causally attributable to each concept explanation. As a training objective, CCW-Net shapes a model's concept representations such that they are both necessary and sufficient for the outputs they are credited with and independent of other concepts' contributions. Counterfactual concept representations anchor a set of causal alignment criteria: necessity, sufficiency, and independence. Necessity drives irrelevant concept effects toward zero, sufficiency ensures relevant concept representations fully reconstruct a model's output, and independence enforces the total effect decomposes linearly across concepts. We evaluate CCW-Net across aircraft control, driving, and image classification. CCW-Net provides a step toward concept-based explanations that are not merely interpretable, but quantifiably causal, supporting safer evaluation, certification, and deployment of transparent and trustworthy neural models.
papers.summary: Concept-based explanations of neural models are typically correlational, so a cited concept may be neither necessary nor sufficient for the output it supposedly explains. Causal Concept Wrapper Network (`CCW-Net`) uses interventional mediation analysis, borrowed from economics, medicine and epidemiology, as a training objective that **shapes concept representations to be necessary and sufficient for the outputs they are credited with and independent of other concepts' contributions**. The same analysis serves as an evaluation tool that quantifies how much of any model's output is causally attributable to each concept explanation. The method is evaluated on aircraft control, driving and image classification; the abstract reports no quantitative results.

papers.title: Bits or permutations? Spending a fixed inference budget on weight precision or on option-order averaging in small local language models
papers.abstract: Local language models can save memory by storing weights in fewer bits, and they can reduce sensitivity to the order of answer options by averaging a few reorderings. We ask whether the first makes the second worse, and which is the cheaper way to spend a fixed budget. On Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B with simulated round-to-nearest weight quantization (8, 6, 4 and 3 bits, fp16 reference), read from the logits of the letters A to D on ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, MMLU and HellaSwag (300 items each), 6 bits lose no accuracy against fp16 (they score +1.8 (+1.0 to +2.5) and +0.9 (+0.3 to +1.5) points higher, which we do not explain), and 8 bits change it by -0.7 (-1.1 to -0.3) and -0.4 (-0.7 to -0.2) points. At 4 bits the answer-slot skew rises from 0.15 to 0.53 (0.6B) and from 0.07 to 0.12 (1.7B); Gaussian noise at the same weight SNR gives 0.15 and 0.37 (two draws) and 0.19 (one draw), so the control is inconclusive on whether rounding adds slot skew beyond equal-power noise. Flip rates rise but stay below an accuracy-matched baseline of independent uniform errors. Averaging four cyclic orders recovers +12.6 points at 4 bits for 0.6B (+5.3 at fp16). We price bits and passes in one machine-independent unit, weight bytes read times passes. In cost-matched pairs, extra orders beat extra bits only when the weights have 6 or more bits, and the decision table reduces to: use 6-bit weights and spend the rest of the budget on up to four orders, one pass each. Everything is simulated on two small models with the simplest quantizer; a title-level search found no earlier study of quantization together with option order.
papers.summary: For small local language models, a fixed inference budget can go to higher weight precision or to averaging predictions over reorderings of multiple-choice options, and this study asks which is cheaper and whether quantization worsens option-order sensitivity. Using simulated round-to-nearest quantization of `Qwen3-0.6B` and `Qwen3-1.7B` on `ARC-Easy`, `ARC-Challenge`, `MMLU` and `HellaSwag`, 6-bit weights lose no accuracy against fp16, while at 4 bits answer-slot skew rises (0.15 to 0.53 for the smaller model) and averaging four cyclic orders recovers 12.6 points. Pricing cost as weight bytes read times passes, the decision reduces to **using 6-bit weights and spending the remaining budget on up to four option orders**. A Gaussian-noise control is inconclusive on whether rounding adds skew beyond equal-power noise, and the authors note everything is simulated on two small models with the simplest quantizer.

papers.title: Exploring Post-Hoc Disentanglement of Audio Foundation Models for Music Similarity
papers.abstract: Audio foundation models like CLAP, MuQ, and MERT excel at capturing general musical similarity. On the other hand, their entangled latent spaces limit interpretability and fine-grained attribute control. Conditional Similarity Networks (CSN) address this by pairing a backbone representation model with learned masks that gate the embedding space into attribute-specific subspaces. However, existing methods train the backbone from scratch, rather than leveraging pretrained foundation models. We instead present a systematic study of post-hoc disentanglement, adapting CSN to gate frozen pretrained embeddings. We evaluate adding trainable parameters to adapt the embedding under different masking and pooling regimes across two datasets. Our findings show that minimal adaptation capacity is sufficient for post-hoc gating to improve both attribute-specific disentanglement and overall retrieval performance, while pooling, masking, and depth choices yield limited additional gains.
papers.summary: Audio foundation models such as `CLAP`, `MuQ` and `MERT` capture general musical similarity but have entangled latent spaces that limit interpretability and attribute-level control. Conditional Similarity Networks (CSN) address this with learned masks that gate an embedding into attribute-specific subspaces, but have required training the backbone from scratch; this study instead applies them post hoc to frozen pretrained embeddings. Across two datasets and various masking, pooling and adaptation settings, **minimal added adaptation capacity is enough for post-hoc gating to improve both attribute-specific disentanglement and overall retrieval**, while pooling, masking and depth choices yield limited further gains.

papers.title: Precision on Demand: Escalating Weight Bits at Uncertain Decoding Steps in a Small Local Model
papers.abstract: Local decoding usually fixes one weight precision for the whole generation. We study a different allocation: store 8-bit weights, decode with their top 4 bits, and redo a step at 8 bits only when the low-precision output distribution looks uncertain (entropy above a threshold or a small top-two margin). Quantization is simulated, the model is Qwen3-0.6B, and the benchmark is GSM8K. Cost is counted in weight bytes read per token. On 36724 replayed steps the entropy of the low pass ranks argmax flips with AUC 0.93. At a 15% escalation budget it catches 78% of flips and the margin gate 94%, against the 15% expected for a random gate of equal rate (a computed expectation, not a run). In 150 live problems all-high scores 64.0% and all-low 55.3% (McNemar p=0.053). An entropy gate with a 16% escalation rate scores 62.7% at 0.87 of the all-high weight bytes. Its paired difference is -1.3 (-8.0 to +5.3) points to all-high and +7.3 (+0.0 to +14.7) points to all-low (p=0.080), so the live data do not separate the gate from either end. Verified speculation reaches zero KL at similar bytes in the same cost model. A live random control, a thinking-mode phase rule, a second model and live KL were not run.
papers.summary: Instead of fixing one weight precision for a whole generation, this study stores 8-bit weights, decodes with their top 4 bits, and redoes a step at 8 bits only when the low-precision output looks uncertain by entropy or top-two margin. With simulated quantization of `Qwen3-0.6B` on `GSM8K`, low-pass entropy predicts argmax flips with AUC 0.93, and at a 15% escalation budget the entropy gate catches 78% of flips and the margin gate 94%. On 150 live problems, **an entropy gate escalating 16% of steps scores 62.7% at 0.87 of the full-precision weight bytes**, against 64.0% for all-high and 55.3% for all-low, but the differences are not statistically separated from either end. The authors note that a live random control, a second model and other checks were not run.

papers.title: Evaluating LLM-Generated World Models for Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning
papers.abstract: Formal world models can support planning, verification, and safety reasoning, but constructing them from open-ended natural-language situations is difficult, particularly in multi-agent settings where several formalizations may be plausible. We study whether five LLMs can generate such world models as partially observable stochastic games and whether mechanical validity is sufficient to establish that the resulting model faithfully represents the intended decision problem. We introduce a benchmark of 44 scenarios spanning game, situational, and cultural settings and evaluate generated world models along three dimensions: mechanical validity, reference-relative structural agreement, and semantic criteria. Across three empirical tracks, we analyze 410 first-pass generations. In the reference-backed game track, 134/135 generated world models pass a strict mechanical audit, yet mean permutation-invariant structural F1 is only 0.366, with just 28/134 mechanically valid models exactly matching the authored reference. In the cultural track, explicitly naming the country changes the generated structural representation for most LLMs while producing only small changes in automated semantic scores. These results show that executability is a necessary but insufficient criterion for LLM-generated world models: models that are mechanically valid can still differ substantially in the structure used by downstream neuro-symbolic reasoning and planning.
papers.summary: Formal world models support planning and verification, and this study tests whether five LLMs can generate them as partially observable stochastic games from natural-language situations, and whether mechanical validity implies faithfulness. A benchmark of 44 scenarios across game, situational and cultural settings is scored on mechanical validity, structural agreement with references and semantic criteria, over 410 first-pass generations. In the reference-backed game track, **134 of 135 generated models pass a strict mechanical audit, yet mean structural F1 is only 0.366 and just 28 exactly match the authored reference**. In the cultural track, naming the country changes the generated structure for most LLMs while automated semantic scores barely move, so executability is necessary but not sufficient.

papers.title: Earlybird: Predictive Streaming Speech Recognition in 29M Parameters
papers.abstract: Streaming speech recognizers output a word only after the speaker has finished it, typically 90-400 ms later. For a voice agent every millisecond counts: the sooner the words are outputted, the sooner the agent can start a search or plan its reply. We present Earlybird, a 29M-parameter streaming recognizer (16.8 MB at 4 bits). Earlybird learns from audio cut off at random points, including partway through a word, and is asked to predict every word that is due by then in full, plus a guess of the next two words. Its raw token probabilities give a confidence for every word including the one still being spoken. On clean audiobook speech (LibriSpeech test-clean), the median word is predicted correctly 90 ms before the speaker finishes it, while released streaming models get it 90 to 400 ms after it ends. Earlybird is the earliest on all six test sets we time, covering audiobooks, TED talks, public speech, earnings calls, and synthetic speech. On the same audiobooks, 69% of words are predicted correctly before they end, against 3-25% for the other models. For words still being spoken, confidence is calibrated, with an expected calibration error (ECE) of 3.7 to 5.5. On the eight English Open ASR Leaderboard sets, it is more accurate than Moonshine Tiny on every set and roughly ties Whistle, a model of the same size.
papers.summary: Streaming speech recognizers normally emit a word 90-400 ms after the speaker finishes it, which delays voice agents. `Earlybird`, a 29M-parameter streaming recognizer (16.8 MB at 4 bits), is trained on audio cut off at random points, including mid-word, to predict every word due by then in full plus a guess at the next two words, with token probabilities serving as per-word confidence. On `LibriSpeech` test-clean, **the median word is predicted correctly 90 ms before the speaker finishes it**, and 69% of words are correct before they end versus 3-25% for other models; it is the earliest on all six timed test sets. Confidence for in-progress words has an expected calibration error (ECE) of 3.7 to 5.5, and accuracy beats `Moonshine Tiny` on all eight English `Open ASR Leaderboard` sets while roughly tying `Whistle`.

papers.title: DnNP: Denoising Input Uncertainty in Neural Processes
papers.abstract: Neural Processes (NPs) are flexible meta-learning models capable of uncertainty quantification across diverse applications. However, the standard NP framework assumes access to noise-free inputs. This is unrealistic in many practical settings, where sensor noise or measurement errors are unavoidable. This discrepancy between model assumptions and real-world data can significantly degrade prediction quality and uncertainty estimates. We introduce Denoising Neural Processes (DnNPs), a principled extension of the NP framework that explicitly models input uncertainty. We train DnNPs via variational inference. DnNPs jointly learn to denoise corrupted inputs and perform meta-learning, making them robust to noisy training data. We demonstrate DnNPs' effectiveness on both synthetic and real-world datasets, showing consistent improvements in prediction and uncertainty quantification compared to standard NPs. On PM2.5 spatial interpolation from real-world air quality sensors, DnNP reduces RMSE by up to 30% and NLL by up to 73% relative to standard NPs. We also provide theoretical grounding: we show that the Bayes-optimal predictor under noisy inputs belongs to the DnNP model class, and that plug-in models with fixed observation variance incur an irreducible KL divergence gap that DnNP provably avoids.
papers.summary: Neural Processes (NPs), a family of meta-learning models with uncertainty quantification, assume noise-free inputs, which fails under sensor noise or measurement error. Denoising Neural Processes (`DnNP`s) extend the framework to model input uncertainty explicitly, trained by variational inference to jointly denoise corrupted inputs and meta-learn. On PM2.5 spatial interpolation from real air-quality sensors, **`DnNP` reduces RMSE by up to 30% and negative log-likelihood by up to 73% relative to standard NPs**. The authors also show that the Bayes-optimal predictor under noisy inputs lies in the `DnNP` model class, and that plug-in models with fixed observation variance incur an irreducible KL divergence gap.

papers.title: Quantifying the Sampling Frequency Invariance of Time-Series Foundation Models for Sensor Data Applications
papers.abstract: Time-Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) are increasingly used in sensor applications, where sampling frequency (SF) varies across sensors, devices, and operating modes (e.g., power saving). Ideally, TSFMs must remain effective during such SF changes, provided the SF retains task-critical bandwidth. In this paper, we stress-test 4 prominent TSFMs: MOMENT, Chronos-2, Moirai-MoE, and TimesFM, to quantify their SF-invariance and investigate whether their behavior tracks the resulting loss of information bandwidth rather than the SF value itself. Our stress-test probes 3 dimensions: (i) the shift in embeddings, (ii) the degradation in forecasting performance, and (iii) the degradation in downstream performance, quantified by three novel metrics: FSI, FDI, and CDI, respectively. To our knowledge, this is the first study to place SF-invariance at the core of TSFM evaluations. Our results characterize: (i) how SF-invariance depends on the margin between signal's native-SF and the bandwidth its task requires, (ii) how much of that invariance the choice of TSFM explains, and (iii) how much of TSFM's performance degradation under a lower SF reflects information loss rather than a limitation of their abilities. These findings reframe SF-invariance as a measurable, signal-aware property of the (signal X TSFM) pair, and guide practitioners on when TSFMs display SF-invariance.
papers.summary: Time-Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) used on sensor data face sampling frequency (SF) changes across sensors, devices and operating modes, and should stay effective as long as the SF retains the bandwidth the task needs. This study stress-tests `MOMENT`, `Chronos-2`, `Moirai-MoE` and `TimesFM` on embedding shift, forecasting degradation and downstream degradation, using three new metrics named `FSI`, `FDI` and `CDI`. The results characterize how invariance depends on the margin between a signal's native SF and the bandwidth its task requires, how much the choice of model explains, and how much degradation reflects information loss as opposed to model limitations. The authors conclude that **SF-invariance is a measurable, signal-aware property of the signal-model pair** and not of the model alone; the abstract gives no headline numbers.

papers.title: Two Communities, One Problem: Branch-and-Bound vs. A* for Resource-Constrained Project Scheduling
papers.abstract: Branch-and-Bound (B&B) and $A^*$ are popular exact search methods originating from Operations Research and Artificial Intelligence, respectively. Although the two methods share fundamental search principles, their different ways of exploring the search space can lead to substantially different computational performance. We investigate these differences using the Resource-Constrained Project Scheduling Problem (RCPSP) as an exemplary problem setting. We first establish the relationships between mixed-integer linear programming, state-action, and timed Petri-net representations. Since B&B and $A^*$ admit numerous algorithmic enhancements, we focus on relatively basic implementations. This allows us to examine the fundamental differences between the methods rather than compare the performance of state-of-the-art solvers. By using the same lower bound and best-first node selection, we isolate the effects of the search mechanisms, particularly the identification of equivalent states reached through different scheduling decision sequences. Experiments on 480 benchmark RCPSP instances show that graph-based $A^*$ substantially outperforms the B&B variants considered. With additional pruning rules, $A^*$ proves optimality for all 480 instances, compared with 445 for best-first B&B under the same time and memory limits. Depth-first B&B uses less memory and can find feasible solutions even when the search does not finish within the time limit. Stronger linear programming relaxations reduce the search space but introduce considerable computational overhead. Our findings highlight the importance of duplicate-state detection and clarify the computational trade-offs between the search approaches. These insights can help researchers select an appropriate method and identify opportunities to incorporate effective mechanisms from one approach into the other.
papers.summary: Branch-and-Bound (B&B) from operations research and A* from artificial intelligence are compared as exact search methods on the Resource-Constrained Project Scheduling Problem (RCPSP), after relating its mixed-integer linear programming, state-action, and timed Petri-net representations. Deliberately basic implementations share the same lower bound and best-first node selection, so the effect of the search mechanism, especially detecting equivalent states reached through different decision sequences, can be isolated. On 480 benchmark instances, graph-based A* with additional pruning rules **proves optimality for all 480 instances, against 445 for best-first B&B** under the same time and memory limits. Depth-first B&B uses less memory and still finds feasible solutions when it times out, while stronger linear programming relaxations shrink the search space at considerable computational cost.

papers.title: One Policy for 100 Household Tasks: Our Solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge
papers.abstract: We describe our solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge: 100 long-horizon household tasks in the OmniGibson simulator. We placed 9th on the final leaderboard, the only independent team in the top 10. The core of the solution is a single vision-language-action (VLA) model, one checkpoint for all 100 tasks, built on our 1st-place 2025 solution, which is based on $\pi_{0.5}$. On the 50 tasks shared with 2025, its Q rises from 0.260 to 0.371; across all 100 tasks it scores 0.392. Our main conclusion from 2025 was that the model was undertrained, so most of the 2026 work went into training the model for longer, optimizing some training parameters, making each training step slightly faster and reducing the gradient noise: a migration from 50 to 100 tasks (semantic stages built from the demonstrations' skill annotations, task and stage embeddings of new tasks warm-started from similar old ones, and a 21-dimensional action space matching the teleoperation controls); variance-reduced multi-sample flow matching with a simple noise-vs-compute model that picks the number of action-expert samples per observation without ablations; and a 200k-step training run, about one pass over the 211M frames of the demonstrations. A cloud evaluation infrastructure keeps a shared record with provenance, episode diagnostics and restorable simulator states, and runs six simulators on one GPU together faster than real time. On top of the learned policy, 14 tasks are routed to a GPT-6 Astra coding agent that controls the robot through observation and motion tools, starting every episode from a frozen copy of its own practice session on training instances. Across these 14 tasks, Astra's mean Q is 0.639, against 0.108 for the learned policy. The public submission included only part of the Astra results and scored 0.446 Q with 27.3% full-task success.
papers.summary: A single vision-language-action (VLA) checkpoint built on `pi0.5` covers all 100 long-horizon household tasks of the 2026 `BEHAVIOR Challenge` in the `OmniGibson` simulator, finishing 9th on the final leaderboard. Most of the work went into training longer with less gradient noise: a migration from 50 to 100 tasks with warm-started task and stage embeddings, variance-reduced multi-sample flow matching, and a 200k-step run over the 211M demonstration frames, which lifts the Q score on the 50 tasks shared with 2025 from 0.260 to 0.371. Fourteen tasks are instead routed to a `GPT-6 Astra` coding agent that drives the robot through observation and motion tools, where it reaches **a mean Q of 0.639 against 0.108 for the learned policy**. The public submission, which included only part of the agent results, scored 0.446 Q with 27.3% full-task success.

papers.title: UGG: Unified Generative Geometry Model
papers.abstract: Understanding 4D scenes is a core challenge in visual intelligence, requiring models to jointly capture scene geometry, appearance, and dynamics from partial observations. However, existing approaches are subdivided into feedforward models for direct geometric prediction, and generative models for visual synthesis. We introduce UGG, a unified framework for 4D scene understanding that jointly models RGB video and geometric representations such as depth and camera pose. By assigning different noise levels across modalities and time, UGG formulates visual generation and geometric prediction as conditional completion within a single generative model. This flexible formulation enables the model to learn from diverse, heterogeneous datasets with different subsets of geometric and visual annotations. Furthermore, our generative formulation enables inference-time search over multiple plausible scene hypotheses, using geometric evidence extracted from observed RGB frames to improve geometric prediction without ground truth geometry. We demonstrate UGG's effectiveness over non-unified baselines across camera-controlled video generation, depth estimation, and camera pose prediction, including in challenging sparse observation settings. Code and visualizations are available at https://ugg-model.github.io/
papers.summary: Work on 4D scene understanding is split between feedforward models that predict geometry directly and generative models that synthesize video. `UGG` jointly models RGB video with depth and camera pose in one generative model, assigning different noise levels across modalities and time so that **both visual generation and geometric prediction become conditional completion within a single model**. This formulation lets it train on heterogeneous datasets carrying different subsets of annotations, and lets it search at inference time over multiple scene hypotheses using geometric evidence extracted from observed frames. The authors report gains over non-unified baselines on camera-controlled video generation, depth estimation, and camera pose prediction, including under sparse observations.

papers.title: When does text encoding matter for language modeling?
papers.abstract: UTF-8's role as the de facto encoding standard in language models introduces cross-lingual inequities due to its variable-length design. However, the effect that this encoding choice has on model performance remains largely unexamined. In this work, we investigate how text encoding impacts the performance of byte-level language models, comparing UTF-8 with a wide range of other encoding strategies, including other Unicode-based approaches, language-specific encodings, and our own customized encodings. To facilitate our analysis, we propose Aether: a hybrid encoding scheme that uses script-specific encodings for our target setting while maintaining full Unicode coverage through UTF-8 fallbacks, using this framework to model four orthographically diverse languages. Surprisingly, we find that while languages with information-dense characters (Chinese, Korean) significantly benefit from compressive encodings, languages whose characters carry less information individually (Georgian, Tamil) are largely insensitive to encoding choice. In light of these findings, we argue that text encoding should be a language-specific design decision, rather than a universal default.
papers.summary: UTF-8 is the default text encoding for byte-level language models, but its variable-length design treats languages unequally and its effect on model performance has been little studied. The authors compare UTF-8 against other Unicode-based, language-specific, and custom encodings, and propose `Aether`, a hybrid scheme that uses script-specific encodings for target languages while keeping full Unicode coverage through UTF-8 fallbacks. Across four orthographically diverse languages, **Chinese and Korean, whose characters are information-dense, benefit substantially from compressive encodings, while Georgian and Tamil are largely insensitive to the encoding choice**. The conclusion is that text encoding should be a per-language design decision rather than a universal default.

papers.title: Accurate predictions of properties of energetic materials with tabular foundation models
papers.abstract: We use TabPFN, a recently developed tabular foundation model, to predict three properties of energetic materials: impact sensitivity, decomposition temperature and crystal density. Without any hyperparameter tuning, TabPFN outperforms the best published models for all three properties. It also substantially outperforms a wide range of established machine-learning models, including tuned gradient boosting (XGBoost), random forests and Gaussian processes. This holds both when the models are given hand-crafted molecular descriptors and when they are given learned representations from Chemprop's message-passing neural network. In particular, for all three properties, TabPFN applied to Chemprop's own embedding is more accurate than Chemprop's predictions. TabPFN is also among the fastest models we consider, more than an order of magnitude faster than XGBoost. As TabPFN predicts the entire distribution of the target rather than just a single value, it offers built-in uncertainty quantification, which we compare with the empirical distributions of compounds with repeated measurements. Finally, we interpret the predictions using Shapley values, which rank the features by their importance.
papers.summary: The tabular foundation model `TabPFN` is applied to predicting three properties of energetic materials: impact sensitivity, decomposition temperature, and crystal density. **Without any hyperparameter tuning it outperforms the best published models for all three properties**, as well as tuned `XGBoost`, random forests, and Gaussian processes, whether the inputs are hand-crafted molecular descriptors or representations learned by `Chemprop`'s message-passing neural network. It is also more than an order of magnitude faster than `XGBoost`, and on `Chemprop`'s own embeddings it beats `Chemprop`'s predictions. Because it predicts a full target distribution, its built-in uncertainty estimates are compared with empirical distributions from compounds with repeated measurements, and predictions are interpreted with Shapley values.

papers.title: A Theory of Cross-Validation Variance
papers.abstract: Cross-validation estimates predictive performance by repeatedly splitting the data into training and validation sets, fitting the model on the first and evaluating it on the second. Every observation influences the estimate in two roles, through its own evaluation when it is held out and through the models it helps fit when it trains. The random splits determine its weight in each role. From this representation, we prove an exact finite-sample identity for the variance of the cross-validated estimate. For a given splitting scheme with a common training set size, the variance is a function of these weights, with constants of the model, the metric, and the population. It covers metrics averaged over observations, such as mean squared error, and over case--control pairs, such as the AUC. The identity shows which schemes to use. The variance decomposes into sampling variance, which depends only on the training size, and variance due to the random fold splitting, which arises when the weights change from one draw of the splits to the next. K-fold cross-validation, whose weights are equal across observations by design, is therefore variance optimal at first order; Monte Carlo and bootstrap cross-validation are not. The first-order variance of K-fold does not depend on K, and under reasonable conditions on the model leave-one-out has the smallest variance of any K-fold scheme. For the AUC the same holds for leave-pair-out, which evaluates every case--control pair. Finally, we show the cross-validated estimate is asymptotically normal with the identity's full variance. Together, these results provide a general theoretical foundation for inference on cross-validated performance and establish principles for selecting variance-optimal cross-validation designs.
papers.summary: Each observation influences a cross-validation estimate in two roles, through its own evaluation when held out and through the models it helps fit, with the random splits setting its weight in each role. From this representation the authors prove an exact finite-sample identity for the variance of the cross-validated estimate, covering metrics averaged over observations such as mean squared error and over case-control pairs such as the AUC. The variance splits into sampling variance, depending only on training size, and variance from random fold splitting, so **K-fold cross-validation, whose weights are equal across observations by design, is variance optimal at first order while Monte Carlo and bootstrap cross-validation are not**. First-order K-fold variance does not depend on K, leave-one-out has the smallest variance among K-fold schemes under reasonable model conditions, and the estimate is shown to be asymptotically normal with the identity's full variance.

papers.title: A Theory of Policy Optimization in Post-Training: Coverage Collapse and Reference Resets
papers.abstract:
Policy optimization is central to language model post-training, yet principled guidance remains limited. We revisit its theoretical foundations to identify algorithms that learn near-optimal policies using total samples and gradient steps governed by the base model's response coverage, a measure of how readily it generates optimal responses. We call such algorithms coverage-preserving. This guarantee captures the goal of amplifying capabilities accessible through sampling from the base model.
  (1) Coverage collapse. REINFORCE, the basis for PPO and GRPO, can drive the probability of optimal responses to near zero, even as reward improves. This coverage collapse stalls optimization, and convergence can require exponentially many steps despite good initial coverage. The failure arises even with exact gradients and persists under KL regularization to the base model.
  (2) Reference resets. We show that repeatedly resetting the KL reference to the most recent policy mitigates coverage collapse. We formalize this intervention in Approximate Policy Mirror Descent (APMD), a meta-algorithm that approximately solves a sequence of KL-regularized RL subproblems. APMD enables stronger regularization, making each subproblem easier to solve, while reference resets allow convergence to global optimality.
  (3) Coverage-preserving algorithms. For softmax linear policies over pretrained features, we use APMD to establish the first global convergence guarantees showing that widely used families of post-training algorithms are coverage-preserving. These include stylized PPO and GRPO variants with explicit KL regularization and reference resets, and squared-loss algorithms that implement them implicitly, including those used to train the Kimi models.
  These results clarify how regularization, clipping, and objective choice affect the sampling and optimization costs of post-training.
papers.summary: Theoretical foundations of policy optimization for language model post-training are revisited to find algorithms whose sample and gradient costs are governed by how readily the base model already generates optimal responses, a property the authors call coverage-preserving. They show that **`REINFORCE`, the basis for `PPO` and `GRPO`, can drive the probability of optimal responses to near zero even as reward improves**, a coverage collapse that can require exponentially many steps to escape and that persists with exact gradients and KL regularization to the base model. Repeatedly resetting the KL reference to the most recent policy mitigates this, formalized as Approximate Policy Mirror Descent (APMD), a meta-algorithm that approximately solves a sequence of KL-regularized subproblems. For softmax linear policies over pretrained features, APMD yields the first global convergence guarantees that stylized `PPO` and `GRPO` variants with reference resets, and squared-loss algorithms implementing them implicitly, are coverage-preserving.

papers.title: Bayesian inverse problems and epidemic-threshold uncertainty for a heterogeneous SIS reaction-diffusion model
papers.abstract: We study Bayesian inference of persistence from early observations of a heterogeneous susceptible--infected--susceptible (SIS) reaction--diffusion model with standard incidence. We show that the leading prevalence dynamics depend on the unknown coefficients only through the difference between the transmission and recovery rates and the infected diffusivity. The same pair determines the principal eigenvalue whose sign governs persistence, so early prevalence can inform the threshold even when the individual rates remain uncertain. We prove global weak well-posedness and quantitative parameter stability for the SIS system and use the resulting observation-map estimates to establish Bayesian well-posedness. For an initial infection of size $\varepsilon$, we derive a uniform second-order expansion that describes how the separate rates enter prevalence. Incidence depends explicitly on transmission at leading order. When the noise standard deviation is proportional to $\varepsilon$, we prove $O(\varepsilon)$ convergence in Hellinger distance of the nonlinear posteriors to their low-prevalence limits for both prevalence alone and joint prevalence and incidence data. We bound the principal eigenvalue using the growth rate of the infected $L^2$ norm between two times. This rate gives a lower bound for the full nonlinear system, and the upper bound separates spatial transients from nonlinear saturation. Uniform spectral estimates and bounds on infection size and measurement error give sufficient conditions for persistence and extinction. We also bound the error in posterior persistence probabilities under forward and eigenvalue approximation, accounting for posterior mass near the threshold. Numerical examples illustrate threshold inference and the predicted \(O(\varepsilon)\) convergence of the nonlinear posteriors to their low-prevalence limits in Hellinger distance.
papers.summary: Bayesian inference of whether an infection persists is studied from early observations of a spatially heterogeneous susceptible-infected-susceptible (SIS) reaction-diffusion model with standard incidence. The leading prevalence dynamics depend on the unknown coefficients only through the difference between transmission and recovery rates and the infected diffusivity, the same pair fixing the principal eigenvalue whose sign governs persistence, so early prevalence can inform the threshold even while individual rates stay uncertain. The authors prove global weak well-posedness, parameter stability, and Bayesian well-posedness, and for an initial infection of size epsilon with noise proportional to epsilon they show **convergence of order epsilon in Hellinger distance of the nonlinear posteriors to their low-prevalence limits**. They also bound the principal eigenvalue from the growth rate of the infected norm and bound errors in posterior persistence probabilities, with numerical examples illustrating threshold inference.

papers.title: C$^2$-Routing: Complementary Cropping and Compression for Efficient Vision-Language Inference
papers.abstract: Visual Question Answering (VQA) imposes substantial computational overhead on vision-language models (VLMs), motivating model-agnostic input reduction methods that can be readily applied across diverse VLMs, including in black-box settings. Simply enforcing a visual-token cap reduces computation, but it can discard information needed to answer the question. A single reduction strategy also struggles to accommodate different scenarios. Our key observation is that cropping and compression are complementary: cropping highlights small targets and local details, whereas whole-image compression better preserves context for large targets or distributed evidence. Based on this observation, we propose C$^2$-Routing, which adaptively selects cropping or compression according to the input image and question. Since both strategies may still discard key information, we further design a safety gate that uses the predicted joint correctness distribution under original and reduced inputs to guide fallback and protect accuracy. To accommodate consumer GPU resource constraints, all training and evaluation experiments run on RTX 3090 GPUs. To measure gains beyond token capping, we use full-image baselines with the same cap of 1,024 visual tokens. We conduct extensive evaluation on three VLMs and 18 datasets spanning local details, global scenes, scene text, and documents. With the visual budget already capped, C$^2$-Routing further reduces end-to-end FLOPs by 36.53% and visual tokens by 42.36% on average, with a mean relative task-score decrease of only 0.77%.
papers.summary: Visual Question Answering (VQA) is computationally expensive for vision-language models (VLMs), and simply capping visual tokens or applying one fixed input-reduction strategy can discard information the answer needs. `C2-Routing` builds on the observation that cropping suits small targets and local detail while whole-image compression preserves context for large or distributed evidence, selecting between them per image and question, with a safety gate that falls back to the original input based on the predicted joint correctness distribution. The method is model-agnostic and applicable in black-box settings, and all training and evaluation ran on RTX 3090 GPUs. Across three VLMs and 18 datasets, against full-image baselines already capped at 1,024 visual tokens, it **further cuts end-to-end FLOPs by 36.53% and visual tokens by 42.36% on average, with a mean relative task-score decrease of 0.77%**.

papers.title: FERN: Cross-Benchmark Table Retrieval for Text-to-SQL with Frozen Retrievers and Learned Ranking
papers.abstract: Text-to-SQL systems over large pooled catalogs must first retrieve the tables a question needs. We compare against the published table recall of RASL, which uses Claude 3.5 models to extract keywords and select tables, on pooled BIRD, Spider, and Fiben catalogs. FERN (Feature-Engineered Ranking with No generative LLM) instead fuses three frozen retrievers into 100 candidates, describes each with up to 120 features, and reorders them with LightGBM rankers fitted once on BIRD's training questions. On Spider, where it was not fitted, its candidate pool alone reaches RASL's published recall at fifteen tables (98.0), and the ranker raises the share of questions with every gold table in the top five (complete@5) from 83.9% to 95.6%. At five tables, FERN's recall is within one point of RASL's on Spider (96.7 vs 97.0) and on BIRD with its evidence hints (96.6 vs 97.5), and 8.2 points below on BIRD without them (89.3). On 121 real BEAVER questions, without BEAVER fitting, its recall at fifteen (82.1) falls between two BEAVER-trained retrievers (80.8, 84.5), but its complete@15 is below both (49.6 vs 54.5 and 62.0). On Fiben, it falls far short at fifteen tables (54.2 vs 69.2, different question sets), although its recall at fifty is numerically close to RASL's question-only retrieval result (80.7 vs 79.4). On BIRD dev with evidence, non-retrieval features raise complete@5 by 7.7 points over retrieval signals alone. On BIRD dev, median latency is 208 ms per question on one A100, without hosted model calls.
papers.summary: Text-to-SQL systems over large pooled catalogs must first retrieve the tables a question needs, a step the compared system `RASL` handles with Claude 3.5 models extracting keywords and selecting tables. `FERN` (Feature-Engineered Ranking with No generative LLM) instead fuses three frozen retrievers into 100 candidates, describes each with up to 120 features, and reorders them with `LightGBM` rankers fitted once on `BIRD`'s training questions. On `Spider`, where it was not fitted, its candidate pool alone matches `RASL`'s published recall at fifteen tables and the ranker lifts the share of questions with every gold table in the top five from 83.9% to 95.6%, with **median latency of 208 ms per question on one A100 and no hosted model calls**. It trails by 8.2 points on `BIRD` without evidence hints, falls well short on `Fiben` at fifteen tables (54.2 against 69.2 on different question sets), and on 121 real `BEAVER` questions sits between two `BEAVER`-trained retrievers on recall but below both on complete-set retrieval.

papers.title: Pterodactyl: Pushing the Limits of Efficient Automated Translation Evaluation
papers.abstract: In this paper, we present 1020 Group's submission to the WMT26 shared task on automated quality evaluation. Our system, Pterodactyl, was engineered specifically for subtasks 2 and 3, that is, segment-level quality score prediction and the detection of error-free segments. Pterodactyl is a highly customizable, ultra-low cost system optimized for binary classification in translation triage and data curation. It is based on an LLM-as-a-judge approach, with prompt engineering and model selection guided by ROC analysis. We also developed several variants of Pterodactyl that were specifically adapted for subtasks 3.
papers.summary: A system description of 1020 Group's submission to the WMT26 shared task on automated translation quality evaluation, covering segment-level quality score prediction and detection of error-free segments. `Pterodactyl` is a customizable, very low-cost system aimed at binary classification for translation triage and data curation, built on an LLM-as-a-judge approach in which **prompt engineering and model selection were guided by ROC analysis**. Several variants were adapted specifically for the error-free segment detection subtask; the abstract reports no scores.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability Needs a Logic of Inference
papers.abstract: Neural networks are increasingly studied not merely as predictive systems, but as complex systems whose internal computations are themselves objects of scientific inquiry. Recent progress in mechanistic interpretability (MI) has made it possible to identify neurons, features, circuits, population structures, and dynamical patterns associated with model behavior. As these tools improve, attention is shifting from what can be observed inside a model to how those observations support mechanistic explanations. We examine the parallel efforts of neuroscience and MI to address this question and identify recurring inferential bottlenecks when inferring mechanisms from complex neural systems. We propose five principles and organize them into a recursive logic for a more rigorous procedure of mechanistic inference. These principles provide a framework that supports scientific discovery in two senses: it helps turn local interpretability findings into cumulative knowledge of mechanisms within models, and it makes those mechanisms sufficiently precise to generate testable hypotheses about domains beyond the models. Evidence beyond MI is ultimately required to establish what model mechanisms reveal about the world.
papers.summary: Mechanistic interpretability (MI) can now identify neurons, features, circuits, population structures, and dynamical patterns tied to model behavior, which shifts the question from what can be observed inside a model to how those observations support mechanistic explanations. Drawing on neuroscience's parallel struggle, the authors identify recurring inferential bottlenecks in inferring mechanisms from complex neural systems. They **propose five principles organized into a recursive logic for mechanistic inference**, meant both to turn local interpretability findings into cumulative knowledge about mechanisms inside models and to make those mechanisms precise enough to generate testable hypotheses about domains beyond the models. They add that evidence from outside MI is ultimately required to establish what model mechanisms reveal about the world.

papers.title: Re-Search: Dissecting LLM Ideation Through a Two-Player Questioning Game
papers.abstract: Research ideation is iterative: researchers refine their ideas step by step based on feedback. Yet existing evaluations obscure this search process, making it difficult to understand how LLMs explore the space of research ideas and what limits their progress. We introduce Re-Search, which adapts the format of Twenty Questions to research ideation: given only the research problem of a published paper, a model must rediscover the paper's core idea by asking yes-or-no questions. Built from 200 ICML 2026 papers, Re-Search tracks how a model's idea evolves as it asks questions and receives binary oracle feedback, isolating ideation from execution. Across six recent LLMs, nearly all progress happens within the first 30 of 100 questions, which largely decide how the game ends; after that, most models plateau. Through controlled interventions on the candidate questions and the hypothesis space, we find that the bottleneck is generation, not judgment: models recognize a good idea or a good question when one is offered, but often cannot produce it on their own. We further analyze the ideation traces and find that models fail by either over-exploiting one direction or over-exploring too many. These findings point to concrete design principles for autoresearch systems: since models can judge candidates they cannot produce, enriching the search with externally sourced ideas and questions may be more effective than improving any single model's generation ability.
papers.summary: Evaluations of large language model (LLM) research ideation usually hide the iterative search that produces an idea. `Re-Search` adapts Twenty Questions to ideation: given only the research problem of one of 200 ICML 2026 papers, a model must rediscover the paper's core idea by asking yes-or-no questions answered by an oracle, which separates ideation from execution. Across six recent LLMs, nearly all progress happens within the first 30 of 100 questions and most models then plateau, failing either by over-exploiting one direction or over-exploring too many. Controlled interventions on candidate questions and the hypothesis space show that **the bottleneck is generation rather than judgment: models recognize a good idea or question when offered one but often cannot produce it themselves**, suggesting that autoresearch systems gain more from externally sourced ideas and questions than from better single-model generation.

papers.title: TimeSeek: Multi-Task and Multi-Domain Pretraining for Generalized Time Series Analytics
papers.abstract: Time series analytics has been widely applied across various domains. While existing time series foundation models (TSFMs) have demonstrated promising results, they still face two major challenges: 1) Most TSFMs mainly rely on stacking Transformer layers to increase parameter size, lacking the ability to adaptively model complex time series patterns from multi-domain data. 2) Current TSFMs are primarily pre-trained for specific tasks, e.g., forecasting or anomaly detection, and a few models support multiple tasks, but they fail to fully leverage task specificity and commonality, resulting in suboptimal performance. To address these challenges, we propose TimeSeek, a novel generalized time series analytics model that adaptively models time series patterns from multi-domain data and unifies multiple tasks in pre-training. Conceptually, TimeSeek is guided by selective information sharing under domain and task heterogeneity. From the perspective of multi-domain data, we propose a Multi-Domain Feature Extractor that adaptively captures temporal dependencies and channel correlations based on domain-specific characteristics, including progressive multi-scale modeling and adaptive slot channel modeling. From the perspective of the diversity of tasks, we propose multi-task collaborative training, which leverages task specificity and task commonality through task customization and cross-task training, effectively unifying multiple tasks in pre-training and better adapting to diverse downstream scenarios. After pre-training on large-scale time series data, TimeSeek achieves state-of-the-art performance in forecasting, anomaly detection, and classification tasks across both few-shot learning and zero-shot situations, together with favorable inference efficiency.
papers.summary: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) largely scale by stacking Transformer layers and are pre-trained for one task such as forecasting or anomaly detection, limiting how well they adapt to multi-domain data and multiple downstream uses. `TimeSeek` adds a Multi-Domain Feature Extractor that captures temporal dependencies and channel correlations according to domain characteristics, using progressive multi-scale modeling and adaptive slot channel modeling. It also uses multi-task collaborative training, combining task customization with cross-task training so several tasks are unified during pre-training. After large-scale pre-training the authors report **state-of-the-art results on forecasting, anomaly detection, and classification in both few-shot and zero-shot settings**, alongside favorable inference efficiency.

papers.title: ReTrace: Distilling Tool-Using Agents into Planner-Free Workflows
papers.abstract: Business process automation runs the same Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) again and again on new inputs. Large Language Model (LLM) agents can follow an SOP written in natural language, but they call an LLM to choose every step of every run, which adds latency and cost at scale. We present ReTrace, which turns an SOP and a few logged agent runs into a reusable workflow in which code, not an LLM, selects the next step. The agent's reasoning, the explanation it writes with each tool call, often states why it took an action; the tool calls alone do not. ReTrace extracts the condition behind each step, merges these conditions across runs into a compact rule document, and generates an executable workflow from it. Only this last stage depends on the platform, so rule documents can be compiled for different orchestration platforms. On $79$ procedures from our production platform, ReTrace workflows reach $93.8\%$ completion, against $96.8\%$ for the agent, at $24\%$ lower cost per task. On $\tau^2$-Bench, they reach $75.8\%$ task success (agent: $80.6\%$) and run in $1.3$s instead of $170$s; three rounds of repair on training failures lift $k{=}2$ workflows from $66.7\%$ to $81.2\%$. On eight SOP-Bench procedures, ReTrace without repair trails few-shot generation ($80.6\%$ vs. $83.6\%$), but repair from labeled training failures lifts it to $87.8\%$ at $0.40$s per task, compared to $85.5\%$ in $46.6$s for the agent.
papers.summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents can follow a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) written in natural language, but calling an LLM to choose every step of every run adds latency and cost when the same procedure repeats at scale. `ReTrace` turns an SOP plus a few logged agent runs into a reusable workflow in which code selects the next step, extracting the condition behind each step from the explanations the agent wrote alongside its tool calls, merging them into a compact rule document, and compiling that into an executable workflow for a given orchestration platform. On `tau2-Bench` the workflows reach **75.8% task success against the agent's 80.6%, running in 1.3 seconds instead of 170**, and on 79 production procedures they reach 93.8% completion against 96.8% at 24% lower cost per task. On eight `SOP-Bench` procedures the unrepaired workflows trail few-shot generation, but three rounds of repair from labeled training failures lift them to 87.8% at 0.40 seconds per task against 85.5% in 46.6 seconds for the agent.

papers.title: Comparative Analysis of Agent Evaluation Frameworks: Stability, Detection, and Discovery in Enterprise Analytics Agents
papers.abstract: Deploying LLM-based analytics agents in enterprise settings requires evaluation frameworks that can reliably detect failures across complex, multi-tool workflows. We present a three-phase comparative study of three evaluation frameworks, each representing a distinct evaluation paradigm (trace-based LLM judging, text-only LLM judging with red-teaming, and deterministic heuristics), applied to two analytics agents in a controlled research setting using frozen execution traces. Phase 1 quantifies evaluation harness stability through repeated measurements, finding that 97% of configurations meet the stability threshold and that stability patterns are agent-independent. Phase 2 measures known risk detection on 72 ground-truth test cases, where the trace-based framework achieves the best precision-recall balance (F1=0.90) while text-only evaluation matches on recall but generates 5x more false alarms. Phase 3 evaluates unknown risk discovery, uncovering 24 novel failures with zero overlap between functional testing and security red-teaming. Our results demonstrate that (1) the information available to the evaluation harness determines evaluation quality, (2) functional and security evaluation are complementary, and (3) LLM-based evaluation harnesses surface subtle errors that human reviewers miss. We recommend a two-framework strategy: trace-based evaluation for functional assessment and adversarial red-teaming for security validation.
papers.summary: Three evaluation frameworks for LLM-based enterprise analytics agents are compared across three phases on two agents using frozen execution traces, each framework representing a distinct paradigm: trace-based LLM judging, text-only LLM judging with red-teaming, and deterministic heuristics. Repeated measurements find 97% of configurations meet the stability threshold, with stability patterns independent of the agent. On 72 ground-truth test cases, **the trace-based framework achieves the best precision-recall balance at an F1 of 0.90, while text-only evaluation matches its recall but generates five times more false alarms**. A third phase uncovers 24 novel failures with zero overlap between functional testing and security red-teaming, leading the authors to recommend pairing trace-based evaluation for functional assessment with adversarial red-teaming for security.

papers.title: Emergent Biological Capabilities in a Foundation Model for Molecular Interactions
papers.abstract: Foundation models trained on large unlabeled corpora develop emergent capabilities, tasks that go beyond the training objective. We extend this paradigm to multimodal biology with Bonbon, a foundation model for molecular interactions trained on approximately 3.2 trillion tokens of paired protein-ligand sequences. From a single representation space, Bonbon exhibits three zero-shot emergent capabilities at hierarchical levels of resolution: functional (mechanism of action), residue (binding site localization, including orthosteric/allosteric discrimination), and bond (covalent versus non-covalent engagement). All three capabilities generalize to out-of-distribution complexes. Bonbon was trained on protein-ligand sequences alone, without any task-specific supervision and without structural coordinates. We conducted controlled scaling experiments across six model scales from 42M to 1.6B parameters; every capability evaluated shows a sharp jump at the largest scale on continuous metrics, even as pretraining loss decreases smoothly. This demonstrates that loss-based scaling laws alone are insufficient to predict when zero-shot emergent capabilities become available. The capabilities reported here emerge after training at a 1:2,000 parameter-to-token ratio to accommodate the sparsity of paired biological interaction data. The same frozen representations achieve state-of-the-art binding and affinity prediction at five orders of magnitude greater speed than co-folding methods. In prospective wet-lab validation across nine disease targets spanning seven protein families, Bonbon achieves a 61.5% dose-response hit rate on de novo compounds, yielding structurally novel molecules not previously reported to inhibit these proteins, including for out-of-distribution targets.
papers.summary: `Bonbon` is a foundation model for molecular interactions trained on roughly 3.2 trillion tokens of paired protein-ligand sequences, with no structural coordinates and no task-specific supervision. From one representation space it shows three zero-shot capabilities at different resolutions: mechanism of action, binding site localization including discrimination of orthosteric from allosteric sites, and covalent versus non-covalent engagement, all generalizing to out-of-distribution complexes. Controlled scaling across six model sizes from 42M to 1.6B parameters shows **every evaluated capability jumping sharply at the largest scale even though pretraining loss falls smoothly, indicating loss-based scaling laws alone cannot predict when such capabilities appear**. The frozen representations also reach state-of-the-art binding and affinity prediction five orders of magnitude faster than co-folding methods, and prospective wet-lab testing across nine disease targets gave a 61.5% dose-response hit rate on de novo compounds.

papers.title: Continual-ARC: Measuring Skill Acquisition over a Working Lifetime
papers.abstract: Agent harnesses have emerged as a promising mechanism for continual learning, alongside test-time parametric learning. However, the current benchmarks have several limitations: they generally focus on a single applied domain, serve each instance only once, and assume a single family of learner, so memory-based and weight-based systems are rarely compared on the same scale. We propose Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream built from the three ARC-AGI editions, whose tasks need no domain knowledge. The same tasks return after dormant gaps with fresh instances, while new tasks keep arriving. On each instance, the learner may pay for demonstrations, submit answers, or act inside the harness, with retries permitted on incorrect submissions, which are paid for. Each instance is scored based on the share of this feedback budget consumed. Since a learner may keep anything between instances, memory-based and weight-based systems are scored on the same scale. After the stream, the learner is frozen and tested on fresh instances of the tasks it met, which measures memorization, and on unseen tasks, which measures generalization. We run an agent harness with frozen weights, with and without persistence, on Qwen3.5-9B and GLM-5.3 Flash, comparing them with two prompting floors, a program-induction method and Qwen3.5-9B's weights trained to imitate GLM-5.3 Flash. Persistence in the harness generally does not improve memorization unless provided with explicit expert guidance. Most harness-based methods still learn less than a floor that simply caches each task's demonstrations, across all models we tested. No harness-based method gains on unseen tasks, whereas weight-based learning shows substantial gains. This opens the door to future weight-based continual learning that could teach models to drive harnesses in new domains.
papers.summary: Benchmarks for continual learning usually cover one applied domain, serve each instance once, and assume a single kind of learner, so memory-based agent harnesses and weight-based methods are rarely measured on the same scale. `Continual-ARC` builds a lifelong stream from the three `ARC-AGI` editions, where tasks recur after dormant gaps with fresh instances while new tasks keep arriving, and learners are scored by how much of a paid feedback budget they consume; afterwards they are frozen and tested on fresh instances of seen tasks to measure memorization and on unseen tasks to measure generalization. Running an agent harness with frozen weights on `Qwen3.5-9B` and `GLM-5.3 Flash`, with and without persistence, against prompting floors, a program-induction method, and `Qwen3.5-9B` trained to imitate `GLM-5.3 Flash`, persistence rarely improves memorization without explicit expert guidance. **Most harness-based methods learn less than a floor that simply caches each task's demonstrations, and none gains on unseen tasks, whereas weight-based learning shows substantial gains.**

papers.title: When Does the Real Wiring Win? Testing connectome structure-function claims against unmeasured physiology
papers.abstract: Connectome-constrained models are often used to argue that a measured wiring diagram outperforms shuffled or rewired wiring, and hence that structure shapes function.
